[Page 103]

**"A disavowal from Allah and His Messenger to those with whom you made covenants among the polytheists."** The surah opens the way covenants (*'uhud*) and contract documents (*suhuk al-'uqud*) open, with the word that best indicates their purpose, as in their saying, "This is what so-and-so has covenanted," or "This is what so-and-so and so-and-so have agreed upon," and as the witnesses to contracts say, "He sold," "he appointed an agent," or "he married." This is what the situation requires in drafting letters, pacts, and similar documents.

The indefiniteness of *barā'a* ("disavowal") is the indefiniteness of variety (*tankir al-tanwi'*). Its position is the subject of a nominal sentence (*mubtada'*). What justifies beginning with it is the sense of variety conveyed by the indefinite form, pointing out that this kind of word is sufficient for understanding the intended meaning, as was mentioned earlier in His saying, ﴿Alif, Lam, Mim, Sad﴾ [al-A'raf: 1] ﴿A Book revealed to you﴾ [al-A'raf: 2].

The two prepositional phrases in His saying, ﴿from Allah and His Messenger to those with whom you made covenants﴾, occupy the position of the predicate (*khabar*), because they are the main point of the benefit conveyed. That is: the disavowal has issued from Allah and His Messenger.

"*Min*" (from) is for origin, and "*ila*" (to) is for endpoint, since the preposition "*min*" already conveys the sense of origin. The meaning is that this is a disavowal that Allah issued through His Messenger, to be communicated to those with whom you made covenants among the polytheists.

*Barā'a* means withdrawing from and being free of what burdens a person, and removing responsibility. Since a covenant obligates those who enter it to act on what they agreed to, and breaking any part of it is considered treachery on the part of the one who breaks it, announcing the cancellation of the covenant is a release from the consequences that would arise from breaking it. Therefore the word *barā'a* here conveys the meaning of annulling the covenant and rejecting it, so that the parties to the covenant may take their precautions. The Arabs used to renounce covenants and return protection (*jiwar*) when they wished to end the obligation to them, as Ibn al-Dughunna did when he returned Abu Bakr's protection against Quraysh, and as 'Uthman ibn Maz'un did when he returned al-Walid ibn al-Mughira's protection, saying, "I am content with the protection of my Lord, and I do not want to seek protection from anyone else." And He, exalted is He, said: ﴿And if you fear treachery from a people, then throw back to them [their treaty] on equal terms. Indeed, Allah does not like the treacherous﴾ [al-Anfal: 58]. That is: do not betray them merely because you suspect they will betray you; but when you have such a suspicion, then annul your covenant with them.

Since the party that initiated the nullification and termination of the covenant was the Prophet (ﷺ), by permission from Allah, this disavowal was attributed to Allah, because He is the one who authorized it, and to His Messenger, because he is the one who carried it out. It was directed to the polytheists who had covenants with the Muslims, because the purpose was to communicate that annulment to them and deliver it to them, so that they would be aware of it and the annulment would not be treachery.

The address in His saying "you made covenants" is to the believers, who are commanded to carry out this disavowal.

Know that the covenant between the Prophet (ﷺ) and the polytheists had been concluded in different forms. Between him and the people of Mecca and their allies was the Treaty of al-Hudaybiyya, by which no one would be barred from the House when he came [for pilgrimage], and no one would be feared during the sacred month. Most of the Arab tribes had entered into the agreement of Quraysh concluded at al-Hudaybiyya, because Quraysh at that time were the leaders of all the Arabs. For this reason, one of the conditions of that peace was that whoever wished to enter into the covenant of Muhammad could do so, and whoever wished to enter into the covenant of Quraysh could do so. Another condition of the peace was the suspension of war among the people for years, during which they would be secure and would refrain from harming one another. Those polytheists who had covenants with the Muslims were thus well known to people on the day this verse was revealed. This covenant, although it was for the benefit of the Muslims against the polytheists, had a counterpart that was binding for the benefit of the polytheists against the Muslims, once the House came under Muslim control after the conquest of Mecca. So what had been binding of it ceased after the conquest of Mecca, and the conversion of Quraysh and some of their allies.

There were also covenants between the Muslims and some tribes of the polytheists, as indicated in Surat al-Nisa' in His saying: ﴿except those who join a people between whom and you there is a treaty﴾ [al-Nisa': 90], and as indicated in this surah in His saying: ﴿except those with whom you made a treaty among the polytheists, then they have not been deficient toward you in anything﴾ [al-Tawba: 4].

Some of these covenants were without a specified term, some had a term that had already expired, and some had a term that had not yet expired. The Treaty of al-Hudaybiyya was, according to some reports, set for ten years; it was also said four years, and it was said two years. The Treaty of al-Hudaybiyya took place in Dhu al-Qa'da in the sixth year [after the Hijra]. So its term had expired according to some reports, but had not expired according to others at the time this verse was revealed. The people assumed it was still in force. Some of those covenants were set for a term that had not yet been completed. However, the polytheists broke the covenant by aiding some polytheists who were not parties to it, and by harming the Muslims. It is reported that when the Battle of Tabuk took place, the hypocrites spread rumors that the Muslims had been defeated, and so many of the polytheists broke the covenant. Among those who broke the covenant were some of Khuza'a, Banu Mudlij, and Banu Khuzayma or Judhayma, as indicated by His saying: ﴿then they have not been deficient toward you in anything or supported anyone against you﴾ [al-Tawba: 4]. Allah therefore announced this disavowal to them so that they could take their precautions. This also placed a constraint on them if they persisted in polytheism, because the land had become the land of the people of Islam, as indicated by His saying, exalted is He, afterward: ﴿So if you repent, it is better for you; but if you turn away, then know that you cannot cause Allah to fail﴾ [al-Tawba: 3].

[Page 105]

The disavowal was made a matter concerning Allah and His Messenger, and the covenant was attributed to the pronoun of the Muslims, to indicate that the covenants which the Prophet (peace be upon him) had concluded were binding on the Muslims, and were equivalent to what they had concluded themselves. This is because the covenants of the Prophet (peace be upon him) were made for the benefit of the Muslims, at a time when they had not yet gathered their strength, and at a time when the polytheists still had some remaining power. Otherwise, the people of polytheism did not deserve from Allah and His Messenger any indulgence or covenant, because the interest of the religion is best served when the Muslims are firm against its enemies. Now, since the interest of the religion is purely in rejecting the covenant that the Muslims had made with the polytheists, Allah and His Messenger (ﷺ) authorized disavowal of that covenant. So there is no blame on the Muslims for rejecting it. Although the Prophet (ﷺ) had concluded it, so that they would know that this was a relief for the Muslims, this is like the exchange that took place between 'Umar ibn al-Khattab and the Prophet (ﷺ) on the day of the Treaty of al-Hudaybiyya. It is also like what Allah, exalted is He, said about the steadfastness of one Muslim against two polytheists. Moreover, there is an elliptical construction (*ihtibak*) in the speech, because it is well known that the Muslims do nothing except by command from Allah and His Messenger. So the meaning of the speech is equivalent to: "A disavowal from Allah and His Messenger, and from you, to those who made covenants with Allah and His Messenger, and with you." The tribes that had a covenant with the Muslims at the time this surah was revealed are all included in the relative clause in His saying: ﴿to those with whom you made covenants among the polytheists﴾. Defining by means of the relative clause here is because it is the shortest way to express the intended meaning, together with pointing out that this disavowal is a disavowal from the covenant. Then He clarified part of it by His saying: ﴿except those with whom you made a treaty among the polytheists, then they have not been deficient toward you in anything﴾ [al-Tawba: 4], and so on.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 9, verse 2:

﴿So travel freely in the land for four months﴾ The fa' (فاء) here marks a consequence (li-l-tafri') of the meaning of disavowal (al-bara'ah), since when God commanded the proclamation of it, it became an announcement to the polytheists, who were the intended target of the annulment of the covenant that existed between them and the Muslims. Thus the pronoun of address in the imperative verb is understood to refer to them, the ones addressed by the speech, and this is a shift (iltifat) of grammatical person. The estimated reading is therefore: "so let them travel freely in the land." The purpose of this iltifat is to convey the warning to them directly.

It is also permissible to estimate a omitted saying following from the disavowal of their covenants, meaning: "so say to them: travel freely in the land for four months."

Page 106
Al-siyahah (السياحة), in its real meaning, is travelling in the land. Since the command to this travel follows from the disavowal of the covenant, and confirms the sanctity of the sacred months (al-ashhur al-hurum), it is known that the intended meaning is travel in security, without fear, in any place of the land. The meaning is therefore: "travel freely, secure, wherever you wish in the land."

This is a specific respite after the disavowal, which began from Shawwal at the time of the revelation of "Bara'ah" and whose end was the end of Muharram at the close of the consecutive sacred months, namely Dhu al-Qa'dah, Dhu al-Hijjah and Muharram. This is the view of the majority. Ibn Ishaq said: "The people were given a respite of four months from the day the proclamation was made to them, so that every people might return to its place of safety." Others said: the four months begin from the tenth of Dhu al-Hijjah and end on the tenth of Rabi' al-Akhir, so that His saying: ﴿So when the sacred months have passed﴾ [al-Tawbah: 5], meaning of that year, is an ending of that term, in which was observed a sufficient period for the people to return to their lands, and that is the end of Muharram.

It is also said: the four months are those known among all the tribes of the Arabs, namely Dhu al-Qa'dah, Dhu al-Hijjah, Muharram and Rajab; that is, no security remained for the polytheists except in the sacred months. On this view, there is no specific respite in the verse for their security, but rather the security established for the sacred months, so the meaning is: disavowal of the covenant that is between them, regarding what exceeds the security established for the sacred months. Al-Suhayli, in al-Rawd al-Unuf, related that it was said that by the passing of the sacred months he meant Dhu al-Hijjah and Muharram of that year, and that he made that a term for those polytheists who had no covenant, and for whoever had a covenant, a term of four months was set, the first of which was the day of sacrifice (yawm al-nahr) of that year.

In this command there is an announcement of the obligation of fighting outside the sacred months, and that what lies beyond those months is war between the Muslims and the polytheists, and this will be stated explicitly.

* * *
﴿And know that you cannot escape God, and that God will humiliate the disbelievers﴾ It is coordinated (atf) upon "fasihu" and falls within the ruling of the consequence, since when He informed them of security during the four months, He followed it with a warning of the might of God, as a precaution against the entry of delusion, and as a threat that they should not feel secure that God would empower the Muslims against them outside the sacred months, even if they remained in their dwellings.

The opening of the speech with "wa-'lamu" (واعلموا) is to alert to the matter that deserves to be comprehended and reflected upon, like His saying: ﴿And know that God comes between a man and his heart﴾ [al-Anfal: 24] in Surat al-Anfal, and the alerting to it has already preceded.

Al-mu'jiz (المعجز) is the active participle of a'jaza fulanan, when one makes him incapable of some action; hence it means the one who overcomes and the one who escapes, beyond the power of anyone. The meaning is: you are not beyond the power of God, but He has granted you security, and if He wills, He can place you in fear and affliction.

His saying: ﴿and that God humiliates the disbelievers﴾ is coordinated upon His saying: ﴿that you are not escapers from God﴾ [al-Tawbah: 3], so it falls within the scope of "wa-'lamu," and its purpose is comprehension of it and knowledge of it, as has preceded.

The mention of "the disbelievers" is a departure from what the apparent wording requires, for the apparent requirement would be to say: "and that God humiliates you." The justification for expressing it as an explicit noun is to indicate that disbelief is the cause of humiliation.

Al-ikhza' (الإخزاء) is to degrade. Al-khizy (الخزي), with a kasra on the kha', is abasement and disgrace; that is, God decrees humiliation for the disbelievers: by killing, by capture, and by the punishment of the Hereafter, for as long as they remain characterised by disbelief.

[Page 108]

﴿And a proclamation from Allah and His Messenger to the people on the day of the greater Hajj: that Allah is free of obligation to the polytheists, and so is His Messenger﴾ is coordinated (*'atf*, conjunction) with the clause ﴿A declaration of disassociation from Allah and His Messenger﴾ [At-Tawbah: 1]. The grammatical position of the word "*adhan*" (proclamation) is the same as that of the word "*bara'ah*" (declaration) in the implied construction. This is an announcement to the polytheists who had covenants that their covenant had been broken.

*Adhan* is a verbal noun (*ism masdar*) of *adhdhanahu*, meaning "he informed him by means of a public announcement," like *'ata'* meaning *i'ta'* (giving) and *aman* meaning *iman* (faith). Thus it means *idhn* (notification).

The attribution of the *adhan* to Allah and His Messenger, rather than to the Muslims, is because it is a legislative ruling concerning the welfare of the community, and so it can only come from Allah through His Messenger ﷺ. This is also a command to the Muslims to notify the polytheists of this disassociation, so that they will not be treacherous, as He, the Exalted, said: ﴿And if you fear treachery from a people, then throw back to them [their treaty] on equal terms. Indeed, Allah does not love the treacherous﴾ [Al-Anfal: 58]. By "the people" is meant all people, believers and polytheists alike, because knowledge of this proclamation concerns all of them.

"The day of the greater Hajj": It is said that it is the Day of 'Arafah, because it is the day when people gather in one place. This is reported from 'Umar, 'Uthman, Ibn 'Abbas, Tawus, Mujahid, and Ibn Sirin. It is the view of Abu Hanifah and al-Shafi'i. In a hadith: "The Hajj is 'Arafah."

It is also said that it is the Day of Sacrifice (*yawm al-nahr*), because on the Day of 'Arafah people were scattered, since the Hums used to stand at Muzdalifah while the rest of the people stood at 'Arafah, but all of them would attend Mina on the Day of Sacrifice, so that was the greatest gathering. Ibn 'Atiyyah attributed this reasoning to Mundhir ibn Sa'id. This is the view of 'Ali, Ibn 'Umar, Ibn Mas'ud, al-Mughirah ibn Shu'bah, Ibn 'Abbas as well, Ibn Abi Awfa, and al-Zuhri. Ibn Wahb transmitted it from Malik. Malik said: "We have no doubt that the Day of the greater Hajj is the Day of Sacrifice, because it is the day on which the jamrah is stoned, the sacrifice is slaughtered, and the Hajj is completed. Whoever reaches the night of the Sacrifice and stands at 'Arafah before dawn has caught the Hajj."

I say: the Day of 'Arafah is a day occupied with worship, through standing at the station and listening to the sermon. As for the Day of Mina, it is their day of 'Id.

"*Al-Akbar*" (greater), in the genitive case, is an adjective (*na't*) of "*al-Hajj*," considering that it is divided into acts. So the greatest of those acts is described as "greater." The difference among them regarding the meaning of "the greater Hajj" shows that this expression was not known before the revelation of this verse, so the early scholars differed about its meaning.

This statement is a performative utterance (*insha'*) of this proclamation, tied to the day of the greater Hajj, and so it returns to the meaning of a command. The meaning is: "Announce to the people on the day of the greater Hajj that Allah and His Messenger are free of obligation to the polytheists."

By "the people" is meant all people gathered by that season, and whoever else it reaches among them, believers and polytheists alike, because this proclamation is something that every Muslim and polytheist must know, since its ruling binds both groups.

His statement ﴿that Allah is free of obligation to the polytheists﴾ is connected to "*adhan*," with the omission of the particle of transitivity, the *ba'*; that is, an announcement of this disassociation mentioned earlier in ﴿A declaration of disassociation from Allah and His Messenger﴾ [At-Tawbah: 1]. Its repetition here is because this announcement is for the polytheists who had covenants and others, affirming that the Muslims would not betray them. The earlier verse was an announcement to the Muslims.

The explicit mention of the act of disassociation a second time, without pronominal reference or abbreviation (such as saying "and an announcement to the people of this, or of it, or of the disassociation"), is because the context calls for clarification and elaboration, given the differing understandings of the listeners. Among them are the clever and the dull. So elaboration and clarity remove their excuses and make the communication thorough.

"And His Messenger" is in the nominative (*raf'*), according to all the readers, because it is a coordination of a clause (*'atf al-jumlah*). The listener understands from the nominative that its implied sense is: "and His Messenger is free of obligation to the polytheists." In this nominative there is an eloquent meaning of clarity together with brevity of expression. This is an eloquent Qur'anic subtlety, and Dabi' ibn al-Harith was guided by it in his saying:

*"Whoever has his saddle-camp in Medina tonight, then I and Qayyar here are strangers."*

He used the nominative "Qayyar" because he meant to make the estrangement of his camel, named "Qayyar," a separate estrangement, not dependent on his own.

Something that must be pointed out: some tafsir books report that al-Hasan recited "*wa rasulihi*" in the genitive. This attribution to al-Hasan is not authenticated. How could the genitive of "*wa rasulihi*" be conceived when there is no governing element requiring it? There is, however, a curious story about it: a Bedouin heard a man recite "*anna Allaha bari'un mina al-mushrikina wa rasulihi*" with the genitive on "*wa rasulihi*." The Bedouin said: "If Allah is free of obligation to His Messenger, then I am free of obligation to Him!" He only meant to confront the reciter. The man seized him and brought him to 'Umar, and the Bedouin recounted the recitation. At that, 'Umar ordered the teaching of Arabic. It is also reported that Abu al-Aswad al-Du'ali heard this and referred the matter to 'Ali. This was the reason for the codification of grammar (*nahw*), and this story is mentioned in some books of grammar in relation to the reason for the founding of the science of grammar.

[Page 109]

This proclamation took place during the pilgrimage that Abu Bakr led with the people, when the Messenger of Allah ﷺ sent 'Ali ibn Abi Talib after Abu Bakr, to arrive at the season and proclaim "*Bara'ah*" (Declaration of Disassociation). 'Ali proclaimed it on the Day of Sacrifice at Mina, from its beginning up to thirty or forty of its verses. This is established in the Sahih and the Sunan through various chains, some of which exceed others. Perhaps his statement "or forty" is a doubt on the part of the narrator. As for what appears in the narration of al-Nasa'i, from Jabir, that 'Ali recited "*Bara'ah*" to the people until he completed it, perhaps its meaning is: until he completed what had been revealed of it that relates to disassociation from the polytheists. This is because Surah "*Bara'ah*" had not finished being revealed on that day, since it is established that the last verse revealed to the Prophet ﷺ was the last verse of Surah "*Bara'ah*."

The Prophet ﷺ sent 'Ali ibn Abi Talib after Abu Bakr al-Siddiq because it was said to the Messenger of Allah that the Arabs did not consider it acceptable for anyone to break his covenant with someone he had made a covenant with except by himself or by a messenger from among his close kin. So the Prophet ﷺ wanted to leave the polytheists no excuse regarding their knowledge of the abrogation of the covenant between them.

It is narrated that 'Ali sent Abu Hurayrah to go around the dwellings of the Arab tribes from Mina, calling out the verses of "*Bara'ah*" until his voice became hoarse. Whenever the polytheists heard that, they would say to 'Ali: "You will see after the four months. There is no covenant between us and your cousin except stabbing and striking."

﴿So if you repent, it is better for you; but if you turn away, then know that you cannot escape Allah. And give tidings to those who disbelieve of a painful punishment﴾

This is a branching (*tafri'*) from the clause ﴿that Allah is free of obligation to the polytheists﴾, and from it two states branch out: the state of repentance and the state of turning away.

[Page 110]

The address is to the polytheists who were notified of the disassociation. The meaning: if you believe, then faith is better for you than the covenant you were under, because faith contains salvation in this world and the Hereafter, whereas the covenant contains only salvation in this world and nothing more. By "turning away" is meant turning away from faith. The verb "you turned away" is intended in the sense of continuation: that is, if you persist in polytheism, then know that you will not escape the power of Allah. That is, know that you have fallen within the power of Allah, and you are about to face the punishment.

The clause ﴿And give tidings to those who disbelieve of a painful punishment﴾ is coordinated with the clause ﴿And a proclamation from Allah and His Messenger﴾, because of the meaning of command contained in that clause. It is as if it were said: "So announce to the people the disassociation of Allah and His Messenger from the polytheists, and that whoever repents among them has been saved, while whoever turns away is about to face the punishment." Then He said: "And give tidings to the polytheists who turn away of a painful punishment."

*Bushra* (tidings) originally means the report of something pleasing, but here it is used metaphorically for warning, which is the report of something displeasing, in the manner of mockery, as was mentioned earlier in His statement: ﴿So give them tidings of a painful punishment﴾ [At-Tawbah: 34] in Surah Al 'Imran.

The painful punishment is the punishment of killing, capture, enslavement, and the seizure of property, as He, the Exalted, said: ﴿And He sent down armies you did not see, and punished those who disbelieved; and that is the recompense of the disbelievers﴾ [At-Tawbah: 26]. Their punishment on the day of Hunayn was partly by killing and partly by capture, enslavement, and the taking of property as spoils. That is: warn the polytheists that you will fight them and overcome them after the expiration of the sacred months, as His statement indicates: ﴿Then when the sacred months have passed, kill the polytheists wherever you find them﴾ [At-Tawbah: 5], and so on.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 9, verse 4:

﴿Except those with whom you made a covenant among the polytheists, then they have not fallen short of you in anything, nor have they supported anyone against you, so complete for them their covenant until their term. Indeed, Allah loves the righteous.﴾

This is an exception from "the polytheists" in His saying: ﴿That Allah is free of obligation to the polytheists﴾ [at-Tawbah: 3], and from "those who disbelieve" in His saying: ﴿And give tidings to those who disbelieve of a painful punishment﴾ [at-Tawbah: 3], because the nature of an exception that comes after a series of sentences is that it refers back to everything those sentences contain that is suitable for that exception. So this is an exception for these people from the ruling of annulling the covenant and from the ruling of warning them of war that follows from the annulment. This group of polytheists remain upon the sanctity of their covenant and upon peace with them.

The relative pronoun here encompasses everyone in whom the relation (ṣilah) is realised, and His saying ﴿so complete for them their covenant until their term﴾ has clarified the meaning of the exception.

The particle "thumma" (then) in His saying ﴿then they have not fallen short of you in anything﴾ indicates a gradation of rank (al-tarākhī al-rutbī), because not failing in even the least thing of what they covenanted upon is more important than fulfilling great matters they covenanted upon, since not failing in even the least thing is rare to occur.

Naqṣ (falling short) regarding something means removing part of it, and the intended meaning is that they did not neglect anything of what they covenanted upon. In this conjunction there is an announcement of honouring this negation, because "thumma," when it conjoins sentences, conveys the meaning of gradation in rank, that is, the distance between the rank of the conjoined and the rank of that to which it is conjoined, a distance of perfection and elevated status. For indeed, among the perfection of a covenant is the preservation of fulfilling it.

These are the ones who preserved their covenant with the Muslims and fulfilled it in the most complete manner, so they did not scheme against the Muslims with any scheme, nor did they support an enemy against them secretly. These are the ones whom the Muslims were commanded not to annul their covenant with until the term for which they were contracted. Among them: Banu Damrah, and the two clans of Banu Kinanah: they are Banu Judhaymah and Banu al-Dil. There is no doubt that they were among those who entered the Treaty of al-Hudaybiyah.

From this it is known that those whom Allah commanded to be freed from their covenant are the opposite of those, and they are a people who fell short of what they covenanted upon, that is, they plotted and betrayed secretly, or they supported the enemy with aid and espionage.

Among these: the Quraydhah, who aided the polytheists more than once, and Banu Bakr, who attacked Khuza'ah, the allies of the Muslims, as has previously been mentioned. Their action was expressed as "naqṣ" because they did not openly break the covenant nor nullify it, but rather they violated it, to the extent they were able to scheme and plot, and because they breached some of what they had covenanted upon.

The mention of the word "shay'an" (anything) is for emphasis in negating falling short, because the word "shay'" is an indefinite general term, and when it occurs in the context of negation it conveys the negation of everything that truly qualifies as existent, as previously mentioned in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And the Jews said, "The Christians are not upon anything"﴾ [al-Baqarah: 113] in Surat al-Baqarah.

Al-muẓāharah (support) means assistance. Its verb may be derived from the solid noun "al-ẓahr" (the back), meaning the spine of a person or a camel, because strength of a person in walking and prevailing lies in the back, and the strength of a camel in travel and carrying lies in it. It is said: "ba'īr ẓahīr," meaning strong for travel, like one who helps another in a task, as if one lends the other his back and the other lends him his back, and therefore the form of mufā'alah came. Similar to it are mu'āḍadah (aid), derived from ʿaḍud (the upper arm), musā'adah (assistance) from sāʿid (the forearm), ta'yīd (strengthening) from yad (the hand), and mukātafah (backing) from katif (the shoulder), all of which are limbs of action.

It may also be that its verb is derived from al-ẓuhūr (appearing), the opposite of concealment, because when a person prevails over another, his condition becomes apparent to people, so it is represented by a thing that became apparent after being hidden. For this reason it is construed with the preposition "ʿalā" for figurative elevation. Allah, exalted is He, said: ﴿And if you support each other against him﴾ [at-Tahrim: 4], and He said: ﴿How, when if they gain the upper hand over you they do not observe regarding you any tie of kinship or pact?﴾ [at-Tawbah: 8], and He said: ﴿That He may make it prevail over all religion﴾ [at-Tawbah: 33], and He said: ﴿And the angels, after that, are supporters﴾ [at-Tahrim: 4], meaning helpers.

The fa' in His saying "fa-atimmū" (so complete) is a consequence of what the exception in His saying ﴿Except those with whom you made a covenant among the polytheists, then they have not fallen short of you in anything﴾ etc. indicates, namely that they are not included in the disavowal of the covenant.

Al-muddah (the term) is the appointed time, derived from al-madd (extension), because the appointed time is an extension in the period of action, that is, a lengthening. For this reason they say: "mād al-qawm ghayrahum," when they postponed the war until a fixed limit. The attribution of the term to the pronoun of the covenanting parties is because it is concluded with them, so its attribution to them is like its attribution to the Muslims, but here the side of them was preferred, because their benefit from the term had become greater than the benefit of the Muslims from it, since the Muslims had become stronger than them and more able to fight them.

The sentence ﴿Indeed, Allah loves the righteous﴾ [at-Tawbah: 7] is a concluding statement (tadhyīl) in the sense of justification for the command to complete the covenant until its term, that this is from taqwā (piety), that is, from obedience to the law that Allah commanded, because the report of Allah's love for the righteous following the command is a metonymy (kinayah) for the commanded act being from piety.

Then, all the tribes of the Arabs desired Islam, and they embraced Islam during that term, and thus the sanctity of the Sacred Months ended under the ruling of Islam.

[p. 115]

**﴿So when the sacred months have passed, kill the polytheists wherever you find them, take them captive, besiege them, and lie in wait for them at every place of ambush.﴾** This is a consequence (tafri') of His words: **﴿So travel freely through the land for four months﴾** [al-Tawbah: 2]. If the "four months" mentioned in the verse it is joined to is taken to mean four months beginning from the time "Bara'ah" (Surah al-Tawbah) was revealed, then His words **﴿When the sacred months have passed﴾** are a consequence intended to add a further condition to the time-limit in His words **﴿four months﴾** [al-Tawbah: 2]. That is: when the term of the four months has ended and the sacred months have passed, then kill the polytheists, etc., because the permission in His words **﴿So travel freely through the land for four months﴾** [al-Tawbah: 2] has come to an end. But if the four months are taken to mean the sacred months themselves, then His words **﴿When the sacred months have passed﴾** are an explicit statement of the implication of the permission to be safe for four months, which implies that there is no safety after the four months have elapsed. This is like His words, exalted is He, **﴿And when you have come out of ihram, then hunt﴾** [al-Ma'idah: 2], after His words **﴿not violating the sanctity of game while you are in ihram﴾** [al-Ma'idah: 1]. Thus it is a postponement for them until the end of the month of Muharram of the tenth year (of the Hijrah), followed by a warning against violating the sanctity of the month of Rajab. The situation continues in this way every year until the abrogation (naskh, the cancellation of an earlier ruling by a later one) of the safe-conduct granted during the sacred months, as will come in His words, **﴿Of them four are sacred﴾** [al-Tawbah: 36], **﴿so do not wrong yourselves therein﴾** [al-Tawbah: 36].

*Insilakh al-ashhur* (the passing of the months) means their ending and completion, and it is the reflexive form (mutawi') of *salkh*. Originally it is a metaphor taken from *salkh jild al-hayawan*, that is, the stripping of an animal's skin, i.e. its removal. Then this usage became common until it became a literal usage (haqiqah).

*Al-hurum* is the plural of *haram* (sacred, inviolable), and it is an irregular plural (sama'i, i.e. one that must be learned from usage), because the pattern *fu'ul* with a damma on the first and second letters is only regular (yanqas) in quadriliteral nouns with an extra long vowel. *Haram* is an adjective. Al-Radi said in the chapter on plurals in his commentary on al-Shafiyah: most broken plurals (jumu' al-taksir) require hearing (i.e. are learned from usage). It was mentioned earlier at His words, **﴿the sacred month for the sacred month﴾** [al-Baqarah: 194], in Surah al-Baqarah. They are Dhu al-Qa'dah, Dhu al-Hijjah, Muharram and Rajab.

[p. 116 begins at the next section.]

Their *insilakh* is the ending of the continuous period of them. Their sanctity remained as long as any tribe of the polytheists remained, for the benefit of both parties. When all the Arabs became Muslims, the ruling of the sanctity of the sacred months was nullified, because the sanctity of Islamic prohibitions made it unnecessary.

The imperative in **﴿kill the polytheists﴾** is for permission and permissibility (idhn wa ibahah), with regard to each of the commanded actions separately. That is: permission has been given to you to kill them, to take them captive, to besiege them, and to prevent them from passing through the land that is under the rule of Islam. Obligation may arise when a great benefit becomes apparent, and among the cases of obligation is what will come in His words, **﴿And if they break their oaths after their covenant and attack your religion, then fight the leaders of disbelief﴾** [al-Tawbah: 12]. The point here is that the sanctity of the covenant has been removed.

In this verse, jihad was legislated, permission for it was granted, and there is an indication that nothing but Islam will be accepted from them. This verse abrogated the verses of truce and treaty. The verse covers all polytheists and all places, except what the evidences from the Book and the Sunnah have specified.

*Al-akhdh* means capture.

*Al-hasr* means preventing them from entering the land of Islam except with permission from the Muslims.

*Al-qu'ud* is a metaphor for remaining in a place and staying with it, because sitting (qu'ud) is a firm and lengthy stability. So the meaning of sitting in the verse is standing guard (murabatah) in the places where the enemy polytheists are likely to enter the lands of Islam, and in the places where the enemy army and its equipment are likely to be present.

*Al-marsad* is the place of watching. *Al-rasd* is observation and following the gaze.

The word **"kull"** (every) is used to generalize the watch-places where it is presumed that they will pass, as a warning to the Muslims against neglecting guard at the watch-places, so that the enemy comes upon them from them, or against negligence in some of the enemy's passages, so that the enemies move about in safety and look down on the Muslims, and the groups of polytheists hear that the Muslims are not men of strength or alertness. Thus the meaning of **"kull"** here is interpreted as meaning "many," to alert [the Muslims] to striving to cover the watch-places thoroughly, like the words of al-Nabighah:

*Therein is every dhayyal and khansa' that turns toward every trembling [sand-hill] of the sand, a wanderer.*

[p. 117 begins.]

The phrase **﴿every watch-place﴾** is in the accusative either as a direct object (maf'ul bihi) by implying the meaning of "keep to" in *uq'udu* (lie in wait), like His words, **﴿I will surely sit in wait for them on Your straight path﴾** [al-A'raf: 16], or by analogy with an adverb of place (zarf), because it is proper for the verb "sit" to take a complement with *fi* of place; so it was made like an adverb of place, and *fi* was dropped for expansion (tawassu').

The mention of **"kull"** was already made at His words, **﴿And if they see every sign, they will not believe in it﴾** [al-An'am: 25], in Surah al-An'am.

\* \* \*

**﴿But if they repent, establish prayer, and give zakat, then let them go on their way; indeed Allah is Forgiving and Merciful.﴾**

This is a consequence of the preceding actions in His words: **﴿kill the polytheists wherever you find them, take them captive, besiege them, and lie in wait for them﴾**.

Repentance from polytheism is faith. That is: if they believe with sincere faith, by establishing prayer, whose establishment indicates that its performer is not lying in his faith, and by giving zakat, whose giving indicates that they are truly believers, because spending wealth on the Muslims is a sign of the sincerity of intention in what is spent. So establishing prayer and giving zakat are conditions for withholding fighting against them if they believe. There is no indication in this that prayer and zakat are part of faith.

The literal meaning of **﴿then let them go on their way﴾** is: leave their path on which they travel, i.e. leave for them every road you were commanded to watch, that is, let them travel passing through or coming toward you, since there is no harm from them to you in either case, for they have become your brothers, as He said in the next verse, **﴿But if they repent, establish prayer, and give zakat, then they are your brothers in religion﴾** [al-Tawbah: 11].

This compound expression is used here as a figure (tamthil) for not harming them and leaving them alone. It is said: *khall sabili* ("leave my way"), meaning: leave me to myself, as Jarir said:

*Leave the way to whoever builds the minaret by it, and emerge through Barzah wherever destiny forces you.*

This is the counterpart of the figure in His words, **﴿and lie in wait for them at every place of ambush﴾**.

The clause **﴿indeed Allah is Forgiving and Merciful﴾** is a concluding statement (tadhyil) intended to urge the Muslims not to treat with ill will those among the polytheists who embrace Islam, and not to hold them accountable for what they did in the past. So the meaning is: forgive them, because Allah has forgiven them, and He is Forgiving and Merciful; or follow the action of Allah, since He forgave them what they had done before, so you too should be in that same position of overlooking what has passed.

[Page 118]

It is coordinated (*'atf*) with the clause "if they repent" (*fa-in tabu*), to elaborate on the implied meaning of the conditional (*mafhum al-shart*). Alternatively, it is coordinated with the clause "So kill the polytheists" (﴿فاقتلوا المشركين﴾ [al-Tawbah: 5]), to specify its generality, meaning: except for a polytheist who seeks your protection for a benefit, either to serve as an envoy from his people or to learn the laws of Islam. The statement is phrased as a conditional to emphasize the ruling of the response, and to indicate that the desire for protection should arise from the side of the polytheists.

The particle "in" (إن) is used, although its condition is normally one of rare occurrence, to alert the listener that this is a hypothetical condition (*shart far·di*), so that the polytheists cannot claim that they were unable to meet the Prophet ﷺ and thus use that as an excuse to persist in polytheism when the Muslims attack them. It is reported in the Tafsir of al-Fakhr (al-Razi) that Ibn 'Abbas said: A man from the polytheists said to 'Ali ibn Abi Talib: "We wish to come to the Messenger after the end of this term to hear the Word of Allah, or for another need. Will we be killed?" 'Ali said: "No. Allah, may He be exalted, said: ﴿And if any one of the polytheists seeks your protection, grant him protection﴾, meaning, grant him security until he hears the Word of Allah." This does not contradict what we have observed, that the condition in the words of the Exalted, ﴿And if any one of the polytheists seeks your protection﴾, and so on, is a hypothetical condition, for it implies that this man's statement occurred after the revelation of the verse. However, I have not come across this report.

The expression "anyone" (أحد) was used instead of the word "a polytheist" (مشرك) to make explicit the generality of the category, because an indefinite noun (*nakira*) in the context of a conditional is, like its use in the context of negation, open to two meanings when it is not built on the vowel "fatha": it may mean the whole class, or only some individuals. Therefore, the use of "anyone" (أحد) in the context of the conditional makes the generality explicit, in the same way that building on "fatha" after "la" in the context of negation does.

"Ahad" (أحد) originally derives from "wahid" (واحد), since its hamza is a substitute for a waw. It is used to mean an individual of humankind, because he is one (*wahid*), just as "fard" is used for it in the terminology of the sciences. Thus the meaning of "anyone among the polytheists" is "a polytheist."

Placing "anyone" (أحد) before "seeks your protection" (استجارك) is for the sake of emphasis on the subject, so that it is the first thing to strike the hearing, and the predicate then falls into the listener's soul in a settled position.

It is permissible to begin with an indefinite noun because the intended meaning is a type, or because the conditional has the same function as negation in conveying generality. There is no obstacle to the particle of condition entering upon the subject, because the predicate being a verb is sufficient to indicate the verbal sentence required by the conditional particle, so it is known that the agent has been placed first from a delay for some purpose. For this reason, it became common among the grammarians to say that it is the agent of a verb understood, but that is only an assumed construction (*taqdir i'tibar*). Perhaps the purpose of stating the generality and placing "anyone among the polytheists" before the verb is to stress the granting of security to whoever among the polytheists asks for it, if his meeting the Prophet ﷺ and entering the lands of Islam serves a benefit, even if he is from one of the tribes that broke the covenant. This prevents their treachery from leading the Muslims to betray them or act treacherously towards them. This is like the words of the Exalted: ﴿And let not hatred of a people prevent you from transgressing; [but deal justly]﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 2], and the saying of the Prophet ﷺ: "Do not betray the one who betrayed you."

"Istijarah" (الاستجارة) means seeking protection (*talab al-jiwar*), and jiwar means being close by. It is used figuratively, in a widespread manner, to mean security, because a person does not settle in a place unless he is secure there. Hence they called the believer a neighbour (*jar*) and the ally a neighbour, and the verb "ajara" (أجار) came to mean "granted security" (أمّن). It is not used to mean "made a person his neighbour." The meaning is: If anyone among the polytheists seeks security from you, grant him security.

The reason for seeking protection is not stated, because its purposes vary, and it is left to the intentions of rational people, for no one seeks protection except for a legitimate purpose.

Since the residence of the polytheist seeking protection with the Prophet ﷺ, may the prayers and peace of Allah be upon him, is never free of presenting Islam to him and having him hear the Qur'an, whether his seeking protection was for that purpose or for another purpose, and because of what is well known of the Prophet's ﷺ eagerness to guide people, He made the hearing of the Qur'an by this seeker of protection the end (*ghayah*) of his temporary residence with the Messenger ﷺ. This end indicates an omitted statement, by way of brevity (*ijaz*), which is what the residence of the seeker of protection includes of discussion about an important matter, or a request to enter Islam, or the presentation of Islam to him. Then, when he hears the Word of Allah, the purposes of his residence have been fulfilled, because some of them belong to the aim of the seeker of protection, who is eager to begin with them, and some belong to the aim of the Prophet ﷺ, who does not let him go until he has repeated his guidance. The last thing that goes on with him, in the final period of his residence, is having him hear the Word of Allah, the Exalted.

"The Word of Allah" (كلام الله) is the Qur'an. It is attributed to the Name of Majesty (*ism al-jalalah*) because it is a speech that Allah brought into existence to indicate His intention to people, and conveyed to the Messenger ﷺ through the angel. It is not the composition of any created being; rather, Allah brought it into existence by His power without anyone's making. This is unlike the Hadith Qudsi.

For this reason, He followed it with the particle of delay "then" (ثُمَّ): ﴿then convey him to his place of safety﴾, to indicate the obligation of continuing to protect him within the land of Islam until he reaches the place where he is secure, even if he reaches it after a long period. Thus the particle "then" (ثم) here denotes a delay in rank (*tarakhi rutbi*), out of concern for conveying him to his place of safety.

The meaning of "convey him to his place of safety" (أبلغه مأمنه) is: give him respite, and do not frighten him, until he reaches his place of safety. Since the Prophet's ﷺ granting him security was the cause of his reaching his place of safety, the granting of security was treated as conveying him, and the Prophet ﷺ was commanded to do it. This includes commanding the Muslims not to harm him until he reaches his land where he is secure. It does not mean that the Prophet ﷺ would take the trouble to transport him or send someone to convey him. The meaning is: leave him to reach his place of safety. This is like the way the Arabs say to someone who interrupts another's speech before he has finished: "Let me swallow my saliva," meaning, give me a moment as long as it takes to swallow my saliva, then I will speak to you. Al-Zamakhshari said: "I said to one of my shaykhs: 'Let me swallow my saliva,' and he said: 'I have let you swallow the two rivers,' meaning the Tigris and the Euphrates."

"Al-ma'man" (المأمن) is the place of security, which is the place where the seeker of protection finds his former security, and that is the abode of his people, where no one can reach him with harm. The word "al-ma'man" has been attributed to the pronoun of the polytheist, to indicate that it is his own particular place of security, so it is known that it is his original home. This is unlike the abode of the neighbourhood, which is a temporary place of security and is not attributed to the one who is granted protection.

The clause ﴿That is because they are a people who do not know﴾ is in the position of a reason (*ta'lil*), to emphasize the command to keep faith with them in granting protection until they reach their homes. For this reason it was separated from the preceding clause. That is, we command this because they are a people who do not know. So the reference is to the content of the clause ﴿grant him protection until he hears the Word of Allah, then convey him to his place of safety﴾, meaning: do not hold them accountable, during the period of their seeking protection, for the harm they previously did, because they are a people who do not know. This is a reproach to them, in that the likes of them are not given any weight. Keep faith with them in this until they reach their homes, because they are a people who do not know what the Qur'an contains of guidance and right direction. The demonstrative (*ism al-ishara*) was the most suitable means of definition in this context, to combine the intended meanings and to be the most concise.

In the statement there is an honouring of the lofty morals of the Muslims, and a disparagement of the morals of the people of polytheism, and that the cause of this disparagement is polytheism, which corrupts morals. For this reason they were described as "a people who do not know," rather than saying "they do not know," to indicate that the negation of knowledge is pervasive among them. It points out that the reason for its pervasiveness among them is that it arises from the single idea that unites their scattered affairs, which is the belief in polytheism.

"Knowledge" (العلم) in the speech of the Arabs means reason (*'aql*) and soundness of judgement (*asalat al-ra'y*). The belief in polytheism is opposed to this. That is, how can a man of sound judgement worship a stone that he himself has carved, while he knows that it cannot benefit him?

[Page 121]

This is an explanatory resumptive clause (*isti'naf bayani*, a clause that answers a question arising from what came before). It arises from His words, ﴿A declaration of immunity from Allah and His Messenger﴾ (9:1), then from His words, ﴿that Allah is free of obligation to the polytheists﴾ (9:3), and from His words, ﴿So kill the polytheists﴾ (9:5). These verses were a gradual process of nullifying the earlier treaties that existed between them and the Muslims, because this would provoke a question in the minds of the Muslim listeners who had not grasped the underlying reason of the matter. Some of the Arab tribes among the polytheists might be astonished at this declaration and ask about its cause, and how the treaties were terminated and war was declared. So the context required an explanation of the reason for this, and that it consisted of two matters: the great distance between the creeds, and the prior act of treachery.

The interrogative with "how" (*kayfa*) is one of denial, a denial of the state of the continuation of the treaty between the polytheists and the people of Islam. That is, the continuation of the treaty in the future with those who had made a treaty with them on the day of Hudaybiyah and after it. Thus the verb "to be" (*yakun*) is used in the sense of continuance, like His words, ﴿O you who believe, believe in Allah﴾ (4:136), as indicated by His words that follow it, ﴿So as long as they remain upright toward you, be upright toward them.﴾ This denial is not, however, an objection to the making of the treaty, for the treaty was concluded with permission from Allah. He called it a victory in His words, ﴿Indeed, We have given you a clear victory﴾ (48:1), and He called the believers' satisfaction with it on that day tranquility in His words, ﴿It is He who sent down tranquility into the hearts of the believers﴾ (48:4).

The meaning is: the proper state is that there should be no treaty for you with the people of polytheism, because of the vast gap between the religion of monotheism and the religion of polytheism, so how could the two parties come to an agreement? That is, the treaty concluded with them was nothing but a matter limited in time by a benefit. In describing them as "polytheists" there is an implicit indication of the reason for the denial of the continuation of the treaty with them.

This confirms what we have explained concerning the reason for attributing the declaration of immunity to Allah and His Messenger, and for ascribing the treaty to the pronoun of the Muslims, in His words, ﴿A declaration of immunity from Allah and His Messenger to those with whom you made a treaty﴾ (9:1).

The meaning of "with" (*'inda*) is figurative stability, in the sense of continuance; that is, it is only a treaty limited in time. The Quraysh had broken their treaty that they had made on the day of Hudaybiyah, when they helped the Banu Bakr with weapons and men against Khuza'ah, and Khuza'ah had been included in the treaty of the Prophet ﷺ. This was the reason for preparing for the conquest of Mecca.

The exception ﴿except those with whom you made a treaty﴾ (9:4) is from the sense of negation in which the interrogative "how" (in ﴿How can there be a treaty for the polytheists?﴾) is used. That is, the treaty of the polytheists is not valid except with those polytheists with whom you made a treaty at the Sacred Mosque.

Those with whom they made a treaty at the Sacred Mosque were the Banu Damrah and the Banu Judhaymah ibn al-Dil from Kinanah, and the Banu Bakr from Kinanah.

[Page 122]

So the relative pronoun here refers to a specific treaty, and these are more specific than those mentioned in His words, ﴿except those of the polytheists with whom you made a treaty and who have not failed you in anything﴾ (9:4).

The purpose of singling them out for mention is to praise their quality of fulfilling what they had pledged to. It is necessary that these had made a treaty with the Prophet ﷺ during the Lesser Pilgrimage of Compensation (*'Umrat al-Qada'*) at the Sacred Mosque, and had entered into the agreement that he concluded with the Quraysh specifically concerning them, in addition to their having entered into the more general agreement. They did not break their treaty, nor did they support an enemy against the Muslims, up until the time of the revelation of "Bara'ah" (Immunity). Furthermore, making a treaty at the Sacred Mosque is further from the suspicion of breaking it, because a treaty made in its presence has a greater effect on the souls of the polytheists than a mere oath, as He said, ﴿Indeed, they have no oaths﴾ (9:12).

The intended meaning is not every person who made a treaty at the Sacred Mosque, as one who has a misconception might suppose, because the Prophet ﷺ was not authorized to make a treaty with any other group from among them.

His words, ﴿So as long as they remain upright toward you, be upright toward them﴾ (9:7), are a consequence (*tafri'*) of the exception. The implied sense is: except those with whom you made a treaty at the Sacred Mosque, so be upright toward them as long as they are upright toward you, that is, as long as they remain upright toward you. The apparent reason for the exception of these is that their treaty has an additional sanctity because it was made at the Sacred Mosque around the Ka'bah.

The "ma" here is temporal, with the implication of the conditional sense, and the "fa" that precedes it is the "fa" of consequence. The "fa" that occurs in His words, ﴿so be upright toward them﴾, is the "fa" of the answer of the condition. The origin of this is that when an adverbial phrase or a prepositional phrase is placed before what it governs, it may take on the meaning of a condition, and so the "fa" enters into its answer. Among examples of this is His words, ﴿and for that let the competitors compete﴾ (83:26). The "fa" here must be non-consequential, because it is preceded by the conjunction "wa" (and). Also the words of the Prophet ﷺ, "As you are, so will you be ruled over," where both verbs are apocopated (jussive). And his words to the man who asked to take part in jihad, when the Messenger asked him, "Do you have parents?" He said, "Yes." He said, "Then exert yourself for their sake," in a narration in which it has two "fa"s.

Uprightness (*istiqamah*) in its real meaning is the absence of crookedness. The *sin* and *ta'* here are for intensification, like *istajaba* (he responded) and *istahabba* (he loved). When a thing stands erect, its uprightness is fully manifest and it has no crookedness in it. Here it is used figuratively [Page 123] for good dealing and abandoning fighting, because bad dealing is described as twisting and crookedness, so likewise its opposite is described as uprightness.

The clause ﴿Indeed, Allah loves the God-conscious﴾ (9:4) is a justification (*ta'lil*) for the command to be upright. The placement of "inna" (indeed) at its beginning is for emphasis. It indicates the justification, because "inna" in such contexts serves the function of "fa" (so). This justification indicates that uprightness toward them comes from God-consciousness (*taqwa*); otherwise it would not be appropriate to inform them that Allah loves the God-conscious. It follows the command to be upright toward them, and this is a form of concision. Moreover, being upright toward them preserves the treaty, which is of the nature of an oath.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 9, verse 8:

﴿How (can there be a covenant for the polytheists with Allah?) — and if they were to prevail over you, they would not observe toward you any tie of kinship (ilL) or covenant (dhimmah).﴾

This "kayfa" is an emphatic repetition of the "kayfa" in the verse before it, so it is parenthetical between the two clauses. The clause ﴿and if they were to prevail over you﴾ etc. may be a circumstantial clause (jumla haliyya), with the waw indicating the state (waw al-hal), or it may be coordinated with the clause ﴿How can there be a covenant for the polytheists﴾ [al-Tawba: 7], as a report about their inner intentions.

The repetition of the interrogative conveys that the circumstantial clause has a greater connection to the direction of the disavowal of a lasting covenant with the polytheists, so much so that it stands almost independently in the disavowal, and is not merely a qualifier of the matter toward which the disavowal was first directed. Thus the meaning produced by this construction returns to two things: the disavowal of a lasting covenant with the polytheists in itself, from the start, because they are not fit for it; and the disavowal of its lasting in particular in this state, which is the state of what they conceal of an intention of treachery if they prevail over the Muslims, as indicated by the evidences and signs, just as the Hawazin did after the conquest of Makkah. Thus the clause ﴿and if they were to prevail over you﴾ is coordinated with the clause ﴿How can there be a covenant for the polytheists﴾ [al-Tawba: 7].

The pronoun in "yazhharu" refers to the polytheists in His saying: ﴿How can there be a covenant for the polytheists with Allah?﴾ [al-Tawba: 7]. The meaning of ﴿yazhharu﴾ [al-Kahf: 20] is "if they were to be victorious." The explanation of this verb has preceded just above, at His saying: ﴿and they have not supported anyone against you﴾ [al-Tawba: 4]. The meaning is: if the polytheists were victorious, after their weakness, and after they had tested from the covenant that it had been a cause of your strength, they would break the covenant. The pronoun in "ʿalaykum" is an address to the believers.

The meaning of ﴿yarqubu﴾ is "they would not fulfil and would not observe." It is said: raqiba al-shay' — when one looks at a thing with a gaze of watchfulness and observance; and from it the Watcher (al-Raqib) is named, and the watch-post (al-marqab), the place of guarding, is named. It is used here for observing and fulfilling the covenant, because whoever nullifies acting upon something is as if he did not see it and turned his gaze away from it.

Al-illu: the alliance and covenant; and "il" is also used for lineage and kinship. Between the polytheists and the Muslims there were ties of lineage and kinship, so it is correct that both of its meanings be intended here.

And "dhimma" is what one is bound by of ties of connection — companionship, friendship, and neighbourliness — which, in manliness, must be guarded and protected. It is said: "fi dhimmati kadha," meaning: I am bound by it and I guard it.

* * *

﴿They please you with their mouths, but their hearts refuse, and most of them are defiant wrongdoers.﴾

This is a fresh, independent resumption: that is, they say to you what pleases you, deceitfully; and if they were able to overpower you, they would not observe toward you any tie or covenant. Whoever hears a statement and rejects it...

The "ibaya" is refusal to do a thing that is demanded; and attributing refusal to the hearts is a metaphor, for their hearts, when they intended treachery, were likened to one from whom something is requested and who refuses.

The clause ﴿and most of them are defiant wrongdoers﴾, in the position of a circumstantial clause from the plural waw in "yurdunakum," is intended for disparagement: that most of them, despite this, are described as having departed from the path of manliness and chivalry, since we find most of them casting off the reins of modesty. Thus they combined religious blame and customary blame. So "fisq" here means departure from customary perfection among people, and the intended meaning is not departure from the path of religion, because that is a description of all of them, not most of them, and because their description with disbelief is already known.

[Page 125]

﴿They have bought with the signs of Allah a small price, and so they have averted [others] from His way. Indeed, evil is what they used to do.﴾ The position of this sentence is that of a fresh, independent sentence (al-istinaf al-ibtida'i, a new sentence that begins a separate statement), which signals that it begins a new account of their strange condition, separate from what precedes it. In this verse the Qur'an describes the polytheists (al-mushrikun) in terms similar to those it used for the People of the Book in Surat al-Baqarah: buying the signs of Allah for a small price. But they are not described in this way in another verse revealed after it, because its revelation came at the end of the period in which the polytheists remained in shirk. Not much time passed before they entered the religion of Allah in multitudes, in the year of the delegations (sanat al-wufud) and after it. The verse indicates those Arabs who remained upon shirk after the conquest of Makkah and the spread of Islam over most of the lands of Arabia. They had no doubt about the truth of Islam or the strength of its proof, but they remained upon shirk for benefits they gained from the customs of their people: raids that some of them launched against others, attachment to pre-Islamic (jahili) ways such as wine, gambling and fornication, and other blameworthy and corrupt pleasures. That is a small thing, which they preferred over guidance and salvation in the Hereafter. Because the signs of the truth of the Qur'an had become established among them, they were treated as if they were a kind of property in their hands, which they squandered in order to acquire small benefits. Therefore their condition was likened to that of one who buys something with something else. The discussion of a verse like this has already passed in Surat al-Baqarah.

The "signs" (al-ayat) here means the proofs (al-dala'il), namely the proofs of the call to Islam, the greatest of which is the Qur'an, because it contains arguments, demonstrations and inimitability (al-i'jaz). The ba' (preposition) in the phrase ﴿with the signs of Allah﴾ is the ba' of exchange (ba' al-ta'wid, the particle marking what is given in return). Its usual use is with that which is given as a consideration by its owner in order to take a counter-value owned by another. Thus the signs of Allah are treated as if they were property belonging to them, because their indication had been firmly established among them; then they turned away from them and exchanged them for following their desires.

The expression of the item acquired by the term "price" (thaman), which normally refers to something given out rather than something kept, is a metaphor (isti'arah), in which the benefits of their desires are likened to a price paid out. Thus two metaphors arise, from the verb ﴿they bought﴾ and from the word ﴿a price﴾, according to two different considerations.

[Page 126]

The clause ﴿and so they have averted [others] from His way﴾ is a consequence of the clause ﴿they have bought with the signs of Allah﴾, because their preference for remaining upon their disbelief necessarily results in their turning people away from following Islam. Their condition is therefore likened to that of one who blocks people from traveling a road that leads to the destination. The object of ﴿averted﴾ is omitted for the sake of generality, meaning: they averted every seeker.

The clause ﴿Indeed, evil is what they used to do﴾ is also a fresh sentence. It is separated from the one before it so that its independence in conveying information is made clear, and because it should not be joined by a conjunction, since conjoining would make the joined clause a complement to the one it is joined to.

It begins with the emphatic particle (inna) to draw attention to this censure of them.

"Sa'a" (evil, it was bad) is one of the verbs of censure, of the same type as "bi'sa" (how wretched), and ﴿what they used to do﴾ is the specified object of the censure. Their action is expressed by ﴿they used to do﴾ to indicate that it was a habit (da'b) for them and something they repeatedly did.

This sentence may be a *badal ishtimal* (a substitute that is included within the previous clause, "comprehensive substitution") for the clause ﴿Indeed, they, how evil is what they used to do﴾ [At-Tawbah: 9], because the absence of regard for *ilL* (a bond of kinship or alliance) and *dhimma* (a covenant or guarantee of protection) toward the believers is part of the evil of their conduct. It may also be a *isti'naf* (a new, independent sentence) begun to complete the meaning of the clause. It conveys a more general and wider meaning than what is conveyed by His saying: ﴿And if they gain the upper hand over you, they will not observe regarding you any bond of kinship or covenant﴾ [At-Tawbah: 8]. This is because the unrestricted statement, free from the condition ﴿if they gain the upper hand over you﴾ [Al-Kahf: 20], indicates that their disregard for the right of alliance and covenant is an entrenched disposition, whether they are strong or weak. And that is due to the evil of their inner intent toward the believers because of their faith. *Al-ilL* and *al-dhimma* were mentioned shortly before.

* * *

[Page 127]
﴿And it is they who are the transgressors﴾
This is a conjunction (*'atf*) upon the clause ﴿They do not observe regarding a believer any bond of kinship or covenant﴾, due to the connection that the affirmation of their great transgression arose from the rancor which they harbored toward the believers, not for anything except that they are believers, like His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And they did not resent them except that they believed in Allah, the Exalted in Might, the Praiseworthy﴾ [Al-Buruj: 8].

The restriction (*qasr*) may be for the purpose of emphasizing the extent of their transgression, because it is a great, inward transgression against a people with whom they had made alliances and covenants, while they did not inflict any harm upon them although they were able to do so. Or it may be a *qasr qalb* (restriction that reverses a mistaken belief), meaning: it is they who are the transgressors, not you, because they initiated the breach of the covenant in the matter of Khuza'a and the Banu al-Dil of Bakr ibn Wa'il, which was a cause of the expedition of the Conquest.

﴿But if they repent, establish prayer, and give zakah, then they are your brothers in religion.﴾ This is a ruling built upon a ruling (tafrī' ḥukmin ʿalā ḥukmin), to make the harshness followed by leniency: if they desist from hostility toward the Muslims by entering Islam, aiming to erase the effect of the resentment against them once they have embraced Islam. It is followed by the clause ﴿Indeed, they have done evil what they used to do﴾ [At-Tawbah: 9] up to His saying "the transgressors," as an alert to them that their rectifying their situation is easy for them. He made it a consequence of repentance that they become brothers to the believers. Since the context here concerns mentioning their enmity toward the believers, their repentance was made the cause of brotherhood with the believers. This differs from the context of His saying before it, ﴿But if they repent, establish prayer, and give zakah, then let them go their way﴾ [At-Tawbah: 5], where what followed repentance there was the command to fight them and to lie in wait for them. So it was appropriate that, upon their repentance, there follow the absence of any harm being done to them. It results from the two verses together that their repentance necessitates their safety and their brotherhood.

Among the subtleties of the two verses is that brotherhood is mentioned second, because it is the more specific of the two benefits of their repentance. Thus this verse reinforces its counterpart regarding the essence of the ruling.

His saying "then they are your brothers" (fa-ikhwānukum) is the predicate of an omitted subject, meaning: "then they are your brothers." This predicate was expressed as a nominal sentence to indicate that their faith requires the permanence and continuation of brotherhood, alerting that they return like the believers who preceded them in the essence of religious brotherhood.

"Al-ikhwān" is the plural of "akh" in both the literal and figurative senses, and "brotherhood" is used here to mean affection and friendship.

The prepositional expression in His saying "in religion" (fī al-dīn) is figurative: it likens the strong attachment to the enveloping of the container by the contained, to increase the indication of firmly being established in Islam and that it erases what came before it.

* * *

﴿And We detail the signs for a people who know.﴾
This is an interjected (i'tirāḍ) concluding clause (tadhyīl), and the "wāw" is parenthetical. The appropriateness of its placement after His saying ﴿They have sold the signs of God for a small price﴾ [At-Tawbah: 9] is that it implies they did not take guidance from the signs of God and rejected them while knowing their truth, like His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Have you seen one who takes his desire as his god, and Allah has misguided him knowingly?﴾ [Al-Jāthiyah: 23]. Considering what it contains of the supposition of their repentance and faith, if they desist from preferring corruption over righteousness, the saying ﴿And We detail the signs for a people who know﴾ encompasses both states, indicating that the signs mentioned just before, in His saying ﴿They have sold the signs of God for a small price﴾ [At-Tawbah: 9], are clear and detailed signs, and that these people's failure to be guided by them is not due to any deficiency in them; rather, they are guided by them only a people who know. So if they believe, they were then of a people who know. It is understood from this that if they sell them for a small price, they are not of a people who know, so their knowledge at that point is treated as its absence, since the effect of knowledge, which is acting upon it, is absent. This contains a rebuke to them by equating them with those who lack understanding, like His saying: ﴿And none understands them except those who have knowledge﴾ [Al-ʿAnkabūt: 43].

The object of "yaʿlamūn" is omitted because the verb is treated as intransitive, since what is intended is: for a people possessing knowledge and intellect.

This concluding clause was joined to the sentence ﴿But if they repent, establish prayer, and give zakah, then they are your brothers in religion﴾ because it is most closely connected to it: if they repent, they have become brothers to the Muslims, and so they become of a people who know, since they share with the Muslims in being guided by the detailed signs.

The meaning of "tafṣīl" (detailing) was explained in His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Thus We detail the signs, that the way of the criminals may be made clear﴾ [Al-Anʿām: 55], in Surat al-Anʿām.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 9, verse 12:

﴿And if they break their oaths after their covenant and revile your religion, then fight the leaders of disbelief—indeed, they have no oaths—that perhaps they may desist.﴾

When he had completed the explanation of the categories of polytheists from whose covenant God commanded disassociation, with His saying: ﴿That Allah is free of obligation to the polytheists﴾ [al-Tawbah: 3], up to His saying: ﴿And give tidings to those who disbelieve of a painful punishment﴾ [al-Tawbah: 3]—and that was only because of their concealed treachery—and those whom He commanded to be held to their covenant until its term, as long as they remained steadfast to the covenant, with His saying: ﴿except those of the polytheists with whom you made a covenant and who have not failed you in anything﴾ [al-Tawbah: 4], and so on, the verse ﴿Those who are [such as to] respond﴾ is conjoined to those [earlier verses] to explain those who openly break the covenant and openly do what angers the Muslims by their speech. This condition is the opposite of the condition in His saying: ﴿If they gain the upper hand over you, they will not observe toward you any tie of kinship or covenant. They satisfy you with their mouths, but their hearts refuse﴾ [al-Tawbah: 8].

Al-nakth (breaking) was already discussed at His saying—exalted is He: ﴿Then when We removed from them the punishment for a term which they were to reach, at once they broke their word﴾ [al-A'raf: 135], in Surat al-A'raf.

The breaking of the covenant was expressed as the breaking of oaths in order to censure the breaking, because the covenant was accompanied by an oath to fulfil it; for this reason the covenant was called ḥilf (alliance-oath).

His saying ﴿after their covenant﴾ was added to increase the record of the abomination of their breaking: by reminding that it is treachery to a covenant and violation of an oath.

Al-ṭa'n (reviling) in its literal sense is piercing a body with a pointed thing such as a spear, and it is used figuratively in the sense of defamation. It is ascribed to deficiency, by likening a person's honour, which was whole and unblemished, to a sound body. When its defects are made apparent through defamation and abuse, it is likened to skin whose join has been corrupted.

The command here is for obligation, and it is one of the states of the permission mentioned in His saying—exalted is He: ﴿Then when the sacred months have passed, kill the polytheists﴾ [al-Tawbah: 5]. In this state fighting them becomes obligatory, in defence of the sanctity of the religion and in suppressing their evil before they rebel against it.

A'immah is the plural of imam (leader), which is that which is made a model in an action performed upon its pattern, or upon the pattern of its action. He—exalted is He—said: ﴿and make them leaders﴾ [al-Qasas: 5], i.e., those who are followed. And Labid said:

"And for every people there is a path and its leader."

(Continued on the next page)

And the imam is the model that is fashioned upon a form or measure, being made. So "the leaders of disbelief" here are those who reached the extreme of it, to the point that they became models for the people of disbelief.

What is meant by "the leaders of disbelief" is the polytheists who broke their oaths after their covenant. This designation was placed in the position of a pronoun, when it was not said "then fight them," in order to add to the censure against them by their reaching this rank of disbelief, namely that they are models for others. For those who hid the intent to break the covenant remain hesitant to reveal it; then when some of them begin to openly break it, the rest follow them, so the breakers become leaders for the remainder.

The clause ﴿indeed, they have no oaths﴾ is a justification for fighting them: that they deserve it because of their contempt for the oaths they swore for peace, and then betrayed. It also serves to inform the Muslims, so that they do not begin fighting them without knowing the wisdom of the command to do so, in which case their fighting would be merely for the sake of obeying God's command, and they would not have the rage against the polytheists that sharpens their resolve against them.

The negation of oaths for them is a negation of the true reality of the oath, which is intending to honour it and to fulfil it. Since they did not fulfil their oaths, their oaths were treated as nonexistent, because its most essential property, acting upon what it required, was absent.

Nafi', Ibn Kathir, Abu 'Amr, and Ruways from Ya'qub read ʼa'immah (أيِمَّةَ) with the second hamza made easy, between the hamza and the ya'. The rest read with both hamzas fully pronounced. Hisham from Ibn 'Amir and Abu Ja'far read with a madd (elongation) between the two hamzas.

The majority read ﴿lā ʼaymāna lahum﴾ with a fatḥah on the hamza of ʼaymān, as the plural of yamīn (oath). Ibn 'Amir read it with a kasrah on the hamza, meaning they are not believers; and whoever has no faith has no covenant, since there is no restraint.

The conjunction of ﴿and reviled your religion﴾ is the conjunction of one division to its counterpart, so the wāw in it has the meaning of "or." For when one of these two acts occurs—breaking oaths, or reviling the religion—the occurrence of either one necessitates fighting them, that is, without reconciliation, without covenant, and without truce after that.

The mention of their reviling the religion of the Muslims indicates that such reviling was among their habits during the period of the treaty, so it was intended to restrain them from returning to it. I have not found that it was stipulated upon the polytheists in the treaty and covenant agreements with the Muslims that they must not revile Islam—apart from this verse—so this became a condition upon them thereafter, because the Muslims had become powerful.

His saying "(﴿fight the leaders of disbelief﴾)" is a command of obligation.

The clause ﴿that perhaps they may desist﴾ may be a justification for the clause "(﴿fight the leaders of disbelief﴾)": i.e., fighting them in hope that they will desist. It is evident that fighting destroys many of them, so the desistance hoped for is that of those who remain alive after the war has laid down its burdens.

The object of the verb "desist" is not mentioned, and it cannot be that the desistance is from breaking the covenant, because their covenant is not accepted after they broke it, by God's saying: ﴿indeed, they have no oaths﴾. Nor can it be desistance from reviling the religion, because if their reviling of our religion occurs during the period of fighting, there is no benefit in hoping they will desist from it; and if it occurs after the war has laid down its burdens, it is not sound, since there is no end to the killing between the Muslims and them.
