Therefore it is determined that the meaning is: "that perhaps they may desist from disbelief."

It is also permissible that the clause be a fresh independent resumption, not connected to the clause ﴿and if they break their oaths﴾ and the verse, but arising from His saying: ﴿And if they repent, establish prayer﴾ [al-Tawbah: 11], up to His saying: "(﴿the leaders of disbelief﴾)."

The meaning: the hope is that they desist from polytheism and embrace Islam. This was indeed realized, for this verse was revealed after the conquest of Makkah and after the day of Hunayn, no breaking occurred after that, and the polytheists entered Islam in multitudes in the year of the delegations.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 9, verse 13:

﴿Will you not fight a people who broke their oaths, and resolved to expel the Messenger, and they began the attack against you the first time? Do you fear them? Allah has more right that you should fear Him, if you are believers.﴾ This is a warning against slackness in fighting them, apart from those who were exempted from them after the command to kill them, take them captive, besiege them, and block every route of escape for them, in His words: ﴿Then kill the polytheists wherever you find them﴾ (9:5) up to His words: ﴿every ambush﴾ (9:5). After eight attributes were established for them that incite against showing them any leniency in fighting them, namely His words: ﴿How can there be a covenant with the polytheists?﴾ (9:7), His words: ﴿How, when if they gain the upper hand over you﴾ (9:8), His words: ﴿They please you with their mouths, but their hearts refuse﴾ (9:8), His words: ﴿and most of them are defiantly disobedient﴾ (9:8), His words: ﴿They have sold the signs of Allah for a small price﴾ (9:9), His words: ﴿They do not observe toward a believer any tie of kinship or covenant﴾ (9:10), His words: ﴿and it is those who are the transgressors﴾ (9:10), and His words: ﴿Indeed, they have no oaths﴾ (9:12).

So the clause ﴿Will you not fight a people who broke their oaths﴾ is a warning against delay in taking the initiative to fight them.

The word ʾalā (ألا) may be a combination of two particles: the interrogative hamza (هَمْزَةُ الِاسْتِفْهامِ, the interrogative particle) and the negative lā (لا النّافِيَةُ, the negating particle). It may also be a single particle of exhortation (لِلتَّحْضِيضِ, taḥḍīḍ: urging or exhortation), like His words: ﴿Do you not wish that Allah should forgive you?﴾ (24:22).

On the first possibility, the interrogative may be disapproving (إنْكارِيًّا, inkārī: denial), negating the fighting of the polytheists, which is what al-Bayḍāwī held. It would then serve to rule out the possibility that the Muslims might imagine these covenants to be sacrosanct. The interrogative may also be confirmatory (تَقْرِيرِيًّا, taqrīrī: seeking affirmation), which is the apparent meaning of what al-Zamakhsharī (Ṣāḥib al-Kashshāf) understood, as a confirmation of a negation, treating them as those who have abandoned fighting, so that they deserve to be asked to acknowledge their abandonment. In al-Kashshāf he said: its meaning is urging to fight, by way of emphasis. In Mughni al-Labib (Mughnī al-Labīb, Ibn Hisham's grammar), it is stated that ʾalā, when used as an interrogative for affirmation of a negation, is restricted to entering upon a nominal sentence, and his two commentators accepted this. It is not hidden that the words of al-Kashshāf call out against this.

On the second possibility, that ʾalā is a single particle of exhortation, then it is an exhortation to fight. Ibn Hisham in Mughni took this verse as an example of this usage, in the manner of emphasis in warning. Perhaps the reason for this variety of expression in warning against negligence in fighting them, while stating that they deserve it, is that many Muslims had rejoiced in the victory on the day of the Conquest of Mecca and had turned toward gathering the fruit of peace, by devoting themselves to improving their conditions and their wealth. Therefore, when they were commanded to fight these polytheists, they were liable to be reluctant to do so, out of fear of defeat, after they had gained the reputation of victory. In His words following it, ﴿Do you fear them?﴾, there is something that makes this clearer.

As for their breaking of their oaths, it is evident from what preceded at His words: ﴿except those among the polytheists with whom you made a covenant﴾ (9:4), and His words: ﴿except those among the polytheists with whom you made a covenant, then they have not failed you in anything﴾ (9:4), and the verse. That was their breaking of the covenant of al-Hudaybiyya, when they aided Banu Bakr against Khuza'a, while Khuza'a was on the side of the Muslims' covenant, as has preceded.

As for their resolve to expel the Messenger, its apparent meaning is that this resolve occurred together with their breaking of their oaths, and that what is intended is the expulsion of the Messenger from Medina, that is, his banishment from it. This is because his expulsion from Mecca is a matter that occurred years ago, and because forcing him into fighting is not known to be described as expulsion. So the apparent meaning is that they concealed this resolve in their souls, and Allah, may He be exalted, knew it and alerted the Muslims to it. It was that when they broke the covenant, they longed to resume fighting, and imagined themselves victorious, and that if they prevailed they would expel the Messenger, peace and blessings be upon him, from Medina.

(The resolve, al-hamm, is the determination to do something, whether or not one does it, or turns away from it.) Their being held to account in this verse for the mere resolve to expel the Messenger indicates that they did not actually expel him. Otherwise it would have been more fitting to censure them for the expulsion, not the resolve to it, as in His words: ﴿when those who disbelieved expelled him﴾ (9:40). It also indicates that they did not give up what they had resolved upon except when they were prevented from carrying it out. Al-Hasan reported: they resolved to expel the Messenger from Medina when they attacked him at Uhud and when they attacked in the Battle of the Confederates, meaning that Allah sufficed him against the evil they had resolved upon. It is not permissible that what is meant is his expulsion from Mecca for the Hijra, because that occurred before the covenant between them and the Muslims at al-Hudaybiyya was concluded.

So my view is that those meant by ﴿those who resolved to expel the Messenger﴾ are tribes who had been allied to the Muslims by covenant, and who broke the covenant in the year eight, the day of the Conquest of Mecca. They resolved to support the people of Mecca on the day of the Conquest, and to betray the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, and the Muslims, and to come upon them unawares, so that they and Quraysh would be a single confederacy against the Muslims, and would expel the Messenger ﷺ and the Muslims from Mecca. But Allah turned them away from that after they had resolved upon it, and exposed their secret to the Prophet ﷺ, and commanded him to fight them and to cast off their covenant in the year nine.

We do not know whether the Prophet ﷺ fought them after the revelation of this verse, or whether the announcement of the command to fight them (while they knew that they were its intended target) was the cause of their becoming Muslims and Allah's accepting their repentance, fulfilling the hope expressed in His words: ﴿so that perhaps they will desist﴾ (9:12). Perhaps some of these had declared war against the Muslims on the day of the Conquest, breaking the covenant, and supplied Quraysh with troops. When no battle broke out between the Muslims and the polytheists that day, they despaired of their support and returned to their homes. The Prophet ﷺ overlooked them, did not hold them to account for their treachery, and remained observing that covenant, and this continued until the revelation of this verse. That is His words: ﴿and they began the attack against you the first time﴾

[p. 134]

That is, they were the first to break the covenant. This is because Quraysh took the side of their allies from Kinana, and fought Khuza'a, the allies of the Muslims.

﴿The first time⦆ (awwala marrah) is in the accusative as an adverbial of manner (منصوب عَلى المَصْدَرِيَّةِ, accusative of the verbal noun). The annexation of "awwal" to "marrah" is an annexation of the attribute to the thing described. The implied sense is "a first time," and "marrah" (time, instance) is the single occurrence of an act, from "ḥadatha yaḥduthu" (to happen). So the meaning of ﴿they began the attack against you the first time﴾ is: they began against you the first beginning in breaking the covenant, that is, a first beginning. "Marrah" is an indefinite noun denoting a single instance of some act, and its indefiniteness is most commonly specified by context, as here, though sometimes the wording itself specifies it.

"Awwal" is an elative (اسْمُ تَفْضِيلٍ, ism al-tafḍīl: comparative/superlative form) that comes in the masculine form, even though the thing it describes is feminine in wording, because when the elative is annexed to an indefinite noun it must remain singular and masculine, the annexed noun indicating the gender. One says "thānī marrah" (second time) and "thālith marrah" (third time).

The purpose of this statement is to threaten them for the breaking of the covenant which they had concealed, and that there is no leniency in it. In any case, what is meant by the expulsion of the Messenger, peace and blessings be upon him, is either his expulsion from Mecca in defeat after he had entered it victorious, or his expulsion from Medina after he had returned to it following the Conquest, by their having resolved to attack Medina and to expel the Messenger and the Muslims from it and scatter the community of Islam.

The clause ﴿Do you fear them?﴾ is a substitute of inclusion (بَدَلُ اشْتِمالٍ, badal ishtimāl: a substitute related to the first by inclusion) for the clause ﴿Will you not fight﴾. The interrogative in it is either disapproving or confirmatory, concerning the cause of hesitation in fighting them. The sense is: does your not fighting them stem from your fear of them? This is an added incitement to fight them.

Upon this confirmation the clause ﴿Allah has more right that you should fear Him﴾ is built, meaning: Allah, who commanded you to fight them, has more right that you should fear Him, when the thought of not complying with His command crosses your minds, if you are believers, because faith requires fear of Allah and no hesitation about the success of complying with Him.

The condition concerning the future was introduced, though there is no doubt about it, for the purpose of stirring up their religious resolve, so that they would prove that they are truly believers who put the fear of Allah before the fear of people.

[Page 135]

﴿Fight them; Allah will punish them by your hands, disgrace them, give you victory over them, and heal the breasts of a believing people﴾ ﴿and remove the rage from their hearts﴾ [al-Tawbah 9:14–15]

This is a fresh resumption (isti'naf ibtida'i) returning from the theme of warning to the explicit command to fight them, which appears in His words: ﴿So fight the leaders of disbelief﴾ [al-Tawbah 9:12]. It is the nature of such a return in speech to come as a resumption, as occurs here.

The verb ﴿yu'adhdhibhum﴾ (will punish them) and what is conjoined to it are in the jussive mood as the answer to the command (jawab al-amr). By making it an answer and a condition (jaza'), Allah guarantees the Muslims five benefits from that fighting, which resolve into twelve, since each benefit includes both an honour for the believers and a humiliation for these polytheists. In each benefit the most important purpose was observed, and it was stated explicitly, while what lies beyond it was made to occur by way of metonymy (kinayah).

The first benefit: the punishment of the polytheists by the hands of the Muslims. This is a humiliation for the polytheists and an honour for the Muslims.

The second: the disgracing of the polytheists, which entails the might (izzah) of the Muslims.

The third: the victory of the Muslims. This is an explicit honour for them, and it entails the defeat of the polytheists, which is a humiliation for them.

The fourth: the healing of the breasts of a group of the believers. This is explicit in the healing of the breasts of a company of the believers, who were Khuza'ah, and it entails the healing of the breasts of all the believers, and it entails the vexation of the breasts of their enemies. Thus these are three benefits in one benefit.

The fifth: the removal of the rage of the hearts of a group of the believers, or of all the believers. This entails the departure of the rage of the rest of the believers, which they had borne from the provocation of their forbearance, and it entails the rage of the hearts of their enemies. Thus these are three benefits in one benefit.

"Punishment" (ta'dhib) here means punishment by killing and wounding. The punishment is attributed to Allah, and the hands of the Muslims are made an instrument for it, as an honouring of the Muslims.

"Ikhza'" (disgracing) is humiliation (idhlal), and it was discussed earlier in al-Baqarah. Here it means humiliation by capture.

[Page 136]

"Nasr" (victory) is the attainment of the desired outcome of fighting, and it was discussed at the beginning of al-Baqarah.

"Shifa'" (healing) is the removal of illness and the treatment of its removal. It is used here metaphorically (isti'arah) for the removal from the souls of the fatigue of rage and resentment, just as its opposite, illness, is used metaphorically for the corrupt thoughts in souls, in His words: ﴿In their hearts is a disease﴾ [al-Baqarah 2:10]. Qays ibn Zuhayr said:

I have healed my soul from Hamal ibn Badr, and my sword has healed me from Hudhayfah.

The attribution of "al-sudur" (breasts) to ﴿a believing people﴾, rather than to a pronoun of the addressees, indicates that those whose breasts Allah heals through the victory of the believers are a company of the believers addressed with the command to fight. They were peoples in whose hearts there were grudges against some of the polytheists who had harmed them and aided against them, but they were bound by the covenant of the Prophet (ﷺ), so they could not requite them for their evil conduct. They had wished to be permitted to fight them, and when Allah commanded the annulment of the covenants of the polytheists, they rejoiced and were glad. These are a group whose condition differs from the condition of the group addressed with the incitement to fight and the warning against neglecting it. On the authority of Mujahid and al-Suddi, the believing people were Khuza'ah, the allies of the Prophet (ﷺ), and the souls of Khuza'ah harboured grudges against Banu Bakr ibn Kinanah, who had attacked them with fighting. In mentioning this group there is additional incitement to fighting, by increasing the mention of its benefits, and by comparing the condition of those eager for it with the condition of those who were being urged to it, against whom the command to fight was pressed.

The conjunction of ﴿and remove the rage of their hearts﴾ [al-Tawbah 9:15] to ﴿and heal the breasts of a believing people﴾ indicates a difference between the conjoined and that to which it is conjoined, and the difference between the two concepts and the two conditions suffices for the difference. Thus the removal of the rage of the hearts is equivalent to the healing of the breasts, so the first sentence is emphasised by the second, along with the clarification of the object of the healing. It is also permissible that the difference be in the referent (al-masdaq) together with a difference in concept, so that by "the healing of the breasts" is meant what results from gladness and relief through victory, and by "the removal of rage" is meant their rest from the fatigue of rage and the burning of resentment. The pronoun in "their hearts" refers to a believing people, so they are promised both matters: the healing of their breasts from their enemy, and the removal of the rage of their hearts over the breaking of their covenant by those who broke their oath.

"Al-ghayz" (rage) is anger mixed with the will for revenge. It was discussed earlier in His words: ﴿They bite their fingertips at you out of rage﴾ [Al 'Imran 3:119], in Surat Al 'Imran.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 9, verse 15:

Page 137
﴿And Allah turns in forgiveness to whom He wills, and Allah is All-Knowing, All-Wise.﴾

This is an independent nominal sentence (jumla ibtida'iyya mustaʼnafa), because it begins a new statement that does not follow from the command to fight, but rather mentions those who were not killed. For this reason the verb in it is in the nominative (marfu'an), and this structure indicates that it refers to another group, namely the polytheists who betrayed and broke their covenants and were not killed, but embraced Islam either before this command or after it. Allah's turning in forgiveness toward them (tawbat Allah 'alayhim) is the acceptance of their Islam or their entry into it. In this there is a granting of an excuse and a respite for those who came late. The sentence was not separated (from what precedes it) only to indicate that its content is part of the remaining circumstances of the polytheists, so its linking with what came before is appropriate. Allah did indeed turn in forgiveness toward Abu Sufyan, 'Ikrima ibn Abi Jahl, and Suhayl ibn Abi 'Amr (Al-Qurtubi mentioned this third one, but I have not found his name among the Companions).

The concluding phrase ﴿And Allah is All-Knowing, All-Wise﴾ serves to convey that Allah deals with people according to what He knows of their intentions, and that He is All-Wise, who commands only what achieves wisdom. Therefore it is obligatory for people to comply with His commands, and that He accepts the repentance of whoever turns to Him, as an increase in righteousness.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 9, verse 16:

﴿Or did you think that you would be left alone while Allah has not yet known those among you who strove and did not take other than Allah and His Messenger and the believers as intimate allies (wali-ja)? And Allah is Acquainted with what you do.﴾

"Am" here is disconnective (munqati'ah), serving to indicate a turning away (idrab) from one topic of speech to move on to another topic. The speech following "am" (disconnective) always carries the force of a question, so His saying "ḥasibtum" (you thought) is in the sense of "a-ḥasibtum" (did you think), and the implied interrogation is one of denunciation (inkari).

The address is to the Muslims, across their varying ranks in the duration of their Islam, and so it includes the hypocrites, because they displayed Islam.

"Ḥasibtum" means "ẓanantum" (you supposed). The verbal noun of ḥasiba in the sense of ẓanna is al-ḥisbān with a kasra on the ḥa'. As for the verbal noun of ḥasiba in the sense of counting the number, it is with a ḍamma on the ḥa'.

Al-tark (leaving) is the lack of something and neglecting it; that is, that Allah would leave you. The subject of the verb "tark" has been omitted because it is evident. The verb tark must be linked to a complement: either a circumstantial phrase (ḥal) or a prepositional phrase (majrur), indicating the state in which the one who leaves parts from what he leaves. As in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Did the people think that they would be left alone on saying "We believe" and they would not be tested?﴾ [al-'Ankabut: 2]. And like the saying of 'Antara:

"So I left him as prey for the beasts, which tear at him,"

and the saying of Kabsha bint Ma'd Yakrib, speaking on behalf of her brother 'Abd Allah when the Banu Mazin ibn Zubayd killed him in the land of Sa'da in the lands of Yemen:

"And I am left in a dark house in Sa'da."

The complement of "tutrakū" in the verse has been omitted, the context indicating it: that you would be left alone without striving; that is, that you would be left in ease after the conquest of Makkah.

The meaning: how do you suppose that you would be left alone? That is, do not suppose that you would be left alone without striving against the enemies of Allah and His Messenger.

The clause ﴿while Allah has not yet known those among you who strove﴾ and so on is in the place of a circumstantial clause (ḥal) from the pronoun in "tutrakū", meaning: do not suppose that you would be left in a state where Allah's knowledge is not attached to the occurrence of the eagerness of those who strive for jihad, and to the occurrence of the sluggishness of those who were sluggish, and to the occurrence of the abandonment of jihad by those who abandon it.

"Lamma" is a particle of negation, a sister of "lam." Its explanation and the difference between it and "lam" have already been given at His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Or did you suppose that you would enter Paradise while the example of those who passed before you has not yet come to you?﴾ [al-Baqarah: 214], and His saying, exalted is He: ﴿while Allah has not yet known those among you who strove and known the patient﴾ [Al 'Imran: 142], in Surat Al 'Imran.

The meaning of Allah's knowledge of those who strove is His knowledge of the occurrence of that from them and the realization of their compliance, and it is from the attachment of divine knowledge to events that occur. It is more specific than His eternal knowledge, exalted is He, that a thing will occur or will not occur, and it is fitting that it be described as an actual (tanjizi) attachment. Some of this has already been mentioned at His saying, exalted is He: ﴿while Allah has not yet known those among you who strove﴾ in Surat Al 'Imran.

"Al-walījah" is on the pattern fa'īlah in the sense of maf'ūlah, that is, the intimate secret, which is the deed that its doer conceals, as if he inserts it (yūlijuhā), that is, places it in a hidden place so that it does not appear. What is meant by it here includes deception and the incitement of the enemy against the Muslims, and includes taking allies from among the enemies of Islam to whom one reveals and to whom one discloses the secrets of the Muslims; because the indefiniteness of "walījah" in the context of negation generalizes all its instances.

"Min dūni Allāh" is attached to "walījah" in the place of a descriptive circumstantial clause.

"Min" here is initial (ibtida'iyyah), that is, a walījah existing in the state of marking the place which is the starting point of distance from Allah, His Messenger, and the believers.

The clause ﴿and Allah is Acquainted with what you do﴾ is a concluding clause (tadhyīl) for the denunciation of that supposition, meaning: do not suppose that while you know that Allah is Acquainted with everything you do.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 9, verse 17:

﴿It is not for the polytheists to maintain the mosques of Allah while bearing witness against themselves of disbelief. Those—their deeds have become worthless, and in the Fire they will abide eternally.﴾

This is the beginning of a theme from the themes of dealing with the polytheists, namely the prohibition of the polytheists from entering the Sacred Mosque in the coming year. It is connected to what the declaration (al-bara'ah) included in His saying: ﴿A declaration of disassociation from Allah and His Messenger to those with whom you made a treaty among the polytheists﴾ [al-Tawbah: 1], and to what is connected to that verse of the explanation of the Prophet (ﷺ) which he sent with Abu Bakr al-Siddiq: "That no polytheist should perform Hajj after this year, and no naked person should circumambulate the House." It is a preparation (tawti'ah) for His saying: ﴿O you who have believed, the polytheists are but impure, so let them not approach the Sacred Mosque after this, their year﴾ [al-Tawbah: 28].

The construction "ma kana lahum an yaf'alu" (it was not for them that they should do such) indicates that they are distant from that, as was previously explained at His saying: ﴿It is not for a human that Allah should give him the Book and the judgment and prophethood﴾ [Al 'Imran: 79] in Surat Al 'Imran; that is, they are not worthy of maintaining the mosques of Allah with what they are maintained by of acts of worship.

And "masajid Allah" (the mosques of Allah) are the places of His worship through prostration and bowing. What is intended is the Sacred Mosque and what follows it of al-Safa and al-Marwah, 'Arafat, the Sacred Monument (al-Mash'ar al-Haram), the Jamarat, and the place of sacrifice in Mina.

The maintenance (''umr'') of mosques is worship in them, since they were only established for worship; so their maintenance is by those who dwell in them of worshippers. From this the word 'umrah (lesser pilgrimage) is derived. The meaning: it is not right for the polytheists to worship Allah in the mosques of Allah. Attaching this negation to them with the description of being polytheists is an indication that polytheism necessitates their deprivation of maintaining the mosques of Allah.

The circumstantial clause in His saying: ﴿bearing witness against themselves of disbelief﴾ has come explaining the reason for their disassociation from maintaining the mosques of Allah. It is a circumstantial clause (hal) from the pronoun in "ya'muru" (they maintain), and it specifies the governing element of the pronoun, which is "ya'muru" falling under the rule of negation. That is: their fitness to maintain the mosques of Allah is negated, in the state of their bearing witness against themselves of disbelief. So this state has added specificity to this particular deprivation from maintaining the mosques of Allah, which is the deprivation after which there is no entitlement.

By "disbelief" is meant disbelief in Allah, that is, in His oneness, so disbelief is synonymous with polytheism. Disbelief in itself necessitates the deprivation of its adherents from maintaining the mosques of Allah, because they are the mosques of Allah, so no right belongs to other than Allah in them; moreover, they were established for the worship of Allah alone and not for other than Him. Abraham (peace be upon him) established the first mosque, which is the Ka'bah, as a sign of monotheism and a proclamation of it, as was previously explained at His saying: ﴿Indeed, the first House established for mankind is that at Bakkah, blessed﴾ [Al 'Imran: 96] in Surat Al 'Imran. This is the first degree of deprivation. Then, that their disbelief is established by their own acknowledgment of it necessitates the absence of even the least share in this maintenance, and their disassociation from entitlement to it; this is a second degree of deprivation.

Their bearing witness against themselves of disbelief is established in many of their statements and actions, such that they cannot deny it, like their saying in the talbiyah: "Here I am, O Allah, no partner for You, except a partner who is Yours; You own him and what he owns," and like their prostration to idols, their circumambulating them, and their placing them inside the Ka'bah, around it, and on its roof.

Ibn Kathir, Abu 'Amr, and Ya'qub recited "masjid Allah" in the singular, meaning the Sacred Mosque, which is what is intended, or the definition by annexation to denote the category. The rest recited "masajid Allah" in the plural, which then encompasses the Sacred Mosque and what we have enumerated along with it just now.

The clause ﴿Those—their deeds have become worthless﴾ is the beginning of a censure of them. The demonstrative was used because they have been distinguished by the attribute of bearing witness against themselves of disbelief, as in His saying: ﴿Those are upon guidance from their Lord﴾ [al-Baqarah: 5] after His saying: ﴿Guidance for the righteous﴾ [al-Baqarah: 2], and so on.

"Habitat" (ḥabiṭat) means became void, and it was previously mentioned at His saying: ﴿And whoever of you reverts from his religion and dies while he is a disbeliever—those are the ones whose deeds have become worthless in this world and the Hereafter﴾ [al-Baqarah: 217] in Surat al-Baqarah.

The placing of ﴿in the Fire﴾ before ﴿they will abide eternally﴾ is for the sake of the rhyme (ri'ayah 'ala al-fasilah), and from it results the hastening of distress for the disbelievers when they hear it.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 9, verse 18:

﴿Only he who believes in God and the Last Day, establishes the prayer (salah), gives the zakat, and fears none but God—it is they who may be among the guided.﴾

The position of the clause ﴿Only he who believes in God's mosques is the one who maintains them﴾ is that of the explanatory resumptive clause (al-isti'naf al-bayani), because the clause ﴿It is not for the polytheists to maintain the mosques of God﴾ [al-Tawbah: 17], since it required the exclusion of the polytheists from worship in the mosques, was such that it would provoke a question in the minds of the hearers: who are those deserving to maintain the mosques? So this clause came to answer this questioner.

The use of the restrictive form (qasr) in it indicates that the intention is the exclusion of other groups from maintaining the mosques of God, other than the polytheists whose exclusion was stated explicitly. Therefore it is necessary that what is meant by the relative pronoun and its clause is specifically the Muslims, because the totality of the attributes mentioned in the clause does not apply to anyone else. The Jews and Christians believe in God and the Last Day, but they do not establish the prayer and do not give the zakat, because what is meant by the prayer and zakat are the two acts of worship known by these two names and prescribed in Islam. Do you not see His saying—exalted is He—﴿They will say: "We were not of those who prayed, nor did we feed the needy"﴾ [al-Muddaththir: 43], as a metaphor for their not being Muslims?

He dispensed with mentioning belief in His Messenger Muhammad (ﷺ) by what indicates it of the effects of his law: namely belief in the Last Day, the establishing of the prayer, and the giving of the zakat.

The restriction of their fear to attachment to the side of God—exalted is He—by the restrictive form does not mean that they fear nothing other than God, for they may fear a lion and fear an enemy. Rather its meaning is that when their situation is ambiguous between their fear of God and their fear of other than Him, they give precedence to the fear of God over the fear of other than Him, as in His saying earlier ﴿Do you fear them? God has more right that you fear Him﴾ [al-Tawbah: 13]. So the restriction is relative, with regard to the conflict between two fears.

This is among the characteristics of the believers. As for the polytheists, they fear their associates and violate the sanctities of God to please their associates. As for the People of the Book, they fear people and disobey God by distorting His words and conforming to the desires of the common folk. God has admonished them with His saying: ﴿So do not fear people, but fear Me﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 44].

He related the hope that they may be among the guided (al-muhtadin) as a consequence of describing the Muslims with those attributes; that is, among the group described as "the guided," namely the group for whom guidance is a disposition in these deeds and in others. The basis of this hope is that, since they have performed what is undoubtedly guidance, hope is strong that they will remain steadfast in it and it will become a disposition for them, so they will be of its people. For this reason He said ﴿that they may be among the guided﴾, and did not say ﴿that they may be guided﴾.

In this is an exhortation to increase this guidance and a warning against delusion and relying on some righteous deeds, under the belief that some deeds suffice in place of the rest.

The expression of them by the demonstrative noun (ism al-isharah) is to draw attention to the fact that they deserved this hope regarding them because of those deeds that were enumerated for them.

[Page 143]

﴿Do you consider the providing of water for the pilgrims and the maintenance of the Sacred Mosque equal to one who believes in God and the Last Day and strives in the way of God? They are not equal in the sight of God, and God does not guide the wrongdoing people.﴾ The apparent meaning of this verse requires that it is addressed to a people who equated providing water for the pilgrims and maintaining the Sacred Mosque with jihad and emigration (hijrah), in that all of these are acts of righteousness. It therefore indicates that it is addressed to believing people who held back from emigration and jihad, on the pretext that they were satisfied with providing water and maintenance. Its connection to the preceding verses is this: when the discussion had established that the believers are the most entitled to maintain the Sacred Mosque, rather than the polytheists, that discussion implied that the Sacred Mosque is not lawful for a non-Muslim to perform in it any of the works specific to it. This became a cause for the suspicion that performing the rites of the Sacred Mosque is equal to performing the best of the works of Islam.

The best of what has been related concerning the occasion of revelation of this verse is what al-Tabari and al-Wahidi transmitted from al-Nu'man ibn Bashir, who said: "I was beside the pulpit of the Messenger of God (ﷺ) with a group of his companions. One man among them said, 'I would not mind if I did no deed after Islam except giving water to the pilgrims.' Another said, 'Rather, [I would not mind if I did no deed except] the maintenance of the Sacred Mosque.' And another said, 'Rather, jihad in the way of God is better than what you have said.' 'Umar ibn al-Khattab rebuked them and said, 'Do not raise your voices beside the pulpit of the Messenger of God (ﷺ), and that on Friday. But when I have prayed the Friday prayer, I will enter upon the Messenger of God (ﷺ) and ask him for a ruling concerning what you have disputed.' So God revealed: ﴿Do you consider the providing of water for the pilgrims...﴾ up to ﴿and God does not guide the wrongdoing people.﴾"

It has also been related that this delusion spread to some of the Muslims. It is related that al-'Abbas intended to stay in Mecca and abandon emigration, due to being occupied with providing water to the pilgrims and visitors; and that 'Uthman ibn Talha intended the same, in order to undertake the custody of the House (hijabah). Al-Tabari and al-Wahidi also transmitted that a dispute took place between al-'Abbas and 'Ali ibn Abi Talib at Badr, and that 'Ali reproached al-'Abbas for disbelief and severing the ties of kinship. Al-'Abbas said: "What is the matter with you that you do not mention our virtues? Indeed, we maintain the mosque of God, guard the Ka'bah, and provide water to the pilgrims." So God revealed ﴿Do you consider the providing of water for the pilgrims﴾, the verse.

The interrogative here is for denial (inkar).

The word (al-siqayah) is a form denoting a craft, i.e., the craft of providing drink, and it means giving drink from the water of Zamzam. For this reason, al-siqayah is attributed to the pilgrims.

Likewise (al-'imarah) is the craft of maintenance, i.e., undertaking the upkeep of something through repair, guarding, and the like. Here it is other than what is meant in His saying: ﴿It is not for the polytheists to maintain the mosques of God﴾ [al-Tawbah: 17] and His saying: ﴿Only those maintain the mosques of God﴾ [al-Tawbah: 18]. It is attributed to the Sacred Mosque because it is a work performed within the Mosque itself.

The definite article in "al-hajj" (the pilgrims) is the definite article of the genus (ta'rif al-jins).

[Page 144]

The providing of water for the pilgrims and the maintenance of the Sacred Mosque were among the greatest offices (manasib) of Quraysh in the pre-Islamic period. The offices were ten in number, and they were called al-ma'athir (the honours). The providing of water belonged to the Banu Hashim ibn 'Abd Manaf ibn Qusayy, and when Islam came it belonged to al-'Abbas ibn 'Abd al-Muttalib. The maintenance of the mosque, which is the sidanah, and which is called al-hijabah, belonged to the Banu 'Abd al-Dar ibn Qusayy, and when Islam came it belonged to 'Uthman ibn Talha.

They had other offices, eight in number, which Islam abolished. I saw them in the handwriting of my grandfather, the scholar and minister: They are: al-diyat wal-hamalat (blood-money and guarantees), al-safarah (embassy), al-rayah (banner), al-rifadah (provisions), al-mashurah (council), al-a'innah wal-qubbah (the reins and the dome), al-hukumah wa amwal al-alihah (arbitration and the property of the gods), and al-aysar (the arrows of divination).

As for al-diyat wal-hamalat: diyah is the plural of diyah, which is the compensation for the blood of a slain person, whether by error or intention, when settled upon. Hamalah (with an unpointed initial ha, fathah) is the plural of hamalah, which is the indemnity that one people bear on behalf of another people. This belonged to the Banu Taym ibn Murrah ibn Ka'b. Murrah is the grandfather of Qusayy. When Islam came, it was in the hand of Abu Bakr al-Siddiq.

As for al-safarah (with the sin vowelled either kasrah or fathah): it is the striving to make peace between tribes, and the one who undertakes it is called safir (envoy). It belonged to the Banu 'Adi ibn Ka'b, paternal cousins of Qusayy. When Islam came, it was in the hand of 'Umar ibn al-Khattab.

As for al-rayah, which is also called al-'uqab (with the ayn vowelled with dammah) because it flutters over the army like an eagle, it was the banner of the army of Quraysh. It belonged to the Banu Umayyah, and when Islam came, it was in the hand of Abu Sufyan ibn Harb.

As for al-rifadah: it is wealth that Quraysh would spend to honour the pilgrims, so they would feed them throughout all the days of the season, buying camels, food, and raisins (for nabidh, a drink). It belonged to the Banu Nawfal ibn 'Abd Manaf, and when Islam came, it was in the hand of al-Harith ibn 'Amir ibn Nawfal.

As for al-mashurah, it is the administration of the Dar al-Nadwah (the assembly house), and it belonged to the Banu Asad ibn 'Abd al-'Uzza ibn Qusayy. When Islam came, it was in the hand of Zayd ibn Zam'ah.

[Page 145]

As for al-a'innah and al-qubbah: it is a dome they would pitch, gathering beneath it when equipping the army, and it was called al-a'innah. It belonged to the Banu Makhzum, who are paternal cousins of Qusayy. When Islam came, it was in the hand of Khalid ibn al-Walid.

As for al-hukumah and amwal al-alihah (I have not come to know its reality): I suppose that it was named al-hukumah because the wealth gathered by it is what is obtained from the compensation for game hunted in the sacred precinct (haram) or while in the state of ihram. As for calling it amwal al-alihah, it is because it is wealth obtained from things such as the sa'ibah and the bahirah, and what is dedicated to the gods of weapons and goods. It belonged to the Banu Sahm, who are paternal cousins of Qusayy. When Islam came, it was in the hand of al-Harith ibn Qays ibn Sahm.

As for al-aysar, which are the arrows with which they sought the decision of fate (istiqsam): it belonged to the Banu Jumah, who are paternal cousins of Qusayy. When Islam came, it was in the hand of Safwan ibn Umayyah ibn Khalaf.

Islam has abolished all of these offices, except the sidanah and the siqayah, owing to the Prophet's saying in the sermon of the Farewell Pilgrimage: "Verily, every honour of the honours of the Jahiliyyah is under these two feet of mine, except the providing of water to the pilgrims and the custody of the House."

The offices of the Arabs which were in the hand of Qusayy ibn Kilab were five: al-hijabah, al-siqayah, al-rifadah, al-nadwah, and al-liwa'. When Qusayy grew old, he gave the offices to his son 'Abd al-Dar. Then, after his death, the sons of Qusayy disputed, and they summoned one another to war, then summoned one another to reconciliation, on condition that they give the Banu 'Abd al-Dar the hijabah, the liwa', and the nadwah, and that they give the Banu 'Abd Manaf the siqayah and the rifadah. Offices were then created for some of Quraysh who were not sons of Qusayy, so the offices reached ten, as we have mentioned.

The mention of faith in God and the Last Day is not because it is the locus of the equating that was rejected against them, for they did not claim equality between the providing of water or the maintenance without faith. Rather, the mention of faith is an inclusion (idmaj), to allude to the fact that jihad is the effect of faith, and it is inseparable from faith. So it is not lawful for the believer to disengage from it on the pretext of being occupied with providing water to the pilgrims or maintaining the Sacred Mosque. The mention of faith in God and the Last Day does not mean that those who regarded the excellence of providing water to the pilgrims and maintaining the Sacred Mosque as equal to the excellence of faith were not believers. For if they had not been believers, they would not have made the offices of their religion equal to faith; rather, they would have made them greater. They merely imagined that these two were deeds equivalent to jihad, and that occupation with them was an excuse for lagging behind jihad, or a religious merit equal to the merit of the mujahidin.

[Page 146]

The mention of providing water and maintenance on the side of the comparison (al-mushabbah), and the mention of those who believed and strove on the side of what is compared to (al-mushabbah bihi), indicate that the two deeds and those who perform them are not equal to the other two deeds and those who perform them. Thus there occurred an ihtibak (interlocking omission) at both ends of the comparison: that is, the two deeds are not equal to the two other deeds, nor are the doers of these two equal to the doers of those two. The implied meaning is: "Do you consider the providing of water to the pilgrims and the maintenance of the Sacred Mosque like faith in God and the Last Day and jihad in the way of God? And do you consider the providers of water and the maintainers of the mosque like the believers and the strivers in the way of God?" And since equality was mentioned in His saying ﴿They are not equal in the sight of God﴾, it was attributed to the doers rather than the deeds, because it was not common in speech to attach equality to abstract meanings but to beings (dhawat).

The clause ﴿They are not equal﴾ is a resumptive, explanatory new sentence (isti'naf bayani), to explain what is asked about regarding the meaning of denial contained in the interrogative in His saying: "Do you consider..." the verse.

The clause ﴿and God does not guide the wrongdoing people﴾ is a concluding clause (tadhyil) to the clause ﴿Do you consider the providing of water for the pilgrims﴾ and so on. Its placement here is obscure if the surah was revealed after the Battle of Tabuk, and this verse was among what was revealed together with the surah and not before it, according to what we have preferred from the report of al-Nu'man ibn Bashir concerning its occasion of revelation. For at that time there was no one left who would make the providing of water for the pilgrims and the maintenance of the House equal to faith and jihad, so that it would be refuted by evidence showing his lack of guidance. What has been related from 'Umar ibn al-Khattab concerning its occasion of revelation has already been mentioned, and it increases the obscurity of its placement.

So the view I hold regarding the placement of the clause ﴿and God does not guide the wrongdoing people﴾ is that its placement is as a parenthetical insertion (i'tiraD) between the clause ﴿Do you consider the providing of water for the pilgrims﴾ and the clause ﴿Those who believed and emigrated and strove﴾ [al-Tawbah: 20] and so on.

Its purpose is to further emphasize the status of faith, informing that it is a guide to good things and a leader towards them. Those who believe, their faith has guided them to the virtue of jihad. And those who disbelieve, what they were engaged in of maintaining the Sacred Mosque and providing water to the pilgrims did not benefit them, so God did not guide them to good. That is a proof that faith is the root, and that the branches arising from it are the best of deeds, and that other nobilities and good things are in the second rank in merit, because they are not among the branches of faith, although both attributes benefit only when they are accompanied by faith, especially jihad.

[Page 147]

In it is also an allusion to the fact that: were it not for jihad, the people of the providing of water and the maintenance of the Sacred Mosque would not have been believers. For their faith was among the effects of the Conquest of Mecca and the army of the Conquest, when al-'Abbas ibn 'Abd al-Muttalib, who was the holder of the siqayah, believed, and 'Uthman ibn Talha, who was the holder of the maintenance of the Sacred Mosque, believed.

As for what al-Tabari and al-Wahidi transmitted from Ibn 'Abbas: that the revelation of this verse was on the day of Badr, owing to the dispute that took place between 'Ali ibn Abi Talib and al-'Abbas, then the placement of the tadhyil with His saying ﴿and God does not guide the wrongdoing people﴾ is clear: that is, He does not guide the polytheists who provide water to the pilgrims and maintain the Sacred Mosque, since that is of no avail with polytheism. Thus it became clear that what they imagined of equality between those deeds and jihad, and their dispute over that, was an error in reasoning. For it is not correct to equate the follower with the followed, or the branch with the root. Had the providing of water and the maintenance been equal to jihad, their doers would have been guided to supporting faith, just as the mujahidun were guided to supporting it. Observation has shown otherwise: the mujahidun were guided, whereas the people of the providing of water and the maintenance were not guided. Thus guidance has commonly come to be used figuratively, by borrowing it for the meaning of directing towards the sought-after goal, and according to this usage it means a specific goal, namely what one who performs a deed by which he draws near to God seeks, as is required by the placing of the mention of the providing of water for the pilgrims and the maintenance of the mosque immediately before this clause.

The negation of guidance is used as a metonymy (kinayah) for the negation of achieving the purpose of the deed.

The meaning is: God does not accept the deeds of the polytheist people.

It is attributed to Ibn Wardan that he transmitted from Abu Ja'far that he recited: suqat al-hajj (with the sin vowelled with dammah), the plural of saqi (provider of water); and he recited 'amarah (with an open ayn, without an alif, and with a fathah on the ra'), the plural of 'amir. The reports differ concerning these readings from Ibn Wardan.

Page 148

﴿Those who believed, emigrated, and strove in the way of God with their wealth and their lives are greater in rank with God. And those are the triumphant.﴾

This sentence explains the negation of equality in the phrase ﴿they are not equal with God﴾ [al-Tawbah: 19], and it details the jihad mentioned in His saying ﴿like one who believes in God and the Last Day and strives in the way of God﴾ [al-Tawbah: 19], specifying that it is jihad with wealth and lives. It also serves as an *idmaj* (incorporation of a further purpose, bringing in a related aim) to show the excellence of the emigrants (*muhajirun*) among the strivers.

Those who emigrated (*alladhina hajaru*) are the believers from the people of Makkah and its surroundings who migrated from it to Madinah after the Prophet ﷺ permitted them to emigrate there, after they had embraced Islam. This was before the Conquest of Makkah.

*Muhajarah* (emigration, *hijrah*) means leaving one's homeland and settling in another land. It derives from *al-hajr*, which means abandonment. The form *mufa'alah* was used for it because it specifically denotes a strong abandonment, namely leaving one's homeland. In the technical usage of the Sharia, it refers to a particular emigration, namely the emigration from Makkah to Madinah. It therefore does not include the emigration of those Muslims who went to the land of Abyssinia, because that was not intended as permanent settlement but was a temporary emigration. The discussion of emigration has already occurred at the end of Surat al-Anfal.

The comparative *afdal* has an omitted object of comparison, which is understood: that is, greater in rank with God than the companions of the watering of the pilgrims and the maintenance of the Sacred Mosque, who believed but did not emigrate and did not carry out the great jihad that the Muslims waged during the days when those others remained in disbelief. The intended purpose is to exalt their qualities.

The word *darajah* (rank) has already appeared in His saying ﴿And the men have a degree over them﴾ [al-Baqarah: 228] in Surat al-Baqarah, and in His saying ﴿For them are ranks with their Lord﴾ [al-Anfal: 4] at the beginning of Surat al-Anfal. In all of these it is used figuratively to mean elevation in status. The phrase *'inda Allah* (with God) indicates that their elevation in status is an elevation of good pleasure from God and an exaltation through honour, because the basic meaning of *'inda* is a adverb of nearness.

The sentence ﴿And those are the triumphant﴾ is coordinated with ﴿greater in rank﴾, meaning: greater, and they are the people of triumph. The definition of the predicate with the definite article *al-* conveys a restriction (*qasr*), and it is a hyperbolic restriction (*qasr idda'i*) for the sake of emphasising the greatness of their triumph, to the point that the triumph of others, in comparison with theirs, is counted as though it were non-existent.

Page 149

The use of the demonstrative *ulaika* (those) serves to draw attention to the fact that they deserved triumph because of those qualities that distinguished them: namely belief, emigration, and jihad with wealth and lives.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 9, verses 21–22:

﴿Their Lord gives them good news of mercy from Him, and of approval, and of gardens for them wherein is lasting bliss,﴾ ﴿abiding therein forever. Indeed, with Allah is a great reward.﴾

This is an explanation of the great rank mentioned in His words: ﴿greater in rank with Allah﴾ [al-Tawbah: 20]. That rank is the care of Allah – exalted is He – for them, by bringing joy to them, confirming their success, informing them of His approval of them, His mercy toward them, and what He has prepared for them of enduring bliss. The totality of these matters was not granted to others among the people of the siqayah (giving water to the pilgrims) and the 'imarah (tending the Sacred Mosque), who, although they were fit to attain some of these privileges, did not attain all of them.

Al-tabshir (good news) is: informing someone of a good thing that will come to the one informed, of which he had no knowledge.

The attribution of the good news to the Name of Majesty (Allah) in the present tense, which indicates renewal (tajaddud), signifies the succession of good things upon them and the continual renewal of joy brought to them. This is because the renewal of good news indicates that the thing announced was not known to the one who receives the good news (the mubashsharun, with the shin vowelled with fatha); otherwise, informing him of it would be the obtaining of what is already obtained.

That the subject of the predicate is the word al-Rabb (the Lord), rather than any other term that indicates the Creator – glorified is He – is an allusion to mercy toward them and care for them, because the meaning of lordship (rububiyyah) returns to the management of the one who is nurtured (al-marbub), kindness toward him, and gentleness with him; and so that the attribution to their pronoun is an attribution of honour (idafat tashrif).

Mercy has already been mentioned in His words: ﴿the Most Merciful, the Most Compassionate﴾.

Al-ridwan – with the ra' vowelled with kasra or with damma – is complete and intense approval, because this form indicates intensification, like al-ghufran (forgiveness), al-shukran (gratitude), and al-'isyan (disobedience).

As for al-jannat (gardens), the discussion of them has preceded in the mention of Paradise in Surat al-Baqarah. Its plural is used in view of its levels, its kinds, and the kinds of bliss within it.

Page 150
Al-na'im is that by which the soul delights in sensory pleasures, and it is more specific than al-ni'mah (blessing). Allah – exalted is He – said: ﴿Indeed, the righteous are in bliss﴾ [al-Infitar: 13], and He said: ﴿Then you will surely be asked that Day about the bliss﴾ [al-Takathur: 8].

Al-muqim is the enduring, the continuous; the word iqamah (residence) is used figuratively for permanence and continuance.

The indefiniteness in (bi-rahmatin, wa-ridwanin, wa-jannatin, wa-na'imin) is for magnification, indicated by the context, by His words "from Him" (minhu), and by the fact that these are the things announced as good news.

The sentence ﴿Indeed, with Allah is a great reward﴾ is a concluding statement (tadhyil) and an honouring of the status of the believers who emigrated and struggled (in the way of Allah), because the meaning of this sentence encompasses the meaning of what precedes it and beyond it. In this concluding statement is the benefit that what has been mentioned of the great ranks of the believers who emigrated and struggled is only part of what is with Allah of good things. From this arises encouragement to increase in righteous deeds so that they may increase in elevation with their Lord, as Abu Bakr al-Siddiq – may Allah be pleased with him – said: "There is no harm upon whoever is called from all those gates." 

Al-ajr (reward) is the compensation given for a deed, and it has preceded in His words: ﴿when you have given them their dowries (ujurahunna)﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 5] in Surat al-'Uqud.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 9, verse 23:

﴿O you who have believed, do not take your fathers and your brothers as allies if they prefer disbelief over faith. And whoever among you allies with them, then it is those who are the wrongdoers.﴾

This is an independent resumptive sentence (isti'naf ibtida'i) opening a new theme, which is the reproof of the hypocrites (munafiqun) and those who are allied with them. Since the beginning of the surah laid down the manner of dealing with those who openly displayed disbelief, it was fitting that the discussion move on to those who concealed disbelief while displaying faith: the hypocrites from among the people of Madinah and from the remnants of the Arab tribes, those who were known as such or who were not known, and whom Allah informed His Prophet ﷺ about. He warned the believers who had knowledge of them about their intimates and close relatives and about associating with them.

صفحة ١٥١
Most of this applied to the people of Madinah, because the majority of them were sincere believers, while among them there remained a remnant of hypocrites who were their close relatives. For this reason the address was opened with ﴿O you who have believed﴾, indicating that what would be conveyed to them of admonitions is among the requirements of faith and its emblem.

The expedition of Tabuk, after which this surah was revealed, revealed that a remnant of hypocrisy remained among the people of Madinah and the Bedouins surrounding them, as in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And there came those who make excuses among the Bedouins, seeking permission﴾ [al-Tawbah: 90], and His saying: ﴿And among those around you of the Bedouins are hypocrites, and among the people of Madinah are those who have become accustomed to hypocrisy﴾ [al-Tawbah: 101], and their likes among the verses.

Al-Tabari related from Mujahid, and al-Wahidi from al-Kalbi, that when they were commanded to emigrate, al-'Abbas said: "I will give drink to the pilgrims," and Talhah, a brother of the Banu 'Abd al-Dar, said: "I am the doorkeeper of the Ka'bah, so we will not emigrate." Some of the wives and children clung to some of the believers and said, "Will you abandon us?" So they felt compassion for them and sat with them, and this verse was revealed.

The meaning of ﴿they prefer (istahabbu) disbelief﴾ is that they loved it with a firmly established love. The sin and ta' here are for emphasis, like in istaqama and istabshara.

Allah warned the believers against allying with those who preferred disbelief over faith, whether outwardly or inwardly, when they became aware of them and the signs of that appeared upon them through the attributes mentioned in this surah. He made the warning concerning those specifically as fathers and brothers, as an alert to the utmost degree of suitability for allegiance, so that it would be known by implication of the address that those below them are more deserving of the ruling of the prohibition. He did not mention sons and wives here, because they are followers and so they do not remain behind their leaders.

His saying: ﴿then it is those who are the wrongdoers﴾ is intended to mean that they are wrongdoers to themselves, because they fell into what Allah forbade them, so they deserved punishment, and thus wronged themselves by causing punishment to befall them. So "wrongdoing" here is in its linguistic meaning and is not intended to mean shirk. The form of restriction (hasr) is for emphasis, in the sense that the wrong done to others is as nothing in comparison with the enormity of their wrong. It is also possible that ﴿they﴾ in ﴿the wrongdoers﴾ refers back to what the pronoun of object in His saying ﴿whoever allies with them﴾ refers to, namely the fathers and brothers who preferred disbelief over faith,

صفحة ١٥٢
and the meaning would be: whoever allies with them has indeed allied with the wrongdoers, so the wrongdoing here is intended to mean shirk, as is most common in its usage in the Qur'an.

The use of the demonstrative (ism al-isharah) serves to further distinguish these or those, and to alert that their suitability for the ruling mentioned after the demonstrative was due to those attributes, namely preferring disbelief over faith.

﴿Say, "If your fathers, your sons, your brothers, your spouses, your kindred, the wealth you have acquired, the commerce whose slump you fear, and the dwellings you are pleased with are dearer to you than Allah and His Messenger and striving in His cause, then wait until Allah brings His command. And Allah does not guide the defiantly disobedient people."﴾

This is an escalation in warning against the attachments that may lead to neglect in carrying out the obligations of Islam. Therefore the detailed enumeration of the categories of kinsfolk and of the causes of association that exist between believers and disbelievers is extended. Among the things to which people's souls attach themselves, and whose attachment prevents them from fulfilling some of the rights of Islam, is the mention of sons here, because attachment to them is stronger than attachment to brothers. Other close relatives are also mentioned.

Beginning the address with "Say" (qul) indicates its severity and is a rebuke through it.

The addressees in the plural pronouns are the believers who fell short in some of the obligations, or who were expected to do so, as is indicated by the conjunction of the conditional with the particle of doubt, "in" (if). It is understood from this that those who persist in this and are immersed in it are the people of hypocrisy, and they are the ones targeted with the threat in His words: ﴿So wait until Allah brings His command. And Allah does not guide the defiantly disobedient people.﴾

This verse has gathered categories of relationships and those who hold them, which by their nature souls become accustomed to and desire to remain close to and not to part from. If steadfastness in faith leads to abandoning some of them, such as fathers and brothers who are disbelievers, who abandon one another when they differ in religion, and such as sons, spouses and kin among whom a person is accustomed to living, perhaps that will keep him from going out to fight; and such as wealth and commerce, which divert from fighting and from spending in the cause of Allah; and likewise the dwellings in which a person is accustomed to residing, whose familiarity keeps him from fighting. When there is conflict and opposition between what Allah wants from the believers and what those attachments drive them toward, it becomes obligatory for the believer to dispel them and seek the pleasure of his Lord.

This meaning is conveyed by the expression "dearer" (aḥabb), because preference in love requires satisfying the stronger of the beloved things. In this expression there is a warning against negligence regarding the obligations of religion, together with a kinayah (indirect expression) that this negligence is caused by preferring love of those attachments over love of Allah. Thus there is an awakening to what such preference leads to of ruin in religion, and this is among the most eloquent forms of expression.

Striving (jihad) is singled out for mention from among the general things that Allah loves from them, to honor its status, and because what it entails of danger to souls, of spending wealth and of leaving behind what is familiar makes it the most likely thing to be neglected. This is especially so since the surah was revealed after the expedition of Tabuk, from which many hypocrites and some Muslims stayed behind.

Al-'ashira (kinsfolk) are the nearest relatives, and it appears to be derived from ʿishra, which means close association and companionship.

The majority of readers recited "wa-ʿashiratukum" (and your kinsfolk) in the singular form, while Abu Bakr, from ʿAsim, recited "wa-ʿashiratukum" in the plural, ʿashīrāt, the plural of ʿashīra, and its justification is that each one of the addressees has a kinsfolk group. It is reported from Abu al-Hasan al-Akhfash that the Arabs only pluralize ʿashīra as ʿashāʾir and hardly ever say ʿashīrāt. This is a claim on his part, and the recitation is a transmitted report, so it refutes his claim.

Al-iqtiraf (acquiring) means earning, and it is derived from qarafa, meaning to approach a thing.

Al-kasad (slump) is a decline in trading, the opposite of brisk sales and popularity, and this occurs through the boycotting by groups of polytheists with whom they used to trade, and through ceasing trade during the days of jihad.

The preference in love among these categories and the love of Allah, His Messenger and jihad is made, because preferring the love of Allah, His Messenger and jihad necessitates cutting off these categories. Thus preferring these things over the love of Allah leads to allegiance to those who love disbelief, and to sitting back from jihad.

[p. 154]

Al-tarabbus (waiting) means expectation, and this is a command of threat, because what is intended is the waiting for evil. This is what is meant by His words: ﴿until Allah brings His command﴾, that is, the matter by which the evil outcome of your preferring love of relatives, wealth and dwellings over love of Allah, His Messenger and jihad becomes manifest.

Al-amr (the command) is an indefinite noun meaning "thing" and "matter," and the purpose of this vagueness is to inspire awe, so that the souls of those threatened may go every possible way. Thus the command of Allah may be punishment, killing or the like. Whoever interprets the command of Allah as the conquest of Mecca has erred, because this surah was revealed after the conquest.

The clause ﴿And Allah does not guide the defiantly disobedient people﴾ is a concluding statement (tadhyil), and the waw is parenthetical. This is a threat that they have preferred their kin and wealth over the love of Allah and His Messenger and over jihad, so it has been established that they are defiantly disobedient, and Allah does not guide the defiantly disobedient people. Thus the position of the concluding statement contains an implicit allusion to them, that they are among the defiantly disobedient.

[Page 155]

Since the preceding verses contained the exhortation to fight the polytheists, beginning with His saying, ﴿Then kill the polytheists wherever you find them﴾ [al-Tawbah: 5], and since the preparation for undertaking this was gradually built up by nullifying the sanctity of their covenant because of their polytheism, and by showing that they intend to initiate the breaking of the covenants between them and the Muslims if victory over the Muslims were ever granted to them, and the evidence for this is their aggression against Khuza'ah, the allies of the Muslims, and their intention to expel the Messenger (ﷺ) from Makkah after the Conquest. When this gradual preparation reached the exhortation to fight them and the guarantee of God's victory of the Muslims over them, along with what is connected to that and stirs the zeal of the Muslims, this verse came with proofs of what had preceded concerning God's granting victory to the Muslims in many battlefields, and as a reminder of comparing divine support with the state of obedience to His commands, and that the Battle of Hunayn contains proofs that testify to both states. Thus the speech is a fresh, independent beginning, linked to the purpose of what came before.

[Page 155 continued]

The victory is attributed explicitly to God in order to show that preferring the love of God, even if it forfeits some worldly portions, contains a portion of the Hereafter and contains other worldly portions, namely the portions of victory with what it entails: the protection of the community, the spoils of war, and the defense of the Ummah against the aggression of its enemies. This is part of God's bounty, since they preferred His love over the love of their worldly attachments.

He emphasized the statement with qad (قَدْ) to affirm this victory, because the people were as if they had forgotten it or doubted it, so they were treated as one who needs the reinforcement of the news.

Mawatin (مَوَاطِنَ) is the plural of mawtin (مَوْطِن). Its original meaning is the place of settling down, i.e., residence. It is also applied to the position and station of battle, meaning: your victory in many sites of war.

"Yawma" (يَوْمَ) is coordinated (ma'tuf) upon the prepositional phrase in His saying "fi mawatin" (فِي مَوَاطِنَ). It is therefore connected to what the coordinated element is connected to, which is "nasarakum" (نَصَرَكُمْ), and the implied meaning is: "and He gave you victory on the day of Hunayn," and it is one of the battlefields, because the sites of war require days in which the fighting takes place. Thus the sites indicate the days just as the days indicate the sites. When "the day" was made an annexed term (mudaf) to the name of a place, it was known that it was one of the sites of victory. For this reason it was coordinated with the conjunction "wa" (وَ), because had it not been coordinated, it would have been assumed that all the sites were on the day of Hunayn, and that is not the intended meaning. Therefore the implied meaning is: "in many sites and many days, among which is the site of Hunayn and the day of Hunayn."

The singling out of the day of Hunayn for mention from among the days of battles is because the Muslims were defeated in the course of the victory, then victory returned to them. Singling it out for mention contains a lesson: victory is achieved when the command of God and His Messenger (ﷺ) is obeyed, and defeat occurs when immediate worldly portions are preferred over obedience. Therefore it contains an example and a proof for the two states of preference mentioned just before, in His saying, ﴿more beloved to you than God and His Messenger and striving in His cause﴾ [al-Tawbah: 24], so that they would be alert to the fact that this preference may arise in the course of another preference. When they went out to the Battle of Hunayn, they had preferred the love of jihad over the love of their families and attachments. Then, in the course of the jihad, the preference for immediate worldly portions over obeying the command of God and His Messenger (ﷺ) recurred to them, and this is a consequence of preferring the love of those portions. This is a subtle lesson in which two opposites occurred. For this reason the placement of His saying, ﴿when your great number pleased you﴾ is wondrous, because it is an admonition about their error in adab with God appropriate to their station, i.e., it was not fitting for you to rely upon your great number.

Hunayn (حُنَيْنٌ) is the name of a valley between Makkah and al-Ta'if, near Dhu al-Majaz. A great battle took place there after the Conquest of Makkah between the Muslims with the Prophet (ﷺ), who numbered twelve thousand, and Hawazin and Thaqif with their allies, when they rose to fight the Prophet (ﷺ) out of zeal and anger over the defeat of Quraysh and the Conquest of Makkah. Malik ibn 'Awf, the brother of Banu Nasr, was in command of Hawazin, and 'Abd Yalil ibn 'Amr al-Thaqafi was in command of Thaqif. They were in a great number and marched toward Makkah, so the Prophet (ﷺ) went out to meet them until they gathered at Hunayn. The Muslims said, "We will not be defeated today through lack of numbers," and they trusted in victory because of their strength. So a defeat befell them at the outset of the encounter. It was a divine reproach for their forgetting to rely upon God for victory and their dependence upon their great number. It is narrated that when the Messenger of God (ﷺ) heard the saying of some of the Muslims, "We will not be defeated through lack of numbers," it grieved him. When they descended into the valley of Hunayn, the enemies had lain in ambush for them in its ravines and bends. The Muslims, while descending into the valley, were not alarmed except by the battalions of the enemy that had attacked them. It was said that the Muslims charged the enemy, the enemy fled, and the Muslims pursued them to seize their spoils. Hawazin were skilled archers, and they showered the Muslims with arrows, so the Muslims turned back in retreat, not looking back at anyone, and they scattered in the valley. The polytheists pressed upon them, while the Messenger of God (ﷺ) remained firm on the right side of the valley with ten men from the Muhajirun and the Ansar. The Messenger of God (ﷺ) ordered al-'Abbas, his uncle, to cry out to the people: "O companions of the tree, or the samurah," meaning the people of the Pledge of Ridwan, "O company of the Muhajirun, O companions of Surat al-Baqarah," meaning the Ansar, "come to me!" So a hundred gathered to him, and they fought Hawazin together with those who remained with the Prophet (ﷺ). The people engaged in fierce combat, the defeated ones returned, the fighting intensified, and the Messenger of God (ﷺ) said, "Now the furnace has become hot" (al-ana hamiya al-watis). Then the tide turned against the polytheists, they were routed with the worst defeat, their wealth was seized as spoils, and their women were taken captive.

That is His saying, ﴿and the earth, for all its vastness, closed in upon you﴾. This construction is a figurative depiction of the state of the Muslims when severe hardship overtook them, they were agitated, and they could not find a way to repel the enemy from themselves. It is like the state of one who sees the wide earth as narrow.

[Page 157]

The narrowness is not literal, as indicated by His saying, "for all its vastness" (بِمَا رَحُبَتْ). The expression is used as a metaphor (isti'arah) of the kind called a "representational metaphor" (isti'arah tamthiliyyah), depicting the state of one who cannot escape from hardship because of the disruption of the power of his thinking, by the state of one who is in a narrow place of the earth and wants to leave it but cannot pass beyond it or move from it.

The "ba'" (بِ) here indicates accompaniment (mula'abah), and "ma" (مَا) is a verbal-source particle (masdariyyah). The implied meaning is: "the earth closed in upon you while it was in a state of being accompanied by its vastness," i.e., while in a state in which there is no narrowness in it. This meaning is like the saying of al-Tirimmah ibn Hakim:

"I filled the earth around him until it seemed, from the narrowness, in his eyes like the palm of a hunter's net."

Al-A'lam said: "That is, from terror." It is derived from the saying of another:

"As if the roads of the earth, though broad, were to the fearful one being hunted like the palm of a hunter's net."

This is better than the view of some exegetes that the meaning of "the earth closed in upon you for all its vastness" is that you did not find a place on the earth to flee to, so it was as if the earth had closed in upon you. Among them is one who spoke in general terms, saying: "That is, because of the severity and difficulty of the situation."

The position of "thumma" (ثُمَّ) in His saying, ﴿then you turned back in retreat﴾, is the position of graded sequence (al-tarakhi al-rutbi), meaning: "and greater than the evil that befell you is that you turned back in retreat."

Al-tawalli (التَّوَلِّي) means turning back. "Mudbirin" (مُدْبِرِينَ) is a circumstantial clause (hal), either emphatic of the meaning of "tawallaytum," or it is intended to indicate a retreat more specific than tawalli, because tawalli is general and may be for fleeing, and it may be for a feigned withdrawal as a stratagem of war, whereas idbar (retreat) is commonly used for flight that is not intended as a stratagem. Thus the distinction between it and tawalli becomes a technical military distinction.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 9, verse 26:

﴿Then Allah sent down His tranquility upon His Messenger and upon the believers, and sent down hosts you did not see, and He punished those who disbelieved. That is the recompense of the disbelievers.﴾

This is a conjunction (ʿatf) upon His saying: ﴿and on the day of Ḥunayn, when your great number pleased you﴾ [al-Tawbah: 25].

The particle (thumma) indicates a delay in rank (al-tarākhī al-rutbī), since the sending down of tranquility and the sending down of the angels is greater than the victory of the first day, at Ḥunayn. Yet the temporal delay may also be intended, by way of treating the magnitude of the hardship and the terror of the calamity as if it were the length of its duration, for the times of hardship are imagined to be long even when they are brief.

Al-sakīnah (tranquility) means steadfastness and the calm of the soul. Its explanation has already preceded at His saying, ﴿that there should come to you the ark, in which is tranquility from your Lord﴾ [al-Baqarah: 248], in Surat al-Baqarah. Attaching it to Allah's sending down, and ascribing it to His pronoun, is an honouring of its status and blessing, and an indication that it is a tranquility that breaks custom, having no apparent causes or preliminaries, but arising solely by Allah's decree and creative will, as a gift of honour to His Prophet ﵁ and a response to his call to the people. For this reason the Messenger was mentioned before the believers.

The repetition of the preposition (ʿalā) after the conjunctive particle (wa) is a signal of renewing the attachment of the verb to the second genitive, to hint at the difference between the two tranquilities: the tranquility of the Messenger, peace be upon him, is a tranquility of reassurance regarding the Muslims who are with him and confidence in victory, while the tranquility of the believers is a tranquility of steadfastness and courage after dismay and fear.

Al-junūd is the plural of jund. Al-jund is a collective noun (ism jamʿ) with no singular from its own form; it means a body of people prepared for war, and its singular is formed with the nisba suffix: jundī. It has already been discussed at His saying, ﴿So when Ṭālūt went forth with the hosts﴾ [al-Baqarah: 249], in Surat al-Baqarah. The word jund is sometimes applied to a great nation possessed of power, as in His saying, ﴿Has there come to you the report of the hosts, [of] Pharaoh and Thamud?﴾ [al-Burūj: 17–18], in Surat al-Burūj. What is meant by the hosts here are companies of angels entrusted with defeating the polytheists, as the verb "sent down" indicates; that is, Allah sent them to support the believers and to cast terror into the hearts of the polytheists. For this reason He said, ﴿you did not see them﴾, and because the angels were angels of victory, the name "hosts" was applied to them.

His punishment of those who disbelieved is the punishment of killing, capture and taking of captives.

The demonstrative in ﴿That is the recompense of the disbelievers﴾ refers to the punishment derived from ʿaḏḏaba (He punished).

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 9, verse 27:

﴿Then Allah relents after that toward whom He wills. And Allah is Forgiving and Merciful.﴾

Thumma (ثُمَّ) indicates a sequence of rank (al-tarakhi al-rutbi), and it is conjoined to the clause ﴿Then Allah sent down His tranquility upon His Messenger﴾ [al-Tawbah: 26] up to His words: ﴿And that is the recompense of the disbelievers﴾ [al-Tawbah: 26]. This refers to the conversion to Islam of the Hawazin after that defeat, for they came to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) as Muslims, repentant, and asked him to return to them their captives and their spoils. That was the greatest favour in the victory of the Muslims, since the enemy troops became Muslims alongside them, and they no longer feared them after that day.

The meaning is: Then Allah relented toward them, that is, toward those among them who embraced Islam. So His saying ﴿Allah relents after that﴾ is evidence for what is conjoined by (thumma). For this reason the present tense was used in His saying "yatubu Allah" rather than the past tense, because the intended meaning includes the repentance of the Hawazin and the repentance of others, to indicate that the repentance is renewed for everyone who turns back to Allah and is not restricted to the Hawazin. Their repentance was already known to the Muslims, so they were informed that Allah treats everyone who regrets and repents in the same way. Thus the meaning is: Then Allah relented toward them, and Allah relents toward whom He wills.

The clause ﴿And Allah is Forgiving and Merciful﴾ is a concluding appendage (tadhyil) to the speech, to convey that forgiveness is among His attributes, and that He is Merciful to His servants if they turn back to Him in repentance and abandon associating partners with Him.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 9, verse 28:

﴿O you who have believed, indeed the polytheists are unclean, so let them not approach al-Masjid al-Haram after this, their year.﴾

This is a fresh resumptive sentence (isti'naf ibtida'i) returning to the theme of keeping the polytheists away from al-Masjid al-Haram, which was indicated by His words: ﴿It is not for the polytheists to maintain the mosques of Allah﴾ [al-Tawbah: 17] and what follows. It was brought to emphasize the command to remove them from al-Masjid al-Haram, while giving another cause that requires their removal from it: that they are unclean.
