Earlier, the cause given was that they bear witness against themselves to disbelief, so they are not fit to maintain the mosque built for monotheism. Here the cause given is that they are unclean, so they should not maintain the mosque, because of its purity.

Najas (unclean) is an adjective of the form sifah mushabbahah, a name for a thing in which uncleanliness is a constant attribute. The attribute of uncleanliness has been attached to them through the attribute of association (ishrak), so we know that it is a spiritual, inner uncleanliness and not an essential, physical uncleanliness.

Spiritual uncleanliness is the regarding of the bearer of an attribute as despised and avoided by people, so that he is not fit for any excellence as long as he is characterized by the attribute that made him so. Thus the polytheist is unclean because of the belief of his association. His body may be clean and pleasantly scented, not repulsive, and he may at the same time have a body that is repulsive and smeared with impurities, because his religion does not require him to purify himself; yet their cleanliness varies according to their customs and environment. The intended purpose of this description for them in Islam is to belittle them and keep them away from the gatherings of good. There is no doubt that the corruption of belief brings its bearer closer to being despised than the filth of the body does. For this reason, a polytheist who embraces Islam is obliged to perform ghusl, as a stripping away of that spiritual filth through sensory purification, to remove the corruption of his soul. The purification from minor ritual impurity (hadath) is close to this.

The prohibition from approaching al-Masjid al-Haram, that is, the prohibition from attending the season of the Hajj after this year of theirs, is made a consequence of their uncleanliness through association.

The reference to "this year" is to the year in which this verse was revealed, which was the ninth year after the Hijrah. In it the polytheists attended the season of the Hajj, and it was announced to them that they would not return to the Hajj after that year. They were given a respite until the rest of the year, because they had already arrived during the season, and their return to their distant lands varies; so by "the year" is meant the season of the Hajj. Otherwise, the end of the year comes with the passing of Dhu al-Hijjah, and they were given respite until the end of Muharram by His words: ﴿So travel freely in the land for four months﴾ [al-Tawbah: 2].

The attachment of "the year" (al-'am) to the pronoun "them" (hum) is for the added emphasis of their being specially subject to a great ruling in that year, like the words of Abu al-Tayyib:

"If this year of yours has pleased you, then return to Egypt next year."

The form of restriction (hasr) in His words ﴿indeed the polytheists are unclean﴾ serves to exclude any doubt about considering them unclean; it is for the exaggeration of their attribution of uncleanliness, to the point that as if they have no attribute except uncleanness.

Describing "the year" with the demonstrative (ism al-isharah) is to increase its distinction and clarification.

His words ﴿so let them not approach the mosque﴾ apparently are a prohibition addressed to the polytheists against approaching al-Masjid al-Haram. Addressing the believers with it requires prohibiting the Muslims from allowing the polytheists to approach al-Masjid al-Haram. The prohibition was cast in the form of a prohibition addressed to the polytheists in order to exaggerate the prohibition to the believers, since they were made responsible for keeping the polytheists from approaching al-Masjid al-Haram, in the manner of the Arab saying, "I shall not see you here." So the prohibition is not on the polytheists in its outward sense.

The intended meaning of the prohibition against their approaching al-Masjid al-Haram is the prohibition against their attending the Hajj, because all the rites of the Hajj are preceded and followed by a visit to al-Masjid al-Haram. For this reason, when (Bara'ah) was revealed, the Prophet ﷺ sent someone to proclaim during the season that no polytheist should perform the Hajj after this year. The indication of this is that the beginning of the prohibition is timed to what follows their present year. This shows that the prohibition looks to an act that is completed as the year nears its completion, and that act is the Hajj. Had this not been intended, there would have been no wisdom in timing the prohibition on approaching the mosque to the end of the year, and the prohibition would have been immediate.

* * *

﴿And if you fear poverty, Allah will enrich you from His bounty, if He wills. Indeed, Allah is Knowing and Wise.﴾

This is conjoined to the sentence of prohibition. The purpose of this sentence is the promise to the believers that Allah will enrich them, freeing them from the benefits that came to them from the polytheists when they used to come to the Hajj, spending and bringing gifts for offering, so that benefits from them returned to the people of Makkah and its surroundings. Its people had become Muslims, so there is no doubt that what comes to them of provision returns to the believers.

Al-'aylah means need and poverty. That is, if the fear of poverty from the cutting off of support from you through the prevention of many tribes from the Hajj arises in your minds, then Allah will enrich you against that. Allah enriched them by guiding the people of Tabalah and Jurash in the lands of Yemen to Islam, and they embraced Islam right after that. Their lands were lands of fertility and crops, so they carried food and provisions to Makkah. The people of Jeddah also embraced Islam; their town was a port to which foodstuffs came from Egypt and elsewhere, and they carried food to Makkah. The people of San'a' in Yemen also embraced Islam; their town receives ships from many regions of India and elsewhere.

His words "if He wills" (in sha'a) open for them the door of hope, together with supplication to Allah for the fulfillment of His promise, because He does whatever He wills.

His words ﴿indeed Allah is Knowing and Wise﴾ are the reason for His words ﴿and if you fear poverty﴾, meaning that Allah enriches you because He knows the benefits you have from the coming of the tribes. When He prevented them from being allowed to perform the Hajj, He did not abandon your benefit; rather, He decreed your independence from them through other means, which He knows and whose arrangement He perfected.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 9, verse 29 (part 1 of 2):

﴿Fight those who do not believe in Allah or in the Last Day, and who do not forbid what Allah and His Messenger have forbidden, and who do not adopt the religion of truth, from among those who were given the Book, until they pay the jizyah (poll tax) willingly, while they are humbled.﴾

The apparent meaning is that this verse is a fresh, independent statement (isti'naf ibtida'i) and is not linked to the verse before it. The discourse thus shifts from the theme of repudiating the covenant with the polytheists and the dealings between them and the Muslims, to the theme of dealings between the Muslims and the People of the Book, namely the Jews and the Christians. The two groups had been at peace with the Muslims at the very beginning of Islam, and they used to think that the Muslims' repelling of the polytheists was enough to spare them the task of confronting the Muslims, in the hope of discrediting Islam and causing its affairs to vanish. Then, when Islam began to spread in the lands of the Arabs day by day, and its affair became established in Madinah, some Jews began to display their enmity towards the Muslims, so hypocrisy arose in Madinah, and Qurayzah and al-Nadir backed the (Meccan) confederates (al-Ahzab) when they attacked Madinah, but Allah removed them from it.

Then, when the victory of Islam was completed with the conquest of Makkah and al-Ta'if, and its generality reached the lands of the Arabs through the arrival of their delegations as Muslims, and it extended to the borders of the Syrian lands, the Arab Christians became apprehensive of its reaching them, and the eye of the Roman state, the protector of the Arab Christians, did not close to the approach of the lands of Islam to their lands. So they began preparing to fight the Muslims through the mediation of the kings of Ghassan, the lords of the lands of Syria under Roman rule. In the Sahih of al-Bukhari, it is related from 'Umar ibn al-Khattab that he said: "I had a companion from the Ansar; when I was absent he would bring me the news, and when he was absent I would bring him the news. We were fearful of a king from the kings of Ghassan, of whom it was mentioned to us that he intended to march against us, and that they were shoeing horses for raiding us. Then my Ansari companion knocked at the door and said: 'Open, open!' I said: 'Has the Ghassani come?' He said: 'Rather, something greater than that: the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) has withdrawn from his wives'" – and the hadith continues to its end.

Therefore, when the Muslims felt safe from the might of the polytheists and found themselves in security from them, it was only natural that they should take up preparations to be safe from the might of the People of the Book, the Jews and the Christians. This began with the expedition against Khaybar, Qurayzah and al-Nadir, who had been defeated, and Allah sufficed the Muslims against their might and made them inherit their land. No fighting with them occurred after that. Then He followed it with the expedition of Tabuk, which lies at the frontiers of Syria.

It is related from Mujahid that this verse was revealed concerning the command to the expedition of Tabuk, so that the intended meaning of "those who were given the Book" is specifically the Christians. This does not agree with what the reports have unanimously established, that the surah was revealed after Tabuk.

The "min" (from) is explanatory (bayaniyyah), and it clarifies the relative pronoun preceding it.

The apparent meaning of the verse is that the people commanded to be fought have all the meanings of the three coordinated verbs in the relative clause established for them, and that the clarification occurring after the clause, by His saying ﴿from among those who were given the Book﴾, refers back to the relative pronoun in terms of its being the possessor of those clauses. This requires that the group commanded to be fought is a single group, from whom faith in Allah and the Last Day is absent, and who do not forbid what Allah has forbidden, and who do not adopt the religion of truth. The People of the Book were not known for not believing in Allah and the Last Day. The Jews and the Christians affirm the existence of Allah, the Exalted, and believe in the Day of Recompense.

On this basis, the exegetes were perplexed in interpreting this verse, and therefore they interpreted it as meaning that the Jews and Christians, although they affirm the existence of Allah and the Last Day, have ascribed to Allah attributes that contradict divinity, so that it is as if they did not believe in Him. For the Jews affirmed corporeality for Allah, the Exalted, or said ﴿The hand of Allah is chained up﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 64]. And many of them said: "'Uzayr is the son of Allah."

The Christians affirmed a plurality of gods through the Trinity, and so they came close to the saying of the polytheists, and thus they are further than the Jews from true faith. And as for the saying of both groups affirming the Last Day, they attached to it imaginings and falsehoods that contradict the reality of recompense, such as their saying ﴿The Fire will not touch us except for a few numbered days﴾ [al-Baqarah: 80], so it is as if they did not believe in the Last Day. The exegetes exerted great effort to repel what is objected to their interpretation, which is a varied array of arguments, and that is expounded in the tafsir of al-Fakhr (al-Razi), and all of it is forced interpretation (ta'assufat).

صفحة ١٦٤
The view I hold regarding the interpretation of this verse is that the most important intended aim of it is the fighting of the People of the Book, from among the Christians, as you have known. But the polytheists were incorporated along with them, lest anyone imagine that the command to fight the People of the Book requires devoting oneself exclusively to fighting them and abandoning the fighting of the polytheists.

So the intended aim of the verse is the third attribute: ﴿and who do not adopt the religion of truth﴾.

As for His saying ﴿who do not believe in Allah or in the Last Day﴾ up to His saying (and His Messenger), it is incorporation (idmaj). The intended aim is not to restrict fighting to those in whom the four attributes are combined; rather, the whole intended attribute is the one that is followed by the clarification with His saying ﴿from among those who were given the Book﴾, and what is other than it is incorporation and emphasis of what has passed. The polytheists do not believe in Allah or in the Last Day, and they do not forbid anything of what Allah and His Messenger have forbidden, because they have no sharia; there is no lawful and unlawful among them; and they do not adopt the religion of truth, which is Islam.

As for the Jews and the Christians, they believe in Allah and the Last Day, and they forbid what Allah has forbidden in their religion, but they do not adopt the religion of truth, which is Islam. The Magians are associated with them. These religions were the dominant ones among the nations of the known world of that time. The Romans were Christians, and among the Arabs there were Christians in the lands of Syria, Tayy, Kalb, Quda'ah, Taghlib and Bakr. The Magians were in the lands of Persia, and there were groups of Magians among the tribes that followed the kings of Persia, from Tamim, Bakr and Bahrain. The Jews were in Khaybar, Qurayzah and al-Nadir, and scattered groups in the land of Yemen. The causes of the command to fight these adherents of these religions were abundant, and this is what the choice of the relative (mawsuliyyah) construction points to, in order to identify them by those attributes, because the relative construction is the most suitable method in the language for narrating the states of their disbelief.

Do not think that the coordination of clauses upon the relative clause necessitates that all those attributes be combined in every entity to which the name of the relative pronoun applies. For the conjunction only conveys general combination in the ruling. The relative noun may be intended to refer to one person, in which case it is like the definite with al-, and it may be intended to refer to a kind or kinds of things to which the meaning of the clause or clauses applies. Moreover, the conjunctive particle acts as a substitute for the governing verb, so it is equivalent to repeating the relative pronoun, whether the conjunction alone is used, as in this verse, or the conjunction is combined with repeating the relative pronoun after it, as in His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And the servants of the Most Merciful are those who walk upon the earth in humility, and when the ignorant address them, they say, "Peace"﴾ [al-Furqan: 63] ﴿And those who spend the night before their Lord prostrating and standing﴾ [al-Furqan: 64] ﴿And those who say, "Our Lord, avert from us the punishment of Hell; indeed its punishment is ever adhering"﴾ [al-Furqan: 65] ﴿Indeed, it is evil as a settlement and residence﴾ [al-Furqan: 66] ﴿And those who, when they spend, are neither extravagant nor stingy, but are ever moderate between that﴾ [al-Furqan: 67] ﴿And those who do not invoke with Allah another god﴾ [al-Furqan: 68]. In these, eight relative nouns are coordinated upon the relative noun, and that does not imply that each relative noun is exclusively applied to a specific group; rather, what matters is the attribution of the content of one of those clauses, all of them together, by the first one, and reliance in such matters is upon the indicators (qara'in).

His saying ﴿from among those who were given the Book﴾ is a clarification of the nearest clause to it, which is the clause ﴿and who do not adopt the religion of truth﴾. The basic principle of clarification is that it be attached to what it clarifies, because clarification is like the corresponding substitute (badal mutabiq). This is not among the branches of the issue of the adjective and similar things that come after coordinated sentences. It is a single phrase, not a clarification of the whole relative clause, and furthermore the context returns it to its proper reference. The benefit of mentioning it is to censure them for being given the Book yet not adopting the religion of truth which their Book brought, and they only adopted what they distorted from it, what they denied from it, and what they attached to it. Had they adopted the religion of truth, they would have followed Islam, because their Book which was given to them enjoined upon them following the Prophet who would come after, ﴿And when Allah took the covenant of the prophets: "Whatever I have given you of Book and wisdom, and then there comes to you a messenger confirming what is with you, you must believe in him and support him." He said, "Do you affirm and accept My commitment on that?" They said, "We affirm." He said, "Then bear witness, and I am with you among the witnesses"﴾ [Al 'Imran: 81] ﴿So whoever turns away after that, those are the defiantly disobedient﴾ [Al 'Imran: 82] ﴿Do they seek other than the religion of Allah?﴾ [Al 'Imran: 83].

His saying ﴿and who do not forbid what Allah and His Messenger have forbidden﴾ means: who do not make unlawful what Allah has made unlawful. The pattern fa''ala is used to mean making the object acquire the verbal noun of the verb; so His saying ﴿and who do not forbid what Allah and His Messenger have forbidden﴾ conveys that they make it not unlawful, and the intended meaning is that they make it permissible. The purpose of this is to vilify their condition and to stir up their hatred, by saying that they consider lawful what Allah has forbidden to His servants. Since what Allah has forbidden is ugly and reprehensible, by His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿He makes lawful for them the good things and prohibits for them the evil things﴾ [al-A'raf: 157],

صفحة ١٦٦
it is no wonder that those who consider it lawful have shown the corruption of their minds, and so they were fit to be restrained from their falsehood. Moreover, what Allah and His Messenger have forbidden encompasses the universal necessities of the sharia: the preservation of life, lineage, property and honor, and the polytheists do not forbid these.

By "His Messenger" is meant Muhammad (ﷺ), as is the common usage of the Qur'an. Had another of the messengers been intended, He would have said "and His messengers," because Allah did not forbid through the tongue of His Messenger except what truly deserves prohibition.

On this interpretation, this verse is a preparation for the Muslims to fight the Romans and the Persians, and the remaining tribes of the Arabs who take shelter under the support of one of these two nations, such as Quda'ah and Taghlib on the borders of Syria, until they either believe or pay the jizyah.

And "until" (hatta) indicates the endpoint of the fighting, meaning: your fighting of them shall continue until they pay the jizyah.

The pronoun in "yu'tu" (they give) refers back to ﴿those who were given the Book﴾ [al-Baqarah: 101].

Al-jizyah is a name for money that men of a people give as a recompense for being allowed to remain alive, or for acknowledging possession of the land. It is formed on the pattern of the noun of state (ism al-hay'ah), and there is no relevance in considering the state here. So the apparent view regarding this noun is that it is arabized from the Persian word (kizit) meaning tribute (kharaj). The exegetes transmitted this from al-Khwarazmi. I have not come across this word in Arabic speech in the pre-Islamic period, and al-Raghib did not touch upon it in Mufradat al-Qur'an. Nor did they mention it among the arabized words of the Qur'an, because of the uncertainty in this matter, since they found the Arabic derivational root suitable for it. There is no doubt that it was a known meaning among those among whom the Qur'an was revealed, and for this reason it is defined in this verse.

His saying "'an yadin" (with willing hand / by hand) is an emphasis on the meaning of "yu'tu" for the sake of explicitly stating the giving, and "'an" in it indicates passing from (al-mujawazah). That is, they pay it with their own hands, and their sending it through others or their assigning it through a transfer is not accepted from them. The place of the prepositional phrase is a circumstantial phrase (hal) from the jizyah. The meaning of "yad" here is the hand of the giver, i.e., they give it without refusing or disputing its payment, and this is like the saying of the Arabs "a'ta bi-yadihi" (he gave with his hand) when he submits.

The nominal clause ﴿while they are humbled﴾ is a circumstantial clause from the pronoun in "yu'tu".

صفحة ١٦٧

The adjective al-ṣāghir is an active participle from ṣaghira (with kasra on the ghayn), ṣaghaaran and ṣaghaar, meaning "to be humiliated." The term ṣaghaar has already been mentioned in His words, exalted is He: ﴿Those who committed crimes will be struck with humiliation before Allah﴾ [al-An'am: 124], in Surat al-An'am. That is, they will be abased. This is a condition necessarily attached to paying the jizya "from the hand" (ʿan yadin). The purpose of it is to magnify the authority of the Islamic rule and to belittle the people of disbelief, so that this becomes an incentive for them to abandon their false religion and follow the religion of Islam.

This verse indicates that the jizya is taken from the Magians (al-majus), since they are people of a Book. Ibn al-Mundhir transmitted: "I know of no disagreement that the jizya is taken from them." Ibn Wahb, one of the companions of Malik, disagreed regarding taking the jizya from the Magians of the Arabs. He said: "No jizya is accepted from them, and there is no alternative to killing or Islam." Just as the verse indicates that the jizya is taken from the Christians of the Arabs, it does not extend to the polytheists of the Arabs. This is because the ruling on fighting them has already passed in the preceding verses, and it did not address the jizya there. Rather, the final outcome mentioned in them was His words: ﴿If they repent, establish prayer and give zakat, then let them go their way﴾ [al-Tawbah: 5], and His words: ﴿If they repent, establish prayer and give zakat, then they are your brothers in religion﴾ [al-Tawbah: 11], and His words: ﴿Allah turns in forgiveness to whom He wills﴾ [al-Tawbah: 15].

Moreover, if the jizya were taken from them, that would necessitate their remaining in their homes, because Allah did not legislate their expulsion from their homes, and the Prophet ﷺ did not do that.

[Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 9, verse 30]

﴿The Jews say, "'Uzayr is the son of God," and the Christians say, "The Messiah is the son of God." That is what they say with their mouths, imitating the saying of those who disbelieved before them. May God fight them. How are they deluded?﴾

This is conjoined to the clause ﴿nor do they follow the religion of truth﴾ (At-Tawbah: 29). The implied meaning is: some of the Jews say, "'Uzayr is the son of God," and some of the Christians say, "The Messiah is the son of God," as a condemnation of those among the People of the Book who utter these two statements, showing that they have reached the extreme of disbelief, to the point that they have become equal to the polytheists.

'Uzayr is the name of a great rabbi among the rabbis of the Jews who were in the Babylonian captivity. His name in Hebrew is ('Izra) with a kasra on the unpointed ayn, son of (Saraya), from the tribe of the Levites. He was a memorizer of the Torah. (Kurash) king of Persia showed him favor, freed him from captivity, and freed with him the Children of Israel from the captivity they were under in Babylon, and permitted them to return to Jerusalem and to build their Temple there. That was in the year 451 BC. 'Izra became the leader of the rabbis of the Jews who returned with their people to Jerusalem, renewed the Temple, and restored the Torah's law from memory. The Jews exalted 'Izra to such an extent that most of them claimed that 'Izra is the son of God, out of excess in sanctifying him. Those who described him thus were a group of rabbis of the Jews in Medina, and a large number of their common people followed them. I think that what moved them to this statement was that they did not want to be free of attributing to one of their great men the sonship of God, exalted is He, like the saying of the Christians about the Messiah. As their predecessors said: ﴿Make for us a god as they have gods﴾ (Al-A'raf: 138).

This saying was uttered by a faction of the Jews, but it was attributed to all of them, because the silence of the rest concerning it and their failure to change it obliges them to agree with it and be content with it. The name 'Izra is mentioned in the verse in the diminutive form. It is possible that when it was Arabicized, it was given a form resembling the diminutive, so that his name in the speech of the Jews of Medina was likewise. It is also possible that its diminutive form was used by the Jews of Medina out of affection for him.

The majority read ('Uzayr) without tanwin (nunation), because it is non-Arabic (ajamiyyah) and thus diptote. Al-Zamakhshari affirmed this reading. ('Asim), al-Kisa'i and Ya'qub read it with tanwin, treating it as Arabic because of the diminutive form applied to it, since the diminutive does not enter foreign proper names. 'Abd al-Qahir affirmed this in the chapter on composition (fasl al-nazm) of Dala'il al-I'jaz. Al-Zamakhshari did not accept the two interpretations offered for the reading without tanwin.

As for the Christians' saying of the sonship of the Messiah, it is known and well established. The discussion of the Messiah has already passed at His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And We gave Jesus son of Mary clear signs﴾ (Al-Baqarah: 87), in surah Al-Baqarah, and at His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Whose name is the Messiah, Jesus son of Mary﴾ (Al 'Imran: 45), in surah Al 'Imran.

The demonstrative "that" (dhalika) refers to the saying indicated by "The Jews say" and "the Christians say." The purpose of the reference is to make the saying prominent and distinct, increasing its condemnation among the Muslims.

"With their mouths" (bi-afwahihim) is a circumstantial clause (hal) describing the saying. The meaning is that it is a saying that does not go beyond being uttered by the tongue, and has nothing in reality that realizes it. This is a metaphor (kinayah) for its being false, like His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Grave is the word that comes out of their mouths; they say nothing but a lie﴾ (Al-Kahf: 5). This also binds them to this saying and closes the door to their disowning it, since it is their acknowledgment with their own mouths and their clear speech.

Al-mudahah (imitation) means resemblance. Attributing it to the speakers is by way of an implied, apparent noun in the speech, meaning: it resembles the saying of those.

"Those who disbelieved before" (alladhina kafaru min qablu) are the polytheists: from the Arabs, from the Greeks, and others. That they came before the Christians is clear. As for their coming before the Jews, it is because the belief in the sonship of 'Uzayr arose among the Jews later and was not part of the creed of their earliest ancestors.

The clause "May God fight them" (qatalahumu Allah) is a supplication used for astonishment. It is a construction used to express wonder at a shameful deed, and the form of the verb with the infix (mufa'alah) here intensifies the supplication, meaning: may God kill them with a severe killing. The clause of astonishment is a new independent clause, as is the nature of expressions of wonder.

The clause "How are they deluded?" (anna yu'fakun) is also an independent new clause. The interrogative in it is used to express astonishment at their condition in following falsehood, to the point that the place to which they are turned by their belief is likened to an unknown place about which one would ask with the interrogative for place. The meaning of "are deluded" (yu'fakun) is "are turned away." It is said: afakahu ya'fikuhu, when he turned him away. God, exalted is He, said: ﴿Turned away from it is whoever is turned away﴾ (Al-Dhariyat: 9). The word al-ifk meaning "lie" has come from this same root, because the liar turns the listener away from the truth. This has been mentioned more than once before.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 9, verse 31:

﴿They have taken their rabbis and their monks as lords besides Allah, and [also] the Messiah, son of Mary. Yet they were commanded only to worship one God; there is no god except Him. Glory be to Him above what they associate with Him.﴾

This sentence restates the content of the sentence ﴿The Jews say, "Ezra is the son of Allah," and the Christians say, "The Messiah is the son of Allah"﴾ [al-Tawba: 30], so that upon this restatement is built an added censure, by His saying: ﴿Yet they were commanded only to worship one God﴾, etc. The pattern of this sentence is like the pattern of the sentence ﴿they took it, and they were wrongdoers﴾ [al-A'raf: 148], after the sentence ﴿And the people of Musa, after him, took from their ornaments a calf, a body with a lowing sound﴾ [al-A'raf: 148]. The pronoun refers to the Jews and the Christians.

Al-Ahbar (the rabbis) is the plural of habr, with a fatha on the ha', and it means a scholar among the scholars of the Jews.

Al-Ruhban (the monks) is a collective noun for rahib, who is the pious one devoted entirely to the worship of Allah among the adherents of the Christian religion. The term habr was restricted to the scholar of the Jews because the great figures of the Jewish religion occupy themselves with the editing of the sciences of the Torah's law, so they are scholars in religion; and the term rahib was restricted to the great figures of the Christian religion because the Christian religion is founded on the principle of asceticism in this world and devotion to worship.

The meaning of their taking these people as lords is that the Jews claimed for some of their number the sonship of Allah, exalted is He, and that is deification. The Christians were even more extreme in this than they, for they used to prostrate to the images of the great figures of their creed, such as the image of Maryam, the images of the disciples, and the image of Yahya ibn Zakariyya. Prostration is a symbol of lordship, and they would seek help from them in their wars, and not seek help from Allah.

This is the state of many of their sects and factions. Moreover, they used to take the sayings of their rabbis and monks, which contradicted what is known by necessity to be part of the religion, so they believed that their rabbis and monks made lawful what Allah had made unlawful and made unlawful what Allah had made lawful. This applies to all the adherents of both religions. For this reason the Prophet ﷺ silenced 'Adi ibn Hatim with it, when he came to him shortly before his conversion to Islam, when he heard His saying, exalted is He: ﴿They have taken their rabbis and their monks as lords besides Allah﴾. 'Adi said: "We do not worship them." He said: ("Do they not make unlawful what Allah has made lawful, so you make it unlawful, and make lawful what Allah has made unlawful, so you make it lawful?" I said: "Yes." He said: "That is their worship.")

Thus there results from the totality of the sayings of the Jews and the Christians that they gave some of their rabbis and monks the rank of lordship in their belief, so the abomination applied to both communities. Even if there were among them someone who did not say their saying, as 'Adi ibn Hatim claimed, the community is held accountable for what issues from its individuals if it approves of it and does not denounce it. The meaning of their taking them as lords besides Allah is that they took them as lords instead of singling out Allah with oneness.

The mention of the Messiah specifically is because the Christians' deification of him is more abominable and more well known.

The sentence ﴿Yet they were commanded only to worship one God﴾ is in the position of a circumstantial clause (hal) from the pronoun in ﴿they have taken their rabbis﴾, and it is the locus of the added censure against them and of the denunciation of their conduct, that they have no excuse for what they claimed, because the scriptural injunctions of both religions are replete with warning against the worship of creatures and against associating them with the attributes of divinity.

The sentence ﴿there is no god except Him﴾ is a second attribute of ﴿one God﴾.

The sentence ﴿Glory be to Him above what they associate with Him﴾ is a resumptive sentence for the purpose of declaring Allah exalted and free from what they have invented against Allah, exalted is He, and for this reason that is called association (shirk).

Ibn 'Ashur, *al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir*, on Surah 9, verse 32:

﴿They wish to extinguish the light of Allah with their mouths, but Allah refuses except to perfect His light, even though the disbelievers dislike it.﴾

This is an initiatory resumption (*isti'naf ibtida'i*), intended to further provoke the anger of the Muslims against the People of the Book by exposing what they conceal against Islam of collusion (*mumalah*) and of gathering together to oppose the religion, once they had confirmed that it was spreading and becoming manifest. Their envy was aroused, and they feared the manifestation of its superiority over their own religion. The pronoun in His saying "*yuridun*" (they wish) refers back to ﴿those who were given the Scripture﴾ [al-Tawbah: 29]. *Itfa'* (extinguishing) is the nullification of a lamp's illumination and the removal of its light by blowing upon it, or by the blowing of winds, or by pouring water upon the illuminated thing, whether a lamp or an ember.

*Nur* (light) is radiance, and it was discussed earlier at His saying ﴿a light and guidance for the people﴾ [al-An'am: 91] in Surat al-An'am. The statement is an allegory (*tamthil*) of their condition: attempting to belie the Prophet (ﷺ), turning people away from following Islam, aiding the adversaries of Islam with speech, rumor-mongering and incitement to resistance, and joining the ranks of the enemies in wars, as in the attempt of the Christians of Syria to attack Madinah. It is like the condition of one who tries to extinguish a light by blowing into it with his mouth. Thus this statement is a compound expression (*murakkab*) used in other than its original sense, in the manner of comparing one state with another (*tashbih al-hay'ah bi-al-hay'ah*). Among the perfections of its eloquence is that it admits of dismantling the comparison: Islam alone may be likened to light, those who attempt to nullify it to those who wish to extinguish light, and the rumor-mongering and denial to blowing. Among its elegance is that the instrument of blowing and the instrument of denial are one and the same, namely the mouths. The well-known example of an allegory that admits both the composite and the separated readings is the verse of Bashshar:

*As if the dust-clouds raised above our heads,*
*and our swords, were a night whose stars are falling.*

However, the separation in the allegory of this verse is more independent, unlike Bashshar's verse, as becomes evident upon reflection.

[Page 172]

The attribution of the light to the Name of Majesty (*ism al-jalalah*) indicates that the attempt to extinguish it is futile, and that its proponents will not attain their aim.

*Al-iba'* and *al-ibayah* mean refusal to perform an act. Here it is an allegory for Allah's, Exalted is He, will to complete the manifestation of Islam, in the manner of one who attempts an action from another while that other refuses to do it. Since they attempted to obliterate Islam, they were in reality attempting to nullify the will of Allah, Exalted is He, so their condition in reality was like that of one who attempts an act of someone else who refuses to do it.

The exception (*istithna' mufarragh*) is of the "emptied" type, even though no negation precedes it, because the verb *ya'ba* (refuses) was treated as negating the will (*ajrya fi'l ya'ba majra nafy al-iradah*), as if he had said: "Allah does not will except to perfect His light." This is because the verb *aba* and its like contain an aspect of negation, since refusing something is a rejection of it. The aspect of negation is strengthened here because it stands in opposition to His saying ﴿they wish to extinguish the light of Allah﴾. Thus the refusal of what they wish amounts to the negation of Allah's will concerning what they wished. By this the difference between this verse and saying "I disliked except your brother" becomes evident.

This construction was used here because of the intensity of the obstinacy of the People of the Book and their rigidity in their religion. It was not used in Surat al-Saff, where He said ﴿they wish to extinguish the light of Allah with their mouths, and Allah will perfect His light﴾ [al-Saff: 8], because the hypocrites used to plot against the Muslims covertly, with softness and flattery.

The author of *al-Kashshaf* mentioned, at His saying ﴿then they drank from it, except a few of them﴾ [al-Baqarah: 249], in the reading of al-A'mash and Ubayy, with the *raf'* (nominative) of *qalil* (few), that the nominative of the exception is in apposition (*badaliyyah*) to the subject of *fa-shariba* (then they drank), on the basis that *shariba* was given the implied meaning (*tadmin*) of "did not taste," so that it means "none tasted it except a few," inclining with the sense of the statement.

The word *itmam* (perfecting) implies increase and spread, and for this reason He did not say "and Allah refuses except to keep His light [as it is]."

The *law* (لو) in ﴿even though the disbelievers dislike it﴾ is *ittisaliyyah* (of continuation), and it conveys emphasis that what follows is more worthy of the absence of what precedes, even if that were absent. The emphasis on the disbelievers' dislike returns to emphasis on the effects of that dislike, which are gathering together and collaborating to resist and nullify the religion. As for their mere dislike, it has no value with Allah, Exalted is He, such that it would be emphasized. The disbelievers here are the Jews and the Christians.

[p. 173]
﴿It is He who sent His Messenger with guidance and the religion of truth, that He may make it prevail over all religion, even if the polytheists dislike it.﴾

This is an explanation of the clause ﴿And Allah refuses except to perfect His light﴾ [al-Tawbah: 32], by stating that He sent His Messenger with this religion. Therefore He does not intend its removal, and He does not render His decree void and vain. In this explanation there is also an honouring of the Messenger after the honouring of the religion.

In His saying ﴿It is He who sent His Messenger﴾ there is a form of restriction (qasr), meaning: it is He, and no other, who sent His Messenger with this light. How, then, would He leave its opponents to extinguish it?

The use of the relative pronoun (ism al-mawsul) serves to indicate that the content of the relative clause is the reason for the sentence upon which this sentence is built, namely the sentence ﴿And Allah refuses except to perfect His light﴾ [al-Tawbah: 32].

He expressed Islam as ﴿guidance and the religion of truth﴾, honouring its excellence and implying indirectly that what they follow is neither guidance nor truth.

The verb of manifestation (al-izhar), when it is followed by ʿala (over), carries the implication of support (al-nasr) or superiority (al-tafdil). That is, ﴿to make it prevail over all religions﴾ means to support it over all religions, so that it may be the most noble and most dominant of religions. From the same root is al-muzaharah, which means support (al-munasarah), and it has already been mentioned just before, at His saying ﴿and have not supported anyone against you﴾ [al-Tawbah: 4].

Islam was the most noble of religions, because the miracle (mu'jizah) of its truthfulness is the Qur'an, and it is a miracle that is grasped by the intellect; the perception of its inimitability is shared by all ages. Moreover, this religion is free of all defects in belief and in practice: it is free of affirming what does not befit Allah the Exalted, free of imposing burdensome obligations, and free of calling to abandon the soundness of the order of the world. I have explained this in detail in the book I named Usul al-Nizam al-Ijtima'i fi al-Islam (The Foundations of the Social Order in Islam).

The manifestation of Islam over all religion has come about in the world through the adherence of the people of the faiths (milal) to it in all regions, despite the dislike of their peoples and the leaders of their faiths for that, and their opposition to it by every means. Nevertheless, it has appeared, risen, and its excellence has become evident over the religions that neighbour it, and its freedom from the superstitions

[p. 174]
and illusions to which they have clung. Some of their affairs were only put right by imitating what they observed of the conditions of the Muslims and the causes of their advancement. And it does not follow from its manifestation over the religions that those religions must become extinct.

As for ﴿even if the polytheists dislike it﴾, the word "even if" (law) here is a concessive particle similar to the one in its counterpart. The polytheists are mentioned here because the manifestation of the religion of Islam is a more bitter grief for them than for any other community, since they were the ones who began opposing it and hostility towards it, called the nations to unite against it, and sought help from them, but these did not avail them anything. Furthermore, the fullest manifestation of Islam's victory was in the Arabian Peninsula, which is the land of the polytheists, because Islam prevailed there and all other religions disappeared from it. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Two religions shall not remain in the Arabian Peninsula." Therefore the polytheists' dislike of its manifestation was the greatest in its degree of intensity, with regard to the circumstances of its manifestation over all religion, as becomes clear upon reflection.

[Page 175]

Ibn 'Ashur, *al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir*, on Surah al-Tawbah (9), verse 34:

﴿O you who have believed, indeed many of the rabbis and the monks consume the wealth of people unjustly and avert [them] from the way of Allah.﴾

This is a fresh, independent sentence (*istinaf ibtida'i*, a resumptive sentence that begins a new topic), meant to alert the Muslims to the faults of the People of the Book, so that they may belittle them in their own minds and be firm with them in their dealings. After mentioning that the common people among them deified some of their eminent rabbis and monks of earlier times, such as 'Uzayr, the verse shows the Muslims that many of the later rabbis and monks are not in a state of perfection and do not deserve the religious station they claim. The purpose of this alert is for the Muslims to know that the elite and the common people among the People of the Book are united in misguidance and in opposition to Islam. Their aim is that the elite may monopolize leadership (*al-istithar bi al-siyadah*), and the common people may monopolize distinction among the Arabs.

Opening the sentence with the vocative (*al-nida'*) and reinforcing it with the two emphasizing particles serves to draw attention to its content and to remove any suspicion of exaggeration, because it is so strange.

The mention of the rabbis and monks has already preceded.

The judgment is attributed to "many of them" rather than to all of them, because there have never been lacking among them righteous people, such as 'Abd Allah ibn Salam and Mukhayriq.

*Al-batil* is the opposite of *al-haqq* (truth). That is, they consume the wealth of people in a manner that is tainted with falsehood, i.e., a consumption for which there is no justification. The use of "consume" (*akl*) for taking another's property is a widespread usage. Allah says: ﴿And you devour the heritage, devouring greedily﴾ [al-Fajr: 19], and He says: ﴿And do not consume one another's wealth unjustly, nor send it [as bribes] to the rulers in order that you may consume a portion of the wealth of people in sin while you know﴾ [al-Baqarah: 188], which has been discussed in Surah al-Baqarah, and the term *al-batil* was discussed there too.

*Al-batil* includes many aspects: among them, altering religious rulings to suit people's desires; among them, judging between people without giving the rightful claimant his right as prescribed in the Shari'ah; among them, denying trusts to their owners or to their heirs; and among them, consuming the property of orphans, endowments (*awqaf*) and charities.

*Sabil Allah* (the way of Allah) is its path, used metaphorically for His religion, which leads to Him, i.e., to His pleasure. *Al-sadd 'an sabil Allah* (averting from the way of Allah) means turning away from following the true religion in one's own self, and enticing people to turn away from it. This applies to the rulings of their own religion, since they change the practice of them and mislead the common people about their reality until they come to act contrary to them, while they think they are following their religion. It also applies to the religion of Islam, since they deny the prophethood of Muhammad (ﷺ) and inform the followers of their religion that Islam is not the religion of truth.

Because of the sense of *sadd* in which the subject himself averts, the present tense of this verb takes a *damm* on the 'ayn (*yasuddu*), being treated as a doubled, transitive verb. For this reason, it does not occur in the Qur'an except with a *damm* on the *sad*, even in places where it is not meant that he averts others. Some of this was mentioned when discussing the words of Allah, ﴿Those who avert [others] from the way of Allah and seek to make it crooked﴾ [al-A'raf: 45], in Surah al-A'raf.

* * *

[Page 176]

﴿And those who hoard gold and silver and do not spend them in the way of Allah, give them tidings of a painful punishment.﴾

This clause is conjoined (*ma'tufah*) to the clause ﴿O you who have believed, indeed many [of them]﴾. The relation between the two clauses is that both alert to the faults of groups whom people place in positions of elevation and nobility, although they are not worthy of that. The content of the first clause explains the faults of groups whom people raised in rank for their knowledge and religion, while they harbored hidden corruptions. The content of the second clause explains the faults of groups whom people raised for the sake of their wealth. Allah thus makes clear that those riches, if not spent in the way of Allah, will not avail them anything against the punishment.

As for the occasion of the revelation of this verse in this surah: this surah was revealed directly after the Battle of Tabuk, which took place in a time of hardship (*'usrah*), when the need for equipment and mounts was great, as indicated by the verse ﴿Nor [is there blame] upon those who came to you that you might provide them mounts, [and] you said, "I find nothing to mount you on," and they turned back while their eyes overflowed with tears from grief that they could not find anything to spend﴾ [al-Tawbah: 92]. It is related in the *sirah* (biography of the Prophet) that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) urged the wealthy to spend and to provide mounts in the way of Allah. 'Uthman ibn 'Affan spent a thousand dinars in gold on the army of the Battle of Tabuk, and many of the wealthy provided mounts. Those who shrank back from spending are the ones the verse meant by ﴿those who hoard gold and silver and do not spend them in the way of Allah﴾, and there is no doubt that they were among the hypocrites.

*Al-kanz* (hoarding), with a *fatha* on the *kaf*, is the verbal noun of *kanaza*, meaning to store up wealth, and it is applied to the wealth of gold and silver that is stored, by the usage of the verbal noun for the object, like *al-khalq* meaning "the created thing."

*Sabil Allah* is the Islamic struggle (*al-jihad*), and this is what is meant here.

The relative pronoun (*al-mawsul*) refers to a known group who understand that they are the target of the threat, and the Muslims also know them. For this reason, it is not established that the Prophet (ﷺ) rebuked any people by name.

* * *

[Page 177]

The meaning of ﴿and do not spend them in the way of Allah﴾ is the absence of obligatory spending, namely the obligatory charities and obligatory expenditures, whether of a continuous obligation, such as *zakah* (obligatory almsgiving), or of an incidental obligation, such as the expenditure for the obligatory *hajj*, and expenditure in the calamities of the Muslims for which the rulers of justice call people.

The feminine pronoun in His saying "*yunfiquna-ha*" (they spend them) refers to gold and silver.

The threat is tied to hoarding and to not spending. So hoarding alone is not what is threatened, and the verse is not in the context of the rulings on storing wealth, nor in the context of making spending obligatory, nor does it specify the paths of righteousness and goodness for which wealth must be paid out. There is no need to interpret *kanz* as wealth whose *zakah* was not paid when it was due, nor to interpret *infaq* as paying the obligatory *zakah*, nor to interpret *sabil Allah* as obligatory charities; because the relative pronoun does not mean generality but is intended to refer to a specific known group. So there is no need to claim that it was abrogated (*naskh*, the cancellation of a ruling by a later one) by the verse of the obligation of *zakah*, for the obligation of *zakah* came before the revelation of this verse.

It is reported in the *Muwatta'* that 'Abd Allah ibn 'Umar was asked about hoarding, i.e., the blameworthy hoarding that is threatened in the verse ﴿And those who hoard gold and silver﴾, the verse, what it is. He said: It is the wealth from which *zakah* is not paid. In the authentic hadith from Abu Hurayrah that the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Whoever has wealth from which he does not pay its *zakah*, it will be depicted for him on the Day of Resurrection as a bald, poisonous snake with two black spots, which will coil around him, then it will seize him by his two cheeks, meaning his jaws, then it will say: 'I am your wealth, I am your hoard.'" Its interpretation is that this is a part of his wealth and a part of his hoard, i.e., it is a part of the blameworthy hoarding mentioned in the Book and the Sunnah, and not every hoard is blameworthy.

Abu Dharr deviated (*shadha*) by taking the verse as covering all hoarders in every state of hoarding, and as covering all spending, and by taking "the way of Allah" as covering all paths of goodness. He held that hoarding wealth is forbidden. It seems he interpreted "and do not spend them" as an explanatory conjunction (*'atf al-tafsir*), i.e., a conjunction only for the sake of linking the two expressions together. Abu Dharr used to be in Syria forbidding people from hoarding and saying: "Give the hoarders the good news of a branding with fire, by which their foreheads, sides, and backs will be branded." Mu'awiyah, who was governor of Syria during the caliphate of 'Uthman, said to him: "The verse was only revealed about the People of the Book." Abu Dharr said: "It was revealed about them and about us." Abu Dharr's words became harsh upon the people, and they saw them as a saying that no one had said in the time of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and his two companions. So Mu'awiyah complained about him to 'Uthman, who summoned him from Syria. Abu Dharr feared strife in Medina, so he withdrew from it and settled in al-Rabadhah, and he remained steadfast in his opinion and his statement.

The particle *fa* in His saying "*fa-bashshir-hum*" (so give them tidings) enters upon the predicate of the relative clause, as the relative clause is treated as a conditional clause, because it contains an indication of the cause of the relation (*sillah*) in the predicate. So the plural pronoun refers to "those who," and it is permissible for the pronoun to refer to the rabbis, the monks, and those who hoard. The *fa* is the *fa* of explanation (*al-fa' al-fasihah*), meaning that after mentioning those who consume wealth and turn people away from the way of Allah, and mentioning the hoarders, He commanded His Messenger to warn all of them of the punishment. So the *fa* indicates an omitted condition, whose estimate is: "If you know these are their conditions, then give them tidings." The "tidings" (*tabshir*) is used metaphorically for a threat, in the manner of irony (*al-tahakkum*).

[Page 179]

The phrase ﴿on the Day it is heated﴾ is in the accusative of time (ẓarfiyyah), governed by "torment" (ʿadhāb), because the word "ʿadhāb" carries the sense of "they will be tormented." The pronoun in ﴿upon them﴾ refers to "gold and silver," understood as dinars and dirhams. Alternatively, it refers to "the wealth of people" and ﴿the gold and the silver﴾ [al-Tawbah: 34], if the pronoun in His words ﴿so give them good tidings﴾ [al-Tawbah: 34] refers to the rabbis, the monks, and those who hoard.

Al-ḥamy (heating) is intense heat. It is said: "ḥamiya al-shayʾ" when its heat has intensified.

The pronoun governed by ʿalā refers to ﴿the gold and the silver﴾ [al-Tawbah: 34], in consideration of their being dinars or dirhams, which are plural. The verb is in the passive voice because the purpose does not depend on the agent. It is as if it were said: "on the Day when those who heat will heat them." The passive verb is attributed to the preposition-object phrase because the purpose does not depend on mentioning the heated object, which is evident: it is the fire that is heated. For this reason, it is not joined with the feminine marker. It is construed with ʿalā, which indicates figurative elevation (istiʿlāʾ majāzī), to convey that the heating has taken hold of the wealth such that it acquires the entire heat of what is heated. Then the sense of taking hold is reinforced by the sense of location in His words ﴿in the fire of Hell﴾, so the wealth becomes heated upon by the fire and placed within the fire.

[Page 180]

By the annexation of "fire" to "Hell," it is known that what is heated is the fire of Hell, which is the most intense fire in heat. Thus the construction comes as a wonderful composition of eloquence and emphasis, in brevity.

Al-kayy (branding) is placing an ember or something burning upon the skin.

Al-jibāh is the plural of jabhah, which is the upper part of the face adjacent to the head.

Al-junūb is the plural of janb, which is the side of the body, right and left.

Al-ẓuhūr is the plural of ẓahr, which is what lies between the lower lip's hollow (al-ʿanfaqah) and the end of the spinal bone.

The meaning is the generalization of the directions of the bodies by branding, for those directions vary and differ in their sensation of the pain of branding. Thus, along with the generalization of branding, there is a tasting of various kinds of pain.

In expressing the generalization, the style of elaboration (iṭnāb) by enumeration was adopted, to evoke the state of that painful punishment and to magnify its gravity. For this reason, He did not say: ﴿and their bodies will be branded therewith﴾.

The manner of bringing those dirhams and dinars to be heated is among the matters of the Hereafter that break customary habits. By the power of God, those dinars and dirhams, or their like, will be brought, as it is reported in the hadith about the one who withholds zakāt in the Muwaṭṭaʾ and the two Ṣaḥīḥs, that "his wealth will be represented to him as a bald venomous snake that seizes him by his two cheeks, saying: 'I am your wealth, I am your treasure.'" By the power of God, those who refused to spend them in the way of God will be branded, even though many people in this world may have circulated their very substance by its passing from hand to hand, from land to land, and from age to age.

The clause ﴿This is what you hoarded for yourselves﴾ is the object of an omitted verb of saying (maqūl qawl maḥdhūf), and omitting the verb of saying in such a context is common in the Qur'an. The demonstrative refers to what was heated. The addition of His words ﴿for yourselves﴾ serves reproach and severity. The particle of causation (lām al-taʿlīl) indicates the intention of benefit, because the act for which the cause is given is an act of the addressed, and he does not do anything for the sake of himself except because he intends by it its comfort and benefit. So when their hoarding led them to painful punishment, they had lost and were ruined in what they had taken benefit from of gold and silver, by an amount that was multiplied manyfold of the pain of punishment.

The clause ﴿So taste what you used to hoard﴾ is a rebuke and reproach.

The fāʾ in "fa-dhūqū" is for the consequence of the content of the rebuke clause upon the first reproach clause.

[Page 181]

Al-dhawq (tasting) is a figurative use in the sense of sensation, by the relation of generality (ʿalāqat al-iṭlāq), and it was discussed earlier at His words, exalted is He: ﴿that he may taste the consequence of his affair﴾ [al-Māʾidah: 95], in the surah of al-ʿUqūd.

﴿What you used to hoard﴾ is the object of the verb "taste," with an implied modifier understood from the context: that is, "taste the punishment of what you used to hoard."

He expressed with the relative form in His words ﴿what you used to hoard﴾ to draw attention to their error regarding what they hoarded, for the purpose of reproach.

**Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 9, verse 36 (part 1 of 2):**

﴿Indeed, the number of months with Allah is twelve months in the Book of Allah, the day He created the heavens and the earth; of them, four are sacred.﴾

This is an initial resumptive sentence (*istinaf ibtida'i*, a new sentence that begins a fresh topic) to establish the system of timekeeping for the community in the true manner, one suitable for all of mankind and appropriate to the system upon which God established the terrestrial world and what is connected to it of the celestial worlds, in a firm manner into which human arbitrary decisions have no entry. It also serves to clarify the specification of the sacred months from His words: ﴿Then when the sacred months have passed﴾ [al-Tawbah: 5], after what followed that verse of detailed rulings concerning security and war with the various groups of disbelievers among the polytheists and others.

The purpose is: to fix the sacred months, and to nullify what the polytheists had introduced into them of *nasi'* (the practice of intercalation, postponing a sacred month by shifting its sanctity to another month), which corrupted their times, led to their confusion, removed the sanctity of what had sanctity among them, and conferred sanctity upon what had no sanctity.

Indeed, the fixing of timekeeping is among the foundations of establishing the order of the community and warding off chaos from its affairs.

The opening of the speech with the emphatic particle is for the sake of drawing attention to its content, so that people's ears and minds may be directed to comprehending it.

By "the months" is meant the lunar months, by the indication of the context, because they are the ones known to the Arabs and to most nations, and they are the oldest and most precise months of timekeeping among mankind, since the variation in the states of the moon
[p. 181]
helps in taking those states as markers for appointments and deadlines, and for dating past events, by mere observation. The moon is a body following the system of the earth. He, the Exalted, said: ﴿that you may know the number of years and the reckoning﴾ [Yunus: 5]. Also, relying on celestial states is more precise and further from error, because they are not subject to people's hands altering or changing them. The solar months and their year did not come into being except after the knowledge of astronomy and the calculation of times became manifest. Thus people benefited from the course of the sun in regulating the four seasons, and they made it a reckoning for timing those works which are suitable only in some seasons, such as tilling, harvesting, and the conditions of livestock. The solar reckoning was known among the Copts and the Chaldeans, and the Torah came with fixing the lunar times for the months and the solar times for the festivals. It is well known that festivals are of secondary rank among human affairs, since they relate to embellishment, whereas the regulation of months relates to necessity (*hajiyy*). So God inspired mankind, among what He inspired them with of establishing the foundations of their civilization, to adopt a system for timing their works that required timing, and to make it rest upon clear observations evident to all people, which are not hidden from them except briefly, and then soon become manifest to them in a clear and dazzling way. He also inspired them to discover indicators, among what God created for them, of a regular system. These are the stars of the sky and their stations, as He said in explaining the wisdom of that: ﴿It is He who made the sun a radiance and the moon a light and determined for it stations that you may know the number of years and the reckoning. Allah did not create that except in truth﴾ [Yunus: 5]. And they made their daily timing rest upon the appearance of the sun's light and its setting away from them, because they found it to be on a system that does not change, and because people share in observing that; by it the day and night are arranged. And they made their monthly timing begin with the first appearance of the first part of the moon, which is called the crescent (*hilal*), until the end of its disappearance (*mihaq*). Then when it returns to the same appearance as the first, that is the beginning of another month. They also arranged the degrees of the numbers of the parts of the period called the month in sequence according to the increase of the light of the illuminated half of the moon each night, and with the aid of the stations of the moon's appearance each night in line with a shape of the stars, which they called the stations (*manazil*). They found this to be on a regular system. Then He inspired them, so they observed the period in which the fruit or the pasture returned, from which they began counting, and that is the times of the four seasons. They found that it contained twelve months, so they called that period a year (*'am*). Thus the months were twelve for that reason, because whatever exceeds that returns to the same time at which they began the reckoning the first time. They named them with names to distinguish some from others, to prevent error. And they made the beginning of the years by events according to their fame
[p. 182]
among them, if they wished to do so, and that is open to them. When God wished to give people worships, seasons, and recurring festivals that occur once every year, He commanded them to make the worship at a time corresponding to the time of its counterpart. So He prescribed upon Abraham and his descendants the pilgrimage to the House every year in the twelfth month, and He made for them a respected time among them in which they would be secure for their lives and their wealth and could undertake long journeys. That is the sacred months. When all of that was achieved through the totality of Allah's, the Exalted's, ordering of the stars, His placing in them the inspiration to perceive their wisdom, the capacity to fix the regular states of them, and His specifying of the worships and works that were prescribed with their timings, all of that was willed by Him. Therefore He said: ﴿Indeed, the number of months with Allah is twelve months in the Book of Allah, the day He created the heavens and the earth.﴾

So the meaning of His words ﴿Indeed, the number of months with Allah is twelve months﴾ is that they are thus in the system upon which He established this earth, which He made the abode of mankind, with regard to the distinction of each one from the other. When it exceeds twelve, what exceeds twelve becomes similar to a counterpart of it at the time of its arrival, so it is considered a repetition of something.

"With Allah" means in His judgment and decree. So "with Allah" is a metaphor for consideration and reckoning. It is an adverbial complement governed by *'iddah* (number), or a circumstantial state (*hal*) of *'iddah*. And ﴿in the Book of Allah﴾ is a qualifier of ﴿twelve months﴾.

The meaning of ﴿in the Book of Allah﴾ is in His decree, which is the decree by which the things decreed came into existence, meaning the connection of His power to them as an effective connection, like His words: ﴿a decree, a fixed term﴾ [Al 'Imran: 145], that is, a specified measure. So *kitab* here is a verbal noun (*masdar*).

The explanation of this: when He created the moon upon that system, He willed, in His wisdom, that it be a means for reckoning time, as He said: ﴿and determined for it stations that you may know the number of years and the reckoning﴾ [Yunus: 5]. For this reason He said here ﴿the day He created the heavens and the earth.﴾ So ﴿the day﴾ is an adverbial complement of ﴿the Book of Allah﴾ in the sense of the specific decree, for when He created the heavens and the earth, this system linking the moon and the earth was among what He created.

For this reason, the earth was mentioned along with the heavens, rather than limiting it to the heavens. This is because those phenomena of the moon, by which the moon was divided into parts from its being a crescent, to its first quarter, to full moon, to its third quarter, to its disappearance, and which are the measures of the weeks, are only
[p. 183]
manifestations according to its position relative to the earth and the impression of the sun's light upon the amount visible from it to the earth. And because the stations in which it alights according to the number of nights of the month are stations of imagination, by the sight of the eye, according to its alignment with the earth from the direction of one of those masses of stars, which appear to the eye as gathered together, while in reality they have varying distances and no harmony or unity among them. And because the rising of the crescent at the same time as it rose eleven times before, from whatever time the counting of the seasons began, is only with regard to terrestrial conditions.

Therefore, the system of the lunar months and their year necessarily resulted from the totality of the system of the creation of the earth and the creation of the heavens, that is, the celestial bodies and their states in their orbits. For this reason, the earth and the heavens were mentioned together.

These months are known by their names among the Arabs, and they agreed to begin their reckoning after the season of the pilgrimage. So the start of the year for them is the appearance of the crescent after the end of the pilgrimage, which is the crescent of Muharram. Therefore, the first month of the Arab year was undoubtedly Muharram. Do you not see the words of Labid:

*"Until, when they had completed Jumada, six parts of it, so its fasting was long and their fasting [too]."*

He meant the second Jumada, and he described it with "six" because it is the sixth month of the Arab year.

Al-Jumhur (the majority of readers) read ﴿twelve﴾ (*ithna 'ashar*) with a fatha on the shin of *'ashar*, while Abu Ja'far read it *ithna 'ashar* with a sukun on the ayn of *'shar* and with an extended alif in *ithna*, lengthened fully.

The four sacred months are the ones known among them: three of them are consecutive, about which there is no disagreement among the Arabs, namely Dhu al-Qa'dah, Dhu al-Hijjah, and Muharram. The fourth is single, and it is Rajab according to the majority of the Arabs, except the tribe of Rabi'ah, who make the fourth Ramadan and call it Rajab. I suppose they describe it as the second, like Rabi' and Jumada. These are not taken into account, because they deviated, just as the tribe that used to make all the months of the year lawful was not taken into account, and that is Qudaah. The Prophet (ﷺ) clarified the general sense of this verse in his sermon at the Farewell Pilgrimage with his words: "﴿Of them, four are sacred﴾: Dhu al-Qa'dah, Dhu al-Hijjah, Muharram, and Rajab of Mudar, which is between Jumada and Sha'ban."

The sanctification of these four months is among what Allah legislated for Abraham, peace be upon him, for the benefit of people and the establishment of the pilgrimage, as He said: ﴿Allah has made the Ka'bah, the Sacred House, a means of standing for the people, and the sacred month﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 97].

Know that the preference of times and places resembles the preference of people. The preference of people is by the righteous deeds and noble character that proceed from them, and the preference of others that have no will, by the virtues that accompany them, which occur in them or are associated with them. So the preference of times and places is only by Allah's, the Exalted's, making it so, by a report from Him, or by informing about His purpose. For when Allah prefers them, He makes them the occasions for seeking His pleasure, such as being the occasions of answered supplications or multiplied good deeds, as He said: ﴿The Night of Decree is better than a thousand months﴾ [al-Qadr: 3], that is, better than worshipping for a thousand months for those nations before us. And the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "A prayer in this mosque of mine is better than a thousand prayers elsewhere, except in al-Masjid al-Haram." And Allah is the Knower of the wisdom for which one time is preferred over another and one place over another. The matters made by Allah, the Exalted, are affairs and states that Allah willed, so He decreed them, and they resemble cosmic affairs. Therefore, none nullifies them except a nullification from Allah, the Exalted, just as He nullified the sanctity of the Sabbath with Friday. It is not for people to make preferences in religious times, because the matters that people make resemble handmade products, and they have no weight except when they are intended for righteous purposes. So it is not for people to change what Allah, the Exalted, has made of virtue for times, places, or people.

﴿That is the upright religion﴾.

The reference in His words "that" is to what was mentioned: the division of the twelve months and the number of the sacred months. That is, this division is the complete religion, and whatever else is not free of either being altered or subjected to arbitrary decision, due to the specialization of some people in knowing it, with varying degrees of correctness in their knowledge.

Religion (*din*) is the system attributed to the Creator by which people are judged, meaning they are dealt with according to its laws. It was previously mentioned at His words, ﴿Indeed, the religion with Allah is Islam﴾ [Al 'Imran: 19], in the surah of Al 'Imran, just as it was described by that in His words:
[p. 185]
﴿So direct your face toward the religion, inclining to truth, the natural disposition of Allah upon which He created mankind. No change is there in the creation of Allah. That is the upright religion﴾ [al-Rum: 30].

So the fact that the number of months is twelve has been established by the original creation, by His words following it: ﴿in the Book of Allah, the day He created the heavens and the earth.﴾

Ibn 'Ashur's commentary, part 2 of 2:

That four of those months are sacred (ḥurum) was established by the legislative enactment, and this is indicated by His words immediately following: ﴿That is the upright religion﴾. From the whole of this it follows that the months being twelve, and that four of them being sacred, is regarded as part of the religion of Islam. By this, what was in the law of the Torah concerning fixing the times of the religious festivals according to the solar calendar was abrogated (naskh), and what the people of the Jahiliyyah (pre-Islamic period of ignorance) practised was nullified.

The sentence ﴿That is the upright religion﴾ is a parenthetical clause (i'tirad) placed between the sentence ﴿Indeed, the number of months﴾ and the sentence ﴿so do not wrong yourselves therein﴾.

﴿So do not wrong yourselves therein﴾

This is a consequence (tafri') of ﴿of them four are sacred﴾. Since their sanctity is among what Allah has legislated, Allah has obligated people to honour their sanctity by avoiding evil deeds in them.

The pronoun governed by (fi), namely "therein" (fihinna), refers to the four sacred months, because they are the nearest thing mentioned, and because it is more suited to the context of warning against committing wrong in them. Otherwise it would be a mere abrupt shift without relevance. Moreover, al-Kisa'i and al-Farra' claimed that the usage is that the feminine pronoun for the plural of paucity (jam' qillah), such as hunna (they), as in "therein" (fihinna) here, and the feminine pronoun for the plural of abundance (jam' kathrah), such as ha (it), are both treated as the singular, as in ﴿of them four are sacred﴾. It is well known that the plurals of non-rational things are treated as feminine singular. Al-Kisa'i said: "This is one of the wonders of Arabic usage, and for this reason they say of fewer than ten nights 'khalawna' (they have passed) and of more than ten 'khalat' (it has passed)."

It is also related from Ibn 'Abbas that he interpreted the pronoun in "fihinna" as referring to the twelve months. So the meaning in his view is: "do not wrong yourselves by acts of disobedience throughout the year," meaning that the sanctity of the religion is greater than the sanctity of the four months of the Jahiliyyah. This implies no distinction in feminine pronouns between "fiha" and "fihinna," and that the variation between them in the verse is stylistic variety (tafannun).

Wronging oneself (zulm al-nafs) is doing what Allah has forbidden and threatened for, for doing it is casting oneself into punishment, and so it is a wronging of oneself. He, exalted is He, said: ﴿And if, when they wronged themselves, they had come to you and asked Allah's forgiveness﴾ [an-Nisa': 64], and He said: ﴿And whoever does an evil or wrongs himself﴾ [an-Nisa': 110].

The word "anfus" (selves) may be understood as the selves of the wrongdoers in His words "fa-la tazlimu" (so do not wrong), meaning that each one should not wrong himself.

The reason for specifying the prohibition of sins in these months is that Allah made them appointed times (mawaqit) for worship. So if one is not engaged in worship during them, let him at least not be engaged in sins. The prohibition of sins in them does not imply that sins outside these months are not forbidden; rather, the intended meaning is that sin in them is greater and that righteous deeds in them are more rewarding. A parallel to this is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿There shall be no obscenity, no disputing during the Hajj﴾ [al-Baqarah: 197], for obscenity (fusuq) is forbidden during the Hajj and outside it.

It is also possible that wrongdoing (zulm) here means aggression (i'tida'), and the intended "selves" are the selves of those who are not wrongdoers. Its being attributed to the pronoun of the addressees serves to draw attention to the fact that the community is like a self within a body, in the manner of His saying, exalted is He: ﴿So when you enter houses, greet one another as a greeting from Allah﴾ [an-Nur: 61], meaning, upon the people who are in them, according to the more preferred of the two interpretations of that verse; and like His saying: ﴿Certainly did Allah confer [a favour] upon the believers when He sent among them a messenger from themselves﴾ [Ali 'Imran: 164]. The meaning on this view is to confirm the rule of safety (amn) in these months, that is, no one should attack another with fighting, as in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Allah has made the Ka'bah, the Sacred House, a means of stability for the people, and [also] the sacred month﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 97]. This meaning is only correct with regard to the dealings of the Muslims with the polytheists. Thus this is a confirmation of the explicit content of His saying: ﴿So travel freely in the land for four months﴾ [at-Tawbah: 2], and of the implicit meaning (mafhum) of His saying: ﴿So when the sacred months have passed, then kill the polytheists﴾ [at-Tawbah: 5]. The latter is restricted by His saying: ﴿So as long as they are upright toward you, be upright toward them﴾ [at-Tawbah: 7], and by His saying: ﴿The sacred month for the sacred month, and violations are [subject to] retribution. So whoever has assaulted you, then assault him in the same way that he has assaulted you﴾ [al-Baqarah: 194].

For this reason, the matter is not problematic regarding the Messenger's fighting against Hawazin, peace and blessings be upon him, for some days of Dhu al-Qa'dah, because they had begun fighting the Muslims before the sacred months entered. The war continued until they entered the month of Dhu al-Qa'dah, and he would not have halted the fighting when the defeat of the polytheists was near, given that they had initiated it the first time. On this interpretation, the ruling of this verse has ended with the disappearance of the polytheists from the lands of the Arabs after the Year of Delegations (sanat al-wufud).

The first interpretation of the verse was adopted by the majority (al-jumhur). The second interpretation was adopted by a group: Ibn al-Musayyab, Ibn Shihab, Qatadah and 'Ata' al-Khurasani said: the verse made fighting forbidden in the sacred months, then it was abrogated by the permission of jihad at all times. So this verse would be complementing what remained of the period of the sanctity of the sacred months, until the rule of Islam would encompass all the lands of the Arabs, through the conversion of most of the tribes and the imposition of the jizyah (poll tax) on some Arab tribes, namely the Christians and the Jews. 'Ata' ibn Abi Rabah said: raiding is forbidden in the sacred months unless the enemy begins fighting in them, and there is no abrogation in the verse.

* * *

﴿And fight against the polytheists all together as they fight against you all together. And know that Allah is with the righteous﴾

I think the position of this verse is that of a safeguard (ihtiras) against the assumption that the prohibition of violating the sacred months entails the prohibition of fighting the polytheists in them when they begin fighting the Muslims. With this the causal comparison (al-tashbih al-ta'lili) in His saying ﴿as they fight against you all together﴾ is understood. So the meaning is: do not violate the sanctity of the sacred months by sins, or by aggressing against your enemies.
