But if they initiate fighting against you, then fight them, in the manner of His saying, exalted is He: ﴿The sacred month for the sacred month, and violations are [subject to] retribution. So whoever has assaulted you, then assault him in the same way that he has assaulted you﴾ [al-Baqarah: 194]. Thus the main purpose of the speech is the command to fight the polytheists who fight the Muslims in the sacred months, with the justification that they consider those months lawful in their fighting of the Muslims.

"Kaffatan" (all together) is a word that indicates generality and comprehensiveness, equivalent to "kull" (all). Its form does not change with the change of what it emphasizes in singular, dual, or plural, nor in masculine or feminine. It seems to be derived from "kaff" (restraint), in the sense of withholding from excepting any individuals. Its position is accusative as a circumstantial qualifier (hal) of what it emphasizes. In the first case it is an emphasis of "al-mushrikin" (the polytheists), and in the second it is an emphasis of the pronoun of the addressees. The purpose of generalizing the entities is the generalization of states, since it follows from the generality of entities; that is, every group of the polytheists, whatever state they are in, and who had initiated fighting against the Muslims, the Muslims are commanded to fight them. Among this: every group that is so in the sacred months, and every group that is so in the Sacred Precinct (haram).

The kaf in "kama yuqatiluna-kum" (as they fight against you) is originally the kaf of comparison, used figuratively for causation by comparing the caused thing with its cause, since it occurs in the pattern of that cause. Among examples of this is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And remember Him as He has guided you﴾ [al-Baqarah: 198].

The sentence ﴿And know that Allah is with the righteous﴾ is an assurance and guarantee of victory when they fight the polytheists, because the "being with" here is the "being with" of support (ta'yid) in action, not the "being with" of knowledge, since the "being with" of knowledge is not restricted to the righteous.

The sentence begins with "i'lamu" (know) for the sake of emphasis on its content, as already mentioned in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And know that whatever you obtain of war booty﴾ [al-Anfal: 41], so that they must know it and retain it.

The sentence serves as a conclusion (tadhyil) to what precedes it, because of the generality contained in "al-muttaqin" (the righteous), rather than saying "and know that Allah is with you," so that the explicit noun conveys the meaning of generality. This indicates that those characterised by the state described in the preceding speech are counted among the righteous. This avoids the mention of the sentence ﴿And know that Allah is with the righteous﴾ being foreign to the context. Thus there results an independent statement that works like a proverb, and a concise expression indicating that they are at that time among the righteous, that Allah supports them for their piety, that fighting in the sacred months in that situation is obedience to Allah and piety, and that the polytheists at that time are the aggressors against the sanctity of the months, and they are the ones who compel retaliation in kind for the defence of oneself.

**Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 9, verse 37 (part 1 of 2):**

﴿Indeed, the postponement [al-nasi'] is an increase in disbelief by which those who disbelieve are led astray. They make it lawful one year and unlawful another year, to match the number of what Allah has made unlawful, so that they make lawful what Allah has made unlawful. The evil of their deeds has been made attractive to them. And Allah does not guide the disbelieving people.﴾

This is an explanatory resumption (istinaf bayani) arising from His statement, exalted is He: ﴿Indeed, the number of months with Allah﴾ [al-Tawbah: 36], and so on, because that verse serves as an introduction to the intended purpose, which is the nullification of the nasi' and the condemnation of it.

[p. 189]

The word al-nasi' (the postponement) is applied to a sacred month whose sanctity has been deferred and transferred to another month. Thus al-nasi' is a fa'il in the sense of a maf'ul, from nasa'a, a verb with a hamza as its third radical, meaning "he postponed" (akhkhara). It is also used as a verbal noun (masdar) on the pattern fa'il, like nadhir, from His statement: ﴿Then you will know how My warning was﴾ [al-Mulk: 17], and like al-nakir and al-'udhr. Its verb is nasa'a with a hamza, meaning "he postponed." So al-nasi' (with a hamza after the ya') is the commonly known reading, and it is the reading of the majority of the Ten Readers. Warsh, from Nafi', read it with a shaddah on the final ya', by softening the hamza into a ya' and assimilating it into its counterpart. The statement that the nasi' is an "increase" is a predication of the verbal noun, just as the Qur'an describes Harut and Marut with "trial" in His statement: ﴿We are only a trial﴾ [al-Baqarah: 102].

In the usage of the Arabs, al-nasi' is a postponement which they make for a sacred month, so that they render it lawful, and they make another month of the lawful months unlawful in its place during that same year.

The factor that prompted the Arabs to institute the nasi' is that their year was lunar, following the months. They therefore had twelve complete lunar months in their year, and they continued on this for long centuries. Then it occurred to them to institute the nasi'.

The best that has been related describing this is the statement of Abu Wa'il: The Arabs were people of wars and raids, and it was hard for them to remain three consecutive months without raiding in them. So they said: "If three months in succession pass over us in which we obtain nothing, we will surely perish." The commentators have remained silent about what arose after this statement of the Arabs. What occurred in some of what al-Tabari and al-Qurtubi related gives the impression that the first person to institute the nasi' for them was Junada ibn 'Awf, but this is not the case, because Junada ibn 'Awf lived to see Islam, whereas the matter of the nasi' is ancient. What must be relied upon is that the first person to institute the nasi' was Hudhayfah ibn 'Abd Nu'aym or Fuqaym. Perhaps "Nu'aym" is a distortion of "Fuqaym," in reference to the statement of Ibn 'Atiyya that the name Nu'aym is not known for this. He was known by the nickname al-Qalammas. The Banu Fuqaym are not mentioned in the Jamharat of Ibn Hazm, but the author of the Qamus and Ibn 'Atiyya mention them. Ibn Hazm said: The first to postpone the months was Sarir (thus, but perhaps it is Sari) ibn Tha'labah ibn al-Harith ibn Malik ibn Kinanah, then his nephew 'Adiyy ibn 'Amir ibn Tha'labah. Ibn 'Atiyya has a different account on this. He said: al-Qalammas, who is Hudhayfah ibn 'Abd Fuqaym, undertook the task and instituted the postponement of the months for them.

[p. 190]

Then his son 'Abbad succeeded him, then his son Qal', then his son Umayyah, then his son 'Awf, then his son Abu Thumamah Junada, and upon him Islam arrived. Ibn 'Atiyya said: The Banu Fuqaym were people of religion among the Arabs and adherents of the law of Ibrahim. From among them al-Qalammas, who is Hudhayfah ibn 'Abd Fuqaym, undertook the task and instituted the postponement of the months for the Arabs. In the tafsir of al-Qurtubi, on the authority of al-Dahhak, on the authority of Ibn 'Abbas: The first to institute the postponement was 'Amr ibn Luhayy (i.e., the one who introduced the worship of idols among the Arabs, who slit the ears of the she-camel [bahirah] and let loose the free camel [sa'ibah]). Al-Kalbi said: The first to institute it was a man from the Banu Kinanah called Nu'aym ibn Tha'labah.

Ibn Hazm said: Everyone who came to hold this position, namely the position of the nasi', was called al-Qalammas. Al-Qurtubi said: The one who held the office of the nasi' would gain leadership, because the Arabs gave him that status. Al-Qalammas used to stand at the Jamrat al-'Aqabah and say: "O Allah, I am the postponer of the months, and the one who places them in their positions, and I am not blamed and I am not answered. O Allah, I have made lawful one of the two Safars, and I have made unlawful the delayed Safar. Set forth in the name of Allah, exalted is He." The last of the postponers was Junada ibn 'Awf, who was called Abu Thumamah. He was a man of opinion among them, and he used to attend the season (mawsim) on his donkey, and he would call out: "O people, indeed Abu Thumamah is not blamed and is not answered, and there is no refuting what he says." Then they would say: "Postpone for us a month," meaning: delay from us the sanctity of the Muharram and place it in Safar. So he made the Muharram lawful for them and would call out: "Indeed your gods have made Safar sacred this year." So they would make it sacred that year. When they performed the Hajj in Dhu al-Hijjah, they would abandon the Muharram and call it Safar. Then when Dhu al-Hijjah ended, they would go out in the (new) Muharram, and they would fight in it, raid and take booty, because it had become Safar. Thus in that year they would have two Safars. In the following year, Dhu al-Hijjah would become, for them, Dhu al-Qa'dah, and the Muharram would become Dhu al-Hijjah. So they would perform the Hajj in the Muharram. They would do this for two consecutive years. Then they would change, and perform the Hajj in the month of Safar for two years in succession, and so on.

Al-Suhayli said in al-Rawd al-Unuf: "The postponement of some months after a period was for the purpose of postponing the Hajj from its lunar time, in an effort by them to match the solar year. They would postpone it every year by eleven days or a little more, until the cycle returned after thirty-three years, and then it would return to its proper time." It is related of his teacher Abu Bakr ibn al-'Arabi that this was a consideration on their part of the non-Arab (ajami) months. Perhaps he followed in this the statement of Iyas ibn Mu'awiyah which al-Qurtubi mentions, but I think this is a confusion.

[p. 191]

The nasi' was in the hands of the Banu Fuqaym of Kinanah, and the first to postpone the months was Hudhayfah ibn 'Abd ibn Fuqaym.

The approximate time when the practice of the nasi' began was at the end of the third century before the Hijrah, that is, around the year two hundred and twenty before the Hijrah.

The form of restriction (qasr) in His statement: ﴿Indeed, the postponement is an increase in disbelief﴾ requires that it is nothing more than an effect of disbelief, arising from the love of aggression and raids. This is a true restriction (qasr haqiqi). And it follows from its being an increase in disbelief that those who devised it were none other than disbelievers, and they were not reformers. Likewise, those who followed them were none other than disbelievers, and they were not pious.

The reason it is disbelief is that they know that Allah prescribed the Hajj for them and fixed its time to one of the lunar months, which are counted and named with names that distinguish them from confusion. When they devised the nasi', they knew that they were placing some months out of their proper position and naming them by other than their names, and they were coinciding the performance of the Hajj with a month other than the specified one, namely the month of Dhu al-Hijjah. For this reason they called it al-nasi', a name derived from the root of al-nasa', which means postponement. Thus they acknowledged that it is the postponement of something from its time, and in doing so they treated the law of Allah, exalted is He, lightly, and opposed what He set for them, deliberately, establishing the lawfulness of a sacred month and the sanctity of a month that is not sacred. That is audacity against the religion of Allah and treating it lightly. Therefore this resembles their making partners for Allah. Just as they made partners for Allah in divinity, they made, from themselves, partners for Allah in legislation, opposing Him in what He legislated. So by this consideration it is like disbelief. The verse therefore contains no proof that evil deeds necessitate disbelief in their doer. Rather, the disbelief of these people is what made their deed false.

The letter fi (in) here indicates location (zarfiyyah) and is connected to ziyadah (increase), because ziyadah is transitive with fi, as in: ﴿He adds to creation what He wills﴾ [Fatir: 1]. Increase in physical bodies necessitates that the increase inhere in a body that resembles a container. It is also possible that its interpretation is: since its introduction was among the actions of the polytheists in matters of their religion, and since it involved the nullification of the times of the Hajj and the sanctity of the sacred month, it was regarded as an increase in disbelief, meaning in the actions of disbelief, even though in itself it is disbelief. This is like what the early generations (al-salaf) say: "Faith increases and decreases." They mean by this that it increases with the increase of righteous deeds and decreases with their decrease, along with the firm conviction that the reality (mahiyyah) of faith neither increases nor decreases.

[p. 192]

This is like His statement, exalted is He: ﴿And Allah would not let your faith go to waste﴾ [al-Baqarah: 143], meaning: your prayer. Moreover, applying the name "faith" to the deeds of the religion of Islam and applying the name "disbelief" to the deeds of the Jahiliyyah is something that pervades the statements of the Book and the Sunnah, along with the agreement of the majority of the scholars of the Ummah that deeds other than belief do not necessitate faith or disbelief.

On the second possibility, the interpretation is by supposing an omitted genitive construction (mudaf), meaning: an increase in the conditions of the people of disbelief, that is, a matter of error added to what they already have of disbelief. This is the opposite of His statement, exalted is He: ﴿And Allah increases in guidance those who are guided﴾ [Maryam: 76]. These two interpretations are close to each other, with no real disagreement between them except in terms of perspective. The first interpretation implies that the use of "disbelief" here is a metonymy (majaz mursal), while the second implies that the use of "disbelief" here is a concision by omission (ijaz al-hadhf), by supposing an omitted genitive construction.

The clause ﴿by which those who disbelieve are led astray﴾ is a second predicate about the nasi', meaning: it is a continuous error, because of the continuity implied by the present tense verb.

The clause ﴿They make it lawful one year and unlawful another year﴾ is an explanation of the reason why it is an error.

The present tense was chosen for these verbs because it indicates renewal and continuity, meaning: they are in a renewed and continuous error, through the renewal of its cause, which is its being made lawful at one time and unlawful at another, and the matching of the number of what Allah has made unlawful.

Attributing the error to "those who disbelieve" implies that the nasi' was a practice widespread among all the polytheistic Arabs. What is related in the tafsir of al-Tabari on the authority of Ibn 'Abbas and al-Dahhak, that they said: "Hawazin, Ghatafan and the Banu Sulaym used to do it and glorify it," does not mean that it was exclusive to them, but rather that they began to follow it first.

Al-Jumhur read yadill (with a fatha on the ya'), while Hafs on the authority of 'Asim, Hamzah, al-Kisa'i, Khalaf and Ya'qub read yudillu (with a damma on the ya'), meaning that they cause others to go astray.

The indefiniteness and singularity in His statement "'aman" in both places are for the sense of type (nau'iyyah), meaning: they make it lawful in some years and unlawful in some years. It is like the singularity in the statement of the poet:

"One day at Huzwa, and another day at al-'Aqiq."

It does not mean that this is one day after another, and likewise in the verse it does not mean that the nasi' occurs every other year, as some commentators have supposed. A similar example is the statement of Abu al-Tayyib:

"One day with horses that drive the Romans away from them, and another day with generosity that drives away poverty and drought."

(He means: at times it repels the enemy from them, and at times it repels from them poverty and drought.) This happens only when the enemy descends upon them and poverty and drought strike their lands. For this reason al-Ma'arri explained it in the book Mu'jiz Ahmad by saying: "If the Romans intend to attack them, you repel them with your horses, and if poverty and drought befall them, you lift it from them by your generosity and bounty."

The speech has been left general (mujmal), since explaining the manner in which the nasi' was practiced is not the aim in this context, and perhaps they had various manners of it which were known to the listeners.

The point of blame lies in what happens in the practice of the nasi': the changing of the appointed times of the Hajj set by Allah, to other days, over many years, and the changing of the sanctity of some of the sacred months over many years. The statement ﴿so that they match the number of what Allah has made unlawful﴾ is connected to the statement ﴿they make it lawful one year and unlawful another year﴾, meaning: they do this in order to conform to the number of the sacred months, so that four remain.

Al-mu'awatah (matching) means conformity. It is a form of mufa'alah derived from al-wati' (treading). It likens the equivalence in quantity and in action to conformity and the treading of feet. From this comes their saying: "the hoof falling upon the hoof."

And ﴿the number of what Allah has made unlawful﴾ is the number of the four sacred months.

This passage clearly reads as an excuse and a kind of justification from them, so it does not fit in the context of condemning their deeds and rebuking them. Rather, he mentioned it so that he could build on it the statement: ﴿so that they make lawful what Allah has forbidden﴾. For their attempt to match the number of what Allah has forbidden entails that they make lawful what Allah has forbidden. This is a demonstration of the corruption and confusion of their religion. They preserve the number of the sacred months, which has no added significance in the religion and is merely a number subordinate to the determination of the sacred months, while they neglect the sanctity itself, making the sacred month lawful and then inventing another falsehood by making a permitted month forbidden. Thus they preserved the number and corrupted what is numbered.

[p. 194]

The grammatical basis for coordinating ﴿fa-yuhillū﴾ (so that they make lawful) with the genitive of the purpose particle in his statement ﴿li-yuwāṭi'ū ʿiddata mā ḥarrama Allāh﴾ (to match the number of what Allah has forbidden) is the treatment of an outcome that follows from a cause as if it were the intended purpose of the causal clause, even when the person doing the act did not intend it as a cause. This is in the manner of sarcasm and censure, like His statement, exalted is He: ﴿Then the family of Pharaoh picked him up, so that he would become for them an enemy and a grief﴾ (al-Qasas: 8).

The use of the relative pronoun in his statement ﴿ʿiddata mā ḥarrama Allāh﴾, rather than expressing it as something like "the number of the sacred months", indicates the cause of their action in their own belief: that they were preserving the number of the months that Allah forbade, out of reverence. Therefore there is an allusion to sarcasm toward them.

The use of the explicit noun in his statement ﴿fa-yuhillū mā ḥarrama Allāh﴾, rather than saying "fa-yuhillūhu", serves to add emphasis in recording the ugliness of their action, which is their opposition to Allah's command and their nullifying the sanctity of some of the sacred months, a sanctity for whose sake they claimed to make some permitted months forbidden, in order to preserve the number of the months that Allah has forbidden.

The clause ﴿Zuyyina lahum sūʾu aʿmālihim﴾ (The evil of their deeds was made attractive to them) is a resumptive clause (istiʾnāf bayānī, an explanatory resumption), because what has been described of the disorder of their condition provokes the question of the questioners about the cause of this mass of error with which they have filled themselves. So it was said: "Because the evil of their deeds was made attractive to them," that is, because Satan made the evil of their deeds attractive to them and made the ugly seem good to them.

Tazyīn (embellishment) is tahsīn (making something beautiful), that is, making a thing into an adornment. It therefore attributes to something whose reality does not change that it does not become good, which indicates that the making-beautiful is a form of disguising. Tazyīn has already been mentioned in His statement, exalted is He: ﴿The life of this world was made attractive to those who disbelieved﴾ (al-Baqarah: 212) in Surat al-Baqarah, and in His statement: ﴿Thus We made attractive to every community their deeds﴾ (al-Anʿam: 108) in Surat al-Anʿam.

In this resumption there is the sense of giving a reason for their strange condition, so that the listener's wonder at it may cease.

The clause ﴿Wa-Allāhu lā yahdī al-qawm al-kāfirīn﴾ (And Allah does not guide the disbelieving people) is coordinated with the clause ﴿Zuyyina lahum sūʾu aʿmālihim﴾, so it is included in the meaning of the explanatory resumption, whose purpose is to give the reason for that strange state. For wonder at that state entails wonder at their persistence in their error and their failure to be guided to the disorder in their conduct, so that they might abandon their error. So after the questioner was informed that the cause of that disorder is Satan's making the evil of their deeds attractive to them, he was informed that their persistence in it is because Allah withheld from them the kindness and success by which the misguided person perceives his error and abandons it, as a recompense for the disbelief they had committed; so they continued in the depths of error to the utmost extent.

The use of the explicit noun in place of the pronoun, in his statement ﴿al-qawm al-kāfirīn﴾, is intended to convey a generality that includes them and others; that is, this is Allah's way with all disbelievers.

Know that the sanctity of times and places is only received from divine revelation, because Allah, who created this world, is the One who lays down its order. Thereby the sanctity of every sacred thing becomes firmly established in the souls of all people, since there is no action in this matter for some of them over others. When alteration is introduced into what Allah has established in this regard, the sanctity dissipates from souls, and no group is satisfied with what another group has set up. For this reason al-nasīʾ (the intercalation of months) was an increase in disbelief, because it is among the arrangements that people have agreed upon, just as they agreed upon the worship of idols through the instruction of ʿAmr ibn Luhayy.

Allah revealed to His Messenger ﷺ that in the year in which he performs the pilgrimage, the Day of the Pilgrimage falls on the ninth of Dhū al-Ḥijjah, according to the reckoning that runs from the day Allah created the heavens and the earth, and that in it the effect of al-nasīʾ is nullified. Therefore the Prophet ﷺ said in the sermon of the Farewell Pilgrimage: "Indeed time has returned to its form on the day Allah created the heavens and the earth." They said: The pilgrimage of Abū Bakr in the year nine happened to fall in the month of Dhū al-Qaʿdah according to the reckoning of al-nasīʾ, so the pilgrimage of the Prophet ﷺ came in the month of Dhū al-Ḥijjah according to the reckoning that Allah established on the day He created the heavens and the earth.

This is the beginning of an address to the believers, urging them to fight in the cause of God by way of reproach for their slowness in answering the call to march forth (*nafir*) to jihad. The intended event is the expedition of Tabuk. Ibn 'Atiyya said: "There is no disagreement among the scholars that this verse was revealed as a rebuke to those who stayed behind from the expedition of Tabuk, when tribes and some of the believers, as well as the hypocrites, remained behind."

The discourse is connected to God's words, ﴿Fight the polytheists all together﴾ [al-Tawbah: 36], and to His words, ﴿Fight those who do not believe in God nor in the Last Day﴾ [al-Tawbah: 29], up to His words, ﴿Taste what you used to hoard﴾ [al-Tawbah: 35], as I have indicated in the commentary on those verses. This address is directed to those among whom sluggishness had occurred. The Messenger of God ﷺ had called the Muslims to that expedition, and it took place in a time of intense heat, facing a long journey and a desert crossing, when the fruits had ripened and the shade was pleasant. The Muslims at that time were in dire need of mounts and provisions. For this reason the expedition was named "the expedition of hardship" (*ghazwat al-'Usrah*), as will come in this surah. The Messenger of God then made his affair clear to the Muslims so that they might prepare the readiness of their enemy, and he informed them of the direction he intended. Before that, whenever he wished to undertake an expedition, he would use allusion (*tawriyah*), indicating a place other than the one intended. So some of the Muslims showed sluggishness, and some of them stayed behind. God therefore directed this blame at them, followed by a warning.

If we proceed on the view that the surah was revealed all at once, and that this happened after the expedition of Tabuk, as is the more likely opinion and the view of the majority of exegetes, then the meaning of this verse is that it is a rebuke for what had already passed. In that case, the word *idhā* (when) is used as a time adverb referring to the past, contrary to its most common usage, as in His words, ﴿And when they see trade or amusement, they scatter toward it﴾ [al-Jumu'ah: 11], and His words, ﴿Nor is there blame upon those who came to you that you might provide them mounts, and you said, "I cannot find anything"﴾ [al-Tawbah: 92], and so on. His words, ﴿What is the matter with you that you do not fight in the cause of God?﴾ [al-Nisa': 75], are suitable for conveying this meaning and for warning against returning to it, because His words, ﴿Unless you march forth﴾ [al-Tawbah: 39], and ﴿Unless you support him﴾ [al-Tawbah: 40], and ﴿March forth, light and heavy﴾ [al-Tawbah: 41], refer to what is to come, when they are called to another expedition. We will explain this in detail in its place among the verses.

If, however, we follow the view attributed by Ibn 'Atiyya to al-Naqqash, that His words, ﴿O you who believe, what is the matter with you that when it is said to you, "March forth in the cause of God," you cling heavily to the earth?﴾ are the first verse revealed from Surat Bara'ah, then the verse was a rebuke for laziness and heaviness that had appeared among some people. In that case, *idhā* is a time adverb referring to the future, as is its usual function, and His words, ﴿Unless you march forth, He will punish you with a painful punishment﴾ [al-Tawbah: 39], are a warning against abandoning departure to the expedition of Tabuk. All of this is far from what is established in the biography (*sirah*) and from what is preponderant concerning the revelation of this surah.

The "mā" in His words, "mā lakum" (what is the matter with you), is an interrogative of disapproval, meaning "what thing," and "lakum" (for you) is the predicate of the interrogative, meaning: what thing has been established for you?

*Idhā* is an adverbial of time governed by the meaning of the disapproving interrogative, in the sense that the disapproval is present at that time when they were told, "March forth." It does not carry the meaning of a conditional, because it is a time adverb of past tense.

The clause "ithaqaltum" (you cling heavily) is in the position of a circumstantial clause (*hal*) relating to the pronoun of the group, and this state is the object of the disapproval, meaning: what is the matter with you being heavy [in movement]? One says *mā laka fa'alta kadhā* (what is the matter with you that you did such-and-such), and *mā laka taf'alu kadhā*, as in His words, ﴿What is the matter with you that you do not help one another?﴾ [al-Saffat: 25], and *mā laka fā'ilan*, as in His words, ﴿Why have you become two groups concerning the hypocrites?﴾ [al-Nisa': 88].

*Al-nafr* (marching forth) is quick departure from one place to another for an event that occurs, and it is most commonly applied to going out to war. Its verbal noun in this case is *al-nafir*.

*Sabil Allah* (the way of God) means jihad. It was so named because it is like the path leading to God, that is, to His good pleasure.

*Ithaqaltum* originally was *tathaqaltum*. The *ta'* was changed to a *thā'* because the two articulation points are close, for the sake of assimilation (*idghām*). A hamzat al-wasl was added because it is possible to make the first letter of the word quiescent when it is assimilated.

*Al-tathaqul* (heaviness) is the affectation of heaviness, that is, displaying that one is heavy and unable to rise.

*Al-thiql* (heaviness) is a state in the body that requires intense pulling toward descending and difficulty in moving. It is used here metaphorically, by way of *majaz mursal*, to mean slowness. In this there is an implicit suggestion that their slowness is not from incapacity, but from attachment to remaining in their lands and possessions.

The verb *tathaqul* is followed by *ilā* (to) because it is taken to include the meaning of inclination and clinging, as if it were a heaviness whose doer seeks to reach the earth to sit and settle upon it.

*Al-ard* (earth) is that upon which people walk.

The whole of His words, ﴿you cling heavily to the earth﴾, is a figurative representation of the state of those who dislike fighting and seek excuses to avoid jihad out of laziness and cowardice, by comparison with the state of one who is asked to rise and go forth, and who responds to that request by clinging to the earth and settling down, refusing to rise, let alone to travel.

His words, ﴿to the earth﴾, form a wonderful phrase, because their slowness regarding the expedition and their seeking of excuses had as its greatest motive their desire to remain in their orchards and fruit trees. So some exegetes made the meaning of ﴿you cling heavily to the earth﴾ to be: you inclined toward your land and your homes.

The interrogative in His words, ﴿Are you pleased with the life of this world?﴾ is one of disapproval and reproach, since that does not befit believers.

*Min* in His words, ﴿instead of the Hereafter﴾ is for substitution (*badal*), meaning: how can you be pleased with the life of this world in place of the Hereafter? Such a thing is not to be accepted. By "the life of this world" and "the Hereafter" what is meant is their benefits. When they sought to stay behind from jihad, they preferred comfort in this world over the reward attained by the fighters in the Hereafter.

The verb *radītum* (you were pleased) was chosen rather than something like *āthartum* (you preferred) or *faddaltum* (you favored), for the sake of emphasis in the disapproval, because the verb (*radiya bi-kadhā*, to be pleased with such-and-such) indicates the expansion of the soul. From this is the saying of Abu Bakr al-Siddiq in the hadith of the cave: "So he drank until I was satisfied" (*fa-shariba hattā radītu*).

*Al-matā'* (enjoyment) is the verbal noun of *tamatta'a*, so it means delight and luxury, as in His words, ﴿as an enjoyment for you and your cattle﴾ [al-Nazi'at: 33]. Describing it as *qalīl* (little) means weak and base. The word "little" is used metaphorically for trivial.

It is possible that *al-matā'* here refers to the thing enjoyed, by the usage of a verbal noun for the object, as *al-khalq* means "the created thing." In that case, describing it as "little" is literal.

The particle *fī* in His words, "fī al-ākhirah" (in the Hereafter), indicates the meaning of comparison. The grammarians have made comparison one of the meanings of *fī*, as in *al-Tashīl* and *al-Mughnī*, and they cited this verse as evidence, following *al-Kashshāf*. Their commentators did not discuss this meaning, nor did the commentators of *al-Kashshāf*. A similar usage occurs in the Qur'an, such as His words in Surat al-Ra'd, ﴿And the life of this world, in comparison with the Hereafter, is nothing but enjoyment﴾ [al-Ra'd: 26]. Also, the Prophet ﷺ said in the hadith of Muslim: "The world, in comparison with the Hereafter, is only like what one of you dips his finger into the sea and then looks to see what it brings back." In reality, this is the figurative sense of *min* (from) of place (*zarfiyyah majaziyyah*): that is, the enjoyment of the life of this world, when placed alongside the goods of the Hereafter, is little in comparison with the abundance of the Hereafter's goods. Thus it follows that its littleness becomes apparent only when it is measured against great goods and related to them. Therefore, the correct view is that comparison is a meaning arrived at through the use of the particle of place, not a meaning that the particle *fī* was coined to express.

[Page 199]

﴿Unless you go forth, He will punish you with a painful punishment and replace you with another people, and you will not harm Him at all. And Allah is over all things competent.﴾

This is a warning and a threat, following the preceding reproach, because the reproach was directed at a sluggishness that had already occurred. Since that sluggishness was leading to staying behind from fighting, the warning and threat were stated explicitly, in case they return to the same sluggishness. Thus it relates to the future, as the conditional particle requires. The sentence is therefore a resumptive sentence (isti'naf) serving the purpose of rebuke after reproach.

If this is a warning, then it implies that the departure of the addressees to the jihad to which the Messenger ﷺ summoned them has become obligatory upon each of them individually, such that some cannot substitute for others. That is, the obligation has become fixed upon them (ta'yin al-wujub). This fixing may be due to the Messenger ﷺ's specific designation of them to depart in response to the general call to mobilize (al-nafir al-'amm), or it may be due to the large number of the enemy against whom they were summoned to fight, such that the departure of all capable Muslims became obligatory, because the enemy army was twice the number of the Muslim army.

It is reported from Ibn 'Abbas that this ruling is abrogated (mansukh), abrogated (naskh) by His saying, exalted is He: ﴿The believers should not all go forth [to battle]. Why should there not go forth from every division of them a group [remaining behind] to obtain understanding in the religion?﴾ [al-Tawbah: 122]. Thus, jihad had previously been subject to the ruling of individual obligation (fard 'ayn), and then it was transferred to collective obligation (fard kifaya).

This is based on the premise that the intended meaning of "a painful punishment" in His saying ﴿He will punish you with a painful punishment﴾ is the punishment of the Hereafter, as is customary in the use of the term "punishment" and its description as "painful." It has also been said that the intended meaning of "a painful punishment" is the punishment of this world, as in His saying: ﴿that Allah should afflict you with a punishment from Him or by our hands﴾ [al-Tawbah: 52]. In that case the verse contains no proof that this jihad was obligatory upon each individual. Rather, Allah threatened them that, if they did not comply with the command of the Messenger ﷺ, He would afflict them with a punishment in this world. The statement then becomes a threat (tahdid), not a warning (wa'id). This view may be preferred because the verse is linked to worldly consequences in His saying: ﴿and replace you with another people﴾. Worldly punishments are calamities that follow from neglecting the causes of success, especially failing to heed the advice of the Messenger ﷺ, as happened to them on the day of Uhud. The intended meaning is thus a threat that, if they hold back from the call to mobilize, the enemy will attack them in their homes, destroy them completely, and Allah will bring a people other than them.

[Page 200]

Al-ALim (al-'Alim, "the painful") means "the one who causes pain" (al-mu'lim). It is a form of fa'il derived from the quadriliteral root, contrary to analogy, as in His saying: ﴿Those are the verses of the wise Book﴾ [Yunus: 1], and in the verse of 'Amr ibn Ma'd Yakrib:

"Did you depart from Rayhana, the caller who hears?"

i.e., the one who makes [others] hear.

In the mushafs (codices), the word written after "illa" in ﴿illa tanfiru﴾ is written with a hamza followed by a lam and alif, following the manner of its pronunciation as assimilated (mudghama). Analogically, it should be written as (in la) with a nun after the hamza, then lam and alif.

The concealed pronoun in "yu'adhdhibkum" refers to Allah, since He was mentioned earlier in His saying: ﴿in the way of Allah﴾ [al-Tawbah: 38]. The indefiniteness of "qawman" (a people) is for generality (nau'iyya), since these people have no specific identity, as it is contingent upon the condition of not mobilizing, and they had in fact mobilized when summoned, except for a small number, who were those left behind.

(Wa-yastabdil) means "yubaddil" (He will replace). The sin and ta' are for emphasis. The substitute (badal) is what is taken as an alternative, as in His saying: ﴿And whoever exchanges disbelief for faith﴾ [al-Baqarah: 108], i.e., and He will replace you with others.

The pronoun in (tadurruhu) refers to what the pronoun in (yu'adhdhibkum) refers to, and the waw is for the circumstantial clause (hal). That is: (He will punish you and replace) a people other than you, in a state where you do not harm Allah at all by your staying behind. That is, harm will befall you, but harm will not reach the One who summoned you in His way. The statement thus takes on the force of restriction (hasr), as if it were said: "Unless you go forth, you will harm none but yourselves."

The clause ﴿And Allah is over all things competent﴾ is a concluding statement (tadhyil) for the discourse, because it confirms the content of harm befalling them, since He is competent over them as part of all things, and it confirms the absence of harm reaching Him, since He is competent over all things, so that the things capable of causing harm are included.

**Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on Surah 9, verse 40 (part 1 of 2)**

﴿If you do not support him, Allah had already supported him when those who disbelieved drove him out, the second of two. When they were both in the cave, he said to his companion, "Do not grieve; indeed Allah is with us."﴾

This is an explanatory resumption (istinaf bayani, a new clause that answers a question the previous statement may raise) to His saying: ﴿And they will not harm Him at all, and Allah is competent over all things﴾ (At-Tawbah 9:39). The negation that their staying behind from the expedition harms Allah and His Messenger prompts a question in the listener's mind about how victory could be achieved without a helper. So He clarifies that Allah supports him just as He supported him when he was the second of two, with no army with him. The One who supported him when he was the second of two is capable of supporting him, even though he was in a great army. Thus it becomes clear that their staying behind from the expedition does not harm Allah at all.

The pronoun object of ﴿تَنْصُرُوهُ﴾ (you support him) refers to the Prophet (ﷺ), even though he has not been previously mentioned, because it is clear from the context.

The clause ﴿فَقَدْ نَصَرَهُ اللَّهُ﴾ (Allah had already supported him) is the answer to the conditional. It is made the answer because it serves as evidence for the meaning of the implied answer, since it carries the sense of a cause for the omitted answer. The content of ﴿فَقَدْ نَصَرَهُ اللَّهُ﴾ has already occurred in the past, so it cannot be the answer to a conditional that refers to the future. Therefore the sense is: "If you do not support him, he is independent of your support, by the support of Allah for him, since He supported him at a time when there was with him only one person by whom there could be no victory. Just as He supported him on that day, He will support him when you do not support him." The explanation of this support will come later in the passage, in His saying: ﴿So Allah sent down His tranquility upon him and supported him with hosts you did not see﴾ and the verse that follows.

﴿إذْ أخْرَجَهُ﴾ (when they drove him out) is connected to ﴿نَصَرَهُ﴾ (supported him), meaning at the time of the disbelievers' expulsion of him from Makkah. What is meant is his emigration (hijrah). The expulsion is attributed to those who disbelieved because they were its cause: they schemed to drive him out more than once, as He said: ﴿And [remember] when those who disbelieved plotted against you to restrain you, or kill you, or expel you﴾ (Al-Anfal 8:30). It was also because they harmed him and oppressed him regarding his calling to the religion, and oppressed the Muslims with harm and boycott. So the causes of his departure were fulfilled, but they were nevertheless hesitant to let him leave, fearing that the matter of Islam would become manifest among another people. Therefore in the end they were determined to prevent him from leaving. They stationed people to watch him, tried to send riders after him in order to bring him back to them, and offered a generous reward to whoever would capture him, as occurs in the hadith of Suraqah ibn Ju'shum.

In the mushafs, the word ﴿إلّا﴾ in His saying ﴿إلّا تَنْصُرُوهُ﴾ (If you do not support him) is written with a hamzah followed by a lam and alif, according to the way it is pronounced when assimilated. The analogical spelling would be (إنْ لا), with a hamzah, a nun, then a lam and alif, because they are two particles: (إنْ) the conditional particle and (لا) the negative particle. However, the orthography of the Mushaf is a followed tradition, and in the first century there were no agreed rules of orthography. Similarly, ﴿إلّا تَفْعَلُوهُ تَكُنْ فِتْنَةٌ في الأرْضِ﴾ (Al-Anfal 8:73) was written in the same way in Surat al-Anfal. They also wrote His saying ﴿بَلْ رانَ﴾ (Nay, but rust has covered) (Al-Mutaffifin 83:14) in Surat al-Mutaffifin with a lam after the ba' and a ra' after it, and they did not write it with a shaddah-marked ba' and ra' after it.

The writing of ﴿إلّا تَنْصُرُوهُ﴾ in this form in the Mushaf has caused concern lest someone suppose that ﴿إلّا﴾ is the particle of exception. Ibn Hisham said in Mughni al-Labib: "A note: this is not among the categories of (إلّا). The (إلّا) in such a phrase as ﴿إلّا تَنْصُرُوهُ فَقَدْ نَصَرَهُ اللَّهُ﴾ is not of that kind; rather, these are two words: (إنْ), the conditional particle, and (لا), the negative particle. It is strange that Ibn Malik, despite his eminence, mentioned it in his commentary on al-Tashil among the categories of (إلّا), and al-Damamini did not follow him in his three commentaries on the Mughni, nor did al-Shumunni." Shaykh Muhammad al-Rassa' said in his book Al-Jami' al-Gharib li-Tartib Ayat Mughni al-Labib: "I have seen one of the scholars of the eastern lands of our age, among those who studied the commentary on this book (i.e., al-Tashil), beginning to excuse Ibn Malik; but in fairness there is some difficulty in it." Shaykh Muhammad al-Amir said in his gloss on the Mughni: "What is in the commentary on al-Tashil is not an explicit statement on this, and it gives that impression, for he defined the exceptive (al-mustathna) as the excluded element by means of (إلّا), and said: 'I excluded from (إلّا) the meaning of (إنْ لا), and gave the verse as an example', i.e., there is no exclusion in it." I say: the wording of the text of al-Tashil is: "The exceptive is that which is excluded, actually or by implication, from something stated or omitted, by means of (إلا) or what has its meaning." Its commentator al-Muradi did not touch upon this, nor did his commentator al-Damamini, on what he excluded in his commentary, and we have not found the commentary of Ibn Malik on his al-Tashil. In my view, what prompted Ibn Malik to make this exclusion is what occurred to al-Azhari when he said: "(إلّا) is sometimes an exception, and sometimes a conditional particle; its origin is (إنْ لا)," as quoted by the author of Lisan al-'Arab. Such a statement from someone of his standing calls for a warning about it.

﴿ثانِيَ اثْنَيْنِ﴾ (the second of two) is a circumstantial accusative (hal) from the object pronoun in ﴿أخْرَجَهُ﴾. The "second" (al-thani) is anyone by whom the number becomes two. So "second" is an active participle which is added to "two" in the sense of (مِن), i.e., second from two. The two are the Prophet (ﷺ) and Abu Bakr, by the mass-transmitted report and the consensus of all Muslims. Because the second was known to all the listeners, there was no need to mention him. Also, the intention is to magnify this support despite the small number.

The (إذْ) in His saying ﴿إذْ هُما في الغارِ﴾ (when they were both in the cave) is an apposition (badal) of the (إذْ) in His saying ﴿إذْ أخْرَجَهُ﴾ (when they drove him out). So it is one time in which the expulsion occurred, considering the departure and the being in the cave.

The definite article in ﴿الغارِ﴾ (the cave) is for previous reference, to a cave known to the addressees. It is the one in which the Prophet (ﷺ) and Abu Bakr hid when they set out as emigrants toward Madinah. It is a cave in Mount Thawr, outside Makkah to its south, about five miles from Makkah, on a mountainous path. A (غار) is a hollow in the earth or the rock.

The (إذْ) added to the clause ﴿يَقُولُ﴾ (he said) is an apposition (badal) of the (إذْ) added to the clause ﴿هُما في الغارِ﴾, an apposition of inclusion (badal ishtimal).

The companion (al-sahib) is the ﴿ثانِيَ اثْنَيْنِ﴾, namely Abu Bakr al-Siddiq. The meaning of "companion" is one characterized by companionship (suhbah), which in most circumstances is accompaniment; from it the wife is called a companion (sahibah), as was mentioned earlier in His saying: ﴿He will not have a companion (sahibah)﴾ (Al-An'am 6:101) in Surat al-An'am. This statement came from the Prophet (ﷺ) to Abu Bakr when they were hiding in the cave of Thawr. Abu Bakr was grieving out of concern for the Prophet (ﷺ) lest the polytheists perceive him and harm him, or return him to Makkah.

The accompaniment here is the accompaniment of help and care, as Allah related of Musa and Harun: ﴿He said, "Do not fear; indeed I am with you both"﴾ (Ta-Ha 20:46), and His saying: ﴿When your Lord inspired the angels, "Indeed I am with you"﴾ (Al-Anfal 8:12).

* * *

﴿So Allah sent down His tranquility upon him and supported him with hosts you did not see, and made the word of those who disbelieved the lowest; and the word of Allah is the highest; and Allah is Mighty and Wise.﴾

The fa' of sequence (tafri') indicates that the tranquility was sent down immediately after settling in the cave, and that it is part of the support. For it is a spiritual support, whereas the support with hosts not seen was a physical support. It does not follow that the sending down of tranquility came immediately after His saying: ﴿Do not grieve; indeed Allah is with us﴾. Rather, that saying is among the effects of the tranquility of Allah which was sent down upon him, and that tranquility is a manifestation of the support of Allah for him. So the sense of the sentence would be: "Allah had already supported him, so He sent down tranquility upon him and supported him with hosts when they drove him out, and when he was in the cave, and when he said to his companion: 'Do not grieve; indeed Allah is with us.'" These three time-expressions are connected to the verb ﴿نَصَرَهُ﴾ (supported him) in the order mentioned. They are like a parenthesis between what is made dependent (the first clause) and what is made dependent upon it (the consequent clause). The composition of the speech in this wonderful arrangement comes to begin with indicating that the support occurred in times and circumstances in which support would not have occurred for anyone else in similar situations, were it not for the care of Allah for him; and that his support was a miracle, a breach of customary norms.

By this explanation the bewilderment that befell the commentators concerning the meaning of the verse is dispelled. Many of them went to extremes, so that they referred the genitive pronoun in His saying ﴿So Allah sent down His tranquility upon him﴾ to Abu Bakr, while being certain that the accusative pronoun in ﴿وأيَّدَهُ﴾ (and supported him) refers to the Prophet (ﷺ). This produced a scattering of pronouns and a breakdown of the style, by mentioning Abu Bakr's condition, whereas the context is about the steadfastness of the Prophet (ﷺ) and Allah's support for him. The mention of Abu Bakr came only as a consequence of mentioning the Prophet's steadfastness. That bewilderment arose from making ﴿فَأنْزَلَ اللَّهُ﴾ a consequence of ﴿إذْ يَقُولُ لِصاحِبِهِ لا تَحْزَنْ﴾ (when he said to his companion, "Do not grieve"), and it forced them to interpret His saying ﴿وأيَّدَهُ بِجُنُودٍ لَمْ تَرَوْها﴾ (and supported him with hosts you did not see) as meaning the hosts of angels on the day of Badr. All of this is an adherence to the apparent order of the sentences, with heedlessness of the stylistic structure of the composition, which requires anticipation and postponement.

Tranquility (sakinah) is the calm of the soul in frightening circumstances; it is derived from sukun (stillness). Its mention has already occurred at His saying: ﴿In it is tranquility from your Lord﴾ (Al-Baqarah 2:248) in Surat al-Baqarah.

Support (ta'yid) means strengthening and aiding; it is derived from the noun "hand" (yad). It was mentioned earlier at His saying: ﴿And We supported him with the Holy Spirit﴾ (Al-Baqarah 2:87) in Surat al-Baqarah.

Hosts (junud) is the plural of jund, meaning army. It was mentioned at His saying: ﴿When Talut set out with the hosts﴾ (Al-Baqarah 2:249) in Surat al-Baqarah, and earlier in this surah.

Then he allowed that the clause ﴿وأيَّدَهُ بِجُنُودٍ﴾ (and supported him with hosts) may be conjoined to the clause ﴿فَأنْزَلَ اللَّهُ سَكِينَتَهُ عَلَيْهِ﴾ (So Allah sent down His tranquility upon him) as an explanatory conjunction (ʿatf tafsir). Then the hosts would be the angels who cast bewilderment into the souls of the polytheists, so they diverted them from thoroughly searching for the Prophet (ﷺ), from intensive pursuit after him, and from lying in wait for him on the roads that lead there and the paths that connect there. Especially since it is evident that he was heading for Yathrib, the place of emigration of his companions and the city of his helpers, so it was easy for them to watch the routes to reach Madinah.

It is also possible that it is conjoined to the clause ﴿أخْرَجَهُ﴾ (drove him out), with the sense: "and when He supported him with hosts you did not see, namely with angels, on the day of Badr, on the day of the Confederates, and on the day of Hunayn," as occurred in His saying: ﴿Then Allah sent down His tranquility upon His Messenger and upon the believers, and sent down hosts you did not see﴾ (At-Tawbah 9:26).

(The word "kalimah") originally means a word from speech; then it was applied to a matter, a affair, and the like, to everything that people speak about and that a person reports about himself concerning his own affairs. He said: ﴿And He made it a lasting word among his descendants﴾ (Az-Zukhruf 43:28) (i.e., he made the disavowal of idols and the monotheism of Allah the lasting affair and emblem of his descendants). He also said: ﴿And when his Lord tested Ibrahim with words﴾ (Al-Baqarah 2:124), i.e., with matters of obligations such as the sacrifice of his son and circumcision. And He said to Maryam: ﴿Indeed Allah gives you good news of a word from Him﴾ (Ali 'Imran 3:45), i.e., of a wondrous matter, or of a wondrous son. And He said: ﴿And the word of your Lord was fulfilled in truth and justice﴾ (Al-An'am 6:115), i.e., His rulings and His promises. From this is the saying: "Do not divide the word of the Muslims," i.e., their matter and their unity. And Allah united the word of the Muslims. So the word of those who disbelieved is their affair, their scheming, and whatever they plotted of kinds of deception.

The meaning of "the lowest" (al-sufla) is the most contemptible, because lowness is used to express contemptibility. Its opposite is His saying: ﴿and the word of Allah is the highest (al-'ulya)﴾; this is the religion and the affair of His Messenger and the believers. His saying ﴿and made the word of those who disbelieved the lowest﴾ indicates that the affair of the polytheists was apparently in a position of strength and firmness, because they were numerous and among them were people of opinion and intelligence. But when they opposed Allah and His Messenger, Allah humiliated them and reversed their condition from height to lowness.

The sentence "wa-kalimatu Allahi hiya al-'ulya" is a resumptive clause, placed as a concluding summary (tadhyil) of the speech, because when He informed us that the word of those who disbelieved had become the lowest, He conveyed that exaltedness is confined to the religion of God and His affair. The pronoun of separation (damir al-fasl, "hiya") here conveys restriction (qasr), and for this reason the phrase "kalimatu Allahi" is not conjoined (ma'tuf) to "kalimatu alladhina kafaru." The intended meaning is not to convey that the word of God was made exalted, since "making" (ja'l) suggests the bringing about of a state, but rather to convey that exaltedness is firmly established for it and restricted to it. Thus the clause serves as a concluding summary for the making of the word of those who disbelieved to be the lowest.

The meaning of its being made so is this: when the two words clashed and contradicted each other, the word of those who disbelieved was nullified, and the establishment of the word of God was secured.

Ya'qub alone read "wa-kalimata Allahi" with the accusative on (kalimata), conjoined (ma'tuf) to "kalimata alladhina kafaru al-sufla," so that the word of God is exalted by the making and decree of God.

The clause "wa-Allahu 'Aziz Hakim" (And God is Mighty, Wise) is a concluding summary of the content of the two clauses: for the Mighty (al-'Aziz) cannot be overcome by anything, and the Wise (al-Hakim) does not miss any aim, so necessarily His word is the exalted one and the word of His opponent is the lowest.

**Commentary of Ibn ʿĀshūr (al-Taḥrīr wa al-Tanwīr) on Surah 9, verse 41:**

﴿Go forth, whether light or heavy, and strive with your wealth and your lives in the way of God. That is better for you, if you only knew.﴾

The address is to the believers whose blame was previously stated in His words: ﴿O you who believe, what is wrong with you that when you are told to go forth in the way of God, you cling heavily to the earth?﴾ [al-Tawba: 38]. So the *nafīr* (going forth) commanded here refers to the jihad that is yet to come. We have already noted that the call (*istinfār*) to the expedition of Tabuk was general to everyone able to go on the campaign, because it was a time of hardship and the enemy was a great one. Therefore the pronoun in ﴿go forth﴾ [al-Tawba: 38] is general to those who were called and then held back, while only those able were summoned. The call was in proportion to the need of the campaign. This command therefore does not require that going forth become obligatory for every Muslim in every campaign, nor for a Muslim who is incapable because of blindness, chronic disability, or illness. Rather, in every campaign the practice follows what its circumstances require and what call is issued to them. And in the hadith: «When you are called to go forth, then go forth.»

*Khifāfan* is the plural of *khafīf* (light), an adjectival form derived from *khiffa* (lightness). It is a state of the body that entails a small quantity of parts compared with other familiar bodies, so that the person is easy to move and easy to carry. *Thiqāl* (heavy) is its opposite, and *thiql* (heaviness) was discussed just above in the words ﴿you cling heavily to the earth﴾ [al-Tawba: 38].

Here *khifāf* and *thiqāl* are used figuratively (*mustaʿāraān*) for things resembling them among the conditions of the army and its ties. Lightness is used for swiftness toward war, and they used to praise one another for this, since it indicates courage and valour. Quraiṭ ibn Unayf al-ʿAnbarī said:

*A people who, when evil bares its fangs at them,*
*rush toward it in groups and singly.*

The heaviness that fits this sense is steadfastness in combat, as in the words of Abū al-Ṭayyib:

*Steadfast when they meet, swift when they are summoned.*

Lightness is also used figuratively for a small number, and heaviness for a large number of the army, as in Quraiṭ's words: "in groups and singly." Lightness is used for repeated attacks on the enemy, and heaviness for firmness in the attack. Lightness is used for scarcity of provisions or weapons, and heaviness for the opposite. Lightness is used for having few dependants, and heaviness for the opposite. Lightness is used for riding, because the rider moves more swiftly, and heaviness for walking on foot, and that is at the time of fighting. Al-Nābigha said:

*Upon mares that know how to thrust, grim-faced, with wounds on them, some bleeding, some fresh,*
*when they are dismounted from them for striking, they hasten toward death at the gait of stubborn camels.*

All these meanings are suitable as intended by the verse. And since ﴿light and heavy﴾ stands as a circumstantial qualifier (*ḥāl*) of the subject of *infirū* (go forth), some of its meanings may be taken to mean that the qualifier is understood as implied (*muqaddara*), and the conjunction *wāw* links one of the two qualities to the other for division (*taqsīm*). Thus it has the sense of *aw* (or), and the intended meaning is the command to go forth in all conditions.

*Mujāhada* is contending against the enemy, and it is derived from *juhd* (with a *ḍamma* on the *jīm*), meaning the exertion of one's capacity in contending. Its literal meaning is defence with weapons, so its application to spending wealth on the campaign, such as providing for the army and buying mounts and weapons, is a figurative usage (*majāz*) based on the relation of causation (*ʿalāqat al-sababiyya*).

God has commanded both matters. Whoever is able to do both together is obligated to both, and whoever is able to do only one of them is obligated to that which he is able to do.

The placing of wealth before lives here is because striving with wealth is less present in the mind when the command to strive is heard. So it was more important to mention it after the general mention of striving.

The demonstrative *dhālikum* (that) refers to the jihad understood from ﴿strive﴾.

The indefiniteness of *khayr* (better) is intended to express the expectation of good in this world and the Hereafter from many branches, the most important of which is being reassured that the Byzantines will not attack them. For this reason he followed it with the words ﴿if you only knew﴾, meaning: if you know that good and its branches. The choice of the verb *ʿilm* (knowledge) rather than, for example, *īmān* (faith) indicates that some of this good is hidden, so the one seeking to identify its branches needs to employ reflection and knowledge.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 9, verse 42:

﴿Had it been a near gain and a moderate journey, they would have followed you. But the distance seemed long to them. They will swear by God, "Had we been able, we would have gone out with you." They destroy themselves, and God knows that they are indeed liars.﴾

This is a resumptive statement (isti'naf) marking the beginning of a new discussion about the hypocrites and the Battle of Tabuk, when they stayed behind, and many of them asked permission to remain behind and made excuses with false pretexts. It arises from His saying: ﴿What is the matter with you, that when you are told, "Go forth in the way of God," you cling heavily to the earth?﴾ [al-Tawbah: 38]

The address shifts from second person to third person because those being spoken of here are certainly some of the reluctant ones, as is shown by His saying after this: ﴿Only those ask your permission who do not believe in God and the Last Day, and whose hearts are in doubt﴾ [al-Tawbah: 45]. From these verses begins the notification to the hypocrites that God had informed His Messenger (ﷺ) of their inner secrets.

Al-'arad (lit. "that which presents itself") is the worldly goods that come to people. It has occurred in His saying: ﴿They take the goods of this lowly life﴾ [al-A'raf: 169] in Surat al-A'raf, and His saying: ﴿You desire the goods of this world﴾ [al-Anfal: 67] in Surat al-Anfal. What is meant here is spoils of war (ghanimah).

"Qarib" (near) means that which is at a short distance, and here it is used metaphorically for that which is easy to obtain. "Qasidan" means moderate in distance, not far. The subject of kana (was) is omitted, indicated by the predicate: that is, "Had the gain been a near gain and the journey a moderate journey," or: "Had what you call them to been a near gain and a journey..."

"Shuqqah" (with a damma on the shin) means a long distance.

Page 209

The construction of ba'udat with the preposition (ʿalā) is because it implies the meaning of thaqulat (became burdensome). For this reason it is good to combine the verb ﴿ba'udat﴾ with its subject ﴿al-shuqqah﴾, given the closeness of their meanings. It is as if it were said: "But the place became far from them, because it was a distance, so the journey became burdensome for them," and so the speech comes in a concise form.

His saying ﴿They will swear by God, "Had we been able, we would have gone out with you"﴾ indicates that this verse was revealed before the return from the Battle of Tabuk, for their swearing was after the return, when they sensed that the Messenger (peace and blessings be upon him) suspected them of lying in their excuses.

Al-istita'ah means power, that is: "We are not able to go out." This is an excuse from them and a confirmation of their excuse.

The clause ﴿we would have gone out with you﴾ is the answer to law (had).

Al-khuruj means moving from one's place to a place, near or far, and it is construed with "ila" for the intended destination and with "min" for the place left. The use of khuruj for travel to war became common. Restricting it with "ma'iyyah" (accompaniment) indicates that the matter of fighting does not concern them at the outset, and that they would only go out if they went out in response to the Prophet's (ﷺ) call to arms, like the going out of a helper to support another. The Arabs say: "The sons of so-and-so went out, and the sons of so-and-so went out with them," when they intend to support them.

The clause ﴿They destroy themselves﴾ is a circumstantial clause (hal), meaning they swear while bringing destruction upon themselves, that is, causing themselves to fall into ruin. Halak means perishing and death, and it is also applied to grave harms, which is the more fitting meaning here: they bring harm upon themselves through false oaths, which is the harm of this world and the punishment of the Hereafter.

In this verse there is evidence that deliberately swearing a false oath leads to ruin. This is supported by what al-Bukhari related in the Book of Blood-Money concerning the Hudhayl who swore the oaths of qasamah in the time of 'Umar and deliberately lied; then rain fell upon them, they entered a cave in a mountain, the cave collapsed upon them, and they all died.

The clause ﴿God knows that they are indeed liars﴾ is a circumstantial clause, meaning they do this while it will not benefit them, because God knows their lying, that is, and He informs His Messenger of their lying. Thus they gained from the oath nothing but the ruin of themselves.

The clause ﴿that they are indeed liars﴾ takes the place of the two objects of ﴿ya'lamu﴾ (knows).

[Page 210]

﴿May God pardon you. Why did you give them permission before it became clear to you who were truthful and you knew the liars?﴾ A group of the hypocrites asked the Prophet ﷺ for permission to remain behind from the expedition. Among them were ʿAbd Allah ibn Ubayy ibn Salul, al-Jadd ibn Qays, and Rifaʿa ibn al-Tabut, and they numbered thirty-nine. They offered false excuses. The Prophet ﷺ granted permission to those who asked him, out of charity toward people by taking them at their word, since the outward state of their affairs was faith, and knowing that those making excuses, if they were compelled to go out, would be of no benefit, as God the Exalted said: ﴿If they had gone out with you, they would only have added to you corruption﴾ [al-Tawba: 47]. So God rebuked His Prophet ﷺ for having granted them permission, because if he had not granted it to them they would have stayed behind, and that would have been a proof to the Prophet ﷺ of their hypocrisy and their lying in claiming faith, as God the Exalted said: ﴿And if We willed, We would have shown them to you, and you would have recognized them by their marks﴾ [Muhammad: 30].

The sentence is resumptive, a fresh beginning (istiʾnaf ibtidaʾi), because its purpose is a new one.

Opening the rebuke with the announcement of pardon is a great honour and a noble gentleness: He informed him of the pardon before engaging him with the rebuke. In this opening there is an implication (kinaya) that the cause for rebuke is light, since it is as if one said: "It was not fitting." Calling the forgiveness of that "pardon" (ʿafw) looks to the meaning of the saying of the people of the haqiqa (the mystical path, a technical term glossed here as "the people of inner realities"): "The good deeds of the righteous are the misdeeds of those brought near."

The rebuke was delivered in the form of a question about the cause (al-ʿilla), as a hint that he granted permission only for a reason he had interpreted and from which he hoped for general good. Thus one asks about the like of it, using the question form of one seeking knowledge. This is one of the forms of gentle expression in disapproval or blame, whereby the one disapproving presents himself as one asking about a cause that was hidden from him. Then he followed it with the statement that not granting permission would have been more fitting for making their condition clear, which is another purpose that the Prophet's ﷺ intention had not been directed toward.

The object of "ādhantа" (you granted permission) is omitted because it is evident from the context, meaning: why did you grant them permission to sit back and stay behind?

[Page 211]

The phrase "ḥattā" (until) marks the limit (ghāya) of the verb "ādhanta," because when it fell within the scope of the interrogative of disapproval, it took the ruling of a negation. The meaning is: there was no justification for granting them permission until the truthful was distinguished from the liar.

The addition of "laka" (for you) after "yatabayyana" (becomes clear) contains an added gentleness, that the rebuke was only for a lapse in something whose benefit returns to him. By "those who were truthful" are meant those who were truthful in their faith, and by "the disbelievers who are liars" (al-kāfirīn al-kādhibīn) those who lied about the faith they displayed, and they are the hypocrites. So by "those who were truthful" is meant the believers.

This sentence stands in the position of explanation for the clause ﴿until it becomes clear to you who are truthful, and you know the liars﴾ [at-Tawbah: 43], and in the position of giving the reason for the clause ﴿Why did you give them permission?﴾ [at-Tawbah: 43]; or it is an explanatory resumption (isti'naf bayani) for what the clause ﴿until it becomes clear to you who are truthful, and you know the liars﴾ [at-Tawbah: 43] raises. These considerations are close to one another, and their outcome is one.

The meaning: the condition of the believers who were called forth to march is that they should not seek permission from the Prophet ﷺ to stay behind from jihad. As for people with valid excuses, such as the blind, the Prophet ﷺ does not call them forth. As for those among the believers who stayed behind, they stayed behind without seeking permission to remain, because they intended to catch up with the army after it had set out.

Al-isti'dhan (seeking permission) means requesting leave, that is, for permission to do an action and to leave its opposite, because the nature of permissibility (al-ibahah) is to entail choice between one of two opposing matters.

Al-isti'dhan is followed by (fi) [in]. Thus His saying, ﴿an yujahidu﴾ [that they strive], is in a position of genitive governed by the omitted (fi) [in], and omitting the preposition before (an) is common and widespread.

Since al-isti'dhan entails two opposing things, as we have said, it is permissible to say: "I sought permission to do such-and-such" and "I sought permission to leave such-and-such." What is usually mentioned along with the verb of seeking permission is the matter which the one seeking permission desires to be allowed, rather than its opposite, although mentioning both is also correct.

Since the condition of the believers is eagerness for jihad, what is mentioned with the believers' seeking permission in the verse is ﴿an yujahidu﴾ [that they strive], rather than ﴿an la yujahidu﴾ [that they do not strive], since it is not fitting for believers to seek permission to abandon jihad. So when the seeking of permission to strive is negated, it is established that they strive without seeking permission. This is one of the subtleties of the eloquence of this verse, which the exegetes did not touch upon, and they strained themselves in establishing the structure of the verse.

The clause ﴿and God is Knowing of the God-fearing﴾ is a parenthetical insertion (i'tiraD) for the benefit of alerting that God is aware of the secrets of the believers, since they are the intended meaning of "the God-fearing," as was previously mentioned in His saying in Surat al-Baqarah: ﴿a guidance for the God-fearing, who believe in the unseen﴾ [al-Baqarah: 2].

The sentence is a resumed explanatory clause (isti'naf bayani, a sentence that answers an implied question), arising from the exoneration of the believers from asking permission to avoid jihad. It explains who are the ones whose habit is to ask permission in this matter, and that they are those who do not believe in God and the Last Day inwardly, because the absence of their faith negates their hope for the reward of jihad, and so they do not expose themselves to it.

The particle *innama* ("only") indicates restriction (al-qasr). Since restriction conveys the meaning of two statements, affirming one thing and negating its opposite, the form of restriction here, in terms of one of its two meanings, emphasizes the sentence ﴿Those who believe in God and the Last Day do not ask your permission﴾ (Al-Tawbah: 44). It would have dispensed with that emphasizing sentence, except that the purpose of placing that sentence first is to draw attention to the virtue of the believers. So the speech is elaboration (itnab) for the purpose of tanwih (drawing attention), and drawing attention is one of the contexts of elaboration.

The object of *yasta'dhinuka* ("ask your permission") is omitted here because it is clear from what came before, namely the verb of asking permission in the statement ﴿Those who believe in God and the Last Day do not ask your permission to strive﴾ (Al-Tawbah: 44). The estimated meaning is: "Only those who do not believe ask your permission not to strive," and for this reason the object of *yasta'dhinuka* is omitted here.

[Page 213]

The eloquent listener estimates for every utterance what suits the intention of the eloquent speaker, and each one weaves according to its own pattern.

The conjunction of ﴿and their hearts are in doubt﴾ to the relative clause, which is ﴿do not believe in God and the Last Day﴾, indicates that the intended meaning of *al-irtiyab* (doubt) is doubt about the manifestation of the affair of the Prophet (ﷺ). Because of that doubt they were two-faced with him: they showed Islam so that what accrues to the Muslims of might and benefit would not escape them, should the affair of Islam prevail, and they concealed disbelief to preserve their corrupt religion and their ties with the people of their creed. As God, exalted is He, said about them: ﴿Those who wait and watch for you: if a victory comes to you from God, they say, "Were we not with you?" and if the disbelievers have a share, they say, "Did we not gain mastery over you and protect you from the believers?"﴾ (Al-Nisa': 141).

Perhaps their greatest doubt was about the outcome of the campaign of Tabuk, because in their disbelief they did not expect that the Muslims would defeat the Romans. This is the correct interpretation of His saying ﴿and their hearts are in doubt﴾, as His saying ﴿so they are wavering in their doubt﴾ indicates.

The phrase "do not believe" uses the present tense to indicate the renewal of the negation of their faith, while ﴿and their hearts are in doubt﴾ uses the past tense to indicate the antiquity of that doubt and its firm establishment. Therefore its effect is the continuation of the negation of their faith. Since doubt is inseparable from the negation of faith, the speech contains something like *ihtibak* (a rhetorical device in which two complementary elements are omitted from two parallel parts of a sentence, each part retaining the other's omitted element), as though it were said: "Those who did not believe and do not believe, and whose hearts doubted and continue to doubt."

He branched His saying ﴿so they are wavering in their doubt﴾ from ﴿and their hearts are in doubt﴾ as the branching of the caused from the cause. This is because doubt is uncertainty about a matter due to hesitation in attaining it. Because of their hesitation, they did not openly disobey the Prophet (ﷺ) when he called them to march forth, nor did they comply with him. Instead they took a course that suits both matters, namely the course of asking permission to stay behind. So asking permission is caused by hesitation, and hesitation is caused by doubt. This shows that the intended purpose of the relative clause in His saying ﴿those who do not believe in God and the Last Day﴾ is His saying ﴿and their hearts are in doubt, so they are wavering in their doubt﴾, because it is what produces the confinement of asking permission to them.

[Page 214]

The phrase *fi raybihim* ("in their doubt") is a stable adverbial phrase, the predicate concerning the plural pronoun. The locative sense is figurative, conveying that the doubt encompasses them, meaning its taking firm hold of their souls. The phrase *fi raybihim* is not connected to *yataraddadun* ("they waver").

Hesitation (*al-taraddud*) is literally going and returning repeatedly to one place, and here it is an image of the state of one who is torn between acting and not acting, by the state of one who walks and turns back. Close to this is the saying: "He puts one foot forward and draws the other back."

The meaning is that they did not resolve to go out to the campaign. In this verse there is an explicit statement to the hypocrites that they are disbelievers, and that God informed His Messenger, peace and blessings be upon him, and the believers of their disbelief, because the matter of their asking permission to stay behind had become known to the people.

[Page 215 marker omitted]

It is coordinated with the clause ﴿they are in their doubt, wavering﴾ [At-Tawbah: 45], because the meaning of what is coordinated with it is that they did not intend to go out to the expedition (ghazw). This is an argument for their not intending to go out, since had they intended it, they would have prepared its equipment. This refutes their claim that they had prepared for the expedition and then excuses came upon them, so they asked permission to stay behind. Their failure to prepare the equipment (*'uddah*) for jihad indicates the absence of their intention to go out on the expedition.

*Al-'uddah*, with a damma on the 'ayn, is what is needed of things, such as weapons for the fighter and provisions for the traveller. It is derived from *al-i'dad*, which is preparation (*al-tahay'ah*).

*Al-khurug* (going out) has been mentioned just above.

The *istidrak* (corrective exception) in His words ﴿But Allah disliked their setting out﴾ is a corrective exception to what the conditional *law* implies from the supposition that they intended to go out, serving to affirm the non-occurrence of that act by asserting its opposite. He expressed the opposite of going out as Allah's discouraging them, because in the divine causation it is the opposite of going out, so He used it to express its cause. The use of *istidrak* in this way after *law* is a well-known usage in their speech, such as the saying of Ubayy ibn Sulma al-Dabbi:

"Had any hoofed creature flown before her, she would have flown, but it did not fly."

And the saying of al-Ghatamshsh al-Dabbi:

"O my friends, had anything other than death befallen you, I would have blamed you, but there is no blame upon death."

However, the *istidrak* of the opposite of the condition in the verse came by mentioning something equivalent to the opposite, namely Allah's discouraging them. This is to amplify the benefit of the *istidrak* by stating the cause of the matter being corrected, and by making this cause follow from its reason, namely that Allah disliked their setting out. The *istidrak* was phrased with mention of its reason to give it importance and to draw attention to the fact that their not intending to go out was a deprivation from Allah for them, and a care for the Muslims. Thus the speech came in a wondrous arrangement, and emphasis was achieved together with additional benefits.

Allah's disliking their setting out is explained in the verse after it with His words: ﴿Had they gone out among you, they would have added nothing to you but corruption﴾ [At-Tawbah: 47].

*Al-inba'ath* is the reflexive form (*mutawi'*) of *ba'atha*, which means to send.

*Al-tathbit* is the removal of resolve. Allah's discouraging them means that He created in them laziness and weakness of determination for the expedition.

*Al-qu'ud* (sitting) is used for abstaining from the expedition, by likening abstention to sitting.

The "saying" (*al-qawl*) in His words "and it was said: sit" is the saying of the command of creation (*qawl amr al-takwin*), meaning that He brought into existence in them the sitting back from the expedition.

The addition of His words "with those who sit" is a rebuke to them, because "those who sit" are those whose habit is to stay back from the expedition, and they are the weak, such as children and women, like the blind and the chronically ill.

[Page 216]
