﴿Had they gone out among you, they would have added nothing to you but corruption, and they would have rushed about between you, seeking to cause you strife, and among you there are those who listen to them. And Allah knows the wrongdoers.﴾

This is an explanatory resumptive clause (*isti'naf bayani*, a clause that answers an implied question) following the phrase ﴿Allah disliked their being sent forth, so He held them back﴾ (al-Tawba 9:46). It explains the wisdom behind Allah's dislike of their going out: Allah wills the safety of the Muslims from the harm of these people's presence among them. This is because they were concealing deceit against the Muslims, and so they would go out only unwillingly. There is no benefit in an army that fights without believing that it is upon the truth. The construction of the verb *al-khuruj* (going out) with *fi* (in) is common when speaking of going out with an army.

*Al-ziyada* means increase, provision.

The object of *zadu-kum* (they added to you) is omitted, as the verb *al-khuruj* (going out) indicates it. The meaning is: they would not have added to you strength, or anything whose increase would benefit the campaign by way of victory over the enemy. Then *al-khabal* (corruption) is made an exception from the omitted object, in the manner of *tahakkum* (sarcasm, mocking irony), by affirming a thing with something resembling its opposite. Corruption in war is a part of the lack of increase in the army's strength; indeed it is even more absolutely the lack of increase. However, it is claimed that it is one of the kinds of increase in the benefits of war, and that it must be excepted from that negation, in the manner of sarcasm.

*Al-khabal* is corruption, and the disintegration of a thing that is joined and fitted together. Here it is applied to the disorder of the army and the breakdown of its order.

The literal meaning of *awda'u* is "they hastened the pace of the riding animals." It is said: *wada'a al-ba'iru wad'an*, when the camel hastened. It is also said: *awda'tu ba'iri*, meaning I drove my camel at a swift pace. This verb is specific to the travel of camels, so the verb *awda'a* is treated as intransitive, because its object is known from the root of the verb. Here it is a figurative depiction of the state of the hypocrites when they exert their utmost effort to cause dissension and fear among the men of the army, and to spread false reports about the strength of the enemy, like the state of one who drives his camel hard to convey an important news or to bring merchandise to a market. Similar to this figure is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿They roamed through the homes﴾ (al-Isra 17:5), and His saying: ﴿And you see many of them hastening toward sin and aggression﴾ (al-Ma'ida 5:62). Its origin is the saying: "he strives for such-and-such"; however, since the use of *al-sa'y* (striving) for eagerness for something became widespread, the awareness of the figure of the depicted state became obscure upon its unqualified use, due to its frequent usage. Therefore the expression *al-iy da'* (driving hard) was chosen here, because of the rarity of this meaning and because of its suitability to disrupt the arrangement, by likening those who cause strife to a caravan, and the means of strife to riding animals.

[Page 217]

In the mention of *khilal-kum* (between you) there is something suitable for likening their searching out of the groups and individuals to the penetration of riding animals through the gaps of roads and valleys.

*Al-khilal* is the plural of *khalal* (with a vowel on the middle letter), meaning the gap between two things. Here it is borrowed for the meaning of "among you," likening the groups of the army to scattered parts.

The word *wa-la awda'u* is written in the Mushaf with an *alif* after the hamza of *awda'u* that comes after the *lam*, so that after the *lam* there are two alifs. Thus the *lam-alif* resembles the *lam-alif* that is not the negative particle of the verb *awda'u*, and the second alif is not pronounced in recitation, so no confusion arises in the words of the verse. Al-Zajjaj said: "They fell into this because the fatha (short vowel) in Hebrew and in many languages is written as an alif." Al-Zamakhshari followed him. Ibn 'Atiyya said: "It is possible that the vowel of the *lam* is prolonged, so that an alif arises between the *lam* and the hamza of *awda'a*. It has also been said: that is due to the roughness of the spelling of the earlier generations," meaning the lack of refinement of the orthography among the early Arabs. Al-Zamakhshari said: "Similar to this they wrote *la-adhbahannahu* in Surat al-Naml." I say: they wrote *la-u'adhdhibannahu* with *lam-alif* only, and it is attached to the word *aw la-adhbahannahu*, and not in the like of *wa-idhan la yattakhadhuka khalilan*. So I do not see that they wrote an alif after the *lam-alif* in what they wrote it in except for a purpose; perhaps they intended to alert the reader that the hamza is fatha-vowelled, and that it is a hamzat qat' (the hamza of cutting, a glottal hamza).

The clause ﴿they seek to cause you strife﴾ is in the position of a circumstantial clause (*hal*) from the pronoun in ﴿and had they desired to go out﴾ (al-Tawba 9:46), which refers to those who do not believe in Allah, in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Only those who do not believe in Allah and the Last Day ask your permission﴾ (al-Tawba 9:45). The intended meaning of them is the hypocrites, as has passed.

*Baghā* is transitive to one object, because it means "sought" (*talaba*). It was mentioned earlier in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Do they seek other than the religion of Allah?﴾ in Surat Al 'Imran. The phrase *yabghunakum* is here transitive to the pronoun of the addressees by way of omitting the preposition (*naz' al-khafid*), and its original form is *yabghuna lakum al-fitna*. This is a common usage of *baghā* in the sense of *talaba*.

*Al-fitna* is the disruption of affairs and corruption of judgment. It was mentioned earlier in His saying: ﴿And they thought there would be no strife﴾ (al-Ma'ida 5:71) in Surat al-Ma'ida.

[Page 218]

His saying ﴿and among you there are those who listen to them﴾ means: among the Muslims, i.e., among the Muslims there are those who listen to them. It is possible that these listeners are Muslims who believe what they hear from the hypocrites. It is also possible that the listeners are hypocrites scattered among the Muslims.

This clause is a parenthetical interjection (*i'tiraḍ*) to alert that their seeking of strife is a greater danger to the Muslims, because among the Muslims there is a group whose tricks deceive them. These are the naive among the Muslims, who are amazed at their reports and are influenced by them, and do not reach the ability to distinguish deceptions and schemes from truth and reality.

The phrase *sammā'ūn* (listeners) comes in the intensive form (*sigha al-mubalagha*) to indicate that their listening is complete, namely the listening accompanied by belief in what is heard, as in His saying: ﴿Listeners to falsehood, listeners to other people﴾ (al-Ma'ida 5:41). From al-Hasan, Mujahid, and Ibn Zayd: the meaning of *sammā'ūn lahum* is spies who listen to news and convey it to them. Qatada and the majority of exegetes said: its meaning is: among you there are those who accept their word and obey them. Al-Nahhas said: "Most often the meaning of *sammā'* is one who hears speech, and similar to it is *sammā'ūna lil-kadhib*. As for one who accepts what he hears, it is hardly said of him except *sami'* (hearer), like *qa'il* (speaker)."

The particle *fi* (in) is used in His saying ﴿and among you there are those who listen to them﴾, which indicates location, rather than the particle *min* (from). So it did not say *wa-minkum sammā'ūna lahum* or *wa-minhum sammā'ūn*, lest it be thought that the listeners are restricted to a group from one of the two parties to the exclusion of the other, because the intended meaning is that the listeners to them are of two groups: a group of the believers, and a group of the hypocrites themselves scattered among the believers to spread rumours and strife, and they are the majority. Thus the use of the particle *fi* fulfils the wondrous brevity of this expression, and because it is the suitable one for both possible senses of the word *sammā'ūn*; thus two benefits are achieved by it.

The clause ﴿and Allah knows the wrongdoers﴾ is a concluding summation (*tadhyil*), intended to inform the Muslims that Allah knows the states of the wrongdoing hypocrites, so that they may be on guard against them, and so that they may recognise in them what the Qur'an has marked them with, and so that they may know that listening to them is a form of wrongdoing.

Here *al-zulm* (wrongdoing) means disbelief and polytheism, as in ﴿Indeed, associating others with Allah is a tremendous wrong﴾ (Luqman 31:13).

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 9, verse 48:

Page 219
﴿Indeed, they had sought discord before, and they had turned matters over for you until the truth came and the command of Allah prevailed while they were averse.﴾
This sentence is a justification (ta'līl) for His saying (﴿They wish to cause you discord﴾ [al-Tawbah: 47]), because it is evidence that this was their habit from before, since they sought discord for the Muslims. That was on the day of Uhud, when 'Abd Allah ibn Ubayy ibn Salul and those hypocrites with him withdrew after they had reached Uhud. They were a third of the army, and they intended to instill fear into the hearts of the Muslims when they saw some of their army withdrawing. Ibn Juraij said: those who sought discord were twelve men from among the hypocrites, who stood at the Thaniyyat al-Wada' on the night of al-'Aqaba in order to assassinate the Prophet ﷺ.

And "qallabū" with a doubled lam is the intensive form (muḍā'af) of qalaba (the unemphatic form), and the doubling indicates the strength of the action. It may be from qalaba al-shay' (he turned a thing over), when one examines its inside and outside to become aware of its finest attributes; the intensification then refers to quantity, i.e., the frequency of turning over, meaning: they repeatedly reconsidered their opinions and devised schemes and tricks to harm the Prophet ﷺ and the Muslims.

It may also be that "qallabū" comes from qalaba in the sense of searching and investigating; the turning-over is used metaphorically for searching and inspecting, because inspecting resembles turning over in comprehending the state of a thing, like His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿So he began to turn his hands over﴾ [al-Kahf: 42]. The meaning then is that they searched and spied to learn about the affairs of the Muslims and inform the enemy of them.

The lam in His saying "laka" ("for you"), on these two readings, is the lam of cause, i.e., for your sake, and it is general, clarified by His saying: ﴿They had sought discord before﴾. The meaning is: they pursued a discord that would appear from you, i.e., in your circumstances and in the circumstances of the Muslims.

It may also be that "qallabū" is an intensive form used for turning around a matter, when what was apparent in it is concealed and what was hidden is revealed, as in the saying: "he turned the back of the shield to him." Its transitivity with the lam in His saying "laka" is then clear.

Page 220
"Al-umūr" is the plural of "amr," which is an indefinite noun like "shay'," as in the verse of al-Mawsili:

But there are decrees that have passed and matters [that have occurred]
The alif and lam in it are for the genus, i.e., matters some of which you know and some of which you do not know.
"Ḥattā" marks the endpoint of their turning over of matters.

The "coming of the truth" means its occurrence and establishment, and what is meant by it is the disappearance of the Muslims' weakness and the exposure of the hypocrites' affair.

What is meant by the manifestation of Allah's command is the victory of the Muslims through the conquest of Makkah and people entering the religion in multitudes. The hypocrites dislike that.

"Ẓuhūr" means dominance, prevailing, and victory.

"Amr Allah" is His religion, i.e., when the truth came and Allah's command prevailed, they knew that their discord would not harm the Muslims, so for that reason they saw no benefit in going out with them on the expedition to Tabuk, and so they made excuses for not going out from the very beginning.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 9, verse 49:

﴿And among them is one who says, "Grant me permission and do not put me to trial." Unquestionably, they have fallen into trial. And indeed, Hell encompasses the disbelievers.﴾

It was revealed concerning some of the hypocrites who sought permission from the Prophet (ﷺ) to remain behind from Tabuk. They did not present an excuse that would prevent them from going on the campaign, but they declared plainly that going out to the campaign would put them to trial by [making them love] their wealth and their families. So God exposed their affair, [showing] that they were hypocrites, because the pronoun of plurality in the genitive case refers back to ﴿those who do not believe in God and the Last Day﴾ [al-Tawba: 45]. It was also said: a group of them said, "Grant us permission, for we are sitting [at home]. Whether you grant us permission or not, grant us permission so that we do not fall into disobedience." This is among the greatest of impudence, because permission in this situation is as if there were no permission. Perhaps they said that because of their knowledge of the Prophet's (ﷺ) gentleness. It was also said: "Indeed, al-Jadd ibn Qays said: 'O Messenger of God, the people already know that I am excessively infatuated with women, and when I see the women of the Banu al-Asfar I am tempted by them. So grant me permission to remain behind and do not put me to trial, and I will help you with my wealth.' So he granted them permission." Perhaps all of that happened.

The use of the particle of opening (ʾadāt al-istiftāḥ, "alā") in the clause ﴿Unquestionably, they have fallen into trial﴾ is to draw attention to what follows of the strangeness of their condition, since God dealt with them in the opposite of what they intended. They guarded themselves against a trial, and so they fell into trial. The definite article in "al-fitna" is not the definite article of prior reference (ʿahd), since there is no previously mentioned referent here; rather it is the definite article of the genus (jins), which indicates the perfection of the defined thing within its kind, i.e., they fell into the great trial. Whatever meaning is assigned to "trial" [in the speaker's words], when he said, "do not put me to trial," what befell him was worse than what he sought to escape. If he meant the trial of religion, then he has fallen into the greatest trial, through polytheism and hypocrisy. If he meant the trial of bad reputation through staying behind, then he has fallen into something greater, the exposure of the hypocrisy of their affair. If he meant the trial of distress through separation from family and wealth, then he has fallen into the greatest distress, by being cursed and hated by people. The explanation of "trial" has already been given shortly before.

The word "al-suqūṭ" (falling) is used figuratively for the occurrence of something suddenly, by way of metaphor (istiʿāra): that occurrence is likened to falling, in terms of being unprepared for it and in terms of its suddenness, since they came to be in the trial while they were secure from falling into it. They are like one who falls into a pit at a time when he thought he was walking on an easy path. And from the speech of the Arabs: "You fell upon the one who knows (ʿalā al-khabīr saqaṭta)."

The fronting of the prepositional phrase before its governing element is for emphasis on it, because it is the intended point of the sentence.

This sentence functions as a proverb (yasīr majrā al-mathal).

The clause ﴿And indeed, Hell encompasses the disbelievers﴾ is a parenthetical insertion (muʿtariḍa), and the "wāw" is parenthetical (wāw iʿtirāḍiyya), meaning: they fell into the trial that leads to disbelief, and disbelief deserves Hell.

The encompassing of Hell is meant to convey that they cannot escape it, so "encompassing" is a metonymy (kināya) for inability to escape. By "the disbelievers" is meant all disbelievers, so it includes those being spoken of, due to the established fact of their disbelief in His saying: ﴿Only those seek your permission who do not believe in God and the Last Day﴾ [al-Tawba: 45].

The reason for shifting from using their pronoun to using the apparent noun in His saying "encompassing the disbelievers" is to establish the encompassing of Hell around them by way of something resembling inference (istidlāl), because the universal noun's applying to some of its particular instances is among the most well-known forms of inference.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 9, verse 50:

Page 222
﴿If good befalls you, it grieves them; but if a calamity strikes you, they say, "We had already taken our precaution before," and they turn away rejoicing.﴾

This sentence stands in the position of an explanation (bayan) for the sentence ﴿Only those ask your permission who do not believe in Allah and the Last Day, and whose hearts are in doubt, so they waver in their doubt﴾ [al-Tawbah: 45]. Between the two sentences there is an argument proving their lying in the excuse they offered and in the permission they showed they were seeking on its account. Here it clarifies that their wavering is that they fear the victory of the Muslims' cause, and therefore they do not openly declare their opposition to them, and they wish for the believers' failure; for this reason they do not like to go out with them.

Al-hasanah (the good) is the event that brings good to the one who is struck by it and befalls him. What is meant by it here is victory and spoils of war.

Al-musibah (the calamity) is derived from asaba, meaning to alight upon, to attain, or to coincide with. In the language, the word musibah is restricted to an event that befalls a person and grieves and saddens him. For this reason it is expressed by sayyi'ah (evil) in the saying of the Exalted, in Surat Al 'Imran: ﴿If good touches you, it grieves them; but if an evil befalls you, they rejoice at it﴾ [Al 'Imran: 120]. What is meant by it in both places is defeat, and this has already been discussed in the saying of the Exalted: ﴿Then We replaced the evil with good﴾ [al-A'raf: 95] in Surat al-A'raf.

Their saying ﴿We had already taken our precaution before﴾ is an expression of their delight at their actions coinciding with what secures their safety; they claim that their alertness and resolve have hit the mark, since they took precautions against it before falling into harm.

Al-akhdh (taking) in its literal sense is receiving or grasping, and here it is used metaphorically for preparation and forestalling.

Al-amr (the matter) is the important affair concerning its possessor; that is, "We have prepared for what concerns us, so we did not fall into calamity."

Al-tawalli in its literal sense is turning back, and it has been discussed in the saying of the Exalted: ﴿And when he turns away, he strives in the land﴾ [al-Baqarah: 205] in Surat al-Baqarah. Here it is a figurative depiction of their state in escaping the calamity that would have befallen them had they gone out with the Muslims, like the state of people who came near a danger, then were spared from it and returned rejoicing and glad at their safety and at the misfortune of their enemies.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 9, verse 51:

[p. 223]
﴿Say: "Nothing will befall us except what Allah has decreed for us. He is our Protector, and upon Allah let the believers rely."﴾

This is a teaching of a response to their statement ﴿We had already taken our precaution before[, and they turn away rejoicing]﴾ [al-Tawbah: 50], which reveals their joy at whatever misfortune befalls the Muslims, by affirming that the Muslims are not distressed by the calamity and that they feel no grief over it, because they know that what has struck them happened only by the decree of Allah for the benefit of the Muslims in it. It is therefore pure benefit, as is indicated by the transitivity of the verb (kataba, "decreed") with the preposition lam (li-), which signifies that He decreed it for their benefit. The point of this response is that the enemy rejoices at the misfortune of his enemy because it troubles and grieves him. So when they know that the Prophet does not grieve over what befalls him, their joy disappears.

In this there is also an instruction to the Muslims to adopt this disposition: that they should not grieve over what afflicts them, lest they weaken and their strength depart, as Allah - Exalted is He - said: ﴿And do not weaken and do not grieve, for you will be superior if you are believers. If a wound should touch you, there has already touched the enemy a wound like it﴾ [Al 'Imran: 139]. And that they should be content with what Allah has decreed for them and hope for the pleasure of their Lord, because they are certain that Allah wills the victory of His religion.

The phrase ﴿He is our Protector﴾ is in the position of a circumstantial clause (hal) relating to the Name of Majesty (Allah), or it is a parenthetical clause (mu'taridah), meaning: nothing will befall us except what Allah has decreed for us, and we have hope that He does not write for us except what contains our good, whether immediate or deferred, because the Protector does not wish disgrace for His protégé.

As for the clause ﴿upon Allah let the believers rely﴾, it may be coordinated (ma'tufah) upon the clause "Say," so it is from the speech of Allah - Exalted is He - a statement in the sense of a command, meaning: say that, and do not rely except upon Allah, rather than upon the support of these people, that is, depend upon His grace upon you.

It may also be coordinated upon the clause "Nothing will befall us," meaning: say that to them, and say to them that the believers rely only upon Allah, that is, they believe that He is their supporter, and their support is not by your assistance. The detail of this summary is in the clause that follows it. The fa' (then) that enters upon ﴿so let the believers rely﴾ is a fa' indicating an implied element derived from what precedes it, which is required by the fronting of the complement, meaning: upon Allah let the believers rely.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 9, verse 52:

Page 224
﴿Say, "Do you await for us except one of the two best outcomes? And we await for you that Allah will afflict you with a punishment from Him or at our hands. So wait; indeed, we are with you waiting."﴾

This sentence stands in the position of an explanation (bayan) of what was contained in the sentence ﴿Say, "Nothing will strike us except what Allah has decreed for us"﴾ [At-Tawbah: 51] and the verse thereafter. For this reason it is not joined to it by a conjunction. The thing being explained is the general statement ﴿what Allah has decreed for us, He is our Protector﴾ [At-Tawbah: 51], as has preceded.

The meaning is: "You do not await from our situation except one of two good outcomes, either an immediate good (victory and booty) or a deferred good (martyrdom and reward). As for us, we await from your situation that Allah will punish you in the Hereafter with the punishment of the Fire, or in this world with a punishment not at our hands, from Allah's punishment in this world, such as hunger and fear, or with a punishment at our hands, which is the punishment of killing, when Allah permits war against you, as in His saying: ﴿If the hypocrites, and those in whose hearts is a disease, and the agitators in the city do not desist, We will surely incite you against them﴾ [Al-Ahzab: 60], and so on."

The interrogative is used in the sense of negation, as indicated by the exception (istithna'). The meaning of the speech is a rebuke for them and a condemnation of their waiting, because they await for the Muslims to be killed, and they overlook the possibility that the Muslims will be victorious. So the meaning is: "You do not wait for us except that we be killed or defeated, and that is one of the two best outcomes."

Tarabbus (tarabbus, waiting) means waiting for the occurrence of a thing whose occurrence is desired, and this is its most common usage. It is waiting for the occurrence of a thing to befall someone other than the one waiting, with the ẓā' vowelled with a kasra (tarabbaṣ/tarabbuṣ). For this reason the verb tarabbuṣ is most often construed with bi- (with), because the one waiting awaits a thing accompanied by another, for which the waiting is undertaken. As for His saying: ﴿And the divorced women shall wait by themselves for three periods﴾ [Al-Baqarah: 228], the phrase "by themselves" (anfusihinna) has been treated as if it were a separate element, for emphasis on the obligation of waiting. For this reason al-Zamakhshari said in al-Kashshaf: "Mentioning the selves is an incitement for them to wait and an added urging." This has already been discussed there. As for His saying: ﴿For those who swear off their wives, a waiting period of four months﴾ [Al-Baqarah: 226], it is according to the original usage, since it is a waiting for their wives.

The sentence ﴿and we await for you﴾ is conjoined to the interrogative sentence by the conjunction of a declarative to an interrogative (ʿatf al-khabar ʿala al-inshaʾ): rather, it is a declarative in the form of an imperative, so it is part of the speech being reported (maqul al-qawl), and there is no meaning of interrogation in it.

Page 225
The meaning: there is a difference between the two groups regarding the outcome of the war, in the two states of victory and defeat.

The sentence ﴿and we await﴾ was made a nominal sentence, and he did not say "wa-natarabbasu bikum," in contrast with the sentence to which it is conjoined, in order to convey the strengthening of the waiting, and as a metonymy (kinayah) for the strengthening of the occurrence of what is awaited, because strengthening the waiting conveys the strength of hope in the occurrence of what is awaited, and so it conveys the strength of its occurrence, which is what is alluded to.

From the sentence ﴿Do you await for us﴾ there branches off the sentence ﴿So wait; indeed, we are with you waiting﴾, because if the waiting of each of the two groups results in one of the two mentioned states, then the group of believers is the more content of the two groups with those who wait, since in both there is its benefit and the harm of its enemy.

The imperative in His saying "tarabbasu" is for an figurative incitement (tahdid majazi) conveying little concern for their waiting, like the saying of Tarif ibn Tamim al-Anbari:

"So assess me, for I am that one, bearing my weapon in calamities, known [for it]."

The sentence ﴿indeed, we are with you waiting﴾ is a threat to the addressees, and the "withness" (ma'iyyah) here is a withness in waiting, or in its time. This sentence is separated from the one before it because it functions like a cause (ʿillah) for the incitement.

The commentary begins a new statement, which is a reply to the words of some of those among them who sought permission to stay behind: "I will help you with my wealth." It is reported that the one who said this was al-Jadd ibn Qays, of the Banu Salama, about whom God's words were revealed: ﴿And among them is one who says, "Grant me permission and do not put me to trial"﴾ [al-Tawbah 9:49], as has already been mentioned. He was a hypocrite. It seems that they said this, despite their extreme stinginess, because they thought it would please the Prophet (ﷺ) regarding their remaining behind from jihad.

As for His words, ﴿tawʿan aw karhan﴾ ("willingly or unwillingly"), this means: with wealth that you give up in place of going on the expedition, or with wealth that you spend willingly while going out on the expedition. So His words "willingly" are an *idmāj* (an embedding, a rhetorical device in which a secondary meaning is included within the main statement) to generalize the states of spending in the non-acceptance. For they spend only unwillingly, as He says after this: ﴿And they do not spend except while they are averse﴾ [al-Tawbah 9:54].

The imperative in ﴿anfiqū﴾ ("spend") is for equality (*al-taswiyah*), meaning: spend or do not spend, as the particle "or" in His words ﴿willingly or unwillingly﴾ indicates. It has the meaning of a conditional statement, because it amounts to saying: "It will not be accepted from you if you spend willingly, or if you spend unwillingly." Do you not see that after such constructions the conditional often comes with the same meaning, as in His words: ﴿Ask forgiveness for them or do not ask forgiveness for them; even if you ask forgiveness for them seventy times, God will never forgive them﴾ [al-Tawbah 9:80]?

*Al-karh* ("unwillingness") is the strongest form of compulsion, and between it and *al-tawʿ* ("willingness") there are degrees whose intended meaning is known by inference. ﴿Tawʿan aw karhan﴾ is in the accusative as a substitute for the absolute object (*al-mafʿūl al-muṭlaq*, the cognate accusative), with the implied sense: "a spending of willingness or a spending of unwillingness." The subject of the passive verb ﴿yutaqabbala﴾ ("be accepted") is ﴿minkum﴾ ("from you"), meaning: nothing from you will be accepted. The implied object is not the spending derived from ﴿anfiqū﴾; rather, the intended meaning is generality.

The clause ﴿Indeed, you have been a defiantly disobedient people﴾ is in the position of a cause for the negation of acceptance. For this reason the emphatic particle *inna*, which conveys the sense of the causal *fā'* ("for, because"), occurs within it, since the disbeliever's good deed is not accepted from him. By "those who defy" (*al-fāsiqīn*) is meant the disbelievers, and for this reason He follows it with His words: ﴿And nothing prevented their expenditures from being accepted from them except that they disbelieved in God and His Messenger﴾ [al-Tawbah 9:54]. The description "defiantly disobedient" was chosen over "disbelievers" because they outwardly display Islam while inwardly concealing disbelief, so they were like those who had turned away from Islam toward disbelief. The purpose of this is to make them despair of benefiting from what they gave of their wealth. It may be that they used to reckon that spending for the expedition would benefit them if the Messenger's call was true, and this stemmed from their doubt about the matter of religion. They imagined that they were doing deeds that would benefit the Muslims, which they would find at the Gathering, on the assumption that the truthfulness of the Messenger would become evident. They would remain on their religion and not expose themselves to destruction on the expedition or to its hardships. This is due to the poor judgment of the people of error, as God related about one of them: ﴿Have you seen the one who disbelieved in Our signs and said, "I will surely be given wealth and children"?﴾ [Maryam 19:77], for he reckoned that he would be resurrected on the Day of Resurrection in the same condition in which he was in this life, if the Messenger's report about the Resurrection were true.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 9, verse 54:

Page 227
﴿And nothing prevented their expenditures from being accepted from them except that they disbelieved in Allah and His Messenger, and they do not come to the prayer except while being lazy, and they do not spend except while being unwilling.﴾
This is conjoined to the clause ﴿Indeed, you were a defiantly disobedient people﴾ [al-Tawba: 53], because this is an explanation of the cause for the non-acceptance of their expenditures, by adding mention of two other causes that prevent the acceptance of their deeds, both of which are among the effects of disbelief and defiant disobedience. They are: that they do not come to the prayer except while being lazy, and that they do not spend except while being unwilling. Although disbelief alone is sufficient for non-acceptance, the mention of these two causes indicates the firm rootedness of disbelief in their hearts, and censures them for hypocrisy, which indicates cowardice and hesitation. So the mention of disbelief explains the mention of defiant disobedience, and the mention of sluggishness in the prayer shows that they are negligent regarding the greatest act of worship, so how could their spending be out of sincerity and desire? And the mention of reluctance in spending shows the absence of sincerity in this trait under discussion.

Hamza and al-Kisa'i read: (an yuqbala minhum) with the yaʾ (third person masculine plural), because the plural of a non-human-feminine noun may be treated with either masculine or feminine agreement.

**Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 9, verse 55:**

﴿So let not their wealth or their children impress you. Allah only intends to punish them through them in this worldly life, and that their souls depart while they are disbelievers.﴾

This is a consequence (tafri') of the censure of their condition regarding their wealth, and of the fact that the abundance of their wealth does not bring them peace of mind. It informs the Muslims that what they see of the worldly enjoyment possessed by some of these hypocrites should not be an object of admiration for the believers, nor should they think the hypocrites have obtained a share of immediate good. It shows that this is a cause of their punishment in this world.

The address is to the Prophet (ﷺ), and the intended meaning is to teach the community (ummah).

[p. 228]

The meaning of this verse is that Allah has revealed a secret of the souls of the hypocrites: He created in their souls stinginess (shuhh) and greed for wealth, and a trial (fitnah) in preserving it and in anxiety about losing it. Because of this, He placed them in hardship and torment on account of their wealth. They are in toil (kabad) in gathering it, in fear for it of loss, and in pain from spending what their circumstances compel them to spend from it. Thus Allah intended to punish them in this world through that which is by nature a cause of comfort and ease, and His intention was fulfilled. This is among the most severe worldly punishments, and this is the condition of misers and of those who are stingy in general. However, believers among them have solace for their calamities through what they hope for in reward for spending or for patience.

It is also possible that Allah has innately fashioned this disposition in them from the time of their existence, so that this would be among the motives of their disbelief and hypocrisy, since a bad disposition calls forth another. Disbelief is a bad disposition, so it is no wonder that the soul of the stingy miser is drawn toward it. Hypocrisy is prompted by a bad disposition of cowardice and stinginess, so that its possessor may avoid dangers. The same applies to their children, since they were in a trial of fear for the faith of some of their children, and in opposition between them and some of their children who were guided to Islam, such as Handhalah ibn Abi 'Amir, known as Ghasil al-Mala'ikah (the one washed by the angels), and 'Abd Allah ibn 'Abd Allah ibn Ubayy. This was among the punishments inflicted on their parents.

Because the mention of the children here is like a supplement, to add clarity that they gain no benefit from everything that is likely to benefit people, the children are coordinated (by 'atf) with the repetition of the negative particle after the conjunction, indicating that their mention is a supplement and a digression (istitrad).

The lam in (*li-yu'adhdhibahum*) is the lam of causation (lam al-ta'lil). It is attached to the verb of intention (iradah) to show that the purpose is wisdom and cause, and so it substitutes for the object of the verb of intention. The original usage of the verb of intention is that it takes its object directly, as in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Allah intends for you ease and does not intend for you hardship﴾ [al-Baqarah: 185]. It is frequently followed by the lam, as in this verse, and in His saying, exalted is He, in surah al-Nisa': ﴿Allah intends to make clear to you﴾ [al-Nisa': 26], and in the verse of Kuthayyir:

*I intend to forget her love, but it is as if Layla appears to me in every place.*

Sometimes they use the lam together with *kay* for emphasis in causation, as in the verse of Qays ibn 'Ubadah:

*I intended, so that the people might know that it [the banner] is the trousers of Qays, and the delegations are witnesses.*

[p. 229]

This lam frequently occurs after the root of intention and the root of command. Some readers call it *lam an* (with a fatha on the hamza). This was discussed earlier in the commentary on His saying, exalted is He, *Allah intends to make clear to you* in surah al-Nisa'.

His saying, "(*fi al-hayat al-dunya*) [in the life of this world]," is connected to (*yu'adhdhibahum*) [He punishes them] (al-Tawbah: 14). Attempting to move it earlier or later is forced (ta'assuf).

The phrase (*wa tazhaqa*) [and their souls depart] is coordinated (by 'atf) with (*li-yu'adhdhibahum*) [that He may punish them], in view of the fact that Allah intended it for them when He granted them wealth and children. From this it is understood that He intended their death in disbelief, so the punishment through their wealth and children encompasses their entire lives. For if they had believed in some part of the end of their lives, they would have gained some benefit from their wealth during that time, even with stinginess.

The clause (*wa hum kafirun*) [while they are disbelievers] is in the position of a circumstantial clause (hal) relating to the pronoun attached to it, because if the soul departs while in the state of disbelief, then they died as disbelievers.

Admiration (i'jab) is approval mixed with astonishment and joy at what is seen. Allah, exalted is He, says: ﴿Even if the abundance of the evil impresses you﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 100], meaning: you approve of the sight of its abundant numbers.

Zuhuq is departure with force and constriction, and its mention has become common regarding the departure of the spirit from the body. A similar verse will come later in this surah.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 9, verse 56:

﴿They swear by Allah that they are surely of you, but they are not of you; rather, they are a people who are afraid.﴾

This sentence is coordinated with what precedes it concerning the reports about the hypocrites (ahl al-nifaq). The plural pronouns refer back to them, and the purpose is to nullify what they put forward to the Muslims, namely the affirmation through oath that they are among the believers.

The meaning of "innahum laminkum" ("surely they are of you") is: some of those addressed. Since those addressed were believers, the partiality (al-tab'id) is understood in terms of their being characterized by faith, by the indication of the oath, because they sensed the doubt of the believers that they were like them.

Page 230

Al-faraq (fear) is intense fear.

The choice of the present tense in His words "wa yahlifuna" ("and they swear") and "yafraqun" ("they are afraid") indicates renewal and that this is their habitual conduct.

The requirement of the istidrak (contrast) is that the thing contrasted be that they are not of you, i.e., disbelievers. So the contrasted element is omitted, being dispensed with by the particle of contrast, and what serves as a response to their outward state of faith is mentioned: that it is a false display, and that what prompted them to display faith while in a state of disbelief is that they are afraid of the believers. Thus there is a wonderful brevity in the speech, as the mentioned part dispenses with two omitted sentences.

The complement of "yafraqun" is omitted because it is evident, i.e., they fear the enmity of the Muslims toward them, their fighting against them, or their expulsion, as He - exalted is He - said: ﴿If the hypocrites and those in whose hearts is a disease and the agitators in the city do not desist, We will surely incite you against them; then they will not remain your neighbors therein except briefly﴾ [al-Ahzab: 60] ﴿Cursed; wherever they are found, they will be seized and killed with [intense] slaughter﴾ [al-Ahzab: 61].

His words ﴿but they are not of you; rather, they are a people who are afraid﴾ are a statement open to multiple directions, since it can also mean: "but they are not of you; rather, they are a people characterized by the quality of cowardice, whereas believers are characterized by courage and honor. Those who are afraid are therefore not among the believers." In this sense is His - exalted is He - saying: ﴿He said, "O Noah, indeed he is not of your family; indeed, his deed is other than righteous."﴾ [Hud: 46], and the statement of Musawir ibn Hind in dispraise of the Banu Asad:

You claim that your brothers are Quraysh, for whom there is a covenant (ilf), and you have no covenant (ilaf).
Those [Quraysh] were granted security from hunger and fear, while the Banu Asad have hungered and feared.

So it is a directing toward praise of the believers, and perhaps the verse mentioned after it is more suitable to this meaning. In this verse is an indication that difference in character prevents close association and agreement.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 9, verse 57:

Page 231
﴿If they could find a refuge, or caves, or a place to enter, they would turn towards it while rushing headlong.﴾
This is an explanation of the clause ﴿But they are a people who are fearful.﴾ [al-Tawbah: 56]

Al-malja' (refuge) is the place of al-lajaʾ (seeking shelter), which is taking refuge and seeking protection.

Al-maghārāt is the plural of maghārah (cave), which is a wide cavity into which a person can enter. For this reason the form mafʿal, which denotes the place of an action, is derived for it, from ghāra al-shayʾ (the thing sank) when it entered into the earth. Al-mudakhkhal is a muftaʿal noun of place, from the idkhāl (entering), which is an iftiʿāl from al-dukhūl (entering). The tāʾ of the iftiʿāl was changed to dāl because it came after a dāl, as it was replaced in iddāna (he borrowed), and the majority (of readers) recited it this way. Yaʿqūb alone recited ﴿aw madkhalan﴾ with a fatḥah on the mīm and a sukūn on the dāl, a noun of place from dakhala (he entered).

The meaning of ﴿lawallaw ilayhi﴾ is that they would turn away towards one of the things mentioned. The basic meaning of tawallā is "to turn away," and since turning away implies two directions, one from which one turns away and one towards which one turns, its transitivity with one of the two prepositions specifies the intended meaning.

(Al-jumūḥ) its essential meaning is recoiling in aversion, and it is used here as a figure for speed combined with fear.

The meaning is: because of their fear of going out to the expedition, if they found a place of the kind in which one who wishes to hide can conceal himself so that people would not notice him, they would head for it hastily, fearing that the decision to go out to the expedition would be imposed upon them.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 9, verse 58:

﴿And among them are those who criticize you concerning the charities. If they are given from them, they are pleased; but if they are not given from them, at once they become resentful.﴾

The hypocrites were known for stinginess (shuhh), as Allah - exalted is He - said: ﴿grudging toward you﴾ and He said ﴿grudging toward the good﴾ [al-Ahzab: 19]. And from their stinginess is that they wish that the charities were distributed among them, and when they see them distributed to others, they find fault with giving them, with faults that they throw into their talk, and they show that they are jealous on behalf of those who deserve them, and that they are repelled by their disbursement to other than their people; but they only aim by this that they be restricted to themselves.

It is narrated that Abu al-Jawwaz, one of the hypocrites, found fault with the Prophet ﷺ giving some of the weak Bedouin shepherds from the wealth of the charities, as help for them and to win their hearts, and he said: "This is not justice, that you place your charities with shepherds, when he has been commanded to distribute them among the poor and the needy." And it is related that he confronted the Prophet ﷺ with this directly.

And on the authority of Abu Sa'id al-Khudri: it was revealed concerning Dhu al-Khuwaysira al-Tamimi, who said to the Prophet ﷺ: "Be just." This was at the division of gold that came from Yemen in the ninth year (AH). So perhaps the cause recurred, and Dhu al-Khuwaysira was among the hypocrites from the Bedouins.

Al-lamz means censure and disparagement; its present tense is from the pattern yadribu, and the majority (al-Jumhur) read it this way; and from the pattern yansuru, and Ya'qub alone read it this way.

The particle (fi) is attached to al-sadaqat, and the censure is only in their distribution, not in their essence, because usage indicates the intended meaning; this is common, the attribution of a ruling to the entities while the intended meaning is their states.

Then His saying: ﴿If they are given from them, they are pleased﴾ may mean: the apparent referent of the pronoun is what it returns to, namely, if the censurers are given; that is, the fault-finders hope to take from the wealth of the charities by way of a gift and assistance, and this is from their reaching the extreme of greed and covetousness. It may also be that the pronoun refers to what the pronoun of "from them" (minhum) refers to; that is: if the hypocrites are given, the censurers are pleased, and if others are given, they are angered. So the meaning is that they aim that the charities be distributed only to their own poor, and for this reason Abu al-Jawwaz disliked that the Bedouins be given from the charities.

The complement of "radu" (they were pleased) is not mentioned, because the intended meaning is that they became content, namely, with you.

The sudden "idha" (then suddenly) indicates that their anger is a matter that surprises the intelligent observer when he witnesses it, because it occurs where anger is not expected, and the nature of sudden matters is that they be strange in their category.

Page 233

﴿And if only they had been content with what Allah and His Messenger had given them, and said: "Allah is sufficient for us; Allah will give us of His bounty, and so will His Messenger. To Allah we are turning in hope."﴾ This is a clause conjoined (*jumla ma'tufa*, a clause linked to another by a conjunction) to the clause ﴿And among them are those who find fault with you concerning the alms﴾ [al-Tawba: 58], with respect to what follows from it, His saying: ﴿If they are given from it, they are pleased; but if they are not given from it, they become angry at once﴾ [al-Tawba: 58]. The conjunction indicates a praiseworthy state after the mention of a blameworthy one.

The answer to *law* (if/if only) is omitted, and what the conjoined clause indicates stands in its place. Its implied sense is: "That would have been better for them."

*Al-Iitā'* (giving) means *al-i'ṭā'* (giving). Its literal sense is giving essences (physical things), and it is used figuratively for determining gifts, as in ﴿Allah gave him the kingdom and wisdom﴾ [al-Baqara: 251], and in ﴿That is the bounty of Allah, which He gives to whom He wills﴾ [al-Ma'ida: 54].

His saying "*mā ātāhumu Allāh*" (what Allah gave them) belongs to this category. That is, what He determined for them, namely for their group, from the alms, by attaching it to attributes realised in them, like His saying: ﴿Alms are only for the poor﴾ [al-Tawba: 60], and so on.

The giving by the Messenger (ﷺ) means his giving property to whomever he sees fit from what Allah has made his to dispose of, such as the *nafl* (extra portion) from the spoils of war, the *salab* (the spoils taken from a slain enemy), gifts, rewards, and the like. It also includes his giving to those whom Allah has made entitled to alms.

It is permissible that the giving of Allah is the very giving of the Messenger (peace and blessings be upon him). The giving of Allah is mentioned to indicate that what the Messenger (ﷺ) determined for them is what Allah determined for them, as in His saying: ﴿Allah will give us of His bounty, and so will His Messenger﴾, that is, what Allah revealed to His Messenger (ﷺ) that he should give them, and in His saying: ﴿Say: The spoils belong to Allah and the Messenger﴾ [al-Anfal: 1].

*Ḥasb* is a noun meaning "sufficient." *Al-kifāya* (sufficiency) is used in the sense of "being content with something" and in the sense of "being in charge of a matter for the one who is sufficed," as in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And they said: Allah is sufficient for us﴾. Here it is in the first sense.

*Raḍiya* (to be pleased), when transitive with a direct object, indicates choosing the thing that is pleased with. When it takes *bi* (with), it indicates that he has become content because of what the *bi* governs, as in His saying: ﴿Are you content with the life of this world instead of the Hereafter?﴾ [al-Tawba: 38].

Page 234

When it takes *'an* (from), its meaning is that he overlooked his shortcoming or his sin: ﴿If you are pleased with them, indeed Allah is not pleased with the defiant people﴾ [al-Tawba: 96].

Here, "saying" is intended to mean speech together with belief. It is therefore a *kināya* (metonymy) for the necessary consequence while the implied meaning (the belief) may also be intended. If they conceal that in their hearts, that is from the praiseworthy state. However, since this speech comes in contrast to the report of their faultfinding about the alms, and faultfinding is by speech indicating dislike, what indicates contentment in speech is made a metonymy for contentment.

The clause ﴿Allah will give us of His bounty, and so will His Messenger﴾ explains the clause "Allah is sufficient for us", because sufficiency in an important matter requires attending to the one who is sufficed with benefits and meeting his need. The giving in it means giving essences.

*Al-fadl* is an increase of good and benefits: ﴿Indeed, Allah is full of bounty toward people﴾ [al-Baqara: 243]. Here *al-fadl* means "what is given," by using the verbal noun to mean the object given, as indicated by the partitive *min* (some of). If *min* were taken as indicating the starting point, it would be correct to intend the meaning of the verbal noun.

The clause ﴿To Allah we are turning in hope﴾ gives the reason, that is, because we hope for His bounty.

The fronting of the prepositional phrase *ilā Allāh* indicates restriction, meaning: "To Allah alone we turn, not to other than Him." The speech contains an elided *muḍāf* (a noun in a genitive construction omitted), and its implied sense is: "We hope for what Allah has determined for us, and we do not seek to be given what is not our right."

*Al-raghba* means seeking with courtesy and good manners.

[Page 235]

This verse is an interjection between the clause ﴿And among them are those who find fault with you concerning the alms﴾ (al-Tawba: 58) and the clause ﴿And among them are those who harm the Prophet﴾ (al-Tawba: 61). It is a digression (istitrad) that arose from the mention of fault-finding concerning the alms, and within it the explanation of the recipients of the alms (masarif al-sadaqat) was inserted.

[Page 236]

The purpose of the particle of restriction (adat al-hasr) is that none of the alms is due to those who found fault concerning the alms. The restriction of the alms to being due to the categories mentioned in this verse is a relative restriction (qasr idafi), meaning: the alms are for these people, not for you.

As for their being confined to the eight categories and not to any other category, this is derived from the limitation to them in a context of explanation, since the form of restriction cannot be used for both the absolute (haqiqi) and the relative (idafi) senses together, except by way of using a homonym (mushtarak) in both its meanings.

Al-faqir (الفَقِيرُ) is an adjective of the form sifa mushabbaha, meaning one characterized by poverty (al-faqr), which is the lack of possessing what suffices for the necessities of a person's living. Its opposite is al-ghaniyy (the rich). It has already been discussed at the words of Allah, the Exalted: ﴿If he is rich or poor, then Allah is more entitled to both of them﴾ (al-Nisa: 135), in Surat al-Nisa.

Al-miskin (المِسْكِينُ) is one possessing maskana, which is the humiliation that results from poverty. There is no doubt that the mention of one of them suffices from mentioning the other. The question arises only when both are mentioned together in one statement. It was said: this belongs to the category of emphasis (ta'kid). This is attributed to Abu Yusuf, Muhammad ibn al-Hasan and Abu 'Ali al-Jubba'i. It was also said: each of the two words is meant to denote a meaning different from that intended by the other. The explanation of this has been disputed in many opinions. The clearest of them is that al-faqir is the one in need to a degree that does not reduce its possessor to supplication and humiliation, while al-miskin is the one in need to a degree that compels him to supplication and humiliation. This is attributed to Malik, Abu Hanifa, Ibn 'Abbas, al-Zuhri, Ibn al-Sikkit and Yunus ibn Habib. Thus al-miskin is in greater need, because supplication occurs when patience weakens in bearing the pain of destitution, and most of that happens from the severity of need upon the needy person himself. The discussion of these two words has already occurred at the words of Allah, the Exalted: ﴿And to the near relative, the orphans, and the needy﴾ (al-Nisa: 36), in Surat al-Nisa.

[Page 237]

﴿Wa-l-ʿamilina ʿalayha﴾ (﴿and those working on them﴾) means those who work for its sake, that is, for the sake of the alms. Here the particle ʿalā (عَلى) denotes causation, as in the words of Allah: ﴿and that you may glorify Allah for having guided you﴾ (al-Baqara: 185), meaning for the sake of His guidance to you. The meaning of work is striving and service, and these are the collectors who go around to the tribes to gather the zakat of livestock. The choice of the particle ʿalā in this context is due to what its basic meaning implies, namely firmness and control, meaning those working for it with strong effort, because the collectors undertake hardship and great labor. Perhaps the indication of this is intended to point out that the ground for their entitlement is composed of two matters: that their work is for the benefit of the alms, and that it is arduous. It is also possible that ʿalā denotes metaphorical elevation, namely elevation of authority, as one says: he is ʿamil over the city (هو عامِلٌ عَلى المَدِينَةِ), meaning those working for the Prophet or for the caliph over the alms, that is, empowered to act in them.

Among those who were in charge of the alms in the time of the Prophet (ﷺ) was Hamal ibn Malik ibn al-Nabigha al-Hudhali, who was in charge of the alms of Hudhayl.

Al-mu'allafa qulubuhum (those whose hearts are to be reconciled) are those whose souls are won over (tu'allafu), that is, made comfortable with Islam, from among those who have entered Islam recently, or from among those who are inclined to enter Islam, since they were close to becoming Muslims.

Ta'lif (reconciliation) means producing ulfa, which is familiarity and comfort. So "qulub" (hearts) means souls, and the use of "qalb" for that by which belief is perceived is common in the Arabic language.

The reconciled ones have various conditions. Among them are those who were recent in Islam and whose Islam was known to be weak at that time, such as Abu Sufyan ibn Harb and al-Harith ibn Hisham, from among those who accepted Islam at the conquest. Among them are those who were fierce unbelievers, such as 'Amir ibn al-Tufayl. Among them are those who were unbelievers but who showed an inclination towards Islam, such as Safwan ibn Umayya. The Prophet (ﷺ) gave such people from the wealth of the alms and other sources in order to win them over to Islam. The number of those whom Ibn al-'Arabi counted among the reconciled ones in his book al-Ahkam reached thirty-nine men. Ibn al-'Arabi said: Abu Ishaq, meaning the judge Isma'il ibn Ishaq, counted Mu'awiya ibn Abi Sufyan among them, but he was not one of them, and how could that be, when the Prophet (ﷺ) had entrusted him with the revelation of Allah and His Qur'an and mixed him with himself?

[Page 238]

Al-riqab (الرِّقابِ) (﴿and for the slaves﴾) means the slaves, the plural of raqaba, which is also used to mean a slave. Allah, the Exalted, said: ﴿then the freeing of a believing slave﴾ (al-Nisa: 92).

The particle fi (في) here denotes metaphorical location (zarfiyya majaziyya). It makes unnecessary the assumption of a hidden phrase "fakk al-riqab" (freeing the necks), because the locative sense makes the slaves as if the wealth were placed within their collective. It was not introduced with the preposition li (لِ) lest it be assumed that the alms are handed over to them. Rather, that wealth is spent on the necks of the slaves by purchase or by assisting them with installments of a contract of manumission (nujum kitaba), or by ransoming captured Muslims, because captives are slaves of those who captured them. The words of Allah ﴿and to the seekers and for the slaves﴾ (al-Baqara: 177) have already passed in Surat al-Baqara.

Al-gharimin (الغارِمِينَ) are debtors whose wealth is insufficient to pay what they owe, to the extent that their creditors would lose some of their wealth, or the debtors would lose what remains of their wealth needed to sustain life. So spending alms wealth on that is mercy to both the creditor and the debtor.

Fi sabil Allah (في سَبِيلِ اللَّهِ) (in the way of Allah) is jihad. That is, from the wealth of the alms is spent what is needed for the means of jihad, such as weapons and guarding on the frontiers, by land and by sea, all of that.

Ibn al-sabil (ابْنِ السَّبِيلِ) (the wayfarer) is a stranger away from his people. He is attributed to the sabil (road), meaning the way, because the road gave him birth, that is, the road that brought him, and he was not born among the people. For this meaning the expression "son of the road" (ibn al-sabil) was applied to him.

The jurists of the Community have many approaches to the rulings derived from this verse, and important understandings. It is appropriate that we touch upon the well-known of them without leading to prolixity. Indeed their meanings are more abundant than what this discussion can contain.

As for what relates to assigning the alms to these categories, leaving aside taking the li (لِ) in His words "li-l-fuqara" (for the poor) to mean ownership or entitlement, the scholars have differed over whether the eligible recipients of these alms must each receive a portion of the alms, and whether equality is required among the categories in what each category receives of their share. What the majority of scholars hold is that giving to all the categories is not obligatory. Rather, the distribution is left to the discretion of the rulers, who assign it according to the need of the categories and the abundance of wealth. This is the view of 'Umar ibn al-Khattab, 'Ali, Hudhayfa, Ibn 'Abbas, Sa'id ibn Jubayr, Abu al-'Aliya, al-Nakha'i, al-Hasan, Malik and Abu Hanifa. It is narrated from Malik that this is among what the Companions reached consensus upon. Ibn 'Abd al-Barr said: we do not know of any dissenter among the Companions on this. It is also narrated from Hudhayfa: Allah only mentioned these categories so that they would be known, and whichever category you give from them will suffice you. Al-Tabari said: the alms are for filling the need of the Muslims, or for filling the need of Islam, and this is understood from the sources of the Qur'an in its explanation of the categories and enumeration of them. I say: this is what the most skilled of the scholars of reasoning chose, such as Ibn al-'Arabi and Fakhr al-Din al-Razi.

[Page 239]

Ikrima, al-Zuhri, 'Umar ibn 'Abd al-'Aziz and al-Shafi'i went to the obligation of distributing the alms to all eight categories, with each category receiving an eighth of the alms. If one of the categories ceases to exist, the alms are divided into parts according to the number of categories remaining. They agreed that it is not obligatory to distribute what is given to one category among all the individuals of that category.

As for what returns to verifying the meanings of the categories and specifying their attributes: regarding the description of the poor and the needy, the more apparent view is that it is left to custom (al-'urf), and that destitution varies, as has been mentioned just above. The scholars differed in determining the sources of income by which a person is not considered poor, but they agreed that a dwelling place and a servant do not count as wealth that removes from their owner the description of poverty.

As for the capacity to earn a living, it was said that one who is capable of it is not counted as poor and does not deserve alms on the ground of poverty. This was said by al-Shafi'i, Abu Thawr, Ibn Khuwayz Mandad and Yahya ibn 'Umar from among the Malikis. Traditions were narrated on this, transmitted by al-Daraqutni, al-Tirmidhi and Abu Dawud. It was also said: if a person is strong and has no wealth, it is permissible for him to take alms. This is what is transmitted from Malik, and al-Tirmidhi chose it. Al-Kiya al-Tabari, from among the Shafi'is, also held it.

As for those working on the alms, they are determined by the appointment of the ruler. It is narrated from Ibn 'Umar that they are given wages according to the amount of their work. This is the view of Malik and Abu Hanifa.

As for the reconciled ones, the Prophet (ﷺ) gave them varied gifts from the alms and other sources. As for the alms, they have a share in them by the explicit text of the Qur'an. As for what is other than the alms, it is by the action of the Prophet (ﷺ). Their giving continued in the caliphate of Abu Bakr and for a period of the caliphate of 'Umar, and they were given according to individual judgment (ijtihad). They were not assigned a specific eighth of the alms. Then the scholars differed over whether this category continues to exist. This is a peculiar question, because it is based on the permissibility of abrogation by rational proof and by analogical deduction (qiyas al-istinbat), meaning in the absence of an original text on which a similar case is analogized. Whether it is based on this principle is open to question. Rather, its basis is that when this category becomes inoperative, to whom is its portion returned? It should be analogized to the ruling on the portion of one who dies among the people of an endowment (habs), where his share passes to the remaining beneficiaries of the endowment.

It is narrated from 'Umar ibn al-Khattab that their portion lapsed because of the might of Islam. This was also said by al-Hasan, al-Sha'bi, Malik ibn Anas and Abu Hanifa. It was also said that the Companions reached consensus on the lapsing of the portion of the reconciled ones from the time of the caliphate of Abu Bakr. This was reported by al-Qurtubi. There is no doubt that 'Umar stopped giving to the reconciled ones although their category still existed. He saw that Allah had made the religion of Islam sufficient by the abundance of its followers, so there is no benefit for Islam in spending the wealth of the Muslims to win over the hearts of those in whose hearts Islam had not yet been firmly established.

Some scholars treated the action of 'Umar and the silence of the Companions regarding it as a tacit consensus (ijma' sukuti, consensus by silence), and so they treated it as abrogating part of this verse. This is abrogation by consensus (naskh bi-l-ijma'). Whether tacit consensus counts as equivalent to explicit consensus is disputed among the masters of the principles of jurisprudence. This structure is also open to question, as you have known just above.

Many scholars said: they continue to exist whenever they are found, because the imam may sometimes need to win people over to Islam. This was said by al-Zuhri, 'Umar ibn 'Abd al-'Aziz, al-Shafi'i and Ahmad ibn Hanbal. 'Abd al-Wahhab and Ibn al-'Arabi from among the Malikis chose it. Ibn al-'Arabi said: in my view the correct position is that if Islam becomes strong, they cease to be given, but if they are needed, they are given. That is, he holds that this category continues to exist, and he holds that the non-giving to them in the time of 'Umar was due to the might of Islam. This is what the later scholars have affirmed as correct. Ibn al-Hajib said in al-Mukhtasar: the correct view is that their ruling continues if they are needed. This is a view that should not be taken in imitation of anyone else.

Then as for the slaves (al-riqab), the majority hold that the meaning of ﴿and for the freeing of slaves﴾ is buying slaves in order to free them, and paying what is owed by the mukatab (a slave who has contracted to buy his freedom from his master) in money through which he gains his freedom. This is the narration of the Madinans from Malik. It was also said that the mukatab is not to be assisted with it, even if he is at the last installment (najm) by which he gains his freedom, and this was narrated from Malik through other than the Madinan transmitters. It was also said: it is only given to assist the mukatab with his installments, not for manumission. This is the view of al-Layth, al-Nakha'i, and al-Shafi'i.

There is disagreement about giving this for the partial manumission of a slave, or for installments of a kitabah (contract of manumission) which do not complete the mukatab's freedom. It was said: it is not permissible. This is the view of Malik and al-Zuhri. It was also said: it is permissible. The ransoming of prisoners of war is included in ﴿freeing the necks﴾, according to the more correct view within the Maliki school. This is the view of Ibn 'Abd al-Hakam and Ibn Habib, in contrast to Asbagh among the Malikis.

As for the debtors (al-gharimun), their condition is that their debt should not be for an act of disobedience, unless they repent. A deceased debtor whose debt cannot be paid from his estate is counted among the debtors according to Ibn Habib, in contrast to Ibn al-Mawwaz.

Regarding ﴿in the way of Allah﴾ (sabil Allah), there is no disagreement that the intended meaning is military campaigning (ghazw), so the needy fighters in the land of the campaign are given, even if they are wealthy in their own land. As for the wealthy fighters in the land of the campaign, the majority hold that they are given. This is the view of Malik, al-Shafi'i, and Ishaq. Abu Hanifa said: they are not given. The truth is that ﴿in the way of Allah﴾ includes purchasing the equipment for jihad, such as weapons, horses, naval and sea vessels, catapults, mounts for carrying, building fortresses, digging trenches, and paying spies who bring news of the enemy. This was stated by Muhammad ibn 'Abd al-Hakam from the Malikis, and no opponent of his view is mentioned. The words of al-Qurtubi in his tafsir suggest that Ibn 'Abd al-Hakam's view contradicts that of the majority. Some of the early scholars (al-salaf) held that the Hajj is among the ways of Allah and enters into the categories of charitable disbursements; this was narrated from Ibn 'Umar, Ahmad, and Ishaq. This is an ijtihad (independent reasoning) and a ta'wil (interpretation). Ibn al-'Arabi said: no report has ever come concerning giving zakat for the Hajj.

As for the wayfarer (ibn al-sabil), there is no disagreement that a stranger in need in the land of his travel is intended, even if he finds someone who would lend to him, since he is not obliged to put himself under obligation. There is disagreement regarding the wealthy: the majority said he is not given; this is the view of Malik. Al-Shafi'i and Asbagh said: he is given, even if he is wealthy in the land of his travel.

His saying ﴿an obligation from Allah﴾ is in the accusative because it is a verbal noun (masdar) emphasizing an omitted verbal noun indicated by his saying ﴿Charity is only...﴾, since it conveys the meaning "Allah has prescribed" or "has made obligatory." So it is emphasized with "obligation" (fari-dah) from the same root as the omitted term and its meaning.

The purpose of this is to magnify the status of this ruling and to command adherence to it.

The clause ﴿and Allah is All-Knowing, All-Wise﴾ is a tadhyil (concluding addition). It conveys, through the restrictive "only" (innama) in his saying ﴿Charity is only for the poor and the needy...﴾, the meaning: Allah is All-Knowing, All-Wise in restricting charity to these categories; that is, it proceeds from the All-Knowing, who knows what suits the rulings, and the All-Wise, who perfected the things He created or legislated. The waw is parenthetical (i'tiradiyya), because the parenthetical insertion occurs at the end of a speech according to the view of the verifying scholars (al-muhaqqiqin).

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 9, verse 61:

صفحة ٢٤١
﴿And among them are those who harm the Prophet and say, "He is an ear." Say, "An ear of good for you, who believes in Allah and has faith in the believers, and a mercy for those of you who believe. And those who harm the Messenger of Allah will have a painful punishment."﴾
This is a conjoined clause in which another of the traits of the hypocrites is mentioned: their making excuses regarding the caution with which the Prophet and the Muslims treat them, and regarding the slips of their hypocrisy that come to light. They claim that this is a slander by slanderers against them, reported to the Prophet ﷺ, and that he believes the rumour about them and accuses them of what he has heard about them, of which they are innocent. By this they make excuses to the Muslims. In it there is also an increase in harm to the Messenger ﷺ and the casting of doubt into the hearts of the Muslims regarding the perfections of their Prophet, peace be upon him. The expression "the Prophet" (al-Nabi) in place of a pronoun is an explicit mention in the place of the implicit pronoun, because before it is the words, ﴿And among them are those who slander you concerning the charities﴾ [al-Tawbah: 58]. So the apparent requirement would have been to say, "And among them are those who harm you," but he turned away from the pronoun to the explicit mention of the Prophet's description, to signal the heinousness of their saying and to add to the exaltation of the Prophet by praising him with the description of prophethood, such that their statement about him is not related except after mentioning what points to his exalted status and alludes to their guilt in what they said.

These are a group who used to say about the Prophet ﷺ what would harm him if it reached him. Among those hypocrites who said such things are counted: al-Jullas ibn Suwayd, before his repentance; Nabtal ibn al-Harith; 'Attab ibn Qushayr; and Wadi'ah ibn Thabit. Some of them said, "If what Muhammad says is true, then we are worse than donkeys," and some of them said, "We say about him whatever we want, then we go to him and swear to him that we did not say it, and he accepts our word."

Harm (adha) is light injury, and it is most often applied to damage through speech and intrigue. From it is His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿They will not harm you except with a little harm﴾ [Al 'Imran: 111], which was discussed earlier in Surat Al 'Imran, and at His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿and they were harmed until Our help came to them﴾ [al-An'am: 34] in Surat al-An'am.

The content of the clause ﴿And they say, "He is an ear"﴾ is a specific subsumed under a general, because their saying that is itself a form of harm.

صفحة ٢٤٢
The ear (udhun) is the organ through which the sense of hearing exists. The meaning of ﴿He is an ear﴾ is the report about him that he is an instrument of hearing.

The report with ﴿He is an ear﴾ is among the forms of eloquent simile: that is, like an ear in receiving what is heard, not rejecting any of it, and it is a metaphor for his believing everything he hears without distinguishing between what is accepted and what is rejected. It is related that the one who said this was Nabtal ibn al-Harith, one of the hypocrites.

The clause ﴿Say, "An ear of good for you"﴾ is a new, independent clause in the form of a dialogue and conversation, to refute their statement by turning their intent around, to enrage them and to frustrate their aims. This is from the wise style (al-uslub al-hakim), in which the addressee carries the speaker's words to other than what he intends, to alert him that it is more fitting that it be intended. It has already passed at His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿They ask you about the crescent moons. Say: they are signs of time for people and for the pilgrimage﴾ [al-Baqarah: 189]. From it is what took place between al-Hajjaj and al-Qaba'thari, when al-Hajjaj said to him in threat, "I will surely make you carry the black one (al-adham)" (meaning: I will surely keep you bound in chains and never let you go). Al-Qaba'thari replied, "Someone like the Amir carries on the black or the grey." He turned his intent toward riding, and toward the horse which is black in color, from the word al-adham. This is from God's jealousy for His Messenger, peace be upon him. For this reason it was not followed by rebuke or reproach, as what came before it was followed by His saying: ﴿And among them is one who says, "Grant me leave"﴾ [al-Tawbah: 49], up to here. Rather, it was followed by an explanation of its falsity, and He commanded the Prophet ﷺ to convey to them what is a refutation of their claim from its root, by turning their statement toward a meaning fitting for the Messenger, so that nothing of the reported saying remains. This is one of the subtleties of the Qur'an.

The meaning of "an ear of good" is that he hears what reaches him about you and does not hold you to account; he hears your excuses and accepts them from you. So his acceptance of what he hears benefits you and does not harm you. Thus this is an ear for good, that is, for hearing and dealing with it, and not an ear for evil.

This statement refutes that "ear" be taken in the sense of blame that they intended, for the description with "ear" is not restricted to one who accepts speech that leads to evil; rather it is more general. Therefore it was valid to restrict it here to what contains good. This is applying the word to other than its intended meaning, and it is a kind of sent metaphor (al-majaz al-mursal) by the relation of generality and restriction on one side. So let it not puzzle you how the description "ear", when intended as blame, can be joined to "good". The locus of blame in this description is accepting everything one hears, without distinction, whether it leads to evil or good, because that throws its possessor into confusion in his affairs and dealings. But when its possessor accepts only good and rejects what is evil in speech, the description has become beneficial, because its possessor has undertaken to accept only good and to bring people to it.

This is the verification of the meaning of the contrast and the correctness of attaching this description to "good." As for taking it to other than this meaning, it reduces it to the manner of "saying by its implication" (al-qawl bil-mujib) as a concession and letting the reins loose: that is, "He is an ear as you said, and you have benefited from his description of this, since he accepted your excuses and your disavowal of what reached him about you." But this is not refined, because what is good for them may be evil for others.

Nafi' alone read "udhun" with the dhal sukun in both places, and the rest read it with the dhal damma in both places.

The clause ﴿He believes in Allah﴾ is a preparation for His saying after it, ﴿and has faith in the believers﴾, since that is the intended meaning of the response, because it is purely good and far from evil: that he believes in Allah, so he deals with people by what Allah has commanded regarding dealing: pardon, forgiveness, enjoining good, and turning away from the ignorant; and that he does not hold anyone to account except on clear evidence. So people are safe from his side in what reaches him, because he does not deal except in the known manner. Thus his believing in Allah is a restraint preventing him from holding people to account on suspicion and accusation.

To have faith "for" the believers means to accept as true what they report. It is said, "He believed for so-and-so," meaning he confirmed him, and for this reason it is transitive with the lam and not the ba', as in His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿You would not be believed by us even if we were truthful﴾ [Yusuf: 17]. So his confirmation of them is because they are truthful and do not lie, since faith restrains them from telling him a lie. Just as the Messenger does not hold anyone to account for the report of a liar, he deals with people by the testimony of the believers. So His saying, ﴿and has faith in the believers﴾, is praise of him for that, which implies a command to it, and it is the opposite of His saying: ﴿O you who believe, if a corrupt person brings you a report, verify it﴾ [al-Hujurat: 6].

The conjoining of the clause "and a mercy" with the two clauses ﴿believes in Allah and has faith in the believers﴾ is because his being a mercy to those among them who believe, after his knowledge of their hypocrisy, is a result of his overlooking their crimes and granting them respite, so that whoever Allah has guided to faith among them may firmly attain it. Had he seized them in their state without delay, it would have been hasty punishment. So the meaning of "faith" in His saying "who believe" is faith in action, not merely the display of faith, as the commentators explained, meaning by "the believers" those who display faith while concealing disbelief, and they are the hypocrites.

Hamza read "wa rahmatin" with a kasra, in coordination with "khayrin", meaning "an ear of mercy," and the outcome is one.

This trait has been mentioned together with the two other traits in keeping with the Qur'an's custom of seizing the opportunity of guidance toward good through encouragement and warning. It encouraged them to believe so that they might expiate their past misdeeds, then it followed the encouragement with a warning of the consequences of harming the Messenger in His saying: ﴿And those who harm the Messenger of Allah will have a painful punishment﴾. This is a warning of the punishment of the Hereafter and the punishment of this world. In mentioning the Prophet by the description "Messenger of Allah" there is an indication that whoever harms him deserves a painful punishment; so it is the attaching of a ruling to a derived term that signals the causal reason.

In the relative construction there is also an indication that the cause of the punishment is the harming, so the cause is compound.

Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on Surah 9, verse 62:
