﴿They swear by Allah to you, that they may please you; but Allah and His Messenger have more right that they should please Him, if they are believers.﴾

He departed from the style of narrating about them with the phrase "wa minhum" (and among them), because what is related here is a state of all of them.

The sentence is therefore a resumptive sentence of initial resumption (isti'naf ibtida'i), to inform the Messenger ﷺ and the believers that the hypocrites swear false oaths, so their oaths should not deceive them. Thus the pronoun in "yahlifuna" (they swear) refers to those who harm the Prophet.

What is meant is false swearing, by the indication of His saying: ﴿Allah and His Messenger have more right that they should please Him﴾, that is, by their abandoning the matters for which they swore, given that He knows their oaths are false, as was mentioned earlier in His saying: ﴿They would swear by Allah, "Had we been able, we would have gone out with you," destroying themselves; and Allah knows that they are liars.﴾ [At-Tawbah: 42]

The address of "kum" (you) is to the Muslims, and this indicates that the hypocrites swear to disclaim what reaches the Muslims of their harmful statements against the Messenger, peace and blessings be upon him, and this angers the Muslims and they denounce them for it, while the Prophet ﷺ overlooks that. Therefore Allah, exalted is He, said: ﴿Allah and His Messenger have more right that they should please Him﴾, meaning, more right than you that they be pleased by you. The reason for the greater right of Allah and His Messenger to be pleased is explained in the following verse. The pleasing of Allah is through belief in Him and in His Messenger and magnifying His Messenger; the pleasing of the Messenger is through affirming him, loving him and honoring him.

He used the singular pronoun in His saying: ﴿that they should please Him﴾ even though there are two referents, because the intention was for the pronoun to return to the first of the two names, and the conjunction is taken as conjunction of sentences, with the implied meaning: "and Allah has more right that they should please Him, and His Messenger likewise." The speech is then two sentences, the second of which is in the manner of a safeguard (ihtiras), and the omission of the predicate is brevity (ijaz). Among the subtleties of this is an indication of the distinction between the two kinds of pleasing. From this is the saying of Dabi' ibn al-Harith:

"And whoever's dwelling has become in Medina, then I and Qayyar therein are indeed strangers."

The implied meaning: "Then I am a stranger, and Qayyar therein is also a stranger," because one of the two estrangements differs from the other.

The object pronoun in "yurdhuhu" (they please Him) refers to the name of Allah, because it is the more important in the predicate, and for this it was placed first. Do you not see that the verse of Dabi' came with the lam of initiation in its predicate, which is among the associates of "inna" in the first sentence, not in the second sentence? And this usage is the most common.

The conditional clause "in kanu mu'minin" (if they are believers) is used to urge and to express hope for their belief, because what is related of them of states leaves no room for doubt in their belief; so the conditional was used to express hope and to urge belief. In it there is also a recording against them: if they repeat the same conduct, they are unbelievers in Allah and His Messenger. In it there is also instruction for the believers and a warning against the anger of Allah and His Messenger.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 9, verse 63:

Page 246
﴿Did they not know that whoever opposes Allah and His Messenger, for him is the fire of Hell, abiding therein forever? That is the great disgrace.﴾
This sentence stands in relation to the sentence ﴿Allah and His Messenger have more right that they should please Him﴾ [al-Tawbah: 62] in the manner of a causal explanation (ta'lil), because the rational person does not find pleasure in himself for an action that leads to such a punishment. Thus none would proceed to that except one who does not know that whoever opposes Allah and His Messenger comes to this evil destination.

The interrogative (istifham) is used here for denunciation and reproach (inkar wa tash'ni'), because their not knowing this is certain by necessity, since they disbelieve in the Messenger, and [it is certain] that Allah's pleasure is with His pleasure. But since their not knowing this was strange, given the presence of the proofs that necessitate that it is something they should know, the state of not knowing it became a reprehensible state. The use of this and similar expressions is frequent for informing about a important matter, like His saying in this surah ﴿Did they not know that Allah—it is He who accepts repentance from His servants﴾ [al-Tawbah: 104], and His saying ﴿Did they not know that Allah knows their secret and their private talk?﴾ [al-Tawbah: 78], and the saying of Mawyal ibn Jahm al-Madhhiji, or Mubashshir ibn Hudhayl al-Fazari:

Did you not know, O 'Amrak—may Allah keep you—that I am generous, when generous people are few?

So it is as if it were said: "Let them know that whoever opposes Allah..." etc.
The pronoun governed by "annahu" is the pronoun of the matter (damir al-sha'n), and the pronoun is explained by the sentence ﴿whoever opposes Allah﴾ up to its end.

The meaning is: Did they not know a great matter, namely that whoever opposes Allah and His Messenger, for him is the fire of Hell?

The two dals in (yuhadid) are not merged (fakk) and not assimilated (idgham) because it occurs in the jussive, so both unmerged and merged forms are permitted. The unmerged form (fakk) is more well-known and more frequent in the Qur'an, and it is the dialect of the people of the Hijaz. Assimilation is also attested in it, such as His saying ﴿And whoever opposes Allah﴾ [al-Hashr: 4] in Surat al-Hashr, in the reading of all ten readers, and it is the dialect of Tamim.

And (al-muhadda) means opposition and contrariness.

The fa' in ﴿then for him is the fire of Hell﴾ serves to connect the response of the conditional (shart) of (man).

Page 247
"Anna" is repeated in the response in order to emphasize the "anna" mentioned before the condition, as a verbal emphasis (tawkid lafzi). For when it entered upon the pronoun of the matter, and the conditional sentence and its response were an explanation of the pronoun of the matter, the rule of "anna" applied to both sentences, such that if it were not mentioned in the response, it would be known that its meaning was present there. So when it was mentioned, its mention was an emphasis of it. There is no harm in separating the emphasis from what is emphasized by the conditional sentence, or separating the fa' of the response from what follows it by a particle, since there is no barrier to that. Of this type is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Then indeed your Lord, for those who did evil in ignorance and then repented after that and amended—indeed your Lord, after it, is Forgiving and Merciful﴾ [al-Nahl: 119], and the saying of the poet al-Hamasi, who was one of the Bedouins:

And indeed a man whose covenant bonds of pledge endure, upon the like of this—indeed he is generous.

Hell has already been mentioned at His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Hell is sufficient for him, and what a wretched resting place﴾ [al-Baqarah: 206] in Surat al-Baqarah.
The demonstrative "dhalika" refers either to the punishment mentioned or to the pronoun of the matter, considering its explanation. The purpose of the demonstrative is to distinguish it so that its meaning is fixed in the mind of the hearer.

Khizy is humiliation and abasement, and it has already been mentioned at His saying, exalted is He: ﴿So what is the recompense of those among you who do that except disgrace in the worldly life﴾ [al-Baqarah: 85] in Surat al-Baqarah.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 9, verse 64:

﴿The hypocrites are wary lest a surah should be sent down against them, informing them of what is in their hearts. Say: "Mock on. Indeed, Allah will bring forth what you are wary of."﴾

This is an initial resumptive sentence (isti'naf ibtida'i, a new sentence that begins a fresh topic) introducing one of the conditions of all the hypocrites, as previously mentioned in His saying: ﴿They swear by Allah to you﴾ (Surat al-Tawbah: 62). It is their display of faith in the miracles and Allah's informing His Messenger ﷺ of unseen matters.

The apparent meaning of the statement is that the wariness proceeds from them. This apparent meaning conflicts with the fact that they do not believe that the Qur'an was sent down from Allah or that its report is true. For this reason the exegetes differed in interpreting this verse. The best of what has been said on this is the statement of Abu Muslim al-Isfahani: "It is a wariness that the hypocrites display by way of mockery. Allah informed His Messenger of this and commanded him to inform them that He would expose their secret, which they were wary of becoming known." The saying ﴿Mock on﴾ is evidence for what we have mentioned, meaning: they display this, intending to deceive the Muslims about the sincerity of their faith, while they are only mocking the Muslims among themselves. The intended meaning of ﴿what is in their hearts﴾ is not disbelief, because they do not display that it is something to be feared. Thus the verb (yahdharu, "is wary") is taken to mean the display of wariness. That is a figurative usage (majaz mursal, a metonymy based on a non-metaphorical relation), with the relation being that of appearance, and the indicator is His saying ﴿Say: "Mock on"﴾. Without this, there would be no fitting connection between genuine wariness and mockery. Since the hypocrites were concealing disbelief, it was not in their nature to be wary of a surah being sent down that would reveal what was in their hearts, because they do not believe it. Therefore the verb (yahdharu) must be understood to mean: they display wariness. According to this view, applying the verb to the display of wariness is one of the rare figurative usages.

Al-Zajjaj interpreted the verse as follows: "yahdharu" is a report used in the sense of a command, meaning "let them be wary." On this interpretation, the clause ﴿Say: "Mock on"﴾ is an initial resumptive sentence with no connection to the clause ﴿The hypocrites are wary﴾. There are other interpretations of the verse, far removed from its clear sense, which al-Fakhr (al-Razi) mentioned.

The pronouns in (ʿalayhim, "against them") and (tunabbi'uhum, "informs them") may refer to the hypocrites, which is the obvious reading given the consistency of the pronouns and their referents. In that case (ʿala, "against") has the meaning of the causal lam (li, "for the sake of"), meaning: it is sent down on account of their conditions, as in His saying: ﴿and that you may glorify Allah for having guided you﴾ (Surat al-Baqarah: 185). This usage is common in speech. The verb (tunabbi'uhum, "informs them") would then have its object, the pronoun of the hypocrites, with the preposition omitted, meaning: it informs about them, that is, it informs the Messenger of what is in their hearts.

It is also possible that the taʼ in (tunabbi'uhum) is the taʼ of address, with the address directed to the Messenger ﷺ, meaning: you inform them of what is in their hearts. Then the clause ﴿informing them of what is in their hearts﴾ is in the position of a qualifier for (surah, "surah"), and the connecting pronoun is omitted, its estimated form being: "informing them of it." This is a description of the surah in itself, not in the belief of the hypocrites. Thus the placement of the clause ﴿informing them of what is in their hearts﴾ is a digression (istitrad).

It is also possible that the two pronouns refer to the Muslims. The difference between the two pronouns does not harm the meaning, nor does it conflict with the pronoun (qulubihim, "their hearts"), which definitely refers to the hypocrites, because the meaning assigns each pronoun to what is fitting for it to refer to.

[Page 249]

The imperfect form (yahdharu) was chosen for what it conveys of bringing the condition to mind, as in His saying: ﴿then it stirs up clouds﴾ (Surat al-Rum: 48), and His saying: ﴿argues with Us concerning the people of Lot﴾ (Surat Hud: 74).

A surah (sūrah) is a specific portion of the verses of the Qur'an, having a beginning and an end. Its explanation has already been given in the commentary on the opening of the Surat al-Fatihah.

Tanbi'ah (informing) means reporting and making known. It is the verbal noun of (naba'a al-khabar, "reported the news"). It was mentioned earlier in His saying: ﴿There has certainly come to you some of the news of the messengers﴾ (Surat al-An'am: 34), in Surat al-An'am.

Istihza' (mockery) was mentioned in His saying: ﴿We are only mockers﴾ (Surat al-Baqarah: 14), at the beginning of al-Baqarah.

Ikhraj (bringing forth) is used figuratively to mean making apparent. The meaning is: Allah makes apparent what is in your hearts by sending down surahs, such as the surah of the Hypocrites, and this surah, the surah of "Bara'ah" (Repudiation, i.e., al-Tawbah). It was called al-Fadihah (the Exposer) because it enumerates their conditions in His saying: "And among them... and among them... and among them."

The use of the relative construction in His saying ﴿what you are wary of﴾, instead of saying "Allah will bring forth a surah that informs you of what is in your hearts," is significant. The more important aspect of their threat is the exposure of their inner secrets, not the sending down of a surah. Mentioning the relative clause covers both matters: the exposure of their inner secrets and its occurring in a surah that is sent down, and this is more painful to them. Thus there is wonderful brevity in it, like His saying in Surat Maryam, ﴿And We will inherit from him what he says﴾ (Surat Maryam: 80), after His saying: ﴿and he says, "I will surely be given wealth and children"﴾ (Surat Maryam: 77), meaning: We will inherit from him his wealth and his children.

The apparent reading is that this clause is coordinated with ﴿They swear to Allah to you, to please you﴾ [al-Tawbah: 62] or with ﴿And among them are those who hurt the Prophet﴾ [al-Tawbah: 61]. On this reading, the meaning of ﴿They swear to Allah to you﴾ [al-Tawbah: 62] is that they swear even when you do not ask them. So the oath they make is an oath covering, in general, their innocence of hypocrisy and of slander. Their answer to a question about specific matters for which they are accused is an answer intended to show that what came from them is not of the kind they are accused of. Thus, when they are asked about a conversation among them that is viewed with suspicion, they reply that it was idle talk and play. They mean that it was a means of relaxing after the hardships of travel, since a person who has undertaken hard labour needs rest through jesting and play.

It is narrated that the verse refers to this: "A group of the hypocrites who went out on the expedition to Tabuk, hypocritically, among them Wadi'ah ibn Thabit al-'Awfi and Makhshi ibn Humayyir al-Ash'ja'i, an ally of the Banu Salamah, stopped at a pass on the road, watching the army of the Muslims, and said: 'Look at this man who wants to conquer the castles of Syria! Far-fetched, far-fetched!' The Prophet (ﷺ) asked them about their private talk, and they answered: ﴿We were only conversing and playing﴾."

In my view, this does not hold, because the conditional form is in the future tense. The verse was revealed concerning what is more general, namely what they would be asked about in the future, as a report of what they would answer. They are asked about what they discuss in their gatherings and assemblies, which Allah, exalted is He, mentioned in His saying: ﴿And when they go apart to their devils, they say: "Indeed we are with you; we were only mocking"﴾ [al-Baqarah: 14], because they often withdrew from the gatherings of the Muslims. The object of the question is omitted because it is evident from the context of their saying: ﴿We were only conversing and playing.﴾ The implied meaning is: "And if you ask them about their talk in their private gatherings," Allah informed His Messenger of this, and in it there is part of the evidences of prophethood. It is also possible that the verse was revealed before the Messenger asked them, and that when he did ask them afterwards, they answered with what the verse had reported.

The restriction (al-qasr, restriction by exclusive specification) here is for specification: that is, "We discussed only in idle talk and play, not in what you suspected of us of slander and harm."

The word al-khawd (idle plunging into talk) was explained earlier, in His saying: ﴿And when you see those who engage in vain talk concerning Our verses﴾ [al-An'am: 68], in Surat al-An'am.

The word al-la'ib (play) was explained earlier, in His saying: ﴿And the life of this world is only play and amusement﴾ [al-An'am: 32], in al-An'am. Since play includes mocking others, the answer to their excuse came with His saying: ﴿You were mocking.﴾ Since their excuse was vague, it was rejected on this point, for Allah commanded His Messenger (ﷺ) to answer them as one certain of their condition, after He had informed him of what they would offer as an excuse. So He said to them ﴿Was it Allah and His verses and His Messenger that you were mocking?﴾, in the manner of His saying: ﴿So they will say: "Who will restore us?" Say: "He who brought you forth the first time"﴾ [al-Isra': 51].

The interrogative is one of denial and reproach. The placement of the object, ﴿Allah﴾, before its governing verb is for the purpose of restriction by specification. Because in their excuse they used a form of restriction by specification, the reply to them uses a form of restriction by specification in order to nullify their evasion in the answer. So He informed them that the play they admitted to was nothing but mockery of Allah, His verses and His Messenger, and not of anyone else. Restricting the mockery to what is connected with those mentioned implies that the mockery had actually occurred, without doubt, because restriction is a qualifier of a verbal predicate, and it entails that the action occurred. This is what 'Abd al-Qahir established regarding the restriction in the statement of a speaker, "I myself strove for your need," which is emphasised by such words as "alone" or "nobody else," and which entails the occurrence of the action. So one does not say, "I did not say this, nor did anyone else," meaning that one does not say, "I strove for your need, and so did someone else." Likewise here, it cannot be understood as "Was it Allah and His verses and His Messenger that you were mocking, or were you not mocking?"

Mockery of Allah and His verses is an argument against them, because they mocked His Messenger and his religion, and so it became binding upon them that they had mocked the One who sent him with the signs of his truthfulness.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 9, verse 66:

﴿Make no excuse; you have disbelieved after your belief.﴾

Since their saying ﴿We were only conversing and playing﴾ [al-Tawbah: 65] was an excuse for their private talk, that is, a display of the justification for which they conferred, and that it is what the wearied person needs, namely relaxation through jesting and talk not in earnest, when God exposed the matter of their mockery, He followed it with a demonstration of how little their excuse was worth, since they had become involved in something more grievous and greater than what they had excused themselves for, namely their involvement in disbelief after displaying belief. For when God made their hypocrisy manifest, what proceeded from them of mockery became of lesser account. Thus the clause ﴿Make no excuse﴾ belongs to the statement which God commanded the Messenger to say, and it is an escalation in rebuke. It contains an emphasis of the content of the clause ﴿Was it God, His signs and His Messenger that you were mocking?﴾ [al-Tawbah: 65], together with a further escalation in rebuke and in censure of them, in that they had become involved in something worse, which is disbelief. Therefore the clause is cut off from the one before it. Moreover, it is the rule that clauses occurring in a context of rebuke are to be disjoined and not conjoined, because rebuke calls for enumeration, so the clauses by which one is rebuked take the place of counted numbers, such as "one, two." The meaning is: you have no need to make excuses for the private talk, for you have already become known for something greater and more grievous.

The prohibition here is used to express equality (indifference) and the futility (of the act).

The clause ﴿you have disbelieved after your belief﴾ is in the position of the cause for the clause ﴿Make no excuse﴾, giving the reason for the prohibition which is used to express indifference and futility.

His saying ﴿you have disbelieved﴾ indicates that disbelief occurred in the past, that is, before the mockery, since their disbelief was already known previously. The intended sense of ascribing belief to them is the display of belief, for otherwise they had not believed with sincere belief. By their belief is meant their display of belief, not the actual occurrence of its reality. This is indicated by the attachment of belief to their pronoun rather than defining belief with the article that denotes the reality, meaning: after a belief that is of your own kind. This is an allusion that it was a formal belief, not a true one. A parallel to it is His saying, exalted is He, later on: ﴿And they disbelieved after their submission﴾ [al-Tawbah: 74]. This is one of the subtleties of the Qur'an.

* * *

﴿If We pardon a group of you, We will punish another group, because they were criminals.﴾

This clause comes in accordance with the Qur'anic practice of following a warning with good news for the one who desires repentance, reminding him of the possibility of rectifying his condition.

Since the state of the hypocrites was strange, the good news for them was mixed with the remainder of the warning. So He informed them that a group of them may be pardoned if they seek the cause of pardon, which is sincere faith, and that another group will remain in the state of punishment. The context indicates that this does not happen in vain or as an arbitrary preference without a determining factor. Rather, it is that one group is hoped to believe, so it is forgiven for what it had committed of hypocrisy, while another persists in hypocrisy until death, so it proceeds to punishment. The verses that come after this increase the clarity of what the context indicates, from His saying ﴿They forgot God, so He forgot them﴾ [al-Tawbah: 67] to His saying ﴿a lasting punishment﴾ [al-Tawbah: 68].

His saying after that: ﴿So if they repent, it will be better for them; but if they turn away, God will punish them with a painful punishment in this world and the Hereafter﴾ [al-Tawbah: 74].

Some of the hypocrites believed after the revelation of this verse. The commentators mention, from this group, Makhshi ibn Humayyir al-Ashja'i, who, when he heard this verse, repented of hypocrisy, and his Islam became good. He was counted among the Companions, and he fought on the day of al-Yamama and was martyred there. It has also been said that the one intended by "a group" is him alone, to the exclusion of others, so it would be an instance of using the word for a group to refer to one individual in a context of concealment and obscurity, like His saying, may God bless him and grant him peace: "What is the matter with people who stipulate conditions that are not in the Book of God?"

The Messenger of God, may God bless him and grant him peace, died while a remnant of the hypocrites remained in Medina, and 'Umar ibn al-Khattab, during his caliphate, used to discern them (by their marks).

The bā' in ﴿because they were criminals﴾ [bi-annahum kanu mujrimin] is causal, and the criminal (mujrim) is the disbeliever.

The majority of readers recited (yu'fa) and (tu'adhdhab) with both verbs in the passive voice, with the deputy of the subject. ʿĀṣim recited them in the active voice with the first-person plural (nūn of majesty) in both verbs, and he put the second (ṭā'ifatan) in the accusative.

The verse: "The hypocrites, men and women, are of one another. They enjoin what is evil and forbid what is good, and they withhold their hands. They have forgotten Allah, so He has forgotten them. Indeed, the hypocrites are the defiantly disobedient."

It appears that this verse is a safeguard (ihtiras) against the hypocrites thinking that the pardon prescribed for a group among them is a pardon that reaches a party of them who remain upon their hypocrisy. So it follows this with an explanation that hypocrisy is one single state and that its adherents are alike, so that it may be known that the divergence of their conditions between pardon and punishment occurs only when their conditions differ in faith and remaining upon hypocrisy. In addition to this, the verse also clarifies some of the states of hypocrisy and its effects which indicate the deserving of punishment. Accordingly, this sentence is separated from the one before it, either because it is like an explanation of the group deserving punishment, or because it is an independent new sentence (isti'naf ibtida'i) in the sense of an interjection (i'tiraD), as will come at His - exalted be He - saying: "Like those before you" [al-Tawbah: 69], or because it and what follows it are an interjection between the preceding sentence and the sentence "Like those before you, they were stronger than you in might" [al-Tawbah: 69], as will come there.

The mention of the female hypocrites is added in this verse to explicitly state the equality of rulings for all who are characterised by hypocrisy, male and female, lest it occur to the mind that the pardon reaches their women while the reckoning is specific to their men. So that people know that the women of the hypocrites have a share in participating with their men in hypocrisy, and so they may beware of them.

The "min" (from) in His saying "some of them are from some" is connective (ittisaliyyah), indicating the meaning of one thing being connected to another. It is a figurative partitive whose meaning is connection and allegiance. The name of allegiance (wilayah) was not applied to it as it was applied to the connection of believers to one another in His saying: "The believing men and believing women are allies of one another" [al-Tawbah: 71], for what will come there.

His saying "some of them are from some" includes all the male and female hypocrites, because each individual is a part of the whole. So when each part is connected to another part, it is known that they are alike in their conditions.

The clause "they enjoin what is evil" explains the meaning of connection and equality in conditions.

Al-munkar (what is evil) refers to acts of disobedience, because Islam denies them (yunkiruha).

Al-ma'ruf (what is good) is its opposite, because the religion recognises it (ya'rifuhu), i.e., approves of it. Both terms have already been discussed in His saying: "Let there be among you a community calling to good, enjoining what is right and forbidding what is wrong" [Al 'Imran: 104], in Surah Al 'Imran.

Qabd al-aydi (withholding hands) is a metaphor (kinayah) for stinginess, and it is a term of blame because it indicates harshness, since what is meant is stinginess toward the poor.

Al-nisyan (forgetting) on their part is used figuratively for associating partners with Allah, or for turning away from seeking His good pleasure and carrying out what He commanded; because neglect and turning away resemble the forgetting of one who is turned away from.

Allah's forgetting of them (nisyan Allahi iyyahum) is an instance of mushakalah (correspondence in wording), meaning His depriving them of what He has prepared for the believers; because that resembles forgetting when shares are being distributed.

The sentence "Indeed, the hypocrites are the defiantly disobedient" is a summary conclusion (fadhlakah) of what precedes it, and for this reason it is separated, because it is like a comprehensive explanation.

The form of restriction (qasr) in "Indeed, the hypocrites are the defiantly disobedient" is a claimed restriction (qasr idda'i) for emphasis, because when they reached the utmost limit in defiant disobedience, others were treated as though they were not defiantly disobedient.

The use of the explicit noun in place of the pronoun in "Indeed, the hypocrites" serves to further fix this ruling in the mind, and so that the sentence stands independently, as though it were a proverb.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 9, verse 68:

﴿Allah has promised the hypocrite men and the hypocrite women and the disbelievers the fire of Hell, abiding therein. It is sufficient for them. Allah has cursed them, and for them is a lasting punishment.﴾

This sentence is either a resumptive explanatory clause (isti'naf bayani, a new sentence that answers an implied question) arising from His saying: ﴿Indeed, the hypocrites are the defiantly disobedient⁠﻿﴾ [al-Tawba: 67]. Or it explains the clause ﴿they forgot Allah, so He forgot them﴾, because abiding in Hell and being cursed clarify what is meant by Allah's forgetting them.

Wa'd (promise) is more general than wa'id (threat). It is used for an informing, by the one informing, of a commitment to something in the future that benefits or harms the one informed, or neither benefits nor harms: ﴿This is what the Most Merciful promised⁠﻿﴾ [Ya-Sin: 52]. Wa'id is specific to what harms.

The past tense verb here is either to inform of a threat that Allah had already made to the hypocrite men and women, as a reminder to strengthen its certainty. Or it is used to shape the threat in the form by which contracts are concluded, like "I sold" and "I gave," indicating that it is a threat that will not fail, like a contract and a binding commitment.

Page 256

The use of the apparent noun in place of the pronoun serves to fix the one judged in the hearer's mind, so that the attribution of the judgment to them is firmly established.

The mention of the disbelievers here, in addition, indicates that the hypocrites are not in a lesser state than the polytheists, since disbelief has united both groups.

The meaning of ﴿it is sufficient for them⁠﻿﴾ is that it is constant with them. The original sense of "hasb" is that it means "sufficient." Since the sufficient thing is always accompanied by the one it suffices, it is used here as a metonymy (kinaya) for constancy. It is also possible that "hasb" retains its original meaning, and its mention in this context is mockery (tahakkum) of them, as if they had asked for bliss, and it was said: ﴿the fire of Hell is sufficient for them⁠﻿﴾.

Al-la'n (cursing) is distance from mercy, contempt, and wrath.

As for ﴿a lasting punishment⁠﻿﴾: if what is meant by it is the punishment of Hell, then it is an emphasis on His saying ﴿abiding therein, it is sufficient for them⁠﻿﴾, to remove the possibility that "abiding" is understood as a long period, and an emphasis on the metonymy in His saying ﴿it is sufficient for them⁠﻿﴾. If what is meant by it is another punishment, then it is necessarily a punishment in this world, namely the punishment of disgrace and humiliation among people.

In this verse there is further affirmation that the hypocrites deserve punishment, and that they are the group that will be punished if they persist in their hypocrisy. Therefore it is established that the group that is pardoned are those among them who believe.

﴿Like those before you, who were stronger than you in might and greater in wealth and children. They enjoyed their share, and you enjoyed your share, as those before you enjoyed their share, and you engaged in vain talk as they engaged in it. Those are the ones whose deeds have failed in this world and the Hereafter, and they are the losers.﴾

It has been said that this address is an iltifat (shift of pronouns) from the third-person pronouns referring to the hypocrites to their second-person address. The purpose is to draw a conclusion and to threaten them with admonition, and to remind them, lest they be deceived by the respite they are enjoying, that the end of that is the failure of their deeds in this world and the Hereafter, and that they are deserving of ruin.

[Page 257]

The kaf (ك) of comparison is in the position of a predicate (khabar) of an omitted subject (mubtada') indicated by the second-person pronoun. Its estimate is: "You are like those before you." Or the kaf is in the position of a accusative governed by an omitted verb, meaning: "You did as the deed of those before you did." It is then in the position of an absolute object (maf'ul mutlaq) indicating its verb. A similar example of omitting the verb and bringing what would be its object is the saying of al-Nimr ibn Tawlab:

"Until, when the dog said to her, 'Like today, pursued and not pursuer.'"

He intended: "I have not seen like today," except that the governing word for the accusative differs between the verse and the line of poetry.

It has also been said that this is part of the speech that the Prophet ﷺ was commanded to convey to them, from His saying: ﴿Say: Was it Allah, His verses, and His Messenger that you were mocking?﴾ [al-Tawbah: 65], and so on. In that case, what lies between them is a parenthetical insertion with His saying: ﴿The hypocrite men and the hypocrite women are of one another﴾ [al-Tawbah: 67], and so on. Then the address pronoun for them follows the apparent sense without iltifat, and the speech is directed to likening their state in their destination to the Fire.

The use of the relative pronoun (al-ladhina) is because it is more comprehensive and inclusive of the earlier nations, such as 'Ad and Thamud, whom the Arabs cited as examples of strength.

"Ashadd" means "stronger." Here "quwwah" means the capacity for difficult deeds, as in His saying: ﴿Do they not see that Allah, who created them, is stronger than them in might?﴾ [Fussilat: 15]. Or it may mean power and the means of victory through completeness of number and equipment. In this sense, "quwwah" is placed as the specification (tamyiz) of "ashadd," just as "shadid" was placed as a genitive-attached noun in His saying: ﴿Taught by one mighty in power﴾ [al-Najm: 5].

Abundance of wealth has many causes: among them, the goodness of the land for planting and grafting, and the grazing of livestock and bees; among them, abundant trade due to the good location of the homeland among the territories of nations; among them, proximity to seas for travel to distant lands and fishing; and among them, the land containing minerals such as gold, silver, and iron, and industrial and food materials from plants, such as spice trees, tanning and dyeing barks, medicines, grains, and oils.

Abundance of children comes from security, by which lives are preserved, and from fertility that produces strong bodies and safety from famines that lead to deaths, and from good climate by safety from deadly plagues, and from wealth through the abundance of wives, concubines, and wet nurses.

[Page 258]

"Al-istimta'" means "tamattu'," which is obtaining some of the enjoyment (mata') by which a person derives pleasure and that which suits him. It was discussed earlier at His saying: ﴿For you on the earth is a dwelling place and enjoyment for a time﴾ [al-A'raf: 24], in Surat al-A'raf.

The sin and ta' in it are for intensifying the strength of the enjoyment.

"Al-khalaq" means one's share of good. It was discussed earlier at His saying: ﴿Among the people is he who says, "Our Lord, give us in this world," and he will have no share (khalaq) in the Hereafter﴾ [al-Baqarah: 200], in Surat al-Baqarah.

﴿So they enjoyed their share﴾ is made a consequence of ﴿who were stronger﴾, because the intended purpose is to bring them into the state to which they are compared, as will come.

﴿So you enjoyed your share﴾ is made a consequence of what the kaf (of comparison) conveyed, through His saying "like those before you," of the meaning of likeness. For this reason, the clause "so you enjoyed" is not joined by the conjunction waw, since this clause is the aim of the comparison and what follows from it. The mention of this clause would have sufficed without mentioning the clause ﴿So they enjoyed their share﴾, were it not for the intent of admonishing both parties: those compared to, and those compared, in that both turn away from taking provision for the everlasting life and are absorbed in hasty enjoyment. So the speech was not limited to the state of only one of the two parties, out of intent to give attention to both. This is what required this elaboration. Had he confined himself to His saying, ﴿So you enjoyed your share, as those before you enjoyed their share﴾, without mentioning before it ﴿So they enjoyed their share﴾, the basic meaning would have been achieved, but the intent of giving concern to both parties would not have been conveyed.

For this reason, when this purpose was established in the minds of the hearers, there was no need to weave a similar structure in His saying: ﴿And you engaged in vain talk as they engaged in it﴾.

His saying: ﴿as those before you enjoyed their share﴾ is an emphasis of the comparison occurring in His saying "like those before you," up to His saying ﴿so you enjoyed your share﴾, to alert that this particular part, from among the compared state and the state compared to, is the locus of admonition and reminder, so that what they are in of the blessing of respite and gradual drawing-on (istidraj) does not deceive them. He placed first His saying ﴿So they enjoyed their share﴾ and brought His saying ﴿as those before you enjoyed their share﴾ as an emphasis of it, rather than limiting himself to this last comparison, so that emphasis could be achieved. Also, mentioning what completes the depiction of the compared state, before stating the comparison, makes the sense of resemblance firmer in the hearer's mind.

[Page 259]

His saying: ﴿And you engaged in vain talk as they engaged in it﴾ is a comparison of the hypocrites' vain talk to the vain talk of those (earlier nations), which is the talk reported of them in His saying: ﴿They would surely say, "We were only conversing and playing"﴾ [al-Tawbah: 65]. Because this comparison is simple, it was not given the same style used in the preceding comparison. That is: "You engaged in disbelief and mockery of the verses of Allah and His Messenger as the vain talk they engaged in on that matter. So you and they are equal, and so it is near that what befell them will befall you." Our discussion of these two comparisons is the most subtle of what has been written about them.

The relative pronoun "alladhi" is singular. Since the pronoun referring back to it in this place is plural, it is necessary that the intended meaning of "alladhi" be interpreted as a group or plural. It is also possible that "alladhi" here is originally "alladhina," lightened by dropping the nun, according to the dialect of Hudhayl and Tamim, as in the saying of al-Ashhab ibn Rumayla al-Nahshali:

"Indeed those whose blood was spilled at Fulj, they are the people, all of the people, O mother of Khalid."

The grammarians of Basra consider this usage restricted to the case where the relative clause is long, as in the line of poetry, so it does not apply to this verse according to them. The grammarians of Kufa permit it even when the relative clause is not long, as in the verse. Al-Farra' claimed that "alladhi" may be a literal relative pronoun interpreted as a verbal noun, and cited this verse as evidence, but this is weak.

When the state of those compared to, from the perished nations, was described, He followed that with pointing to them, to alert that because of that state they were deserving of what will be reported about them. So He said: ﴿Those, their deeds have failed in this world and the Hereafter, and those are the losers.﴾ In this there is an implicit allusion that those who resembled them in their conditions are fit for what befell those. In this implicit allusion there is a great meaning of threat and warning.

"Al-khawd" (vain talk) was previously referred to earlier in its explanation.

"Al-habt" means cessation and invalidation. It was mentioned at His saying: ﴿Then those, their deeds have failed in this world and the Hereafter﴾ [al-Baqarah: 217], in Surat al-Baqarah.

What is meant by "their deeds" is what they did and toiled at: managing wealth and dependents and devoting themselves to them. The meaning of their failure in this world is their eradication and destruction by the descent of various punishments upon those nations, and in the Hereafter, by there being no compensation for them, as in His saying: ﴿We shall inherit from him what he says﴾ [Maryam: 80], meaning in this world, ﴿and he will come to Us alone﴾ [Maryam: 80], meaning in the Hereafter, having no wealth or child, as in His saying: ﴿My wealth has not availed me﴾ [al-Haqqah: 28], ﴿my authority has perished from me﴾ [al-Haqqah: 29].

In all of this is a reminder to the Prophet ﷺ and the believers that they should not think that, because Allah granted respite to the hypocrites, He has pardoned them.

Since their loss was grave, others were made among the losers as if they were not losers, so the loss was restricted to these by His saying: ﴿And those, they are the losers﴾, a restriction intended for emphasis.

The repetition of the demonstrative pronoun is for attention to distinguishing those spoken about, and to increase the establishment of their conditions in the hearer's mind.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 9, verse 70:

﴿Has there not come to them the news of those before them: the people of Noah, ʿAd, Thamud, the people of Abraham, the companions of Madyan, and the overturned cities? Their messengers came to them with clear proofs. Allah would not have wronged them, but they were wronging themselves.﴾ The discourse returns to the hypocrites. The pronoun in (ألَمْ يَأْتِهِمْ, "has there not come to them") and in (مِن قَبْلِهِمْ, "those before them") refers to the hypocrites, whom the pronoun in His words ﴿And if you asked them, they would surely say, "We were only conversing and playing"﴾ [al-Tawbah: 65] refers to, or the pronoun in His words ﴿And for them is a lasting punishment﴾ [al-Tawbah: 68].

The interrogative is directed at the addressee as an affirmation about them, such that it is like calling them to witness that the news of those before them had reached them.

The verb "come" (الإتيان, ʾītiyān) is used to mean the news reaching someone, as in His words ﴿They say, "If you are given this, then take it"﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 41], which was discussed in Surat al-ʿUqud. The arrival of news to the one who hears it is likened to a person coming, on the common ground of attainment after non-attainment. From this category is the saying "the news reached him" (بَلَغَهُ الخَبَرُ). He, exalted is He, said: ﴿That I may warn you thereby, and whoever it reaches﴾ [al-An'am: 19], in Surat al-An'am.

Page 261
"Naba'" (النَّبَأُ, news) means information. It was discussed in His words: ﴿And there has certainly come to you from the news of the messengers﴾ [al-An'am: 34], in Surat al-An'am.

The people of Noah were discussed at His words: ﴿We certainly sent Noah to his people﴾ [al-A'raf: 59], in Surat al-A'raf.

Noah was mentioned at His words: ﴿Indeed, Allah chose Adam and Noah﴾ [Al 'Imran: 33], in Surat Al 'Imran.

ʿAd were discussed at His words: ﴿And to ʿAd, their brother Hud﴾ [al-A'raf: 65], in Surat al-A'raf.

Likewise Thamud. The people of Abraham are the Chaldeans. Abraham and them were discussed at His words: ﴿And when Abraham was tried by his Lord with words﴾ [al-Baqarah: 124], in Surat al-Baqarah.

The idafa of "companions" (أصحاب) to Madyan is by way of applying the name Madyan to the land in which the sons of Madyan dwelt. Just as Madyan is the name of a tribe, as in His words ﴿And to Madyan, their brother Shu'ayb﴾ [al-A'raf: 85], so it is also the name of the homeland of that tribe. Madyan was mentioned at His words: ﴿And to Madyan, their brother Shu'ayb﴾ [al-A'raf: 85], in al-A'raf.

"The overturned cities" (المؤتفكات) is conjoined to "companions of Madyan," meaning the news of the overturned cities. It is the plural of mu'tafikah, an active participle from al-iftifak, which is overturning. That is, the towns that were overturned. What is meant by them is small towns that were the dwellings of the people of Lot, namely: Sodom, Gomorrah, Admah, and Zeboiim. They were neighbouring towns, which were sunk into the earth so that their upper part became their lower part. They were in the regions of the Jordan around the Dead Sea. The news of these people is well known and established: the report of their destruction and annihilation by terrible events.

The clause ﴿Their messengers came to them﴾ is either a causal clause or a explanatory resumptive clause (istiʾnaf bayani) arising from His words ﴿the news of those before them﴾, meaning: their messengers came to them with proofs of truthfulness and right.

The clause ﴿Allah would not have wronged them﴾ is a consequence of the clause ﴿Their messengers came to them﴾, and what is consequent is the whole sentence up to His words "they were wronging" (يَظْلِمُونَ), because what follows from the coming of the messengers is that they wronged themselves through obstinacy, arrogance, denial of the messengers, and deafness to the truth, so Allah seized them for that. But the speech was arranged in this wondrous style, beginning with the negation that Allah wronged them, out of concern for that, because of the intensity of the emphasis upon them for their evil deeds, to the point that this itself appears as if it were the consequent, and the consequent, in terms of meaning, takes the form of an exception (istidrak).

The wronging is negated from Allah, exalted is He, in the most emphatic manner, namely the negation conjoined with the lam of denial after the negated verb of being (kāna), which was discussed at His words: ﴿Allah does not intend to place upon you any difficulty﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 6], in Surat al-'Uqud.

Their wronging themselves is affirmed for them in the most emphatic manner, since it is attributed to them in the past tense form of kāna, which indicates that wrongdoing became firmly established in them since a time long past. And the wronging that occurred in that time is expressed in the present tense form to indicate renewal and recurrence, that is, the repetition of their wronging themselves in past times.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 9, verse 71:

﴿And the believing men and the believing women are allies of one another; they enjoin what is right and forbid what is wrong, establish prayer, give zakat, and obey Allah and His Messenger. Those — Allah will have mercy upon them. Indeed, Allah is Almighty, Wise.﴾

This verse stands in contrast to His saying: ﴿The hypocrite men and the hypocrite women are of one another﴾ [al-Tawbah: 67], to show that the group that will attain pardon is the one joined to the believers.

So the sentence is conjoined to the sentence ﴿The hypocrite men and the hypocrite women are of one another﴾ [al-Tawbah: 67], and between them are sentences that follow one from another in sequence.

His saying ﴿they are allies of one another﴾ corresponds to His saying about the hypocrites ﴿they are of one another﴾ [al-Tawbah: 67].

He expressed regarding the believing men and women that they are "allies of one another" to indicate that the bond uniting them is the wilayah (bond of allegiance) of Islam; they are equal in it, none of them being a blind follower (muqallid) of the other or following him without insight. This is because the meaning of wilayah carries the implication of sincerity and mutual support, unlike the hypocrites, as though some of them arise from others in their blameworthy traits.

Page 263
The phrase "they establish prayer" is added to the description of the believers here to draw attention to the fact that prayer is the greatest of what is right (al-ma'ruf).

His saying ﴿and they give zakat﴾ corresponds to His saying about the hypocrites ﴿and they withhold their hands﴾ [al-Tawbah: 67].

His saying ﴿and they obey Allah and His Messenger﴾ corresponds to His saying about the hypocrites ﴿they forgot Allah﴾ [al-Tawbah: 67], because obedience requires being mindful of the one obeyed, so it is the opposite of forgetfulness.

His saying ﴿Those — Allah will have mercy upon them﴾ corresponds to His saying about the hypocrites ﴿so He forgot them﴾.

The sin (sin, particle of future) is for emphasizing that the mercy will occur in the future; the particle of futurity with the present tense conveys what qad conveys with the past tense, as in His saying: ﴿And your Lord will surely give you, and you will be satisfied﴾ [al-Duha: 5].

The demonstrative is to indicate that what follows the demonstrative noun are deserving of it because of the attributes mentioned before the demonstrative.

The clause ﴿Indeed, Allah is Almighty, Wise﴾ is a justification for the clause ﴿Allah will have mercy upon them﴾, meaning: by His might He benefits His allies, and by His wisdom He places the reward upon the one who deserves it.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 9, verse 72:

﴿Allah has promised the believing men and the believing women gardens beneath which rivers flow, abiding therein, and pleasant dwellings in gardens of perpetual residence (ʿAdn). And approval from Allah is greater. That is the great achievement.﴾

The placement of this sentence after His saying ﴿The believing men and the believing women are allies of one another﴾ [al-Tawbah: 71] is like the placement of the sentence ﴿Allah has promised the hypocrite men and the hypocrite women﴾ [al-Tawbah: 68] after His saying ﴿The hypocrite men and the hypocrite women are of one another﴾ [al-Tawbah: 67], and so on. It is also like a bayani resumptive sentence (al-istinaf al-bayani, a resumption that answers an implied question) arising from His saying ﴿those – Allah will have mercy on them﴾ [al-Tawbah: 71], similar to His saying in the previous verse ﴿Their Lord gives them good tidings of mercy from Him and approval and gardens wherein is lasting pleasure﴾ [al-Tawbah: 21].

The past-tense verb in His saying ﴿Allah has promised﴾ [al-Tawbah: 68] is either because it is a report of a promise that preceded in the verses of the Qur'an, the purpose of reporting it being to remind of it in order to affirm it, or because this promise was phrased in the past tense in the manner of contractual formulas, such as "I sold" and "I gave in charity," because that form is customary in obligations that do not fail. A parallel to this has already occurred just above in His saying ﴿Allah has promised the hypocrite men and the hypocrite women and the disbelievers the fire of Hell﴾ [al-Tawbah: 68].

Using the apparent noun in place of the pronoun, instead of saying "Allah has promised them," is to fix them firmly in the mind of the hearer, so that the action's connection to them is more firmly established in his mind.

The discussion of phrases like ﴿gardens beneath which rivers flow﴾ has already been addressed at His saying – exalted is He: ﴿And give good tidings to those who believe and do righteous deeds that for them are gardens beneath which rivers flow﴾ [al-Baqarah: 25] in Surat al-Baqarah.

The conjunction of ﴿and pleasant dwellings in gardens of ʿAdn﴾ with "gardens" serves to indicate that for them, within the gardens, are palaces and pleasant dwellings, meaning there is nothing in them of the impurity of dwellings, such as filth and the traces of cooking and the like. It is similar to His saying: ﴿And for them therein are purified spouses﴾ [al-Baqarah: 25].

ʿAdn means eternal abiding and continuous settlement, so the "gardens of ʿAdn" are the gardens mentioned before. He mentioned them with this expression, using the apparent noun in place of the pronoun, together with variety in expression and emphasis on the gardens. For this reason He did not say "and pleasant dwellings therein."

The sentence ﴿and approval from Allah is greater﴾ is conjoined to the sentence ﴿Allah has promised the believers﴾.

Ridwan, with a kasra on the ra', may also be pronounced with a damma. The kasra is the dialect of the people of the Hijaz, and the damma is the dialect of Tamim. The majority of readers recited it with a kasra on the ra', while Abu Bakr, from ʿAsim, recited it with a damma on the ra'.

Its equivalent with a kasra is rare among verbal nouns with the alif and nun. It is a verbal noun like ridan (approval), and the addition of the alif and nun in it indicates its intensity, like ghufran (forgiveness) and shukran (gratitude).

The indefiniteness in ﴿ridwan﴾ is for classification, indicating the category of approval. It was not preceded by the definite article of the genus, so that indefiniteness could be used to convey the sense of magnification, for the approval of Allah – exalted is He – is great.

﴿Greater﴾ is a comparative form whose object of comparison is not mentioned, because it is evident from the context, meaning: greater than the gardens, because Allah's approval is the root of all good. In this is evidence that spiritual blessings are higher and more noble than physical ones.

﴿That﴾ refers to everything mentioned: the gardens, the dwellings and their attributes, and the divine approval.

The restriction in ﴿it is the great achievement﴾ is a true restriction, in view of attributing greatness to the achievement.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 9, verse 73:

﴿O Prophet, strive against the disbelievers and the hypocrites, and be harsh with them. Their refuge is Hell, and wretched is the destination.﴾

When His words, may He be exalted, in the preceding verse, ﴿Allah has promised the hypocrite men and hypocrite women and the disbelievers the fire of Hell, to abide therein. It is sufficient for them. And Allah has cursed them, and for them is a lasting punishment﴾ [al-Tawbah: 68], indicated that they have two punishments, a punishment in the Hereafter, which is the fire of Hell, it became clear that the second punishment is a punishment in this world, which is the punishment of killing. So when He followed that with the vile deeds of the hypocrites and with the parable of the perished nations for them, He commanded His Prophet to strive against the hypocrites. This is the striving with which they were warned in Surah al-Ahzab in His words: ﴿Then they will not remain your neighbors therein except for a little, cursed wherever they are found; they will be seized and killed with intense slaughter﴾ [al-Ahzab: 60-61]. So after Allah had warned them of that and they did not desist, and a period of time passed during which their inner intentions were exposed by their repeated outbursts of disbelief and their plotting against the Muslims, Allah fulfilled what He had warned them of, by commanding His Messenger ﷺ to strive against them. Jihad (striving, here meaning fighting in the cause of religion) is fighting to support the religion, and it was mentioned earlier in His words: ﴿They strive in the way of Allah and do not fear the blame of any blamer﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 54], in Surah al-'Uqud (Surah al-Ma'idah).

The hypocrites are joined here with the disbelievers, as an alert that the cause for commanding jihad against the disbelievers has been realized in the hypocrites, so their jihad is like the jihad against the disbelievers. Also, because Allah, when He joined them in the threat of the punishment of the Hereafter, saying ﴿Allah has promised the hypocrite men and hypocrite women and the disbelievers the fire of Hell﴾ [al-Tawbah: 68], and His words there implied that they have another punishment, there is no doubt that He grouped them together in the legislation of this other punishment for them.

So the jihad commanded for the two groups differs, and the word jihad is used in both its literal and figurative senses. The benefit of pairing the disbelievers and the hypocrites in jihad is to instill terror in their hearts, for each one of them fears that his matter will be exposed and he will be treated as an enemy disbeliever, which will break their strength.

As for fighting them in actuality, it is impossible, because they do not openly show disbelief. Therefore most exegetes interpreted jihad with respect to the hypocrites as resisting them with proof and enforcing the prescribed penalties when what necessitates them becomes apparent, and most of those on whom the prescribed penalty was enforced in the time of prophethood were hypocrites. Some of the early scholars (al-salaf) said: their jihad ends in frowning in their faces. Al-Zajjaj and al-Tabari took it as the apparent meaning of the command to jihad, and al-Tabari attributed this to 'Abdullah ibn Mas'ud, but neither of them provided a convincing clarification of the meaning.

This verse is a notice to the hypocrites that hypocrisy necessitates their being fought, definitively, to uproot them from among the Muslims. The Messenger of Allah ﷺ used to teach them, and he informed Hudhayfah ibn al-Yaman of them. The Muslims knew some of them, whose repeated signs of conduct and slips of speech were evident. The Prophet refrained from killing them only to block the means by which doubt could enter the security of those who had entered Islam, as he said to 'Umar: "People should not say that Muhammad kills his companions." This is because the common people and those absent from Medina do not reach, through their knowledge, an understanding of the realities of affairs taking place in Medina, so those who call to sedition can disfigure beneficial actions by presenting them in an ugly form to those who do not know the truth. When the number of those entering Islam increased, and the security of the Muslims became famous such that no doubt remained about the trustworthiness of the Muslims, and the treachery of the hypocrites became widespread so that the tribes heard of it and both Muslim and disbeliever were certain of it, the benefit became clear in uprooting them, and the means for doubt to reach the security of the Muslims ceased. Allah knew that the end of His Messenger, may the blessings and peace of Allah be upon him, had drawn near, and that if this faction of sedition remained after him, their affair would grow and their remedy would become difficult, and everyone with a disease in his heart would follow them. Therefore He definitively announced war against them, so that they would desist and abandon hypocrisy. What makes fighting them obligatory is that they openly uttered words of disbelief, meaning each one of them declared what indicates his concealed disbelief, and the others heard them and approved of them, and from a group of them there proceeded statements and actions indicating that they were mocking the religion,

and the Messenger of Allah ﷺ passed away shortly before the revelation of this verse. Perhaps among the wisdom of announcing this jihad is preparing the Muslims to fight every people who break the bonds of Islam while claiming to be Muslims, as those who withheld zakat did, claiming that they had not disbelieved and that zakat was only the Messenger's right during his lifetime; this was nothing but hypocrisy from their leaders, which their common people followed. Perhaps this verse was also a cause for most hypocrites to refrain from discord and to sincerely adopt faith, as is reported in the story of al-Jallas ibn Suwayd. Allah had already sufficed the Muslims against the evil of the greatest head of hypocrisy, 'Abdullah ibn Ubayy ibn Salul, by his death, so all of this was sufficient to set aside enacting the command to fight them in this verse. ﴿And Allah sufficed the believers in fighting﴾ [al-Ahzab: 25].

This verse indicates excommunication (takfir) on the basis of what clearly indicates disbelief from the one who says or does it, even if he did not openly declare disbelief.

﴿And be harsh with them﴾ is a command to be stern with them. The meaning of harshness (ghilzah) will come at His words: ﴿And let them find in you harshness﴾ [al-Tawbah: 123] in this surah.

This command was directed to the Messenger ﷺ because he was created upon mercy, so he was commanded to set aside his natural disposition regarding the disbelievers and the hypocrites, and not to overlook them as had been his custom before.

This verse necessitates the abrogation of giving the disbelievers whose hearts are to be reconciled to Islam (al-mu'allafah qulubuhum) a share; this remains only for those who have recently entered Islam.

The clause ﴿and wretched is the destination﴾ is a concluding phrase (tadhyil). A similar one has been mentioned many times before. "Ma'wa" (refuge) is the place to which a person retreats, that is, returns to; and "masir" (destination) is the place to which a person proceeds, that is, returns. The difference between them is by consideration, and combining them here is for variety of expression (tafannun).

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 9, verse 74:

[p. 268]
﴿They swear by Allah that they did not say [it]; but they did indeed utter the word of disbelief, and they disbelieved after their Islam, and they resolved upon what they did not attain. And they did not resent except that Allah and His Messenger enriched them from His bounty.﴾ Since the greater part of what was taken against the hypocrites consisted of words indicating disparagement of the Messenger (ﷺ) and similar signs of disbelief, and whenever such things were reported about them they would disclaim them with false oaths, the verse commanding their jihad is followed by an alert that what they disclaim with is a false disclaimer, that there is no trust in their oaths, and by establishing that they did say what is explicit in their disbelief. Accordingly, the clause "They swear" is a resumptive clause (isti'naf) of the explanatory type (bayani), prompted by the command to fight them, together with the observation of the outward appearance of their conditions of disclaiming what was reported of them, if the purpose of the clause is considered to be their being declared liars in their oath.

It may also be in the position of a causal clause (ta'lil) for the command to jihad, if the purpose of the clause is considered to be His saying: ﴿And they indeed uttered the word of disbelief﴾ and what follows it, and that this was only delayed to give importance to refuting their oaths at the outset, and the intended meaning was brought in the form of a circumstantial clause (hali). It is well known that the restriction is the purpose of the restricted speech. What supports this is that most of what is in the clause consists of evidences of their disbelief and their breaking the covenant of Islam; for if the intended meaning were specifically their being declared liars in what they swore, it would have been limited to establishing its opposite, namely ﴿And they indeed uttered the word of disbelief﴾, and what follows it would not have had any further connection to it.

In any case, the clause deserves separation (fasl) rather than conjunction (atf).

The object of "what they said" is omitted, indicated by His saying: ﴿And they indeed uttered the word of disbelief﴾.

He emphasized their utterance of the word of disbelief, in contrast to their emphatic denial of its utterance, by the form of an oath, so that the refutation of their statement would be equal to their statement in emphasis.

"The word of disbelief" (kalimat al-kufr) is the speech that indicates it. The root meaning of "kalimah" is the single word from which speech that conveys meaning is composed together with its like; and "kalimah" is applied to speech when it is comprehensive and concise, as in His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿By no means! It is merely a word he is saying﴾ [al-Mu'minun: 100], and in the hadith: "The truest word spoken by a poet is the word of Labid: 'Verily, everything except Allah is vain.'"

[p. 269]

So "the word of disbelief" is a genus for every utterance in which there is a denial of the Prophet (ﷺ), just as "the word of Islam" is applied to the testimony that there is no god but Allah and that Muhammad is the Messenger of Allah. Thus the words issuing from them, despite their differences, are only instances of this genus, as indicated by the attribution of the saying to the plural pronoun of the group of hypocrites. Qatadah said: "We have no knowledge of which of them it was, since there was no report that would establish proof and by which we could reach knowledge."

It was said: the intended meaning is a word issued by some of the hypocrites indicating denial of the Prophet (ﷺ). On the authority of 'Urwah ibn al-Zubayr, Mujahid, and Ibn Ishaq: that al-Julas (with a dammah on the jim and a light lam) ibn Suwayd ibn al-Samit said: "If what Muhammad says is true, then we are worse than these donkeys of ours upon which we are riding." His stepson reported this about him to the Prophet, who summoned him and asked him about his statement, and he swore by Allah that he had not said that.

It was also said: rather, it was revealed concerning 'Abd Allah ibn Ubayy ibn Salul, because of his saying which Allah related about him: ﴿They say, "If we return to Madinah, the more honorable will surely expel therefrom the more humble"﴾ [al-Munafiqun: 8]. A man among the Muslims reported him, so the Messenger of Allah sent for him and questioned him, and he began swearing by Allah that he had not said that.

On these reports, the attribution of the saying to a plural pronoun is a metonymy for concealing the name of the speaker, as one says: "What is the matter with people who do such-and-such?" when one of them did it; or it is by considering that one person said it and the rest heard it, so they were made partners in the responsibility, as one says: "The sons of so-and-so killed so-and-so," when only one of the clan killed him. And even granting the authenticity of a word being uttered by a specific individual, that does not require that others did not share in it, since they used to plot together concerning what they fabricated; and what issued from one of them was received by his companions and sitters, who would share in it.

As for the attribution of disbelief to the plural in His saying: ﴿and they disbelieved after their Islam﴾, it is similar.

The meaning of ﴿after their Islam﴾ is: after they had displayed Islam outwardly; and for this reason Islam is attributed to them, as was mentioned earlier in His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Do not make excuses; you have disbelieved after your belief﴾ [al-Tawbah: 66].

"Hamm" (resolve) is the intention to do an act, whether it is done or not.

[p. 270]

And "nawal" of a thing is its attainment, i.e., they resolved upon something they did not achieve. What they resolved upon was to assassinate the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) on his return from Tabuk: fifteen of them pledged together to lie in wait for him at a mountain pass on the road, beneath which was a valley; when he ascended it at night, they would push him from his mount into the valley. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) was travelling, and 'Ammar ibn Yasir had taken hold of the halter of his mount, leading it, while Hudhayfah ibn al-Yaman was driving it. Hudhayfah sensed them and shouted at them, so they fled.

The clause ﴿And they did not resent﴾ is conjoined to "they indeed uttered," meaning: while the state is that they did not hold against the Prophet (ﷺ), nor against the entry of Islam into Madinah, anything that would move them to what they do of the signs of hatred and enmity.

"Naqm" is resentment of a thing and disapproval of it; it was mentioned earlier in His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿You resent us only because we believed in the signs of our Lord﴾ [al-A'raf: 126], in Surat al-A'raf.

His saying: ﴿except that Allah and His Messenger enriched them from His bounty﴾ is a sarcastic exception (istithna' tahakkumi). It is of the type of emphasizing a thing by means of what resembles its opposite, like the saying of al-Nabighah:

"There is no fault in them, except that their swords have notches from the clashing of the battalions."

Its subtlety is that the speaker appears to be searching for something that would undo his declarative judgment or the like, so he mentions something that is among the reinforcements of the judgment, to indicate that he has exhausted the search and found nothing that would undo it.

Allah and His Messenger enriched them only by what the Prophet's (peace and blessings be upon him) settling among them brought of the causes of provision: through the abundant work of the Emigrants, through the abundance of spoils in the campaigns, and through the security that Islam brought among them, since it made the believers brothers, so rancours and blood-feuds between them ceased. The Aws and the Khazraj had been enemies before Islam, and there had been wars between them in which they destroyed one another shortly before the Hijrah, namely the wars of Bu'ath.

"Fadl" is increase in giving and generosity. "Min" is for the starting point (ibtida'iyyah). In making enrichment a matter of bounty there is a metonymy for the abundance of the thing with which one is enriched, because the one of bounty gives generously.

The Messenger is conjoined to the name of Allah in the verb of enrichment because he is the apparent and immediate cause.

* * *

[p. 271]

﴿So if they repent, it will be better for them; but if they turn away, Allah will punish them with a painful punishment in this world and the Hereafter, and they will have in the earth no protector or helper.﴾

This is a consequence (tafri') of His saying: ﴿Strive against the disbelievers and the hypocrites﴾ [al-Tawbah: 73], in accordance with the Qur'an's custom of following a threat with a promise and the reverse. When he was commanded to fight them, to be harsh toward them, and to threaten them with the destination of the Fire, He consequently informed that repentance is open to them and that the remedy of their affair is within their power, because the purpose of the command to fight them is to cut off the root of their harm or that their condition be set right.

Repentance is their sincere adherence to faith. The pronoun returns to the disbelievers and the hypocrites, and the pronoun in "yakun" returns to the verbal noun of "yatubu," which is repentance (al-tawb).

"Tawalli" is turning away, and what is meant is turning away from repentance. The punishment in this world is the punishment of jihad and captivity, and in the Hereafter, the punishment of the Fire.

The verb "yakun" is used in the apodosis instead of saying "fa-huwa khayr lahum" (then it is good for them), to emphasize the realization of good upon repentance, and to indicate that good is attained only upon repentance, because the verb of creation (takwin) signals this.

The nun of "yakun" is dropped for lightness, because with its quiescence it is ready for deletion, and what made the deletion good is that a vowel follows it, and vowels are heavy; therefore the deletion of this nun became common in their speech, as in His saying: ﴿And if it is a good deed, He multiplies it﴾ [al-Nisa': 40], in Surat al-Nisa'.

The clause ﴿And they will have in the earth no protector or helper﴾ is conjoined to the clause ﴿Allah will punish them﴾ etc., so it is a second apodosis of the condition. Do not be troubled by its being a nominal clause, which cannot directly follow a conditional particle without a linking fa'; for in subordinate clauses there is latitude that does not apply to the principal ones, since the conjunctive particle suffices to link the clause as a follower of the clause conjoined to it.

The meaning is that if they turn away, they will find none among the tribes to help them, since no Arab remains who has not entered Islam except those whom they do not regard in number or strength. The intended meaning is the negation of a beneficial protector, as is the implication of "wali"; as for one who does not benefit, he is a beloved and a friend, but not a "wali."

[p. 272]

﴿And among them are those who made a covenant with God, saying: "If He gives us of His bounty, we will surely give charity and we will surely be among the righteous."﴾ ﴿But when He gave them of His bounty, they withheld it, and they turned away while being averse.﴾ ﴿So He caused hypocrisy to follow in their hearts until the Day they meet Him, because they broke their promise to God and because they used to lie.﴾

It is said: these verses were revealed about Tha'labah ibn Hatib, one of the hypocrites. He asked the Messenger of God (ﷺ) to pray that he be granted abundance of provision, so he prayed for him, and he became very wealthy. When the zakat collectors (al-Musaddiqun, the officials who collected zakat) came to him to collect the zakat on his livestock, he refused to pay it. Then he regretted it and came with his charity, but the Messenger of God (ﷺ) refused to accept it from him. They also mention in his story that he repented, but his charity was not accepted during the time of the Prophet, nor during the time of the three Caliphs after him, as a punishment for him and to show that they had no need of him, until he died during the caliphate of 'Uthman. It has also been said that the one who said this was Mu'attib ibn Qushayr. On this view, the plural pronouns in "la-nassaddaqanna" and what follows refer to one person, and the act was attributed to the group of hypocrites in accordance with the Arab practice of attributing the act of one member to his tribe.

It is also possible that Tha'labah asked for this, and some of his companions, such as Mu'attib ibn Qushayr, followed him, so they were given the same as Tha'labah was given, and they withheld the same as he withheld, even though no story about them has come down, as was mentioned earlier.

The clause "la-nassaddaqanna" (the Arabic verb whose original form is la-natasaddaqanna, which was contracted by idgham [assimilation of consonants] for ease of pronunciation) explains the phrase "made a covenant with God."

"Al-I'rad" (turning away) refers to their turning away from their covenant and from giving thanks for the blessing of their Lord.

"Fa-a'qabahum nifaqan" means that He made hypocrisy follow after that, i.e., as its consequence. Since "a'qaba" implies the meaning of "a'ta" (to give), it takes two objects, and the original construction is "a'qabahum bi-nifaq."

The hidden pronoun in "a'qabahum" refers either to the states of theirs that have been mentioned, or to the stinginess derived from "bakhilu." Thus the attribution of the causing of consequence is a rational metaphor (majaz 'aqli). Or it refers to the name of God, Exalted, in His words "who made a covenant with God," meaning that their act of this kind became a cause for hypocrisy to remain in their hearts until their death.

[p. 273]
This is the requital for their persistence in hypocrisy. This implies that Tha'labah or Mu'attib died in disbelief, and that his eagerness to avoid giving his charity was ostentation and dissimulation. But how can that be, when both of them are counted among the Companions, and the first of them is among those who attended Badr? It has also been said that they were two other men who shared the same names. Therefore it is possible that "hypocrisy" was used for committing sins while in the state of Islam. This usage existed in the era of prophethood, such as the saying of Hanzalah ibn al-Rabi' to the Prophet (ﷺ): "O Messenger of God, Hanzalah has become a hypocrite." He mentioned committing, in his own personal affairs, what he thought was a sin, and the Prophet (ﷺ) did not rebuke him, but explained to him that what he imagined was not as he imagined. So the meaning would be that they embraced Islam and then continued to commit sins, contrary to the state of the Companions of the Prophet (ﷺ). The indefinite form of "nifaqan" (hypocrisy) may point to this, as it indicates a new hypocrisy. Otherwise, since they were already mentioned as hypocrites, how could hypocrisy be occurring for them as a consequence of this act?

"Liqa'" (meeting) is the coincidence of one thing with another in one place. So the meaning of "ila yawmi yalqawnahu" (until the Day they meet Him) is until the Day of Gathering (hashr), because it is the Day of meeting God for judgment, or until the Day of Death, because death is meeting God, as in the hadith: "Whoever loves to meet God, God loves to meet him." He explained this as a love that comes to the believer at the time of dying. Some of the earlier theologians said that meeting implies seeing, and they took as evidence for the affirmation of the vision of God, Exalted, His words, ﴿Their greeting on the Day they meet Him will be peace﴾ [al-Ahzab: 44] in Surat al-Ahzab. Al-Jubba'i refuted them with His words, ﴿until the Day they meet Him﴾ in this verse, since there is agreement that the hypocrites will not see God. Al-Fakhr (al-Razi) undertook to nullify this refutation with an argument that makes the proof weak. The truth is that meeting does not necessitate seeing. In Nafh al-Tib, in the biography of Abu Bakr ibn al-'Arabi, he mentions a story about an argument from the verse of al-Ahzab against one of the Hanbalis who were Mu'tazilis, and the Hanbali Mu'tazili refuted him with this verse.

The "ba'" (with/because of) is causal or expresses cause, meaning: because of their breaking their promise to their Lord and their lying.

He expressed their lying by the form ﴿they used to lie﴾, because the verb "kana" (used to be) indicates that lying is inherent in them and firmly established in them, and the present tense indicates its recurrence and renewal.

In this there is an indication of the obligation to beware of committing blameworthy acts, for they corrupt good character, and corruption grows more firmly rooted in the soul through the natural process of generation, which is the law of existence.

[p. 272]
