This usage existed in the era of prophethood, such as the saying of Hanzalah ibn al-Rabi' to the Prophet (ﷺ): "O Messenger of God, Hanzalah has become a hypocrite." He mentioned committing, in his own personal affairs, what he thought was a sin, and the Prophet (ﷺ) did not rebuke him, but explained to him that what he imagined was not as he imagined. So the meaning would be that they embraced Islam and then continued to commit sins, contrary to the state of the Companions of the Prophet (ﷺ). The indefinite form of "nifaqan" (hypocrisy) may point to this, as it indicates a new hypocrisy. Otherwise, since they were already mentioned as hypocrites, how could hypocrisy be occurring for them as a consequence of this act?

"Liqa'" (meeting) is the coincidence of one thing with another in one place. So the meaning of "ila yawmi yalqawnahu" (until the Day they meet Him) is until the Day of Gathering (hashr), because it is the Day of meeting God for judgment, or until the Day of Death, because death is meeting God, as in the hadith: "Whoever loves to meet God, God loves to meet him." He explained this as a love that comes to the believer at the time of dying. Some of the earlier theologians said that meeting implies seeing, and they took as evidence for the affirmation of the vision of God, Exalted, His words, ﴿Their greeting on the Day they meet Him will be peace﴾ [al-Ahzab: 44] in Surat al-Ahzab. Al-Jubba'i refuted them with His words, ﴿until the Day they meet Him﴾ in this verse, since there is agreement that the hypocrites will not see God. Al-Fakhr (al-Razi) undertook to nullify this refutation with an argument that makes the proof weak. The truth is that meeting does not necessitate seeing. In Nafh al-Tib, in the biography of Abu Bakr ibn al-'Arabi, he mentions a story about an argument from the verse of al-Ahzab against one of the Hanbalis who were Mu'tazilis, and the Hanbali Mu'tazili refuted him with this verse.

The "ba'" (with/because of) is causal or expresses cause, meaning: because of their breaking their promise to their Lord and their lying.

He expressed their lying by the form ﴿they used to lie﴾, because the verb "kana" (used to be) indicates that lying is inherent in them and firmly established in them, and the present tense indicates its recurrence and renewal.

In this there is an indication of the obligation to beware of committing blameworthy acts, for they corrupt good character, and corruption grows more firmly rooted in the soul through the natural process of generation, which is the law of existence.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 9, verse 78:

Page 274
﴿Did they not know that Allah knows their secrets and their private consultations, and that Allah is the Knower of the unseen things?﴾

This is a resumptive sentence (isti'naf) for the purpose of affirmation (taqrir). The statement affirms to the addressee concerning them, because their being aware of this is known to every listener. The sirr (secret) is what a person conceals of speech and what he harbors within himself, so that people do not become aware of it. It has already been mentioned in His saying: ﴿secretly and openly﴾ [al-Baqarah: 274] in Surat al-Baqarah.

The najwa (private consultation) is conversation carried on in secrecy, meaning He knows what they harbor within their souls and what they speak to one another as a confidential conversation, so that others will not become aware of it.

The najwa was joined to the sirr even though the sirr is more general than it, in order to inform them of His awareness of what they confide to one another of plotting and defamation.

Then He generalized this by His saying: ﴿and that Allah is the Knower of the unseen things﴾, meaning His knowledge of all unseen things is comprehensive.

The ghuyub (unseen things) is the plural of ghayb, which is what is hidden and absent from sight. His saying: ﴿those who believe in the unseen﴾ [al-Baqarah: 3] has already been mentioned in Surat al-Baqarah.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 9, verse 79:

﴿Those who find fault with the volunteers among the believers in their charities, and with those who find nothing to give except their own exertion, so they ridicule them—Allah will ridicule them, and they will have a painful punishment.﴾

This is a new independent sentence (isti'naf ibtida'i). It was revealed because of an event that occurred during the period of the revelation of the surah. The Prophet ﷺ urged the people to give charity. 'Abd al-Rahman ibn 'Awf came with four thousand dirhams, 'Asim ibn 'Adi came with many wasqs of dates, and Abu 'Aqil came with a sa' of dates. The hypocrites said: "'Abd al-Rahman and 'Asim gave only for show (riya'), and Abu 'Aqil wanted to draw attention to himself so that he would be given from the charities." So Allah revealed this verse concerning them.

"Those who find fault" (alladhina yalmizun) is the subject (mubtada'), and its predicate is the clause ﴿Allah will ridicule them﴾.

Al-lamz (ridicule/fault-finding, "al-lamz") means slander (al-ta'n). It has preceded in this surah in His words: ﴿And among them are those who find fault with you concerning the charities﴾ [al-Tawbah: 58]. Ya'qub read it with a dammah on the mim, just as he read His words: ﴿And among them are those who find fault with you concerning the charities﴾ [al-Tawbah: 58].

Al-mutawwi'in (the volunteers) originally was al-mutatawwi'in; the ta' was assimilated into the ta' (ṭā') because their points of articulation are close.

"Fi" (in) is for the figurative sense of location, by making the cause of the fault-finding like a container for the effect.

"Those who find nothing except their own exertion" (alladhina la yajiduna illa juhdahum) is coordinated (ma'tuf) upon "the volunteers," and they are among them, out of concern for their condition. Al-juhd (with a dammah on the jim) means capacity (al-taqah). Capacity was used to refer to its effect that arises from it.

The object of yajiduna is omitted because it is evident from the word "al-sadaqat" (charities); that is, they do not find anything to give in charity except their exertion.

The meaning is that they do not find a way to produce what they could give in charity except their capacity, that is, the exertion of their bodies. Or "wajada" here may be the one meaning "to be possessed of wealth" (kana dha jiddah), that is, to have riches, so no object is supposed for it; that is, those who have no wealth except their exertion. This is the better reading.

In it is praise for the strength of the body and of labor, and that they stand in place of wealth.

This is a great principle regarding the consideration of the foundations of general wealth and the honoring of the status of the worker.

"Al-sukhriyyah" (ridicule) is mockery (al-istihza'). One says: "sakhira minhu," meaning that mockery befell him from such-and-such, so "min" is for connection.

The present tense was chosen in "yalmizuna" and "yaskharuna" to indicate repetition.

The attribution of "sakhira" to Allah, exalted is He, is by way of metaphor, which the correspondence (mushakalah) with their action made fitting. The meaning is that Allah dealt with them in a manner resembling the ridicule of one who mocks, by way of representation (tamthil), in that He commanded His Prophet to apply to them the rulings for Muslims according to their outward state for a time, and then commanded him to expose them.

It is also permissible that the expression ﴿Allah ridicules them﴾ be by way of the metonymic metaphor (al-majaz al-mursal), that is, He despised them and cursed them. And since all of that had already taken place, it was expressed in the past tense in ﴿Allah ridicules them﴾.

The clause ﴿And they have a painful punishment﴾ is coordinated (ma'tuf) upon the predicate, that is: He ridiculed them and decreed for them punishment in the Hereafter.

This is an initial resumptive sentence (*istinaf ibtida'i*, a new sentence not grammatically linked to what precedes it). Its occasion of revelation arose from events concerning the hypocrites described in the preceding verses, so it belongs to the explanation of their conditions and rulings. The verse also indicates that the Prophet ﷺ used to seek forgiveness for them.

The exegetes narrated from Ibn 'Abbas that when some of the preceding verses about them were revealed, up to the words: ﴿Allah has mocked them, and for them is a painful punishment﴾ [al-Tawbah: 79], a group among them said: "Seek forgiveness for us, O Messenger of Allah," meaning for those whose actions were rebuked in the Qur'an without an explicit statement that their doer was a hypocrite. So the Prophet ﷺ promised them that he would seek forgiveness for those who asked him. Al-Hasan said: "They used to come to the Messenger of Allah and make excuses to him, saying: ﴿We intended nothing but good﴾." This is within the meaning of seeking forgiveness, that is, requesting the erasure of what was counted against them as a sin; they meant that it was a request for forgiveness regarding the apparent appearance of their actions. And it is narrated from al-Asamm that 'Abdullah ibn Ubayy ibn Salul, when his hypocrisy became evident and people turned against him from every direction, was met by a man from his people who said to him: "Return to the Messenger of Allah so that he may seek forgiveness for you." He replied: "I do not care whether he seeks forgiveness for me or does not seek forgiveness for me." Concerning him, Allah's words in the Surah of the Hypocrites were revealed: ﴿And when it is said to them, "Come, the Messenger of Allah will seek forgiveness for you," they turn their heads away, and you see them turning away while they are arrogant﴾ [al-Munafiqun: 5], ﴿It is the same for them whether you seek forgiveness for them or do not seek forgiveness for them; Allah will never forgive them﴾ [al-Munafiqun: 6]. That is, this verse is a confirmation of the verse of the Surah of the Hypocrites when a situation similar to the cause for which the verse of the Surah of the Hypocrites was revealed occurs, thereby reconciling the narrations.

[Page 277]

And it is narrated from al-Sha'bi, 'Urwah, Mujahid, Ibn Jubayr and Qatadah that 'Abdullah ibn Ubayy ibn Salul fell ill, and his son 'Abdullah ibn 'Abdullah asked the Prophet ﷺ to seek forgiveness for him, and he did. Then [the verse] was revealed, and the Prophet ﷺ said: "Indeed Allah has granted me a concession, so I will add to the seventy." Then [the verse] was revealed: ﴿It is the same for them whether you seek forgiveness for them or do not seek forgiveness for them; Allah will never forgive them﴾ [al-Munafiqun: 6].

What appears to me is that when the Messenger of Allah ﷺ received the revelation of the verse of the Surah of the Hypocrites, in which it is stated that his seeking forgiveness and not seeking it are equal in their regard, he interpreted that as referring to non-emphatic seeking of forgiveness. His mercy toward people, his eagerness for their guidance, and his distress at their turning away from faith prompted him to seek forgiveness for the hypocrites repeatedly and emphatically, in the hope that Allah would forgive them and His anger toward them would be removed, so that He would guide them to true faith. Since their association with the conditions of faith, even if only in outward appearance, may lead to the attachment of his guidance to their hearts by the slightest cause, the revelation of this verse was a despairing of Allah's pleasure with them, that is, with the remnant that remained among them, to despair them and those who were like them, among those who had perceived their inner states and rejoiced at their condition because they benefited from companionship with the Muslims and the disbelievers. Thus the verse is a despairing without specifying anyone.

The imperative form in His words "seek forgiveness" (*istaghfir*) is used with the meaning of equalization (*taswiyah*), its intended implication being (*lazimuha*) the absence of caution regarding a permissible matter. The purpose of this is to convey the meaning of equalization, which the imperative form frequently conveys. The scholars of the principles of jurisprudence (*usul al-fiqh*) counted equalization among the meanings of the imperative form and illustrated it with His words: ﴿Burn therein; be patient or be not patient﴾ [al-Tur: 16].

As for His words "or do not seek forgiveness for them," its position is unusual, and neither the exegetes nor the grammarians have taken care to explain it. Its being after *la* (not) and jussive makes it resemble the prohibitive form, and the meaning of the prohibitive does not fit this context, since the prohibitive is not used with the meaning of choice or permissibility. Therefore no meaning equivalent to the equalization for which the imperative was used can be derived from it. For this reason we do not find the scholars of the principles mentioning equalization among the meanings of the prohibitive form as they mentioned it among the meanings of the imperative form.

The interpretation of the verse is as follows. Either *la* is negating, and the jussive verb after it is so because it is conjoined to the imperative verb, since the imperative verb is in the jussive by an assumed imperative *lam*, in accordance with the verified view. This is the position of the Kufans, which al-Akhfash of the Basrans chose, as did Ibn Hisham al-Ansari and Abu 'Ali ibn al-Ahwas, the teacher of Abu Hayyan. This is the correct view, because if the verb were indeclinable it would have only one state, and because the endings of its last letter follow the states of the signs of the jussive, so it is not far-fetched that this assumed form was intended in their speech, and it is conjoined to by the jussive through analogy.

It is not valid that this is conjunction of sentences (*'atf al-jumal*), because there would be no basis for the verb to be jussive if it were so, especially since the imperative is interpreted as a declarative statement. Moreover, what the particle of choice conveys indicates the addressee's choice between the two matters, while the benefit is absent from both.

Or the prohibitive form is used with the meaning of equalization, because it accompanies the imperative that indicates the intention of equalization. The meaning would be: your command to them to seek forgiveness and your prohibition of it are equal. This is a metonymy (*kinayah*) for the fact that the commander and the prohibiter does not change his intention regarding them, whether the commanded act is done or the prohibited act is done. It is also possible that both verbs are objects of an omitted verb of saying. The estimate would be: We say to you, "Seek forgiveness for them," or we say, "Do not seek forgiveness for them."

The phrase "seventy times" is not intended as a precise quantity of number; rather, this expression is among the number expressions used to mean abundance. Al-Kashshaf says: "Seventy has become like a proverb in their speech for multiplicity." What supports this is the saying of the Prophet ﷺ: "If I knew that if I added to the seventy he would be forgiven, I would add." This is narrated by al-Bukhari and al-Tirmidhi from the hadith of 'Umar ibn al-Khattab. As for what al-Bukhari narrated from the hadith of Anas ibn 'Iyad and Abu Usamah, from 'Ubaydullah, from Nafi', from Ibn 'Umar, that the Prophet ﷺ said: "And I will add to the seventy," it is a delusion (*tawahhum*) on the part of the narrator, because it contradicts the narration of 'Umar ibn al-Khattab. The narration of 'Umar is more probable because he is the person concerned in the story, and because that addition was not narrated from the hadith of Yahya ibn Sa'id, from 'Ubaydullah, from Nafi', from Ibn 'Umar, in al-Tirmidhi, Ibn Majah and al-Nasa'i.

"Seventy times" is in the accusative as an absolute object (*maf'ul mutlaq*) explaining the number. The discussion of the word "time" (*marrah*) has already preceded, in the phrase of His words: ﴿And they initiated you the first time﴾ [al-Tawbah: 13], in this Surah.

The third-person pronouns refer to the hypocrites whose hypocrisy Allah knew and whom He informed His Prophet ﷺ about. The Muslims used to consider them Muslims, deceived by their outward condition.

[Page 279]

The Prophet ﷺ used to apply to them the rulings of their outward condition among the general body of Muslims, while the Qur'an described them by their marks so that the Muslims would not feel reassured by them and would take precaution against them. Thus, by this, all the interests were fulfilled.

Because of this following of outward conditions, the style of despairing of forgiveness differs between this verse and the verse: ﴿It is not for the Prophet and those who believe to seek forgiveness for the polytheists﴾ [al-Tawbah: 113]. This is because the disbelief of the polytheists is manifest, so the prohibition of seeking forgiveness for them came explicitly. The disbelief of the hypocrites is hidden, so the despairing of forgiveness for them came made dependent on an attribute that they know within themselves and that the Messenger ﷺ also knows. For this reason he used to seek forgiveness for any hypocrite who asked him to seek forgiveness, lest his refraining from seeking forgiveness for him would be a declaration of his inner condition, which the wisdom of the Sharia required not to be disclosed. He said concerning Abu Talib: "I will certainly seek forgiveness for you as long as I am not forbidden from you." When Allah forbade him from that, he stopped seeking forgiveness for him.

The Prophet ﷺ used to perform the funeral prayer over any hypocrite who died, because the funeral prayer is a form of seeking forgiveness. "When 'Abdullah ibn Ubayy ibn Salul, the head of the hypocrites, died after the revelation of this verse, his son 'Abdullah ibn 'Abdullah asked the Prophet ﷺ to pray over him, so he prayed over him out of honor to his son. 'Umar said to the Prophet ﷺ: 'Your Lord has forbidden you to pray over him.' He said to him, in reply: 'Allah only gave me a choice.'" That is, there is no prohibition of seeking forgiveness in this verse. So his praying over them and seeking forgiveness for them had a wisdom other than obtaining forgiveness, namely other interests. Perhaps the Prophet ﷺ took the weaker of the two possibilities in the phrase: ﴿Seek forgiveness for them or do not seek forgiveness for them﴾, and likewise in the numerical expression "seventy times," in pursuit of the hope of mercy, in accordance with what we established in the ninth introduction among the introductions of this tafsir.

The reference in His words: ﴿That is because they disbelieved﴾ is to the absence of forgiveness understood from His words: ﴿Allah will never forgive them﴾.

The particle *ba'* here indicates causation. Their disbelief in Allah is polytheism (*shirk*). Their disbelief in His Messenger is their denial of his prophethood ﷺ. In this verse there is evidence that one who denies the prophethood of Muhammad ﷺ is described as a disbeliever (*kafir*).

[Page 280]

The meaning of: ﴿And Allah does not guide the wicked people﴾ is that Allah does not decree for them guidance to faith because of their wickedness (*fisq*), that is, their distance from reflecting on the evidences of prophethood and from fairness in acknowledging the truth. Whoever has this as his habit, his heart is sealed, and he does not accept guidance. So the meaning of "does not guide" is: does not create guidance in their hearts.

﴿Those who were left behind rejoiced in their sitting [idle] behind the Messenger of Allah, and they disliked to strive with their wealth and their lives in the cause of Allah. And they said, "Do not go forth in the heat." Say, "The Fire of Hell is more intense in heat, if only they could understand."﴾

It is a resumptive sentence (istiʾnāf ibtidāʾī, a new sentence beginning a fresh topic). This verse refers to what happened among the hypocrites when they were called to go out for the expedition to Tabuk. Accordingly, "those who were left behind" refers specifically to those hypocrites who stayed behind from the expedition to Tabuk.

The reason for its placement in this position is that their joy at staying behind grew stronger when the Prophet (ﷺ) asked forgiveness for them. They thought they had deceived him, so they achieved their aim, and then they obtained forgiveness, thinking that Allah's treatment of them would follow the outward appearances of affairs.

Those "left behind" are those who stayed away from the expedition to Tabuk. They asked the Prophet (ﷺ) for permission, and he granted it to them. They were among the hypocrites. Therefore the description "those left behind" is given in the verse in the form of the passive participle (ism al-mafʿūl), because the Prophet (ﷺ) left them behind. In this there is an indication that he only permitted them to stay behind because he knew the corruption of their hearts and that they would be of no benefit to the Muslims, as He said: ﴿Had they gone forth among you, they would have increased you only in corruption﴾ [al-Tawbah: 47].

Mentioning their joy is evidence of their hypocrisy, because if they had been believers, staying behind would have been painful and distressing to them, as happened to the three who were left behind, and then Allah accepted their repentance.

Here al-maqʿad is a mīmī verbal noun (maṣdar mīmī), meaning "by their sitting."

And (khilāf) is a dialectal variant of (khalf). It is said: "He remained khilāf the tribe," meaning after them, i.e. they departed and he did not depart. One of the subtle points in choosing the word khilāf rather than khalf is that it indicates their sitting was an opposition (mukhālafa) to the will of the Messenger of Allah when he called the people all together to go on the expedition. For this reason some exegetes made it an accusative as an object of purpose (mafʿūl lahu), meaning: "by their sitting, opposing the command of the Messenger."

Their disliking of striving with their wealth and their lives in the cause of Allah is another trait of hypocrisy, because Allah commanded this in the previous verse: ﴿And strive with your wealth and your lives in the cause of Allah﴾ [al-Tawbah: 41], and so on. Because it is another trait, its clause was joined by conjunction and was not linked with the particle of causation (lām al-taʿlīl), even though their joy at sitting was caused by their dislike of jihad.

Their saying ﴿Do not go forth in the heat﴾ is addressed by some of them to others. The expedition to Tabuk took place in the time of heat, when the shade was pleasant.

The clause ﴿Say, "The Fire of Hell is more intense in heat"﴾ is a resumptive, new sentence, addressed to the Prophet (ﷺ), and its purpose is to strike their ears with these words.

That the Fire of Hell is more intense in heat than the heat of summer is a known matter, and the purpose does not depend on informing about it. Therefore it is established that the statement is used to remind them of what is known, as a veiled rebuke of their ignorance, because they feared a little heat and thrust themselves into what would bring them to a more intense heat. Thus this reminder is a metaphor (kināya) for their being in the Fire of Hell because of their sitting out the expedition in the heat, and in it there is an incidental metaphor (kināya ʿurḍiyya) for their being destined for the Fire of Hell.

The clause ﴿if only they could understand﴾ is a completion (tatmīm), for the purpose of rebuke and reminder. That is, they are told this if they could understand the reminder, but they do not understand, so the reminder and admonition are of no benefit to them. The meaning of "if only they could understand" is not that the Fire of Hell is more intense in heat, since that is not hidden from them, but rather: if only they could understand that they are destined for the Fire, yet they do not understand that.

[p. 281]

[Page 282 marker omitted]

This is a continuation of the preceding discussion, drawing on their joy mentioned earlier and on the implication of His words, ﴿Say, "The fire of Hell is more intense in heat"﴾ [9:81], which hints that they are its people and destined for it.

Laughing here is a metonymy (kināya) for joy, or it may mean that they laugh with joy because they believe their scheme has succeeded with the Prophet ﷺ, since he permitted them to stay behind.

Weeping is a metonymy for their grief in the Hereafter. The command to laugh and to weep is used to express the certain occurrence of both, since both are presented as coming from God, or it is a command of creation, like His words, ﴿Allah said to them, "Die."﴾ [2:243]. The meaning is that their joy is fleeting and their weeping is lasting.

Laughing is a state in the mouth in which the lips stretch and sometimes part to show the teeth. It occurs at happiness and at wonder at something beautiful.

Weeping is a state in the face and eyes in which the cheeks, the folds of the face, and the nose contract, and tears flow from the eyes. It occurs at grief and at helplessness in resisting a defeat.

His words, ﴿as a recompense for what they used to earn﴾, are a circumstantial phrase (ḥāl) from their pronoun, meaning "as a recompense for them." What is made a recompense is the weeping, which follows the brief laughter, because it removed a blessing and replaced it with a great punishment.

"What they used to earn" refers to the deeds of their hypocrisy. The relative form was chosen for this expression because it is more comprehensive while being concise.

The use of the verb "to be" (kāna) and the imperfect form in "yaksibūn" here parallels its use in His words, ﴿but they were wronging themselves﴾ [9:70].

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 9, verse 83:

﴿So if Allah returns you to a group of them and they ask your permission to go out, say: "You will never go out with me, nor will you fight an enemy with me. You were content with sitting idle the first time, so sit now with those who stay behind."﴾

The fa' (فاء) here is for tafri' (تفريع, consequential connection) upon what was indicated by His saying: ﴿Say: The Fire of Hell is more intense in heat﴾ [al-Tawbah: 81], since a further punishment is made consequent upon the anger toward them and the threat against them: their exclusion from participating with the Muslims in their military expeditions.

The verb raja'a (رجع) may be intransitive or transitive, synonymous with araja'a (أرجع). Here it is transitive, meaning: Allah returns you.

The returning to a group of the hypocrites who stayed behind is expressed in an elliptical manner (ijaz, إيجاز), because the intended meaning is a return to speaking with them about a matter like the one being discussed, as indicated by His saying: ﴿they ask your permission to go out﴾. Since the aim was to explain how he dealt with a group, the speech was abbreviated, and it was said: ﴿So if Allah returns you to a group of them﴾. The intended meaning is not literal return, as the expressions of most of the exegetes have run upon, who took it to be a return from the expedition of Tabuk, even though the whole surah was revealed after the battle of Tabuk. Rather, the intended meaning is figurative: the matter of dealing with them was repeated once more.

The ta'ifah (طائفة) is a group, and it has been discussed previously in His saying: ﴿a group of you who were overcome by drowsiness﴾ [Ali 'Imran: 154] in Surah Al 'Imran, and in His saying: ﴿let a group of them stand with you﴾ [al-Nisa': 102] in Surah al-Nisa'.

The meaning of ta'ifah here is a group of those who stayed behind, indicated by His saying: ﴿they ask your permission to go out﴾, that is, a group of them seeking to go out for the expedition. It is possible that this group was of the hypocrites who wished to go out for the expedition out of greed for the spoils or something similar. It is also possible that it was a group of those who stayed behind who repented and embraced Islam, and so they asked permission to go out for the expedition. In either case, it is possible that his refusal to let them go out was out of fear of their treachery if they were hypocrites, or merely as discipline for them if they had repented and believed.

What the Prophet ﷺ was commanded to say to them suits both possibilities.

The combining of the negation with (لن) and the word abadan (أبدًا) is an emphasis of the meaning of lan, to establish that they will not go out in the future to fight with the Muslims.

The clause ﴿You were content with sitting idle the first time﴾ is a new sentence (mustaanifah) serving as a reproach and rebuke for them, meaning: you love sitting idle and are satisfied with it, so I have increased you in it.

The verb (رضيتم) indicates that what they committed of sitting idle is an act whose nature is that people would turn away from it, to the extent that the verb (رضي), which implies attempt and negotiation, was used for committing it. They were treated as one who tries to bring himself to an act while it resists, until it is satisfied, as in His saying: ﴿Are you content with the life of this world instead of the Hereafter?﴾ [al-Tawbah: 38], and this has been discussed previously.

The phrase ﴿first time﴾ (أوَّلَ مَرَّةٍ) is in the accusative here as an adverb of time, because the occurrence (المرة) here, since it was at a time known to them, namely the time of going out to Tabuk, implied the meaning of time. The accusative of a verbal noun standing in for the noun of time is common in their speech, unlike its accusative in His saying: ﴿and they began with you the first time﴾ [al-Tawbah: 13], and in His saying: ﴿even if you ask forgiveness for them seventy times﴾ [al-Tawbah: 80], as has been discussed. And ﴿the first time﴾ is the expedition of Tabuk, from which they stayed behind.

When the superlative (أفعل التفضيل) is attached to an indefinite noun, it is restricted to the singular and masculine form, even if the noun it is attached to is not singular or masculine, because the attached noun already provides sufficient indication of the intended meaning.

The fa' in (فاقعدوا) is a tafri' upon ﴿You were content with sitting idle﴾, meaning: since you chose sitting idle for yourselves, then sit now, because you love to stay behind.

And (الخالفين) is the plural of khalif (خالف), who is one who replaces the warrior in his family; they used to leave behind for this purpose whoever had no usefulness in war. Thus, their being with the khalifin is a reproach to them.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 9, verse 84:

﴿And do not pray over any of them who has died, ever, nor stand at his grave. Indeed, they disbelieved in Allah and His Messenger and died while they were defiantly disobedient.﴾

When the discussion of seeking forgiveness for the hypocrites, which arose from their excuses and false oaths, was concluded, and the announcement that Allah would not forgive them was mixed with the appearance of an option regarding seeking forgiveness for them, and that still left some of their hope in benefiting from the seeking of forgiveness (because they reckon that Allah's dealing follows the outward appearances of actions and utterances, as we previously mentioned in His saying: ﴿those who were left behind rejoiced﴾ [al-Tawbah: 81]), the situation became ready for an explicit prohibition against seeking forgiveness for them and praying over their dead, since praying over the deceased is a form of seeking forgiveness.

So the sentence ﴿And do not pray﴾ is a conjunction (ʿaṭf) upon the sentence ﴿Seek forgiveness for them or do not seek forgiveness for them﴾ [al-Tawbah: 80], a conjunction of speech intended to be attached to another speech, because the Qur'an was revealed with attention to the positions in which verses were placed.

The pronoun in ﴿of them﴾ refers to the hypocrites who were known by their marks and their past actions mentioned earlier.

The occasion of revelation of this verse is what al-Bukhari and al-Tirmidhi narrated from the hadith of ʿAbd Allah ibn ʿAbbas, from ʿUmar ibn al-Khattab, who said: "When ʿAbd Allah ibn Ubayy ibn Salul died, the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) was called to pray over him. When the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) stood up, I jumped up before him and said: 'O Messenger of Allah, will you pray over Ibn Ubayy when he said on such-and-such a day such-and-such?' I enumerated his words. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) smiled and said: 'Withdraw from me, O ʿUmar.' When I persisted with him, he said: 'I was given a choice and I chose. If I knew that if I added beyond seventy he would be forgiven, I would add beyond it.' He said: So the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) prayed over him, then departed, and he did not remain but a short while until the two verses from 'Bara'ah' were revealed: ﴿And do not pray over any of them who has died, ever﴾ to His saying: ﴿while they were defiantly disobedient﴾. He said: Afterwards I was amazed at my boldness toward the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), and Allah and His Messenger know best." End of quotation. In another narration: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) did not pray over any of them after this verse until he passed away (ﷺ). He only prayed over him and gave him his shirt to be shrouded in, out of honour for his son ʿAbd Allah and to win over the Khazraj."

The phrase ﴿of them﴾ (min-hum) is a qualifier of ﴿any﴾ (aḥad). The clause ﴿who has died﴾ (māta) is a second qualifier of ﴿any﴾.

The meaning of ﴿nor stand at his grave﴾ is: do not stand by it at his burial, because participating in the burial of a Muslim is an obligation upon the Muslims collectively (fard kifāyah), like praying over him. Thus the Prophet's (ﷺ) abandonment of praying over them and attending their burial is a public declaration of the disbelief of the one for whom this is abandoned.

The clause ﴿Indeed, they disbelieved in Allah and His Messenger﴾ is causal (taʿlīliyyah), and for this reason it is not conjoined by a particle; the presence of ﴿inna﴾ at its beginning has made the particle of consequence (fāʾ al-tafrīʿ) unnecessary, as is the usage.

The word "fisq" (defiant disobedience) is intended to mean disbelief, so the expression "fāsiqūn" (defiantly disobedient) in place of "kāfirūn" (disbelievers) is merely a stylistic variation. It is better to interpret fisq here as departure from faith after having been characterised by it, i.e. in the appearance of faith, so the meaning of fisq becomes more heinous than disbelief.

The pronouns in ﴿indeed they disbelieved﴾, ﴿and died﴾ and ﴿while they were defiantly disobedient﴾ refer to ﴿any﴾ (aḥad), because it is general by virtue of being an indefinite noun in the context of a prohibition, and a prohibition is like a negation. As for describing it with the singular in His saying ﴿who has died﴾, it follows the wording of the qualified noun, because the basic principle of the adjective is agreement with the noun it qualifies.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 9, verse 85:

﴿And let not their wealth and their children impress you. Allah only intends to punish them thereby in the worldly life, and that their souls should depart while they are disbelievers.﴾

The address is to the Prophet (ﷺ), but the intended audience is the Muslims, meaning: let it not impress you (lā tu'jibkum). The sentence is conjoined (ma'tuf) to the sentence prohibiting praying over them.

The occasion for mentioning this statement here is that when what indicates their wretchedness in the Hereafter was mentioned, this might stir in people's souls the thought that the hypocrites had obtained the happiness of the worldly life through abundance of wealth and children, and had lost the Hereafter. Perhaps this would cause some confusion among Muslims, who might say: "How does Allah bestow upon them wealth and children when they are His enemies and the enemies of His Prophet?" Perhaps this also served as a consolation for them among the Muslims, so Allah informed the Muslims that those wealth and children, although they appear in the form of a blessing, are for them a curse and a punishment, and that Allah punishes them with them in the world by depriving them of tranquility of mind regarding them. For when they had acquired enmity toward the Messenger and the Muslims, they were wary lest Allah incite His Messenger against them and uproot them, as He said: ﴿If the hypocrites, and those in whose hearts is a disease, and the agitators in al-Madinah do not desist, We will surely incite you against them; then they will not remain your neighbors therein except for a little. Cursed; wherever they are found, they will be seized and slain with [serious] slaughter.﴾ [al-Ahzab: 60-61]. Then He made that continuous until their death upon disbelief, by which they proceed to the everlasting punishment.

The parallel of this verse has already occurred in this surah, at the mention of their stinginess in spending, in His saying: ﴿Say, "Spend willingly or unwillingly"﴾ [al-Tawbah: 53], and the two verses that follow. There it was conveyed that they do not benefit from their wealth and that it is a punishment upon them in the world. Then this verse is repeated here with most of its wording, as an emphasis on the meaning it contains, for the sake of thoroughly removing confusion and bewilderment from people.

However, this verse differs from the preceding one in several respects. The first is that in this one the conjunction at its beginning is with the waw, whereas in the other it is conjoined with the fa'. The reason for the subordinating conjunction there has already been explained, and the reason for not subordinating here is that the meaning of this verse is not a consequence (mufarra') of the meaning of the sentence to which it is conjoined, but there is only a connection between them.

The second is that in this verse "children" is conjoined to "wealth" without repeating the negative particle, whereas in the preceding verse the negative particle lā was repeated. The reason for this is that the mention of children in the preceding verse was merely for completion and digression, since the context is the dispraise of their wealth, as they did not benefit from it. Since the mention of children was a completion, it resembled an independent matter, so the negative particle was repeated in its conjunction. This differs from the context of this verse, for their wealth and their children together are intended to be belittled in the view of the Muslims.

The third is that here came His saying: ﴿Allah only intends to punish them﴾ with the explicit (an), without the lam, whereas in the preceding verse it is ﴿Allah only intends to punish them﴾ with the lam of causation and the omission of (an) after it [al-Tawbah: 55]. Both usages have been combined in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Allah intends to make clear to you﴾ [al-Nisa: 26], up to His saying: ﴿and Allah intends to turn to you in forgiveness﴾ [al-Nisa: 27] in Surat al-Nisa'. The omission of the preposition before (an) is frequent, and the estimation of (an) after the lam is also frequent. Among the elegances of emphasis is variation in wording, and it is a variety of expression. Moreover, that lam and its like have been disputed: it has been said that it is superfluous (za'ida), and it has been said that it conveys causation. Some grammarians named it (lam an). The discussion of it has already preceded at His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Allah intends to make clear to you﴾ [al-Nisa: 26] in Surat al-Nisa'.

The fourth is that in this verse came "to punish them thereby in the world," whereas in the preceding verse came "in the worldly life." The wisdom of this is that the preceding verse mentioned the state of their wealth during their lives, so there was no need to mention life. Here, the state of their wealth after their deaths is mentioned, owing to His saying: ﴿And do not pray over anyone of them who has died, ever﴾ [al-Tawbah: 84]. For they have passed to another life, their worldly life has ended, and it has become a thing of the past.

The rest of the explanation of this verse is like the explanation of the verse before it.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 9, verse 86:

﴿When a surah is sent down, [saying]: Believe in Allah and strive along with His Messenger, those of ampleness among them ask your leave and say, "Leave us that we may be with those who sit [at home]."﴾

This is the conjunction of one purpose to another, intended as a transition to the classification of the groups of those who stayed behind from jihad, among the hypocrites and others, and the varieties of their excuses and their degrees of acceptance. What necessitated it was the severe rebuke (al-ighlaz) of those who stayed behind from jihad, out of hypocrisy and discouraging the Muslims, beginning from His saying: ﴿O you who believe, what is [the matter] with you that, when you are told to go forth in the cause of Allah, you adhere heavily to the earth?﴾ [al-Tawbah: 38], then His saying: ﴿Had it been a near gain﴾ [al-Tawbah: 42]. All of that is directed at the hypocrites.

Because this verse introduces a new purpose, it begins with mention of the sending down of a surah calling to faith and jihad. What is meant by it is this surah, namely Surat Bara'ah (al-Tawbah), and applying the name of the surah to it while it is still in the course of being revealed, before its completion, is an extensive metaphor (majaz muttasi'), like applying the name "the Book" to the Qur'an during its revelation, as in His saying: ﴿That is the Book, there is no doubt in it﴾ [al-Baqarah: 2], and His saying: ﴿And this is a Book which We have sent down, blessed﴾ [al-An'am: 92]. Thus this description is a presumed description, akin to the presumed circumstantial clause (al-hal al-muqaddarah).

Mention of the hypocrites among those who stayed behind is begun with His saying: ﴿those of ampleness among them ask your leave﴾.

The surah is a specific portion of the verses of the Qur'an, having a beginning and an end, and discussion of it has already passed a moment ago and just before this.

Since the surah consists of words and statements, its explanation is validly given by some of what it contains, namely the command to faith and jihad. So His saying ﴿that believe in Allah﴾ is an explanation of the surah, and the "an" (that) in it is explanatory (tafsiriyyah), like that in His saying, exalted is He, quoting 'Isa: ﴿I did not say to them except what You commanded me: that worship Allah, my Lord and your Lord﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 117]. It is permissible to explain a thing by part of it, in the manner of a substitute of part for the whole (badal al-ba'd min al-kull).

What is intended is not the wording "believe" and what is conjoined to it, but what is meant by it. They are like His saying: ﴿O you who believe, what is [the matter] with you that, when it is said to you, "Go forth in the cause of Allah"﴾ [al-Tawbah: 38] and the verses, and His saying: ﴿Those who believe in Allah and the Last Day do not ask your leave to strive with their wealth and their selves﴾ [al-Tawbah: 44].

Al-tawl (ampleness) is abundance in wealth. He, exalted, said: ﴿And whoever among you does not have the ability (tawlan) to marry free believing women﴾ [al-Nisa': 25], and this has already been discussed. Restricting it to "ampleness" indicates that those "of ampleness" are meant to be those who have the capacity for jihad through soundness of body. Thus with the presence of ampleness their excuse is negated, since one who is not able by his body does not look to his being of ampleness, as His saying after it indicates: ﴿Nor is there any blame upon those who find nothing to spend﴾ [al-Tawbah: 91].

Those "of ampleness" are meant to be the likes of 'Abd Allah ibn Ubayy ibn Salul, Mu'attib ibn Qushayr, and al-Jadd ibn Qays.

The conjunction of ﴿and say, "Leave us that we may be with those who sit"﴾ upon "ask your leave" is because of the difference between them in the sentence, with an addition in the conjoined clause, since the asking of leave is general, and their statement reported in it clarifies what they asked leave for, which is sitting [at home]. In its arrangement there is an indication of the fabrication of their excuse and that the reality is their desire to sit. For this reason their saying is reported by beginning with "leave us" (dhurna), which requires a desire for their being left behind in Medina, and [it implies] that they would be followers of those who sit, among whom are the weak, the feeble, and the cowardly, because of what the word "with" (ma'a) indicates of attachment and following.

It has already been mentioned that "dhar" is an imperative from a defective verb, namely "wadhara," for which they have dispensed with a synonym, namely "taraka" (to leave), in His saying, exalted: ﴿And leave those who have taken their religion as play and amusement﴾ [al-An'am: 70], in Surat al-An'am.

This is a continuation (istinaf) whose purpose is to express wonder at the baseness of their souls and the weakness of their manliness, in that they were content for themselves to be followers of women.

In the choice of the verb (radu, "they were content") there is an indication that the state they had fallen into is one that a sensible person would normally hesitate to accept, as was already mentioned in His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Are you content with the life of this world instead of the Hereafter?﴾ [al-Tawbah: 38] and His saying: ﴿You were content to sit at home the first time﴾ [al-Tawbah: 83].

Al-Khawalif is the plural of khalifah, which is the woman who remains behind in the house after her husband has travelled. If she travels with him, she is called al-za'inah (the one who journeys with the caravan). That is, they were content to remain with the women.

Al-tab' (sealing) is a figurative depiction of the state of their hearts in not accepting guidance, like a sealed vessel or a sealed book. Al-tab' is synonymous with al-khatm (sealing). Its explanation has already been given at His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Allah has sealed their hearts﴾ [al-Baqarah: 7] in Surah al-Baqarah. The verb tubi'a (was sealed) is put in the passive form either because its agent is known, namely Allah, or to indicate that they were created thus and naturally disposed to it. Consequent upon the sealing is the absence of their knowledge of the matters that are specific to the knowledge of people of understanding, which is the knowledge expressed by fiqh (deep comprehension), that is, the perception of hidden things. That is, they preferred the blessing of ease over the reputation of courage and over the reward of jihad, since they perceived only tangible things, and therefore they were not people of deep understanding. That is the root of all harms in both abodes.

The predicate in the negation of fiqh from them is expressed as a verbal sentence in order to indicate the strengthening of the report, the affirmation of its attribution to those spoken of, and its firm establishment upon them.

The opening of the speech with the particle of contrast (*harf al-istidrak*, the particle that signals a corrective or contrasting statement) indicates that the content of this statement is the opposite of what precedes it, both in its root and in its branches. Since the hypocrites' staying behind from jihad (striving in the way of God) was caused by their disbelief in the Messenger ﷺ, the believers were the reverse of that. The description of their condition begins with the description of the Messenger's condition, because their attachment to him and their following of him is the root of their perfection and their good. So it is said: ﴿But the Messenger and those who believed with him strove with their wealth and their lives﴾.

His saying ﴿with their wealth and their lives﴾ [al-Tawbah: 81] corresponds to His saying ﴿Those of wealth among them asked your permission﴾ [al-Tawbah: 86].

His saying ﴿And those — theirs are the good things, and those are the successful﴾ corresponds to His saying ﴿And their hearts were sealed, so they do not understand﴾ [al-Tawbah: 87], as has already been explained.

In the particle of contrast there is an indication of being independent of the support of the hypocrites, through the support of the believers for the Messenger, as in His saying: ﴿If these disbelieve in it, then We have entrusted it to a people who are not disbelievers in it﴾ [al-An'am: 89].

The discussion of jihad with wealth has already passed at His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Go forth, light and heavy, and strive with your wealth and your lives﴾ [al-Tawbah: 41].

In His saying ﴿and those who believed with him﴾ there is an implicit reproach that those who did not strive, without an excuse, are not believers.

The word *ma'ahu* ("with him") is in the position of a circumstantial qualifier (*hal*) relative to *alladhina* ("those who"), to show that they are followers of him in every state and in every matter. Their belief "with him" is because they believed in him when he called them to it, and their striving with their wealth and their lives is "with him." In this there is an indication that the good things scattered for them in this world and the Hereafter follow from his good things and his stations.

The clause ﴿And those — theirs are the good things﴾ is conjoined to the clause "strove" (*jahadu*) and was not separated, although separation was permissible, so that by the conjunction it indicates that it is a predicate concerning "those who believed", i.e., that it is among their attributes and conditions. This is because that form is more indicative of the firm establishment of its meaning in them than if it were presented as a separate, independent statement.

The use of the demonstrative *ulaika* ("those") is to convey that their deserving of the good things and success was on account of their striving.

*Khayrat* ("good things") is the plural of *khayr* according to a non-analogical pattern. It is one of those words that came in the form of the feminine plural although it is not feminine and does not bear its marker, like *suradiqat* and *hammamat*.

Many lexicographers took it to be the plural of *khayrah*, with the *ya'* lightened, from *khayyirah* (with the *ya'* doubled), which is the feminine of *khayyir*, or the feminine of *khayr* (with the *ya'* lightened), which means *akhyar* ("better"). They made the feminine form for the description of a woman because they did not intend comparison by it. On all of this, *khayrat* here is interpreted as "good qualities." All of that is an artificial strain for which there is no need, given that the literal reading is sound. What is meant is the benefits of this world and the Hereafter, so the *lam* in it is for comprehensiveness (*istighraq*, encompassing all instances).

The discussion of ﴿And those — they are the successful﴾ is like the discussion of its counterpart at the beginning of Surat al-Baqarah.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 9, verse 89:

﴿Allah has prepared for them gardens beneath which rivers flow, abiding therein forever. That is the great triumph.﴾

This is an explanatory resumptive clause (isti'naf bayani), answering a question that arises from the statement ﴿And those – for them are the good things﴾ [al-Tawbah: 88].

Al-i'dad (preparation) means al-tahy'ah (making ready). It conveys concern for them and attention to their affair. The discussion of the like of this verse has already occurred in His saying earlier ﴿Allah has promised the believing men and believing women gardens beneath which rivers flow, abiding therein forever, and pleasant dwellings﴾ [al-Tawbah: 72], and so on.

[Page 292]

﴿And the excusers among the desert Arabs came, seeking permission to stay behind, and those who lied to Allah and His Messenger sat still.﴾ The clause ﴿And the excusers came﴾ is conjoined (ʿaṭf) to the clause ﴿Those of wealth among them asked your permission﴾ [al-Tawbah: 86], and what lies between them is a parenthetical interjection (iʿtirāḍ). Thus, by "the excusers" is meant a group of truthful believers among the desert Arabs, as the contrast with ﴿and those who lied to Allah and His Messenger sat still﴾ indicates. Ibn ʿAbbās, Mujāhid and Kathīr interpreted it in this sense, and they counted Ghifār among these. Qatādah disagreed: he took them to be the false excusers, namely the Banū ʿĀmir, the kinsmen of ʿĀmir ibn al-Ṭufayl, who said to the Prophet (ﷺ): "If we go out with you, the Arab tribe of Ṭayyiʾ will raid our homes." Among the lying excusers were also Asad and Ghaṭafān.

On both interpretations, the parsing (taqdīr) of the word ﴿al-muʿadhdhirūn﴾ differs. If they were those who were genuinely in excuse, then the underlying form of al-muʿadhdhirūn is al-muʿtadhirūn, from iʿtadhara (to make an excuse). The tāʾ was assimilated into the dhāl because the two articulation points are close, for the sake of lightening (the word), just as the tāʾ was assimilated into the ṣād in the verse ﴿and they are disputing (wa-hum yakhiṣṣimūn)﴾ [Yā-Sīn: 49], meaning yakhtaṣimūn (they dispute).

If, however, they were lying in their excuse, then the parsing of al-muʿadhdhirūn is that it is an active participle (ism fāʿil) from ʿadhdhara, in the sense of "to feign an excuse." On the authority of Ibn ʿAbbās: "May Allah curse the excusers (al-muʿadhdhirīn)." al-Azharī (d. 370 AH) said: "He held that they are those who make excuses without having an excuse; so, in his view, the one who is al-muʿadhdhir (with the doubled ʿayn) is the one who displays an excuse by way of pretext, while he has no excuse." End of quotation. The commentator on the Dīwān of al-Nābigha, on the poet's line:

"Bid farewell to Umāmah, and farewell is an excuse (taʿdhīr)."

said: that is, he finds no excuse other than the farewell.

It may be that the choice of the form al-muʿadhdhirīn is one of the subtleties of the Qur'an, so that it encompasses both those who were truthful in their excuse and those who lied in it.

The word iʿtidhār is an iftiʿāl form, from the pattern in which the iftiʿāl form is used for the effort and deliberate performance of an action, like iktisāb (acquiring) and ikhtilāq (fabricating). This augmented form has no bare verb with the same meaning; the bare verb is ʿadhara, [Page 293] meaning "to accept the excuse." An excuse (ʿudhr) is the clear proof and the circumstance by which the one offering it frees himself from responsibility or blame in the eyes of the one to whom he makes his excuse.

Yaʿqūb read al-muʿdhirūn, with a sukūn on the ʿayn and a lightened dhāl, from aʿdhara, meaning that one who went to great lengths in making excuses.

The word aʿrāb is a collective noun (ism jamʿ). It is said of one individual aʿrābiyy, with the relative yāʾ (nisba), attributed to the collective noun, just as majūsiyy is said of one of the Magians (majūs). The form aʿrāb belongs to the forms of plurals, but it was not a true plural, because it has no singular derived from its own plural form; therefore it was made a collective noun. They are the inhabitants of the desert.

As for His words ﴿and those who lied to Allah and His Messenger sat still﴾, they are those among the desert Arabs who openly declared disobedience regarding the matter of going out to the campaign, as the context indicates. That is, they stayed behind without giving any excuse. Thus sitting still means not going out to the campaign. It is known that the intended meaning is sitting still without excuse from its contrast with His words ﴿And the excusers among the desert Arabs came﴾.

The clause ﴿and those who lied to Allah and His Messenger sat still﴾ is conjoined to the clause ﴿And the excusers among the desert Arabs came﴾. This is another group of the desert Arabs, a mixture of Muslims and hypocrites, who "lied" (kadhdhabū, with the lightened form, meaning they were liars). The meaning is that they lied about the faith they had previously displayed. It is also possible that they lied about their promise of support, and then sat still without excuse, in such a way that their staying behind was not expected, because the ones who gave excuses were known to the Prophet (peace be upon him) as not going out with him, unlike the others, who were counted among the army. Their staying behind was more harmful, because it may weaken the zeal of many of the fighters.

The clause ﴿Those who disbelieved among them will surely be struck by a painful punishment﴾ is a new sentence (mustaʾnafah) introducing a threat.

The pronoun in (minhum) returns to those already mentioned, so it encompasses both those who lied to Allah and His Messenger and those whose excuse arose from hypocrisy and lying.

The indefiniteness of (ʿadhāb) is for magnification, and by it is meant the punishment of Hell.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 9, verse 91:

[294]
﴿There is no blame upon the weak, nor upon the sick, nor upon those who find nothing to spend, when they are sincere to Allah and His Messenger. There is no cause for blaming the good-doers. And Allah is Forgiving and Merciful.﴾

This is a resumptive explanatory clause (isti'naf bayani) answering an implied question that arises from the gravity of staying behind from the military expedition (ghazw) and from the threat directed at those who stayed behind. It completes the classification of those who remained behind into the blameworthy and the excused, whether from the Bedouins or from others.

The repetition of the negative particle with the conjunction of "the weak" and "the sick" serves to emphasise the negation of censure for each group separately.

"Al-du'afa'" is the plural of da'if, the one afflicted with weakness (du'f), meaning the weakness of bodily strength without illness.

"Al-marda" is the plural of marid, the one who has an illness (maradh). Illness (maradh) is a change in the habitual order of the body due to a disturbance that arises in some part of the constitution (mizaj). Among illnesses is the chronic kind, such as blindness and disability (zamanah). It has been mentioned in His words: ﴿And if you are sick or on a journey﴾ [An-Nisa: 43] in Surat an-Nisa.

"Haraj" is narrowness, and what is meant by it is narrowness of obligation, that is, prohibition.

"Nusḥ" (sincere advice) is beneficial action directed at the one advised. It has already been discussed under His words, Exalted is He: ﴿I have conveyed to you the message of my Lord and advised you﴾ [Al-A'raf: 79] in Surat al-A'raf, and the reason for its being transitive with the preposition "li-" was mentioned there. Here it is applied to faith and striving to please Allah and His Messenger, and to obeying and striving for what benefits the Muslims, since that resembles the act of an ally who gives sincere counsel to the one he counsels.

The clause ﴿There is no cause for blaming the good-doers﴾ stands in the position of a causal explanation for the negation of narrowness (haraj) from them, and this clause is composed in the manner of proverbs. Thus His words ﴿There is no cause for blaming the good-doers﴾ indicate an omitted reason. The meaning is: there is no narrowness upon the weak, nor upon those joined to them in the statement, when they are sincere to Allah and His Messenger, because they are good-doers and not wrongdoers; and "there is no cause (sabil) against the good-doers" means no censure or punishment. "Al-muhsinun" are those who perform ihsan, which is what contains complete benefit.

[295]
The word sabil originally means the path, and it is used for the means and causes of blame and punishment, because those means resemble the path by which the seeker of right reaches the place of the one who is owed. Out of regard for this usage, the preposition of elevation (isti'la') is used with the predicate concerning the sabil rather than the preposition of endpoint. A parallel to it is His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿If they obey you, then do not seek a way against them﴾ [An-Nisa: 34] and His saying: ﴿Allah has not given you any way against them﴾ [An-Nisa: 90], both in Surat an-Nisa. Thus those who gave sincere counsel to Allah and His Messenger are included among the good-doers. This is not a case of placing the apparent noun in the position of the pronoun, because this is a different aim, loftier and farther in its goal.

The "min" is emphatic, confirming that the negation covers every sabil.

The clause ﴿And Allah is Forgiving and Merciful﴾ is a concluding appendage (tadhyil), and the waw is parenthetical (i'tiradiyyah). That is: He is exceedingly forgiving, and among His forgiveness is that He does not hold to account those with valid excuses for staying behind from jihad. He is exceedingly merciful toward people, and among His mercy is that He does not impose on those with excuses what would be hardship for them.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 9, verse 92:

﴿Nor [is there blame] upon those who came to you that you might provide them with mounts; you said, "I cannot find anything to mount you on." They turned away while their eyes overflowed with tears from grief that they could not find anything to spend.﴾

This is coordinated (ʿatf) with "the weak and the sick." The negative particle is repeated after the conjunction for the rhetorical point (nukta) mentioned earlier there.

"Ḥaml" (carrying) is used for giving what one is carried upon, that is, "when they came to you that you might give them a ḥamūlah," meaning the mount they ride and carry their weapons and provisions on, namely camels.

The clause "you said, 'I cannot find...'" is either a circumstantial clause (ḥāl) relating to the pronoun of address in "they came to you," or a clause of inclusive apposition (badal ishtimāl) for the act of "they came to you," because their coming for the purpose of being carried includes both a granting and a refusal.

The clause "they turned away" is the answer to "when" (idhā), and the whole phrase is the relative clause (ṣilah) of "those who."

"Tawallī" means to return. It was discussed previously in the commentary on His words ﴿What turned them away from their qiblah﴾ [al-Baqarah: 142] and His words ﴿And when he turns away, he strives in the land﴾ [al-Baqarah: 205], in Surah al-Baqarah.

[Page 296]

"Al-fayḍ" and "al-fayaān" mean the outflow of water or the like from its place of rest and its container. It is literally attributed to the liquid itself, and it is very often attributed to the container of the liquid, so one says "the valley overflowed" and "the vessel overflowed." From this comes "her eye overflowed with tears," which is more eloquent than "her tears overflowed," because the eye is treated as if it were entirely flowing tears. So His words ﴿its eyes overflow with tears﴾ follow this style.

The particle "min" (from) indicates what the overflow consists of, and the noun it governs has the sense of a specifier (tamyīz). It was discussed previously in His words ﴿you see their eyes overflow with tears﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 83] in Surah al-Ma'idah.

"Ḥazanan" (grief) is in the accusative as an object of purpose (mafʿūl li-ajlihi). The phrase ﴿that they cannot find anything to spend﴾ is in the genitive by a deleted preposition "li" (for), meaning: they grieved because they could not find anything to spend.

The verse was revealed concerning a group of seven men from the Anṣār, and it was said that there were others besides the Anṣār among them. There is also disagreement about their names, which need not be mentioned. They were called "the weepers" (al-bakkā'īn) because they wept when they did not find at the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) the mounts, out of grief at being deprived of jihad. It was also said: "It was revealed concerning Abu Musa al-Ash'ari and a company of the Ash'aris who came to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) during the expedition of Tabuk, asking him to carry them. He had no mount for them, and they came at a moment of anger from the Prophet (ﷺ), so he swore that he would not carry them. Then a herd of camels was brought to him, so he summoned them and carried them. They said, 'We have deceived the Messenger of Allah with his oath; we will never prosper.' They returned and informed him, and he said, 'It was not I who carried you, but Allah who carried you. By Allah, if I swear an oath and then see something else as better than it, I will expiate my oath and do what is better.'"

Apparently these were not the ones intended in this verse, because the Ash'aris were carried by the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him. On the authority of Mujahid, they were the sons of Muqarrin from Muzaynah, and they are the ones about whom it was said that His words were revealed: ﴿And among the Bedouins are those who believe in Allah and the Last Day﴾ [al-Tawbah: 99], and so on to the end of the verse.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 9, verse 93:

Page 5
﴿The blame is only upon those who ask your permission while they are rich. They are content to be with those who remain behind, and Allah has sealed over their hearts, so they do not know.﴾
When the two preceding verses negated that there should be any blame upon the weak, the ill, those who find nothing to spend, and those who do not find mounts, this verse confined the blame to those who ask permission to stay behind while they are rich. This is a transition, by way of linking, to a return to the conditions of the hypocrites, as indicated by His words after it: ﴿They will make excuses to you when you return to them﴾ [al-Tawbah: 94]. Thus the restriction (qasr) is relative (idafi), with respect to the categories of people from whom blame was negated.

In this restriction there is an emphasis of the preceding negation, meaning: there is no blame or punishment except upon those who ask your permission while they are rich. Those intended are the hypocrites of Medina who dislike jihad, since they do not believe in what Allah has promised of goods, and they are the people of means mentioned in His words: ﴿And when a surah is revealed, saying: Believe in Allah﴾ [al-Tawbah: 86], and so on.

Al-sabil (the way, path): its literal meaning is the road. It occurred in His words: ﴿There is no blame upon the good-doers﴾ [al-Tawbah: 91], and His words: ﴿The blame is only upon those who ask your permission while they are rich﴾, where it is used metaphorically to mean authority and being held to account for a responsibility. Authority and accountability are likened to a road, because one who holds authority reaches, through it, the execution of accountability upon others. For this reason it is construed with the particle ʿalā (upon), which conveys elevation, and this elevation is metaphorical, meaning the ability to exercise control over what follows ʿalā. So this construction is a metaphorical expression (istiʿārah makniyyah), indicated by what belongs to the likened-to term, namely the particle ʿalā. Within it there is also a serial metaphor (istiʿārah tabiʿiyyah).

The definite article in His words "al-sabil" (the blame) is the definite article of prior reference (ta'rif al-ʿahd), and what is referred to is the blame negated in His words: ﴿There is no blame upon the good-doers﴾ [al-Tawbah: 91], according to the rule that an indefinite noun, when repeated as definite, [refers to the same thing].

Page 6
That is: the blame negated concerning the good-doers is affirmed for those who ask your permission while they are rich. A parallel to this is His words, in Surah al-Shura: ﴿The blame is only upon those who wrong people and transgress in the earth without right; those will have a painful punishment﴾ [al-Shura: 42]. This shows that the intended meaning of al-sabil is punishment.

The meaning is: accountability and blame are only upon those who ask your permission while they are rich, those who wished to stay behind from the expedition of Tabuk while having no excuse that would permit their staying behind. The verse ﴿So Allah has not made for you against them any way﴾ [al-Nisa: 90] in Surah al-Nisa has already preceded, and its interpretation was referred there to what we have mentioned in this verse.

The clause ﴿They are content to be with those who remain behind﴾ is a resumptive clause (mustaʾnafah), answering a question that arises from the cause of their asking permission to stay behind while they are rich; that is, what moved them to this was their contentment to be with the women who remain behind. The discussion of its counterpart has already preceded.

The sealing upon their hearts is attributed to Allah in this verse, unlike in the preceding verse: ﴿And their hearts were sealed﴾ [al-Tawbah: 87]. Perhaps this is to indicate that it is a sealing other than the natural disposition in which they were created; rather it is a sealing upon a sealing, which Allah brought into being in their hearts as a result of His anger against them, depriving them of salvation from the original sealing and increasing them in blindness. For this meaning, the clause "so they do not know" is made consequent upon it, to negate the very root of knowledge from them; that is, they are nearly equal to the dumb beasts.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 9, verse 94:

﴿They will make excuses to you when you return to them. Say, "Make no excuses; we will never believe you. Allah has already informed us of your news. And Allah will see your deeds, and [so will] His Messenger; then you will be returned to the Knower of the unseen and the witnessed, and He will inform you of what you used to do."﴾ This is a fresh, initiating resumption (isti'naf ibtida'i), because this excuse-making is not confined to those who ask your permission to remain behind, for their permission exempts them from disavowing [their conduct] by means of a false oath. The pronoun in (ya'taziruna, "they make excuses") refers to the nearest antecedent (mu'add), which is His saying: ﴿Those who lied to Allah and His Messenger sat [at home]﴾ [al-Tawbah: 90], for they are a group of the hypocrites, and they are the ones who made excuses after the people returned from the expedition of Tabuk.

The predicate is given as a present-tense verb (fi'l mudari') to indicate renewal and repetition.

And "idha" (when) here is used for past time, because the surah was revealed after the return from the expedition of Tabuk.

The return is attributed to the hypocrites because they are the intended subject of the report that occurs upon the return.

The address is to the Muslims, because the hypocrites direct their excuses to the Prophet ﷺ and repeat them before groups of Muslims.

The prohibition in His saying (la ta'taziru, "make no excuses") is used to express despair (ta'yis).

The clause (lan nu'mina lakum, "we will never believe you") is in the position of a causal explanation (ta'lil) for the prohibition against making excuses, since excuse-making is of no benefit. It is said: "amana lahu" when one gives him credence (saddaqahu). His saying, exalted is He, "wa yu'minu lil-mu'minin" ("and he believes the believers"), has already occurred in this surah.

The clause ﴿Allah has already informed us of your news﴾ is an explanation for the negation of their being believed, i.e., Allah has already informed us of your news with what necessitates your being labeled liars. The indefiniteness in the second object of (naba'ana, "informed us") which substitutes for the two objects is relied upon on the basis that the context clarifies it.

And (min, "of") is a noun meaning "some," or it is a qualifier of an omitted element whose estimate is: "Allah has already informed us with certainty of your news."

The clause ﴿And Allah will see your deeds﴾ is coordinated (atf) upon the clause "la ta'taziru" ("make no excuses"), i.e., there is no benefit in your excuses; so if you fear being held to account, then do good for the future, and Allah will see your deeds, and His Messenger [will see them], if you do well. The intent is to open the door of repentance for them and to draw attention to the opportunity to rectify their affair. In this is a threat of warning if they do not repent.

Thus the report that Allah and His Messenger will see their deeds in the future is used as a metaphor (kinayah) for encouraging righteous action and warning against persisting in their present state. The intent is: that they be enabled to correct the outward aspects of their deeds. For this reason it is followed by His saying: ﴿then you will be returned to the Knower of the unseen and the witnessed﴾, i.e., after death you will arrive at Allah. "Radd" here means "returning," as in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿then they are returned to Allah, their true Master﴾ [al-An'am: 62] in the surah of al-An'am.

Radd means restoration (al-irja'). The intended meaning here is the arrival of souls to the world of eternity, over which no control is exercised for anyone other than Allah, even in outward appearance. Since souls are among the creation of Allah, and He has sent them down into the world of worldly perishing, and they have been independent in their deeds throughout the span of life, their arrival after death or at the resurrection under the disposal of Allah becomes similar to returning a thing to its place of settlement or restoring it to its owner.

Al-ghayb is what is hidden from people's knowledge. Ash-shahadah is what is witnessed. The "al-" in "al-ghayb wa al-shahadah" is for totality (istighraq), i.e., every unseen and every witnessed thing.

The shift from saying "to whom you are returned" (i.e., to Allah) to "the Knower..." is for the sake of the explicit mention, which signals that nothing of their deeds escapes Him, adding to the encouragement and warning, so that they know nothing is hidden from Allah.

Al-inba' is informing. "Ma kuntum ta'malun" ("what you used to do") refers to the knowledge of every deed they performed.

And ﴿then He will inform you of what you used to do﴾ is used in its necessary meaning, which is requiting for everything they did, i.e., you will find Him knowing of all that you have done. It is a metonymy (kinayah), because mention of requital in the context of crime and wrongdoing necessarily implies the comprehensive knowledge of the King of the Day of Judgment regarding everything they did.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 9, verse 95:

﴿They will swear to you by Allah when you return to them, that you may turn away from them. So turn away from them. Indeed, they are defilement, and their refuge is Hell, as recompense for what they used to earn.﴾

The sentence is a fresh, independent statement (jumlah mustaanifah ibtida'iyyah), enumerating their conditions. Its meaning arises from the content of the sentence ﴿We will never believe you﴾ [al-Tawbah: 94], as an alert that they do not refrain from lying and deceiving the Muslims. So when they are told ﴿We will never believe you﴾ [al-Tawbah: 94], they swear that they are truthful, to make their deception appear sound.

This is a report of what the hypocrites will meet the Muslims with, before it happens and after the Muslims return from the campaign.

Here (idha) is a adverb of past time.

The object of the oath is omitted because it is evident, and because its counterpart was mentioned earlier in His words: ﴿They will swear by Allah, "If we had been able, we would have gone out with you"﴾ [al-Tawbah: 42], except that what preceded concerned their oath before the departure.

Al-inqilab (انْقِلَاب) means returning, and it was discussed in His words: ﴿Have you turned back on your heels?﴾ [Al 'Imran: 144] in Al 'Imran.

Here the reason for the oath is stated: that it is for the purpose of the Muslims turning away from them, that is, away from their reproach and rebuke. This indicates that they do not intend to console the hearts of the Muslims, but rather wish to escape the sting and pain of reproach. For this reason, in the two other verses He said ﴿They swear by Allah to you, to please you﴾ [al-Tawbah: 62] and ﴿They swear to you, that you may be pleased with them﴾ [al-Tawbah: 96], because that was before going out to the campaign. When the matter had passed and they knew that their oath had not been believed by the Muslims, they began to swear for the purpose that the Muslims would turn away from them.

The particle (an, عَنْ) was attached to the pronoun of the hypocrites by implying an omitted noun (mudaf) that the context indicates, since it is evident that they wish to turn away from being blamed. So the omission of the noun prepares for the consequence of the rebuke that follows in His words: ﴿So turn away from them﴾, that is, if they desire to turn away from you, then you turn away from them completely.

This is a form of rebuke that includes raising hopes in the one being reproached who seeks something, in that his request is granted, until, upon reflection, he finds that what he hoped for has turned into the opposite of what was sought, and so it becomes despair. For they wanted to avoid reproach by refraining from it and continuing to treat them as Muslims; but then they are confronted with turning away from speaking to them and mixing with them, which is worse than what they swore to avoid. This is from affirming a thing by means of something resembling its opposite, or from the saying "by the implication" (al-qawl bil-mujib).

The clause (Indeed, they are defilement) is a justification (ta'lil) for the command to turn away. The placement of (inna) at its beginning indicates the meaning of causation.

Ar-rijs (الرِّجْسُ) means filth. The intended meaning is to liken them to filth in baseness and the defilement of souls. So it is a metaphorical filth, like His words: ﴿Indeed, intoxicants, gambling, idols, and divining arrows are defilement from the work of Satan﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 90].

Al-ma'wa (المَأْوَى) means destination and place of return.

(Jaza'an, جَزاءً) is a circumstantial accusative (hal) from Jahannam, meaning as a recompense for them for what they used to do.

This verse is a substitution of inclusion (badal ishtimal) from the preceding clause ﴿They will swear by Allah to you, when you return to them﴾ [al-Tawbah: 95], because they swear in order that the Muslims turn away from them and not blame them, and this implies their seeking the Muslims' approval.

Allah has made a consequence of this: if the Muslims are pleased with them and turn away from blaming them, then indeed Allah is not pleased with the corrupt people (al-qawm al-fasiqin). This is a warning to the Muslims against being pleased with the hypocrites, by way of kinayah (allusion), since the Muslims already know that what does not please Allah is not something the Muslims should be pleased with.

"Al-qawm al-fasiqun" refers to these hypocrites. The shift away from using the pronoun (hum) to expressing them by their attribute serves to indicate their blameworthiness and to give the reason for not being pleased with them. Thus the speech contains a statement together with its proof, and it conveys the meaning of two statements, because it resolves into: "If you are pleased with them, then indeed Allah is not pleased with them, because Allah is not pleased with the corrupt people (al-qawm al-fasiqin)."

The Bedouins are more intense in disbelief and hypocrisy, and more likely not to know the limits of what Allah has sent down to His Messenger. And Allah is All-Knowing, All-Wise.

This is an initial resumptive sentence (*istinaf ibtida'i*), by which the discourse returns to the conditions of the excuse-makers among the Bedouins and of those among them who lied to Allah and His Messenger. What lies between is a digression (*istitrad*) prompted by the mention of those who lied to Allah and His Messenger together with the Bedouins.
