When the discussion of those people was concluded, it moved on to the remaining conditions of the Bedouins. To draw attention to the connection between the two topics, the predicate-subject was placed first, namely the word *al-a'rab* (the Bedouins), for emphasis on it from this aspect. Behind this is the alerting of the Muslims to the conditions of the Bedouins, because, due to their distance from close contact and association with them, their conditions may remain hidden from the Muslims, who may think well of all of them.

*Ashaddu* and *ajdaru* are superlative forms, and nothing accompanies them that indicates a point of comparison. Thus they may be taken in their apparent sense, so that the point of comparison is the people of the settled areas, i.e., the disbelievers and hypocrites of Madina. This is what all the exegetes have agreed upon.

The increase in their disbelief and hypocrisy is relative to the disbelievers and hypocrites of Madina, and their hypocrites are more intense in hypocrisy than the hypocrites of Madina.

This increase returns to the firm entrenchment of the two attributes in their souls. That is, their disbelief is more firmly rooted in their souls than the disbelief of the disbelievers of Madina, and their hypocrisy is likewise more firmly rooted in their souls, meaning it is more firmly established on the side of disbelief, further from giving it up, and the signs of evil appear more readily among them. This is because harshness of hearts and coarseness of nature increase evil souls in desolation and aversion. Do you not know that Dhu al-Khuwaysira al-Tamimi, who claimed to be Muslim, when he saw the Prophet (ﷺ) give gold to al-Aqra' ibn Habis and those with him from the chieftains of the Arabs, which he had distributed, Dhu al-Khuwaysira said, addressing the Prophet (ﷺ) directly, "Be just!" The Prophet (ﷺ) said to him, "Woe to you! Who will be just if I am not just?"

The Bedouins, due to their upbringing in the desert, were distant from associating with people of sound intellects, their minds were further from knowing realities and fuller of illusions, and due to their distance from witnessing the lights of the Prophet (ﷺ), his character and his manners, and from receiving guidance morning and evening, they are more ignorant of the affairs of religion and of what refines souls. And because they inherit the morals of their ancestors and are distant from the civilized developments that make human souls more noble, and more skilled in placing things in their proper positions, and from a traditional wisdom that develops over time, they are closer in conduct to savagery, more coarse in dealing, and more neglectful of the scientific and moral heritage. For this reason, Uthman said to Abu Dharr when he resolved to settle in al-Rabadha, "Watch over Madina lest you revert to being a Bedouin."

As for the morals that are praised, in which roughness, coarseness and disregard for great matters, such as courage, frankness, refusal of oppression and generosity, are praised, these are stronger in the Bedouins by natural disposition. For this reason, they are closer to good when they believe in it and embrace it.

It is also possible that *ashaddu* and *ajdaru* are stripped of comparison and used to express the strength of the two attributes in those described by them, following the manner of His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿He said: "My Lord, prison is dearer to me than what they invite me to"﴾ [Yusuf: 33]. The meaning then is that their disbelief is very firmly rooted in their souls, and their hypocrisy likewise, without intending that they are more intense in disbelief and hypocrisy than the disbelievers and hypocrites of Madina.

On both interpretations, *kufran* (disbelief) and *nifaqan* (hypocrisy) are in the accusative as specification (*tamyiz*), to clarify the ambiguity in the description *ashaddu*. He took the path of generality and then detail, so that the meaning might be established in the most complete manner.

*Al-ajdaru* means "the most entitled." *Al-jadara* means "priority." They are more deserving of not knowing the Sharia because they are distant from gatherings of admonition and places of revelation, and because of their little association with the people of knowledge among the Companions of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ).

The preposition *ba'* (with), which the verb of entitlement governs, has been omitted, following the manner of omitting a preposition before *an* (that) in its verbal sense.

*Al-hudud* means the measures and the boundaries between things. The meaning is that they do not know the boundaries of rulings and the criteria for distinguishing their ambiguous parts.

In this description the difference between people of knowledge and understanding becomes apparent. This is what the scholars express in technical terminology as verification (*tahqiq*) or wisdom (*hikma*), defined as knowing the realities of things as they are. Thus the addition of the qualifier "as they are" serves to indicate distinction between what is mixed, what is ambiguous, and what is hidden.

The clause "And Allah is All-Knowing, All-Wise" is a concluding appendage (*tadhyil*) to this disclosure of the inner nature and character of the Bedouins. That is: All-Knowing of them and of others, and All-Wise in distinguishing their ranks.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 9, verse 98:

﴿And among the bedouins is one who takes what he spends as a fine (ghurm), and waits for misfortunes to befall you. Upon them is the evil turn of fortune. And Allah is All-Hearing, All-Knowing.﴾

This is a group of the bedouins who display faith and spend in the way of Allah. They do so only out of dissimulation (taqiyyah) and fear of raids, or out of love for praise and conformity to the practice of the community, while they conceal disbelief and await the opportunity that enables them to turn back on their heels. These people, although they are among the hypocrites of the bedouins, are singled out for division here, and this is considered in light of what distinguishes them of the states of hypocrisy; for divisions in rhetorical settings and disputations rely on some difference in the conditions of the one divided, and no regard is given to the inclusion of the division within its counterpart. So His saying: ﴿And among the bedouins is one who takes what he spends as a fine﴾ is, in terms of division, like His saying: ﴿And among the bedouins is one who believes in Allah and the Last Day﴾ [al-Tawbah: 99].

The meaning of (yattakhidh) is "counts" and "considers," because (ittakhadha) is among the sisters of (ja'ala). And (ja'ala) is used in the sense of changing from one state to another, as in "I made the cloth cold" (ja'altu al-shiqqah bardan). It is also used in the sense of counting and reckoning, as in His saying: ﴿And you have indeed made Allah a surety over you﴾ [al-Nahl: 91]. Likewise, (yattakhidh) here.

Al-maghram: that which is paid from wealth under compulsion and oppression. These bedouins give zakat and spend in the way of Allah, and they count that as monetary exactions and calamities which they pay out of dissimulation. Among these are those who refused to give zakat after the death of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ. And one of them from Tayy said, in the time of Abu Bakr, when the collector (al-sa'i) came to them to count the zakat on livestock:

"Say to this man who has come as a collector: 'Come on, for the obligations are the sword (al-mashrafi).'"

That is, the obligations of zakat are the sword: they give the collector a blow of the sword in place of zakat.

Al-tarabbusu: waiting. Al-dawa'ir: plural of dA'ira, which is the change of a state from uprightness to disorder. The discussion of it has preceded at His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿They say, "We fear that a misfortune may befall us"﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 52] in Surat al-'Uqud.

Page 14

The ba' here denotes causation, as in His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿We await for him the vicissitudes of time﴾ [al-Tur: 30]. The object of the preposition ba' has been made the pronoun of the addressees with an elided noun in the reckoning. The estimated meaning is: "And he waits, because of your condition, for the misfortunes upon you," since it is evident that misfortunes do not cause them to await a reversal; rather, their own condition is the cause of their waiting for the state to turn against them, because their present state is harsh upon them.

So the meaning is that they await your weakness and defeat, or they await the death of your Prophet, whereupon they reveal what is latent within them of disbelief. Allah has informed of their condition, which became apparent after the death of the Prophet ﷺ, namely the apostates among the Arabs.

The clause ﴿Upon them is the evil turn of fortune﴾ is an invocation against them and a belittling of them, and for this reason it is separated (from what precedes). Supplication from Allah against His creatures is an decree and determination mixed with humiliation, for nothing overpowers Him, so He has no need to wish for what He wills. The discussion of it has preceded at His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿So the curse of Allah is upon the disbelievers﴾ [al-Baqarah: 89] in Surat al-Baqarah.

The evil turn of fortune did indeed befall the bedouins when the Muslims fought them in the caliphate of Abu Bakr, the year of the apostasy, and defeated them, so they returned disappointed.

The idafa of "dA'ira" to "al-sau'" is an idafa to an inherent attribute, like their saying: "'Isha' al-Akhirah" (the night prayer of the hereafter). For the evil turn of fortune is only in evil. Abu 'Ali al-Farisi said: Had the dA'ira not been attached to al-sau', the meaning of evil would have been known from it, because the dA'ira of time is used only for what is disliked. A parallel is the idafa of "al-sau'" to "di'b" (wolf) in the verse of al-Farazdaq:

"So I was like the wolf of evil when it saw blood, with its companion one day, and turned toward the blood."

For the wolf is wholly devoted to evil, since there is no good in it for people.

Al-sau' with a fatha on the sin is the masdar (verbal noun), and with a damma it is the noun. The majority read it with a fatha on the sin. Ibn Kathir and Abu 'Amr alone read it with a damma on the sin. The meaning is one.

The clause ﴿And Allah is All-Hearing, All-Knowing﴾ is a concluding statement (tadhyil), meaning: He hears what they confer about and what they plot of lying in wait, and He knows what they conceal and intend to hide.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 9, verse 99:

Page 15
﴿And among the Bedouins are those who believe in Allah and the Last Day, and take what they spend as means of nearness to Allah and as [means of obtaining] the prayers of the Messenger. Indeed, it is a means of nearness for them. Allah will admit them into His mercy. Indeed, Allah is Forgiving and Merciful.﴾
These are the believers among the Bedouins, whom Allah has given their due of praise, and they are the opposites of the other two groups mentioned in His saying: ﴿The Bedouins are more severe in disbelief and hypocrisy﴾ [al-Tawbah: 97] and His saying: ﴿And among the Bedouins are those who take what they spend as a penalty﴾ [al-Tawbah: 98]. It is said that they are the Banu Muqarrin of Muzaynah, concerning whom His saying, exalted is He, was revealed: ﴿Nor [is there blame] upon those who came to you that you might provide them with mounts﴾ [al-Tawbah: 92], the verse as previously mentioned. Among these was 'Abd Allah dhu'l-Bijadayn al-Muzani, who is the son of Mughaffal.

The spending here is the same spending mentioned there.

The meaning of "yattakhidh" has been mentioned shortly before.

And (qurubat), with a damma on the qaf and a damma on the ra', is the plural of (qurbah) with a sukun on the ra'. It is used in the sense of the verbal noun, i.e., nearness (al-qurb), which is the intended meaning here: they take what they spend as a means of drawing near to Allah. The plural form "qurubat" is in view of the multiplicity of spending, for each spending is a means of nearness to Allah, because it necessitates an increase in nearness. He, exalted is He, said: ﴿They seek means of access to their Lord, [striving to be] the nearest of them﴾ [al-Isra': 57]. Thus "qurubat" here is a metaphor used for the good pleasure of Allah and the raising of ranks in Paradise, and therefore it is described by "'inda" (with/near), which indicates the place of nearness. "'Inda" is a metaphor for honour and special regard, since Paradise is likened to the abode of honour with Allah. He, exalted is He, said: ﴿Indeed, the righteous will be among gardens and rivers, in a seat of truth near a Sovereign, Omnipotent﴾ [al-Qamar: 54].

"Salawat al-Rasul" means his supplications. The origin of salah is supplication. It is used in the plural here because each spending they present to the Messenger ﷺ brings a supplication from him for them, so with the repetition of spending, the salah is repeated. The Prophet ﷺ used to pray for everyone who brought him his charity and spending, in compliance with what Allah commanded him, saying: ﴿Take from their wealth a charity by which you purify them and cause them to grow, and pray for them﴾ [al-Tawbah: 103].

Page 16
It has come in the hadith of Ibn Abi Awfa that when he brought his charity, the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "O Allah, send blessings upon the family of Abi Awfa."

It is also permissible to conjoin "salawat al-Rasul" to the name of Allah as an object governed by "'inda", meaning: they take the spending as a means of nearness in the presence of the prayers of the Messenger, i.e., they make it a means of nearness existing in the place of closeness to the prayers of the Messenger, likening causation of a thing to drawing near to it; i.e., they make the spending a cause for the Messenger's supplication for them. Thus the adverbial "'inda" is used in two figurative senses. It is also permissible that ﴿wa salawat al-Rasul﴾ be conjoined to ﴿qurubat 'inda Allah﴾, meaning: they take what they spend as the supplications of the Messenger. He describes the spending by taking it as the Messenger's supplications, because they seek through the spending the Messenger's supplications, since he was commanded to do so in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿and pray for them﴾ [al-Tawbah: 103].

The sentence ﴿Indeed, it is a means of nearness for them﴾ is a resumptive sentence, brought in the manner of good tidings to them that what they hoped for will be accepted.

The sentence was opened with the particle of initiation for the sake of attention to it, so that the listener may absorb it, and with the particle of emphasis to confirm its content. The pronoun serving as the subject of "inna" refers to "ma yunfiq" in view of the spendings. The lam is for exclusivity, i.e., it is a means of nearness for them, namely with Allah and with the prayers of the Messenger. That was omitted because the preceding speech indicates it.

The indefiniteness of (qurbah) is because there is no call for definiteness, and because indefiniteness may convey magnification.

The sentence ﴿Allah will admit them into His mercy﴾ stands in the position of explanation for the sentence ﴿indeed, it is a means of nearness for them﴾, because nearness to Allah is the high ranks and His good pleasure, and that is of His mercy. And nearness to the prayers of the Messenger ﷺ is the granting of his supplication. The prayer by which he prays for them is a request for mercy, so the outcome of both matters is Allah's admitting them into His mercy.

The verb of admission has been chosen here because it is suitable to being in Paradise, for it is often said: "he entered Paradise." He, exalted is He, said: ﴿And enter My Paradise﴾ [al-Fajr: 30].

The sentence ﴿Indeed, Allah is Forgiving and Merciful﴾ is a fitting conclusion for what they hoped for and what was granted to them. It is affirmed with the particle of emphasis for attention to this report, i.e., He is Forgiving of their past disbelief, Merciful toward them, bestowing blessings upon them.

Page 17
The majority read (qurbah) with a sukun on the ra', while Warsh alone read it with a damma on the ra', to follow the qaf.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 9, verse 100:

﴿And the foremost, the first of the Emigrants and the Helpers, and those who followed them in excellence—Allah is pleased with them, and they are pleased with Him, and He has prepared for them gardens beneath which rivers flow, abiding therein forever. That is the great triumph.﴾

Having mentioned the groups marked by deficiencies, which differ from one another in that respect, the passage now mentions the righteous model and the perfect example in faith, virtue, and support for the cause of Allah, so that one who seeks righteousness may follow their path. It also ensures that the enumeration of the tribes living in Medina, its surroundings, and its desert areas does not lack mention of the best category, as a way of honouring it.

With this, the survey of the groups and their conditions is complete.

The sentence is a conjunction (ʿatf) upon the sentence ﴿And among the desert Arabs is one who takes what he spends as a loss﴾ [al-Tawba: 98].

The intended meaning of "precedence" (al-sabq) is precedence in faith, because the context of the preceding verses concerns distinguishing the conditions of sincere believers, open disbelievers, and hypocritical disbelievers. It is therefore necessary that the reference be to those who preceded others of their own category. The foremost among the Emigrants are those who believed before the Prophet (ﷺ) migrated to Medina, and the foremost among the Helpers are those who preceded their people in faith; they are the people of the first and second 'Aqaba (pledges).

The exegetes differed in determining the limit at which the description of "the foremost" ends for both the Emigrants and the Helpers together. Abu Musa, Ibn al-Musayyab, Ibn Sirin, and Qatada said: those who prayed towards both qiblas (the Jerusalem and Ka'ba qiblas). ʿAtaʾ said: those who witnessed Badr. al-Shaʿbi said: those who attained the Pledge of al-Ridwan. These three opinions treat the conjunction "wa" in His saying "wa al-Ansar" as a joint marker in the description of precedence, since it is uniform with respect to both groups; but this restricts the reference to the Emigrants. In Ibn al-ʿArabi's *Ahkam al-Qur'an* there is something suggesting that his view is that the foremost are the people of the two 'Aqabas, which restricts the reference to the Helpers. From al-Jubba'i it is reported that the foremost are those who embraced Islam before the Prophet's (ﷺ) migration to Medina; this is perhaps his own preference, since he did not attribute it to any named speaker.

Ibn ʿAtiyya preferred that the foremost are those who emigrated before the migration ceased, i.e., with the conquest of Mecca. This restricts the description of precedence to the Emigrants. It does not accord with the reading of the majority, which uses the genitive case for "al-Ansar."

The particle (min) here is partitive (lil-tab'id), not explanatory (lil-bayan).

Al-Ansar is the plural of nasir, meaning "helper." By this plural form, it became a name that predominantly designated the Aws and the Khazraj who believed in the Prophet (ﷺ), either during his lifetime or after his death, and their descendants until the end of time. The Prophet (ﷺ) addressed them by this description, so it is applied to the sons of the hypocrites among them who grew up in Islam, such as the son of Ibn Sayyad.

The majority of reciters read "wa al-Ansari" in the genitive case as a conjunction upon "al-Muhajirin," so the description "the foremost" is an attribute of both the Emigrants and the Helpers. Ya'qub read "wa al-Ansaru" in the nominative case, which makes it a conjunction upon the predicate "al-sabiqun" (the foremost), and the category divided into foremost and others would then be specifically the Emigrants.

By "those who followed them" is meant the remainder of the Emigrants and the remainder of the Helpers who followed them in faith, i.e., who believed after the foremost: those who believed after the conquest of Mecca, and those among the hypocrites who believed after a period of time.

Ihsan (excellence) is good action (al-'amal al-salih). The "ba'" is for accompaniment (lil-mulabasa). This category is specifically qualified because the foremost first believers were moved to faith by nothing but sincerity, so they are doers of excellence. As for those who followed them, among them were some who believed out of pride in the Muslims when they became the majority of the people of Medina; among them were some whose faith was weak and wavering, like those "whose hearts are to be reconciled" (al-mu'allafa qulubuhum), who might sink into hypocrisy or might rise to complete faith. They are the ones mentioned alongside the hypocrites in His saying: ﴿If the hypocrites do not desist, and those in whose hearts is a disease﴾ [al-Ahzab: 60]. When they reach the rank of excellence, they enter into the promise of Allah's pleasure and the preparation of the gardens.

The clause "Allah is pleased with them" is a predicate concerning "the foremost." Placing the subject before its verbal predicate serves to intensify and emphasize.

Allah's pleasure with them means His care for them, His honouring of them, and His defence of them against their enemies. As for their pleasure with Him, it is a metonymy (kinaya) for the abundance of His beneficence towards them, to the point that their souls are content with what their Lord has given them.

Al-i'dad means preparation. It contains an indication of care and honour.

The meaning of "rivers flowing" has already been discussed.

This verse, according to most reciters, differs from its counterparts in that the word "min" is not mentioned before "tahtaha" in most of the codices and in the transmission of the majority of reciters. Thus it is free of emphasis, since the particle "min" with spatial adverbs has no meaning other than emphasis. The absence of emphasis in the sentence is compensated by what fulfils its purpose: the reinforcement gained by placing the subject before the verbal predicate, and by the verb "a'adda" (prepared), which indicates the perfection of care. Thus what is prepared is only the most perfect of its kind.

The particle "min" is retained in the Meccan codex, and it is the reading of Ibn Kathir al-Makki. In that case the sentence contains two additional emphatic elements.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 9, verse 101:

﴿And among those around you of the Bedouins are hypocrites, and among the people of Madinah are those who have persisted in hypocrisy. You do not know them; We know them. We will punish them twice; then they will be returned to a great punishment.﴾

The Bedouins who were around Madinah had become sincerely devoted to the Prophet ﷺ and obedient to him. They were Juhaynah, Aslam, Ashja', Ghifar, Lihyan, and 'Usayyah. Allah informed His Prophet ﷺ that among these there are hypocrites, so that he would not be deceived by everyone who shows him affection.

The people of Madinah had also become sincerely devoted to the Prophet ﷺ and obedient to him, so Allah informed him that among them there remains a remnant who have persisted in hypocrisy, because it had taken root in them from the time Islam entered among them.

The fronting of the prepositional phrase (al-majrur) serves to draw attention to the fact that it is the predicate (khabar), not a qualifier (na't). The (min) in His saying "wa mimman hawlakum" (and among those around you) is partitive (lil-tab'id), and the (min) in His saying "min al-a'rab" (of the Bedouins) is explanatory (li-bayan) of the relative pronoun (man).

Page 20

The (min) in His saying ﴿wa min ahl al-Madinah﴾ (and among the people of Madinah) is a noun meaning "some of" (bi-ma'na ba'd). "Maradu" (have persisted) is its predicate. Alternatively, the (min) may be taken as partitive, indicating an omitted partitioned noun, its estimated meaning being: "and among the people of Madinah there is a group who have persisted," as in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Among those who are Jews are those who distort words from their places﴾ [al-Nisa': 46] in Surat al-Nisa'.

The meaning of "marada 'ala al-amr" is that he became accustomed to it and trained in it; from it comes "al-shaytan al-marid" (the rebellious devil), meaning one who is adept in devilry (al-shaytanah).

By His saying ﴿You do not know them; We know them﴾ it is indicated that this remaining remnant of the hypocrites is one which Allah has willed to keep knowledge of to Himself, and He did not inform His Messenger ﷺ of them, as He had informed him of many hypocrites before. He informed him of their existence only in general terms, so that the Muslims would not be deceived by them. Thus the intended point is His saying: "You do not know them."

The clause "We know them" is a resumed (mustani'afah) clause. The statement is used in the sense of a threat, like His saying: ﴿And Allah will see your deed, and so will His Messenger﴾ [al-Tawbah: 94]; otherwise the ruling is known to the addressee and does not need to be communicated. It also indicates that there is no benefit for the Messenger ﷺ in knowing them, since Allah's knowledge of them is sufficient. It also serves as a preparation for His subsequent saying: "We will punish them twice."

The clause "We will punish them twice" is an explanatory resumption (isti'naf bayani), answering a question raised by His saying "We know them", namely that someone might ask about the effect of Allah's knowing them. So it is made known that He will punish them for their hypocrisy, and that the Messenger's ignorance of them (peace and blessings be upon him) will not save them from it.

The punishment described as "twice" is a punishment in this world, as indicated by His subsequent saying: ﴿then they will be returned to a great punishment﴾.

The exegetes have been perplexed in determining what is meant by the "twice", and they all took it in its literal numerical sense, and mentioned views that do not satisfy the heart. The apparent view to me is that the number is used merely to intend repetition, which conveys emphasis, like His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Then return the gaze twice﴾ [al-Mulk: 4], meaning: reflect repeatedly. From this is the Arabs' saying: "labbayka wa sa'dayk" (at your service, again and again), where the dual form stands in place of repeating the word. The meaning is: We will punish them with a severe, repeated, multiplied punishment, like His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Its punishment will be doubled twice over﴾ [al-Ahzab: 30]. This repetition varies in its number according to the varying conditions of the hypocrites and the varying times of their punishment.

The great punishment is the punishment of Jahannam in the Hereafter.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 9, verse 102:

Page 21
﴿And others have acknowledged their sins; they had mixed a righteous deed with another that was evil. It may be that Allah will turn to them in forgiveness. Indeed, Allah is Forgiving and Merciful.﴾
The most apparent view is that the clause ﴿And others have acknowledged﴾ is conjoined (ʿatf) to the clause "and among those around you" (wa-mimman ḥawlakum), meaning: and among those around you of the Bedouins are hypocrites, and among the people of Madinah are others who committed sins by staying behind and then acknowledged their sins, through their shortcoming. So his saying "they acknowledged their sins" is concise (ījāz), because it indicates that they committed sins and acknowledged their sins, and that they were not hypocrites, since the expression of sins in the plural form requires that they were evil deeds committed while in a state of faith. Likewise, the expression of committing sins as "mixing a righteous deed with an evil one" (khalṭ al-ʿamal al-ṣāliḥ bi-al-sayyi') indicates the same.

Among these were a group including al-Jadd ibn Qays, Kardam, Aws ibn Thaʿlabah, Wadiʿah ibn Ḥizām, Mirdās, Abu Qays, and Abu Lubabah, along with ten men in total, who acknowledged their sin of staying behind from the expedition of Tabuk, repented to Allah, and tied themselves to the pillars of the Prophet's Mosque for days, until this verse was revealed concerning Allah's acceptance of their repentance.

Al-Iʿtirāf (acknowledgement) is an iftiʿāl form from (ʿa-ra-fa) [to know]. It is for emphasis in knowing, and therefore it came to mean affirming a thing and not denying it. So acknowledging a sin is a metonymy (kināyah) for repentance from it, because affirming a past sin only occurs with regret and resolve not to return to it. Abandonment (al-iqlāʿ), which is one of the pillars of repentance, cannot be imagined regarding it, because it is a past sin; but resolve not to return is required in it.

Their mixing of the righteous deed and the evil one is their mixing of the good aspects of their deeds with the sins of staying behind from the military campaign and of not spending on the army.

His saying ﴿they had mixed a righteous deed with another that was evil﴾ mentions the two mixed things with the conjunction "wa" (and), considering that both are equal in being the object of the act of mixing. It is said: "khalaṭa kadhā bi-kadhā" (he mixed this with that), considering one of the two mixed things as being entangled with the mixing. The two constructions are equivalent in meaning, but the conjunction with "wa" is clearer and better, so it is more eloquent (afṣaḥ).

Page 22
And ("ʿasā," [it may be]) is a verb of hope (fiʿl rajāʾ). It is from the speech of Allah, Exalted is He, addressed to the Prophet ﷺ, so it is a metonymy for the occurrence of the hoped-for matter, and that Allah has indeed turned to them in forgiveness; but mentioning the verb of hope carries the meaning of the speaker's choice regarding whether the thing occurs or does not occur.
The meaning of ﴿that He may turn to them﴾ is that He may accept their repentance. It has already been discussed at His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Then Adam received from his Lord words, and He turned to him [in forgiveness]﴾ [al-Baqarah: 37] in Surat al-Baqarah.

The clause "Indeed, Allah is Forgiving and Merciful" is a concluding statement (tadhyīl) suited to the context.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 9, verse 103:

﴿Take from their wealth a charity by which you purify them and cause them to grow, and invoke blessings upon them. Indeed, your invocations are a comfort for them. And Allah is All-Hearing, All-Knowing.﴾

Since repentance requires making up for what can still be made up of what was missed, and since staying behind from the military campaign involved two matters, namely not taking part in the jihad and not spending wealth on the jihad, this verse gives guidance on the way to make up what can still be made up of what was missed, which is benefiting the Muslims with wealth. The great expenditure on the expedition of Tabuk had used up the wealth set aside for the calamities of the Muslims, so when something of wealth is taken from those who stayed behind, some of the breach that had befallen the wealth of the Muslims is repaired.

This is the reason for mentioning this verse after the one before it. It is narrated that those who acknowledged their sins said to the Prophet (ﷺ): "This is our wealth, because of which we stayed behind from you; take it, give it in charity, purify us and seek forgiveness for us." He said to them: "I have not been commanded to take from your wealth." Then this verse was revealed, and the Prophet (ﷺ) took their charity from them. So the pronoun refers to "others who acknowledged their sins."

The ta' in (tuṭahhiruhum) may be the ta' of address, in view of His saying (khudh, "take"), or it may be the ta' of the feminine third person referring back to the charity.

In either case, the verse indicates that charity purifies and causes to grow.

Page 23
Tazkiyah (purification and growth) means making a thing zakī, that is, abounding in goodness. So His saying (tuṭahhiruhum) points to the stage of takhliyah (clearing away) from bad deeds, and His saying (tuzakkiyhim) points to the stage of taḥliyah (adorning) with virtues and good deeds. Undoubtedly, takhliyah precedes taḥliyah. The meaning is that this charity is an expiation for their sins and a bringer of great reward.

As for "ṣalāh" upon them, it means supplication for them. This was mentioned earlier at His saying: ﴿And the prayers of the Messenger﴾ [al-Tawbah: 99]. After the revelation of this verse, whenever someone came to the Prophet (ﷺ) with his charity, he would say: "O Allah, send blessings upon the family of so-and-so," as occurs in the hadith of 'Abdullah ibn Abi Awfa. In his supplication in this matter, the Prophet (ﷺ) combined the meaning of ṣalāh with its wording, so he would ask Allah, exalted is He, to send blessings upon the one who gives charity. Ṣalāh from Allah is mercy, and from the Prophet it is supplication.

The clause ﴿Indeed, your invocations are a comfort for them﴾ is a reason for the command to invoke blessings upon them, namely that his supplication is a comfort for them, i.e., a cause of tranquility for them, i.e., good. The application of the word sakan (comfort) to this supplication is a loose (mursal) metonymy.

Sakan, with two fatḥahs, is that in which one finds rest, i.e., that to which one is at ease and comforted. It is derived from sukūn in its figurative sense, which is the calm of the soul, i.e., its safety from fear and the like, because fear necessitates much caution and disturbance of judgment, so the soul becomes as if unsettled; for this reason that is called qalaq (anxiety), since qalaq is excessive movement. Allah, exalted is He, said: ﴿And He made the night a sakan﴾ [al-An'am: 96], and said ﴿And Allah has made for you from your houses a sakan﴾ [al-Nahl: 80], and among the names of a wife is sakan. Or it is because his supplication for them increases their souls in righteousness and tranquility toward good deeds, since disobedience is wavering and disturbance, as He, exalted is He, said: ﴿So they are in their doubt wavering﴾ [al-Tawbah: 45], while obedience is assurance and certainty, as He, exalted is He, said: ﴿Verily, in the remembrance of Allah do hearts find rest﴾ [al-Ra'd: 28].

The clause ﴿And Allah is All-Hearing, All-Knowing﴾ is an appropriate concluding appendage (tadhyil) to the command to supplicate for them. What is meant by "All-Hearing" here is the One who responds to supplication. Mentioning it is an indication of the acceptance of the Prophet's (ﷺ) supplication, and so it contains an allusion to honouring his supplication. Mentioning "All-Knowing" is an allusion to the fact that He commanded him to supplicate for them only because in his supplication for them there is great good and righteousness in affairs.

Nafi', Ibn Kathir, Abu 'Amr, Ibn 'Amir, 'Asim in the transmission of Abu Bakr, Abu Ja'far and Ya'qub read ﴿ṣalawātika﴾ in the plural form. Hafs from 'Asim, Hamzah, al-Kisa'i and Khalaf read (ṣalātaka) in the singular form.

Page 24
The two readings are equivalent, because what is intended is the category (jins) of his prayer, upon him be prayer and peace. Whoever reads the plural conveys all the individual instances of the category by direct correspondence (muṭābaqah), because the plural defined by a possessive pronoun is general; and whoever reads the singular, the individual instances of the category are understood by implication (iltizām).

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 9, verse 104:

﴿Did they not know that it is Allah who accepts repentance from His servants and takes the charities, and that Allah is the Accepting of repentance, the Most Merciful?﴾

If those who confessed their sins and offered their wealth for charity still had within themselves agitation out of fear that their repentance might not be accepted, and that the Messenger (ﷺ) might not have been pleased with them, and if His saying ﴿Indeed, your prayer is a comfort for them﴾ [al-Tawbah: 103] was pointing to that, then what indicates it is the conjunction of the acceptance of repentance with the acceptance of charities here, to correspond with His saying ﴿who confessed their sins﴾ [al-Tawbah: 102] and His saying ﴿Take from their wealth a charity﴾ [al-Tawbah: 103], the sentence ﴿Did they not know that it is Allah who accepts repentance﴾ is a explanatory resumptive clause (isti'naf bayani) arising from the causal statement ﴿Indeed, your prayer is a comfort for them﴾ [al-Tawbah: 103]. This is because it raises the question of one who asks about the cause of the agitation of their souls after they had repented. The interrogation then becomes an affirmation (taqrir) mixed with wonder at their hesitation in accepting their repentance.

Its purpose is to remind them of a matter that is known, because they had fallen into a state of forgetting it. The pronoun in (yaʿlamū) refers to those who ﴿confessed their sins﴾ [al-Tawbah: 102].

And if those who confessed their sins had not entertained any doubt about the acceptance of their repentance, and His saying ﴿Indeed, your prayer is a comfort for them﴾ [al-Tawbah: 103] was merely a guidance from Allah to His Messenger regarding the wisdom of his supplication for them, namely that his supplication purifies their souls and strengthens their faith, then the speech concerning them was complete at His saying "and Allah is All-Hearing, All-Knowing." The sentence (Did they not know) would then be a new, independent resumption (isti'naf ibtida'i) by way of digression (istitrad), to encourage those like them who had lagged behind in repenting. The pronoun in (Did they not know) would refer to what is known from the context of the revelation, namely the discussion of the condition of the community, and the interrogation would be a denunciatory one (istifham inkari).

All of them were treated as those who do not know the acceptance of repentance, because their state is the state of one who does not know it, whether one knows its acceptance or does not know it in reality. The speech was also directed toward urging (tahdid) them.

And His saying ﴿and that Allah is the Accepting of repentance, the Most Merciful﴾ is conjoined (atf) to ﴿that Allah is the one who accepts repentance﴾, as an alert that just as it is necessary to know that Allah does this, it is necessary to know that among His exalted attributes is that He is the Accepting of repentance (al-Tawwab), i.e., the One characterized by frequently accepting the repentance of those who repent, the Most Merciful to His servants. There is no doubt that accepting repentance is part of mercy, so the pairing of (al-Tawwab) with (al-Rahim) is most appropriate.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 9, verse 105:

﴿And say: Work, for Allah will see your work, and so will His Messenger and the believers. And you will be returned to the Knower of the unseen and the witnessed, and He will inform you of what you used to do.﴾

This is a conjunction (ʿaṭf) upon the clause ﴿Do they not know that Allah is He who accepts repentance﴾ [al-Tawbah: 104], which in effect carries the meaning of informing them that Allah accepts repentance, and say to them: Work, i.e., after the acceptance of repentance. For repentance only lifts the accountability for what has passed. Therefore it becomes incumbent upon the believer who desires perfection, after his repentance, to increase in righteous deeds so as to make up for what he missed of the times which were truly meant to be filled with good deeds, by populating them with good deeds, whereas he had populated them with evil deeds. When repentance reaches them, the evil deeds are erased and that period becomes empty of righteous deeds. Therefore they were commanded to work immediately following the announcement of the acceptance of their repentance, because once their repentance has been accepted, it is incumbent upon them to demonstrate the sincerity of their repentance and their intense eagerness to rise to the levels of perfection, until they join those who preceded them. This is the intended meaning. For this reason the object of (work) ('mal) was omitted, relying on the context, and because a command from Allah does not come with a deed that is not righteous. The meaning of "deed" ('amal) includes inward deeds of belief and intention. The application of the term "deed" to what includes these is by way of generalization (taghlib).

The branching of ﹛so Allah will see your work﹜ is an added exhortation. It also contains a warning against negligence or against committing sins, because the fact that their deed is in the sight of Allah is something that moves one to make it pleasing to Allah, exalted is He.

This is a reminder to them of Allah's awareness, by His knowledge, of all existing things. This is like the saying of the Prophet ﷺ in explaining ihsan (excellence): "That you worship Allah as if you see Him, and if you do not see Him, then He sees you."

The conjunction of (and His Messenger) upon the Name of Majesty (Allah) is because he, upon whom be prayers and peace, is the one who conveys from Allah, and he is the one who deals with them according to their deeds.

The conjunction of (and the believers) as well is because they are the witnesses of Allah on His earth, and because these, when they repented, returned to the assembly of the community of the Companions; so if they do deeds like theirs, they will be in a place of honour among them, otherwise they will be regarded by them with the eye of anger and disapproval. This is something every person fears, from a people who look at him sidelong and see him as having come with something objectionable.

The seeing attributed to Allah, exalted is He, is a metaphorical seeing. It is the attachment of knowledge to occurrences, whether they are things perceived by sight or events heard or meanings grasped. Likewise, the seeing attributed to the Messenger ﷺ and the believers has the sense of what is requited by the word (your deed).

The clause ﴿And you will be returned to the Knower of the unseen and the witnessed﴾ is part of what is said. It is both a promise and a threat, according to the deeds. For this reason it came with (what you used to do), and its like has been discussed earlier.

**[Page 26]** This is another group, whose matter is joined to the matter of the other groups. It refers to those who remained of the ones who stayed behind and whom Allah had not yet turned to in forgiveness, and whose affair was left pending until Allah decides as He wills. They were three men: Ka'b ibn Malik, Hilal ibn Umayya, and Murara ibn al-Rabi'. All three had stayed behind from the expedition to Tabuk. Their staying behind was not hypocrisy, nor aversion to jihad, but they were occupied when the army set out, thinking that they would catch up with it. The days passed and they despaired of catching up. The Prophet ﷺ asked about them while he was at Tabuk. When the Prophet ﷺ returned, they came to him and told him the truth. He did not speak to them, and he forbade the Muslims from speaking to them or associating with them, and he commanded them to keep away from their wives. They complied and remained in this state for fifty nights. During that period they were deferred for the command of Allah. During that period this verse was revealed: ﴿Then He turned to them so that they might repent﴾ [9:118]. Also revealed concerning them was His saying: ﴿Certainly Allah has turned in forgiveness to the Prophet and the Emigrants and the Helpers﴾ [9:117], down to His saying ﴿and be with the truthful﴾ [9:119].

Concerning Ka'b ibn Malik's account of this matter, there is a long and clear report in Sahih al-Bukhari.

**[Page 27]** ...upon repentance and as an alert to the opening of its door. The exegetes have permitted the pronoun in (Did they not know) to refer to the two groups we have pointed out.

As for His saying: ﴿He it is who accepts repentance﴾ [9:104], (He) is a separating pronoun (damir al-fasl), serving to emphasize the predicate. And (from His servants) is connected to (accepts), because it includes the meaning of (pardons/overlooks), indicating that accepting repentance is overlooking the sins from which one repents.

So it is as if it were said: He accepts repentance and overlooks from His servants. The original construction of the verb (accepts) would have been with the particle (min, from). Al-Fakhr (al-Razi) reported from Qadi 'Abd al-Jabbar that he said: "Perhaps (ʿan) is more eloquent, because it indicates acceptance together with facilitating the path to the repentance that was accepted." He did not explain the reason for this, and I think he means what we have pointed out regarding the implication of overlooking.

The news is given in a general form, because the intent is to generalize the address. Thus (His servants) refers to all people, believers and disbelievers alike, since repentance from disbelief is faith.

The verse is evidence that repentance is accepted with certainty if it is a sound repentance, because Allah has informed of this in more than one verse. This is agreed upon regarding the repentance of the disbeliever from his disbelief, since the evidences reached the level of mass transmission (tawatur) through word and practice. It is disputed regarding the repentance of the believer from sins, since its evidences are no more than indications of apparent meaning. The scholarly jurists, hadith scholars and theologians (al-muhaqqiqun) said: it is accepted with certainty. It is reported from the Ash'ari school, and it is the position of the Mu'tazilah (the rationalist school), chosen by Ibn 'Atiyya and his father, and it is the truth. Imam (al-Haramayn al-Juwayni) claimed consensus (ijma') on it in "al-Ma'alim," and this is more deserving of acceptance. Al-Baqillani, Imam al-Haramayn and al-Mazari said: acceptance is affirmed with certainty only for an unspecified group of people. They meant that the evidences for the acceptance of repentance in general are abundant, mass-transmitted, and have reached the level of certainty, but acceptance of the repentance of a specific individual is not affirmed with certainty. It seems that the disagreement of these scholars goes back to not being certain that the specific repentant person repented a sincere repentance. This requires consideration, because the disagreement concerns a repentance that has fulfilled its pillars and conditions. This was previously discussed at His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Repentance with Allah is only for those who do evil in ignorance﴾ [4:17], in Surat al-Nisa'.

The verb (take) in His saying: ﴿and takes the charities﴾ [9:104] is used in the sense of acceptance, since it is evident that Allah does not take charity in a literal sense. It is therefore a metaphor for accepting it and rewarding it.

**[Page 28]** Nafi', Hamzah, al-Kisa'i, Hafs from 'Asim, Abu Ja'far and Khalaf read (murjawna) with the waw unvocalized and without a hamza, as a passive participle from (arjahu), with alif, which is the lightened form of (arja'ahu) with hamza, meaning to postpone. In its lightened present tense one says (arjaytuhu) with ya', as in His saying: ﴿You may postpone whom you will of them﴾ [33:51] with ya'. So the original form of (murjawna) is (murjayuna). The rest of the readers read (murji'una) with a hamza after the jim, according to the original form of the verb, just as (turji'u man tasha'u) is read. The lam in His saying (for the command of Allah) is for causation, meaning: they are postponed for the sake of the command of Allah concerning their affair. There is an omitted noun in construction here, its estimated meaning being: for the sake of awaiting the command of Allah concerning their affair, because postponement implies waiting for something.

The clause ﴿either He will punish them or He will turn to them in forgiveness﴾ explains the clause (others who are deferred) with regard to the complement of its predicate, which is (for the command of Allah); that is, the command of Allah, which is either their punishment or His forgiveness toward them. From His saying (He will turn to them) it is understood that they repented.

Punishment implies that their repentance would not be accepted at that time, because punishment does not occur except for a grave sin. Their sin was staying behind from the general call to march, as was previously discussed at His saying, exalted is He: ﴿O you who have believed, what is [the matter] with you that when you are told to go forth in the cause of Allah, you adhere heavily to the earth?﴾ [9:38]. And the acceptance of repentance for what has passed is a bounty from Allah.

(Immā) is a particle indicating one of two things or several things. Its meaning is close to that of (aw), which is used for choice, except that (immā) enters upon both nouns between which one is given a choice, and it requires being followed by (wa). (Aw) enters only upon the second of the two nouns. The equality between the two matters is more apparent with (immā) than with (aw), because (aw) implies that the noun it coordinates is intended first. This matter was discussed at His saying, exalted is He: ﴿They said, "O Moses, either you throw or we will be the ones who throw"﴾ [7:115], in Surat al-A'raf.

(yu'adhdhibuhum) and (yatubu 'alayhim) are two verbs with the sense of a verbal noun, from which the particle (an, that) has been omitted, so they are in the nominative case, like the nominative in the proverb "You hear of al-Mu'aydi as good, rather than that you see him." This is because the position of what follows (immā) is for a noun, as in His saying: ﴿either the punishment or the Hour﴾ [19:75] and ﴿either you punish or you take among them a good course﴾ [18:86].

The clause ﴿and Allah is Knowing and Wise﴾ is a concluding phrase fitting the ambiguity of their affair for people, meaning: and Allah is Knowing of what befits them of the two matters, Wise, with a determination (muhkam) of His decree at the time His will is connected to it.

[Page 29]

﴿Those who took a mosque for harm and disbelief, and to cause division among the believers, and as a station for whoever had warred against Allah and His Messenger before. They will surely swear, "We intended nothing but good," but Allah bears witness that they are indeed liars.﴾ ﴿Do not ever stand in it. A mosque founded on piety from the first day is more deserving that you stand in it. In it are men who love to purify themselves, and Allah loves those who purify themselves.﴾

This is speech about another group of those who are called to account for deeds they committed, for which Allah became angry with them. They were a group of hypocrites who built a mosque near Quba' for a wicked purpose: to divert their brethren away from the mosque of the believers and to be alone with them in a mosque of their own. The sentence is therefore a fresh, initial sentence (*istinaf ibtida'i*, a resumptive sentence beginning a new topic) according to the reading of those who recited it without the initial conjunctive *waw*, which is the reading of Nafi', Ibn 'Amir and Abu Ja'far. The point of the resumption here is to draw attention to the difference between the situation of those intended by this sentence and the situation of those intended by the sentence before it, namely those whose matter is deferred by Allah. The rest of the readers recited it with the conjunctive *waw* at its beginning, so it is coordinated with the sentence before it, because it is similar to it in mentioning another group like the one mentioned previously.

On both readings, the speech is a sentence following a sentence, and what comes after the *waw* is not the coordination of a single word.

As for His saying "*alladhina*" (those who): it is the subject (*mubtada'*), and its predicate is the sentence "﴿Do not ever stand in it﴾", as al-Kisa'i said. The linking element (*rabit*) is the prepositional pronoun in "﴿do not stand in it﴾", because that pronoun refers back to the mosque, which is the object of the relative clause. It is therefore a causal link to the subject, since the implied meaning is: "Do not stand in a mosque they took as harm," or "in their mosque," as al-Kisa'i estimated. As for those who parsed "﴿Is one who founded his building﴾" [al-Tawba: 109] as a predicate, they have strayed far from the meaning.

The verse points to the story of the hypocrites taking a mosque near the mosque of Quba' with the intention of harm. They were a faction of the Banu Ghanm ibn 'Awf and the Banu Salim ibn 'Awf from the people of al-'Awali. They were twelve men, whom Ibn 'Atiyyah named. The reason for their building it was that Abu 'Amir, whose name was 'Abd 'Amr and who was called al-Rahib (the monk) of the Banu Ghanm ibn 'Awf, had converted to Christianity in the pre-Islamic period. When Islam came, he was among the hypocrites. Then he openly declared hostility, went out with a group of the hypocrites, and organized the confederates who besieged Medina in the Battle of the Trench. When Allah defeated them, Abu 'Amir stayed in Mecca. When Mecca was conquered, he fled to al-Ta'if. When al-Ta'if was conquered and Thaqif embraced Islam, Abu 'Amir went out to al-Sham seeking help from Caesar. He wrote to the hypocrites of his people, ordering them to build a mosque so that they might be sincere in it among themselves, and promising them that he would come with an army of the Romans and expel the Muslims from Medina. Twelve men from the hypocrites were appointed for this: some of them from the Banu 'Amr ibn 'Awf and some from their allies, the Banu Dubay'a ibn Zayd and others. They built it beside the mosque of Quba', shortly before the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) set out for Tabuk. They came to the Prophet (ﷺ) and said, "We have built a mosque for the sick, the needy, and the rainy night, and we would love for you to pray in it for us." The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said to them, "I am on the verge of a journey and a state of preoccupation, and when we return, if Allah wills, we will pray in it." When he returned from the Battle of Tabuk, they asked him to come to their mosque, and Allah revealed this verse. They swore that they had intended nothing by it but good.

*Al-dirar* (harm) is a verbal noun of (*darra*, to harm) in the intensive form, from *darra*: harm to the people of Islam. "Division among the believers" is what they intended by diverting the Banu Ghanm and the Banu Salim away from Quba'.

*Al-irsad* means preparation. "Those who had warred against Allah and His Messenger" refers to Abu 'Amir al-Rahib, because he waged war against the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) together with the confederates, and fought him together with Thaqif and Hawazin. His saying "*min qabl*" (before) refers to that, meaning before the building of the mosque.

The clause "﴿They will surely swear, 'We intended nothing but good'﴾" is parenthetical (*mu'tarida*), or is in the position of a circumstantial clause (*hal*). *Al-husna* means good.

The clause "﴿Allah bears witness that they are indeed liars﴾" is parenthetical.

The clause "﴿Do not ever stand in it﴾" is the predicate of the relative noun, as we have already mentioned. The meaning of "standing" is prayer, because the beginning of prayer is standing.

The reason for the prohibition on praying in it is that the Prophet's (ﷺ) prayer in it would have given it blessing and sanctity, so the Muslims would have seen no merit for the mosque of Quba' over it. The Banu Ghanm and the Banu Salim would then have restricted their prayer to it because of its proximity to their homes, and by this the hypocrites' aim in establishing it, which was to divide the community of the Muslims, would have been achieved. Since the Prophet's (ﷺ) prayer in it would have led to promoting their corrupt aim, it became a means to a corruption, and so the prohibition was directed at it. This is something only Allah the Exalted can know. This prohibition applies to all Muslims, because when the Prophet (ﷺ) was forbidden to pray in it, he knew that Allah had removed from it the quality of being a mosque, so prayer in it became invalid, since a prohibition implies the invalidity of what is prohibited. For this reason, "the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) ordered 'Ammar ibn Yasir, Wahshi the freedman of Mut'im ibn 'Adi, Malik ibn al-Dukhshum, and Ma'n ibn 'Adi, and said: 'Go to this mosque whose people are wrongdoers, demolish it and burn it.' So they did." Burning it meant burning the timber from which its roof was made and the trunks that had been used as its pillars.

His saying "﴿A mosque founded on piety from the first day is more deserving that you stand in it﴾" is a precautionary qualification (*ihtiras*) against what the prohibition on praying in it entails, namely the loss of an act of worship at the time to which they had invited him to pray in it. So Allah commanded him to pray at that time, when they had invited him to pray in the mosque of harm, in his own mosque or in the mosque of Quba', lest his refusal to pray be one of the portions of Satan, namely that his refusal should turn him away from prayer at a time to which he had been invited to pray. This is a great moral discipline of the soul.

In it there is also the averting of the hypocrites' scheme, which was to slander the Messenger (ﷺ) by saying that he had been invited to pray in their mosque and refused. So His saying "*ahaqqu*" (more deserving), although it is an elative form, has lost the sense of comparison, because the prohibition on his praying in the mosque of harm removed its being truly fitting for his prayer in it at all.

Perhaps the point of using the elative form is sarcasm toward the hypocrites, by means of what they outwardly did in inviting the Prophet (ﷺ) to pray in it: that although it was truly fitting for his prayer, a mosque founded on piety is more deserving than it. Thus it is known from its description as "﴿founded on piety﴾" that this one was founded on its opposite.

It is established in Sahih Muslim and elsewhere, from Abu Sa'id al-Khudri, that "the Prophet (ﷺ) was asked about what was meant by the mosque founded on piety in this verse, and he said: 'It is this mosque of yours.'" He meant the Prophet's Mosque in Medina. It is also established in the Sahih that "the Prophet (ﷺ) described the men who love to purify themselves as the Banu 'Amr ibn 'Awf, the people of the mosque of Quba'." This requires that the mosque founded on piety from the first day be their mosque, according to His saying "﴿In it are men﴾."

In my view, the way to reconcile these two is that His saying, exalted is He, "﴿a mosque founded on piety from the first day﴾" means the kind of mosque that has this description, not one specific mosque. This description is then universal, and it is restricted to two instances: the Prophet's Mosque and the mosque of Quba'. Whichever of them the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) prayed in at the time to which they had invited him to pray in the mosque of harm, that would be more deserving and more fitting. Thus he is saved from Satan's portion in refusing to pray in their mosque, and from their slanders as well, and the two authentic hadiths are reconciled. The Messenger's standing in the Prophet's Mosque was his constant practice.

Among the noble implications of this verse is the evidence it provides for the correctness of the opinion of the Companions of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), since they made the year of the Hijra the starting point of the Islamic calendar. This is what al-Suhayli derived in al-Rawd al-Unuf, in the section on the founding of the mosque of Quba', when he said: "In His saying, glorified is He, '﴿from the first day﴾' (although it is known that it is not the first of all days, nor did He attach it to anything explicit in the apparent wording), there is from jurisprudence the validity of what the Companions, may Allah be pleased with them, agreed upon with 'Umar when he consulted them about the calendar. Their opinion agreed that the calendar should begin from the year of the Hijra, because it was the time when Islam became strong and the Prophet (ﷺ) became secure, so this matched the apparent meaning of the revelation."

The clause "﴿In it are men who love to purify themselves﴾" is a praise of the believing Ansar who pray in the Mosque of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and in the mosque of Quba'. The pronoun came in the singular in consideration of the word "*masjid*," which is a collective noun, like the singular in His saying, exalted is He, "﴿and you believe in the Book entirely﴾" [Al 'Imran: 119].

It also contains an implicit contrast that the people of the mosque of harm are not like that. The believers among the Ansar used to combine cleaning with stones and washing with water, as indicated by a hadith transmitted by al-Daraqutni from Abu Ayyub, Jabir ibn 'Abd Allah, and Anas ibn Malik, from the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) concerning this verse, "﴿In it are men who love to purify themselves﴾." He said: "O assembly of the Ansar, Allah has praised you well for purification. What is your purification?" They said: "When one of us leaves the privy, he loves to cleanse himself with water." He said: "That is it, so hold to it." This applies to all the Ansar. It is not contradicted by the hadith in Abu Dawud that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) asked the people of Quba' about their purification, because the people of Quba' are also from the Ansar, so his asking them was to verify that this practice of purification was widespread among the tribes of the Ansar.

The word "love" in His saying "*yuhibbuna*" (they love) is used as a metonymy (*kinaya*) for doing the beloved thing, because whoever loves something that is possible will certainly do it. The purpose is to honor them, showing that they purify themselves seeking nearness to Allah through purity and pleasing their souls' love of it, to the extent that purity became a disposition for them. Even if it had not been obligatory upon them, they would have done it of their own accord.

The clause "﴿and Allah loves those who purify themselves﴾" is a concluding clause (*tadhyil*). In it there is an indication that their souls agreed with a disposition that Allah the Exalted loves. That is sufficient as a tribute to the purity of their souls.

This is what al-Suhayli derived in al-Rawd al-Unuf, in the section on the founding of the mosque of Quba', when he said: "In His saying, glorified is He, '﴿from the first day﴾' (although it is known that it is not the first of all days, nor did He attach it to anything explicit in the apparent wording), there is from jurisprudence the validity of what the Companions, may Allah be pleased with them, agreed upon with 'Umar when he consulted them about the calendar. Their opinion agreed that the calendar should begin from the year of the Hijra, because it was the time when Islam became strong and the Prophet (ﷺ) became secure, so this matched the apparent meaning of the revelation."

The clause "﴿In it are men who love to purify themselves﴾" is a praise of the believing Ansar who pray in the Mosque of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and in the mosque of Quba'. The pronoun came in the singular in consideration of the word "*masjid*," which is a collective noun, like the singular in His saying, exalted is He, "﴿and you believe in the Book entirely﴾" [Al 'Imran: 119].

It also contains an implicit contrast that the people of the mosque of harm are not like that. The believers among the Ansar used to combine cleaning with stones and washing with water, as indicated by a hadith transmitted by al-Daraqutni from Abu Ayyub, Jabir ibn 'Abd Allah, and Anas ibn Malik, from the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) concerning this verse, "﴿In it are men who love to purify themselves﴾." He said: "O assembly of the Ansar, Allah has praised you well for purification. What is your purification?" They said: "When one of us leaves the privy, he loves to cleanse himself with water." He said: "That is it, so hold to it." This applies to all the Ansar. It is not contradicted by the hadith in Abu Dawud that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) asked the people of Quba' about their purification, because the people of Quba' are also from the Ansar, so his asking them was to verify that this practice of purification was widespread among the tribes of the Ansar.

The word "love" in His saying "*yuhibbuna*" (they love) is used as a metonymy (*kinaya*) for doing the beloved thing, because whoever loves something that is possible will certainly do it. The purpose is to honor them, showing that they purify themselves seeking nearness to Allah through purity and pleasing their souls' love of it, to the extent that purity became a disposition for them. Even if it had not been obligatory upon them, they would have done it of their own accord.

The clause "﴿and Allah loves those who purify themselves﴾" is a concluding clause (*tadhyil*). In it there is an indication that their souls agreed with a disposition that Allah the Exalted loves. That is sufficient as a tribute to the purity of their souls.

**Translation of Ibn 'Ashur's commentary on Surah al-Tawbah 9:109**

﴿Is one who founded his building upon God-consciousness (taqwa) and His pleasure better, or one who founded his building upon the brink of a crumbling precipice, so that it collapsed with him into the Fire of Hell? And God does not guide the wrongdoing people.﴾

This is a consequence of His words: ﴿A mosque founded upon God-consciousness from the first day is more deserving that you stand therein⁠﴾ [al-Tawbah 9:108], to further clarify the greater claim of the mosque founded upon God-consciousness to have prayer offered in it.

The point is that the preference given to that mosque, in that it is deserving of prayer being offered in it, is a preference from which participation is removed, because the Mosque of Harm is not deserving of prayer being offered in it after the prohibition. This is because the prayer of the Prophet (ﷺ), had it been performed there, would have given the purpose of its founders currency among the Community, and their aim was to divide the groups of Muslims, as has already been mentioned.

[Page 34]

The fa' (ف) is placed after the interrogative hamza (ء) because the interrogative particle has precedence in opening the sentence.

The interrogation here is rhetorical (taqriri), meaning it asserts an obvious answer.

Ta'sis (تأسيس) means laying the foundation, which is the base of a wall built of stone and clay or plaster.

Al-buniyan (البنيان) is originally a verbal noun of the pattern of al-ghufran and al-kufran, denoting the act of erecting and setting up a house, whether the house is made of cloth, of leather, or of stone and clay; all of this is called binā' (building). Al-buniyan is also used specifically for what is built of stone and clay. Here it is used in the sense of the thing built (al-maf'ul), that is, the structure.

The referent of "man" (مَن) is the owner of the building and the one who deserves it, so the attribution of al-buniyan to the pronoun of "man" is an attribution in the sense of the lam of possession.

The aim for which the building was erected is likened to the foundation of a building, so the verb ussisa (أُسِّسَ) is used figuratively for it in both places.

Since it is a requirement of a foundation that firm ground be sought for its durability, taqwa was placed as the aim for which one of the two mosques was built. Taqwa is thus likened to that upon which the foundation rests, by way of implicit metaphor (al-makniyya, a metaphor in which only a related attribute of the comparison is mentioned). The omitted comparandum is indicated by one of its necessary attributes, which is the preposition of elevation ('alā, "upon"). It is understood that this comparandum is something firm and stable, by way of contrast in the comparison of opposites with what was founded upon the brink of a crumbling precipice. Thus the corrupt purpose is likened to a building set on the edge of a collapsing ravine, in that what is erected on it is not stable, let alone a building, by way of explicit metaphor (al-tasrihiyya). The preposition of elevation is a supporting element (tarshih) of the metaphor.

On the basis of this last metaphor, there follows a depiction of its state of destruction in this world and its leading its builders to Hell in the Hereafter, through the collapse of the building founded on the brink of a crumbling ravine, carrying its occupant into a pit. Collapsing with it into the Fire of Hell is made to be a leading to the ultimate end of the comparison. The likened image is thus composed of the sensible and the intellectual, and likewise the image of the comparison. What is meant is that the first building achieved the purpose of its builder, because the aim of a builder is the permanence of what he has built. Since they built it for the purpose of God-consciousness and God's pleasure, and no mention is made of anything that would entail their failure in it, as is mentioned in its counterpart, it is known that they had indeed been God-conscious by it and had earned His pleasure, and so they succeeded in attaining Paradise, as the contrast indicates. And the second building did not achieve the purpose of its builder, which was harm and division, so they failed in what they intended. The purpose did not endure, and its failure to endure led them to the Fire, just as a collapsed building leads its occupant to destruction.

Al-shafā (الشفا), with a fatha on the shin and as a shortened form, is the edge of a well or the edge of a pit.

Al-jurf (الجرف), with two dammas, is the side of a valley or the side of a chasm.

Hārin (هارٍ) is a derived form from (هار البناء) meaning that the building cracked and split. It is said its original form was (هَوَر) with two fathas, as they say khalafa for khālafa. The alif after the hā' is not the alif of the active participle pattern (fā'il), but rather the middle radical of the word, changed from a wāw because the wāw is vocalized and the letter before it is open, so it was changed into an alif. It is also said that it is an active participle from (هار البناء), whose original pattern is hāwar, and a transposition occurred between its middle and final radicals for lightness. This occurs in many words of the language, such as their saying shākī al-silāh (armed with weapons), whose original form is shā'ik, and rajul ṣāt (a loud-voiced man), whose original form is ṣā'it. This is supported by their saying inhāra (it collapsed) and not inharā. Hari (هَرٍ) is an intensive form of hārin.

Nāfi' and Ibn 'Āmir alone read the verb ussisa (أُسِّسَ) in both places in the passive voice, with the noun buniyānahu in the nominative in both places. The rest of the readers (qurrā', the authorities on recitation) read it in the active voice, with buniyānahu in the accusative in both places.

The majority of readers read "jurufin" (جُرُفٍ) with a damma on the rā'. Ibn 'Āmir, Hamza, Abu Bakr from 'Āṣim, and Khalaf read it with a sukūn on the rā'.

The sentence ﴿And God does not guide the wrongdoing people﴾ is a concluding statement (tadhyil), which is general in scope, encompassing these wrongdoers who built the Mosque of Harm and others besides them.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 9, verse 110:

﴿Their building which they have built will never cease to be a cause of doubt in their hearts, unless their hearts are cut into pieces. And Allah is All-Knowing, All-Wise.﴾

The clause ﴿Their building will never cease﴾ may be a fresh (resumed) clause enumerating the evils of the Mosque of Harm, by mentioning the bad consequences of it, after having mentioned the bad motive behind it and after having mentioned its bad effect on Islam,

page 36

namely that Allah forbade His Messenger from praying in it and commanded him to demolish it. For when He forbade him to pray in it, all the Muslims became forbidden from praying in it, so it was stripped of the ruling of mosques. For this reason the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) commanded its demolition. This interpretation is preferred because the pronoun referring to the mosque or the building was not used; rather, its apparent noun was mentioned.

It may also be a second predicate (khabar) of ﴿those who took a mosque for harm﴾ [al-Tawbah: 107], as if it were said: "Do not stand in it, and it will not cease to be a cause of doubt in their hearts." In that case, the explicit mention of the word "their building" serves to clarify it further. The linking element (rabit) is the pronoun in "their hearts."

The meaning is that, since they built that mosque for a corrupt purpose, Allah made it a cause for the persistence of hypocrisy in their hearts for as long as their hearts remain in their bodies.

Making the building a "doubt" is an intensification, like describing something by the verbal noun. The meaning is that it is a cause of doubt in their hearts. Doubt (rayba) is uncertainty, for hypocrisy is doubt about the religion, since its adherents waver between allegiance to the Muslims and sincerity toward the disbelievers.

His saying ﴿unless their hearts are cut into pieces﴾ is an ironic exception (istithna' tahakkumi). It belongs to the type of emphasizing a thing by means of something resembling its opposite, like His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And they will not enter Paradise until the camel passes through the eye of the needle﴾ [al-A'raf: 40]. That is, it will remain a doubt forever, unless their hearts are cut off from them, and they will never be cut off.

The clause ﴿And Allah is All-Knowing, All-Wise﴾ is a concluding phrase (tadhyil) suited to this wondrous making and precise, elegant arrangement, namely that this building becomes a cause of anguish and regret for them in this world and the Hereafter.

Al-Jumhur read tuqatta'a with a dammah on the ta'. Ibn 'Amir, Hamzah, Hafs on the authority of 'Asim, Abu Ja'far and Ya'qub read "taqatta'a" with a fatha on the ta', on the basis that its original form was (tatqatta'a). Ya'qub also read "ila an taqatta'a" with the preposition "ila," which denotes the endpoint (intiha').

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 9, verse 111:

[p. 37]
﴿Indeed, Allah has purchased from the believers their lives and their properties in exchange for that they will have Paradise. They fight in the way of Allah, so they kill and are killed. That is a promise binding upon Him in the Torah, the Gospel, and the Qur'an. And who fulfills his covenant more than Allah? So rejoice in the transaction you have made. That is the great triumph.﴾

This is an initial resumptive sentence (isti'naf ibtida'i) to honour the people of the expedition of Tabuk, who were the army of hardship (jaysh al-'usrah), as a preparation and introduction to the mention of the repentance of those who stayed behind from the expedition while they were truthful in their oaths, and to the announcement to those who concealed disbelief as hypocrisy that Allah will not accept their repentance and that His Messenger (ﷺ) will not seek forgiveness for them. The connection is with what preceded of the mention of the circumstances of the hypocrites, whose discourse on them continued from the beginning with His saying: ﴿O you who have believed, what is [wrong] with you that when you are told, "Go forth in the cause of Allah," you adhere heavily to the earth?﴾ [al-Tawbah: 38] and the verses that follow, and what arose from that of the mention of the various circumstances of those who stayed behind from jihad, their excuses, and what followed that of the building of the mosque of harm (masjid al-dirar).

The sentence is opened with the particle of emphasis (inna) to draw attention to the news. It implies that since the opening of the exhortation to jihad was in the form of a reproachful interrogative and their being likened to one who is called to an act and then becomes heavy and clings to the earth, in His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿What [is wrong] with you that when you are told, "Go forth in the cause of Allah," you adhere heavily to the earth?﴾ [al-Tawbah: 38], it was fitting that the believers be placed in the position of one who hesitates and seeks, regarding the reward of jihad being the entitlement to Paradise.

The predicate is expressed as a verbal sentence (jumlah fi'liyyah) to convey the sense of the past tense, indicating that this matter had been established previously, as will come in His saying: ﴿a promise binding upon Him in the Torah, the Gospel, and the Qur'an﴾, and that they are like those who forgot it or feigned to forget it when they did not hasten to the mobilization to which they were summoned, indicating that the promise of this is ancient, recurrent, and well known in the heavenly scriptures.

Purchase (al-ishtira'): is used metaphorically for the promise of reward in exchange for jihad, as indicated by His saying ﴿a promise binding upon Him﴾, by way of the resemblance of a promise to a purchase in that it is the giving of something in return for a payment from the other side.

[p. 38]
Since the usage of the particle "bi" (in) is that it enters upon the price in the forms of purchase, it is introduced here in ﴿that for them is Paradise﴾ because this promise resembles a price. There is no simile (tamthil) in this construction, since there is no comparing figure and compared figure.

The most apparent meaning of "the believers" is that they are the believers of this nation, and this is what fits His saying afterward: ﴿So rejoice in the transaction you have made﴾.

The meaning of His saying ﴿a promise binding upon Him in the Torah and the Gospel﴾ would be what came in the Torah and the Gospel describing the companions of the Messenger who seals the prophethood. This is what His saying, Exalted is He, refers to: ﴿And those with him are severe against the disbelievers and merciful among themselves﴾ [al-Fath: 29], to His saying ﴿That is their example in the Torah and their example in the Gospel﴾ [al-Fath: 29], to His saying ﴿that He may enrage by them the disbelievers﴾ [al-Fath: 29].

It is also permissible that it refers to all the believers in the messengers, peace be upon them, and this is more fitting to His saying ﴿in the Torah and the Gospel﴾. In that case, what is meant are those among them who were commanded to fight, and those who were commanded to endure in adhering to the religion among the followers of the true form of the religion of Christianity, for they endured killing and torture. Thus the application of "fighting in the cause of Allah" to their endurance of killing and the like is metaphorical, and by this the verb "yuqatiluna" (they fight) is used in both its literal and metaphorical senses.

The lam in ﴿for them Paradise﴾ is for ownership and entitlement. The genitive is a verbal noun (masdar), and the estimate is: by the realization of their possession of Paradise. He did not say "bi al-jannah" (with Paradise) because the price was deferred, so this sale is of the type of salam (advance sale).

The clause ﴿They fight in the cause of Allah﴾ is a resumed sentence of explanation (isti'naf bayani), because the purchase of lives and properties, given its apparent strangeness, raises the question of one who says: How do they expend their lives and properties? So its answer was ﴿They fight in the cause of Allah﴾ etc.

Al-Tibi said: So His saying "yuqatiluna" is an explanation, because the place of delivery is the battlefield, since this sale is a salam. For this reason it was said ﴿that for them is Paradise﴾ and not "with Paradise."
