The matter was presented in the form of a report, then Allah bound the sale on His part and guaranteed the delivery of the price to them by His saying ﴿a promise binding upon Him﴾, meaning there is no cancellation (iqalah) nor requested withdrawal from the presence of Might.

[p. 39]
Then He did not suffice with that, but specified the documents in which this transaction is recorded, which are the Torah, the Gospel, and the Qur'an. End of quotation. He intends by this that the verse includes a simile, the reverse of what we explained earlier.

His saying ﴿so they kill and are killed﴾ is a consequence (tafri') of "they fight," because the state of the fighter is not free of one of these two matters. The majority (al-Jumhur) read "fayaqtuluna" in the active voice and what follows it in the passive voice. Hamzah and al-Kisa'i read the reverse. In the reading of the majority there is emphasis on their jihad by killing the enemy, and in the other reading there is emphasis on the cause of martyrdom, which is more fitting for the entitlement to Paradise.

"Wa'dan" (a promise) is in the accusative as an absolute object (maf'ul mutlaq) of "ishtara," because it carries the meaning of "wa'ada" (promised), since the return is deferred.

"Haqqan" (binding) is an adjective of "wa'dan."

"'Alayhi" (upon Him) is an adverbial phrase (zarf laghw) related to "haqqan," placed before its governing word for emphasis on what the particle "'ala" indicates of the sense of obligation.

His saying ﴿in the Torah﴾ is a circumstantial clause (hal) from "wa'dan." The adverbial sense is that of a book to what is written, meaning written in the Torah, the Gospel, and the Qur'an.

The clause ﴿And who fulfills his covenant more than Allah?﴾ is in the position of a circumstantial clause from the pronoun in the genitive in His saying ﴿a promise binding upon Him﴾, meaning: a binding promise upon Him, and there is none more faithful to His covenant than He. The interrogative is one of denial, by placing the hearer in the position of one who considers this promise as possibly fulfilled or not, like most promises, so it is said: "And who fulfills his covenant more than Allah?" as a rebuke to him.

"Awfa" is an elative noun (ism tafdil) from "wafa bi al-'ahd" when one does what he covenanted to do.

[p. 40]
"Min" is comparative, and it is for the starting point according to Sibawayh, meaning the figurative starting point. The name of Allah (al-Jalalah) is mentioned in place of His pronoun to bring to mind the meaning that gathers all attributes of perfection. "Al-'ahd" is a promise with an oath, and a firm promise; the pledge of allegiance is a covenant, and a bequest is a covenant.

On the basis that the promise is binding upon Allah, and that Allah is more faithful to His covenant than every promiser, it follows that the believers should rejoice in this their transaction. So the address is to the believers of this nation.

The transaction is attributed to their pronoun to show their delight in it.

Describing it by the relative pronoun and its clause ﴿which you pledged﴾ is an emphasis for the meaning of "your transaction," so it is a verbal emphasis with a synonymous word.

The clause ﴿That is the great triumph﴾ is a comprehensive concluding statement (tadhyil jami'), for the demonstrative at its beginning comprises the attributes of that transaction with its two considerations. It is emphasized by the pronoun of separation, by the nominal sentence, and by the description "the great," which conveys importance.

[p. 41]

The active participles here are descriptions (*awṣāf*) of the believers mentioned in His saying: ﴿Indeed, Allah has purchased from the believers﴾ [al-Tawbah: 111]. Their original grammatical form was the genitive (*al-jarr*), but they were detached from being qualifiers and made predicates (*akhbār*) of an elided subject, which is the pronoun of the plural, to give these attributes emphasis. This emphasis moved them from the status of qualifiers to that of predicates. This usage is called *na't maqṭū'* (a detached qualifier). It is not a technical qualifier (*na't iṣṭilāḥī*), but it is a qualifier in meaning.

As for ﴿al-tā'ibūn﴾ (those who repent), it means that they turn away from sins, whether this happens without having committed a sin that calls for repentance, as He, Exalted is He, said: ﴿Allah has certainly turned in forgiveness to the Prophet and the Emigrants and the Helpers who followed him﴾ [al-Tawbah: 117], to the end of the verse; or after having committed it, as in His saying: ﴿So if they repent, it will be better for them﴾ [al-Tawbah: 74], after His saying: [p. 41 continued] ﴿And they had certainly uttered a statement of disbelief and reverted to disbelief after their Islam﴾ [al-Tawbah: 74], the verse mentioned just before. The first repentance is faith, because it is a giving up of *shirk* (association of partners with Allah). Then whoever among them had a sin along with faith and repented from it enters into this category. By this, the qualifier differs from the qualified, which is "the believers."

﴿Al-'ābidūn﴾ (those who worship): those who perform what Allah has made obligatory upon them.

﴿Al-ḥāmidūn﴾ (those who praise): those who acknowledge to Allah, Exalted is He, His blessings upon them, and who are grateful to Him.

﴿Al-sā'iḥūn﴾ is derived from *al-siyāḥa*, which is travel through the earth. What is meant by it is a particular journey that is praiseworthy in the Law, namely the journey in which there is drawing near to Allah and compliance with His command, such as the journey of *hijra* (emigration) from the land of disbelief, or travel for the *ḥajj* (pilgrimage), or travel for *jihād* (struggle in the way of Allah). Interpreting it here as travel for *jihād* is more suitable to the context and more inclusive of the believers who are commanded to fight, unlike *hijra* and *ḥajj*.

﴿Al-rāki'ūn al-sājidūn﴾ (those who bow and those who prostrate): they are those who combine both, that is, those who pray, since the obligatory prayer does not lack bowing and prostration.

﴿Al-āmirūn bi'l-ma'rūf wa'l-nāhūn 'an al-munkar﴾ (those who enjoin good and forbid evil): those who call people to guidance and right conduct, and forbid them from what the Law denounces and rejects. The reason that "those who forbid evil" was mentioned with a conjunction (*ḥarf al-'aṭf*), but the rest of the attributes were not, is that although conjunction and its omission are both permissible in predicates and similar constructions, the appropriateness of conjoining these two and not the others is that the attributes mentioned before them in His saying ﴿al-rāki'ūn al-sājidūn﴾ are clearly independent of one another. Then, when ﴿al-rāki'ūn al-sājidūn﴾ was mentioned, it was understood that what is meant is those who combine both, that is, those who pray, in relation to the Muslims. Also, those described as bowing and prostrating, among those whom Allah promised in the Torah and the Gospel, some of their prayer consisted only of bowing. He, Exalted is He, said concerning Dawud, peace be upon him: ﴿And he fell down bowing and turned in repentance﴾ [Ṣād: 24]. And some prayers consisted only of prostration, like some of the prayer of the Christians. He, Exalted is He, said: ﴿O Maryam, be devoutly obedient to your Lord, prostrate, and bow with those who bow﴾ [Āl ʿImrān: 43]. When ﴿al-āmirūn bi'l-ma'rūf wa'l-nāhūn 'an al-munkar﴾ came after it, and these two were independent attributes, they were conjoined with *wāw* so that it would not be supposed that the two were to be treated together like the two attributes preceding them, which are ﴿al-rāki'ūn al-sājidūn﴾. So the *wāw* here is like the one in His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿married women and virgins﴾ [al-Taḥrīm: 5].

[p. 42]

﴿Wa'l-ḥāfiẓūn li-ḥudūd Allāh﴾ (and those who guard the limits of Allah): a comprehensive attribute for acting upon the legal obligations when they are directed at them. The true meaning of *ḥifẓ* (guarding) is seeking that a thing remain in the place where its owner wishes it to remain, out of desire for its continuance and care, lest it be lost. It is commonly used figuratively for persistence in acting upon what one is commanded, in the manner in which one was commanded, and this is what is meant here. That is: "and those who guard what Allah has set for them," i.e., those who do not neglect any of the limits of Allah.

The word *ḥudūd* (limits) is used figuratively for the injunctions and commands. So the limits include the acts of worship and the transactions, as was mentioned earlier in His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿These are the limits of Allah, so do not transgress them﴾ [al-Baqarah: 229], in Sūrat al-Baqarah. For this reason these attributes were concluded with it. It was conjoined with *wāw* so that the omission of the conjunction would not give the impression that it and the one before it are two mutually linked attributes counted after the attribute of enjoining good.

A group of scholars said: the *wāw* in His saying ﴿wa'l-nāhūn 'an al-munkar﴾ is a *wāw* that frequently occurs in the speech of the Arabs when mentioning an eighth counted item, and they called it *wāw al-thamāniya* (the *wāw* of the eighth). Ibn ʿAṭiyya said: Ibn Khalawayh mentioned it in his debate with Abu ʿAli al-Farisi regarding the meaning of His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿until, when they arrive there and its gates are opened﴾ [al-Zumar: 73]. Abu ʿAli al-Farisi denied it. Ibn Hisham said in *Mughni al-Labib*: "A group of men of letters, like al-Ḥarīrī, and of exegetes, like al-Thaʿlabi, mentioned it, and they claimed that when the Arabs counted they said: six, seven, and eight, indicating that seven is a complete number and that what follows it is a new number, and they cited verses, one of which is ﴿They will say: they were three, the fourth of them being their dog﴾ [al-Kahf: 22], to His saying, Glorified is He: ﴿seven, and the eighth of them being their dog﴾ [al-Kahf: 22]. Then he said: The second is the verse of al-Zumar, since it was said that the gates were opened at the verse of Hell, because the gates of Hell are seven, and they were opened at the verse of Paradise, since its gates are eight. Then he said: The third is ﴿and those who forbid evil﴾, for it is the eighth attribute. Then he said: The fourth is: ﴿and virgins﴾ in the verse of al-Taḥrīm, which al-Qadi al-Fadil mentioned and boasted of extracting, though al-Thaʿlabi had mentioned it before him. . . As for al-Thaʿlabi's statement that among them is the *wāw* in His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿for seven nights and eight days, continuously﴾ [al-Ḥāqqah: 7], it is a clear error, for this is merely the *wāw* of conjunction." End of quotation. He elaborated in the course of his statement with refutations and rebuttals.

Ibn ʿAṭiyya said: "My father related to me from the grammarian teacher Abu ʿAbd Allah al-Kafif al-Malaqi, and he said: It is an eloquent dialect of some of the Arabs, whose custom when counting is to say: one, two, three, four, five, six, seven, and eight, nine, ten, and this is their dialect. Whenever the matter of eight comes up in their speech, they insert the *wāw*." End of quotation.

Al-Qurtubi said: "It is the dialect of Quraysh."

I say: Much discussion has been devoted to this meaning of the *wāw*, affirming it and denying it, giving reasons for it and refuting it. In my view, the correct position is that it is an established usage. As for the eighth counted item, it is consistent in the Qur'anic verses cited as evidence. There is no need to be troubled by the fact that some of the items conjoined with *wāw* in them are not the eighth in number, because what matters is that it is the eighth in mention, not in rank.

As for the conjunction of the *wāw* with a matter that carries the meaning of the eighth, as they said about His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿and its gates are opened﴾ [al-Zumar: 73], the *wāw* comes because the gates of Paradise are eight. I do not consider it to be anything other than a subtle point that came about by coincidence. This will come up again at His saying, Exalted is He, in Sūrat al-Zumar: ﴿until, when they arrive there and its gates are opened﴾ [al-Zumar: 73].

The clause ﴿wa-bashshir al-mu'minīn﴾ (and give good tidings to the believers) is conjoined to the clause ﴿Indeed, Allah has purchased from the believers﴾ [al-Tawbah: 111], a conjunction of an imperative (*inshā'*) to a declarative (*khabar*). What made it good is that the purpose of the declarative clause conjoined to it is to act upon it, so it resembles a command. And the purpose of the command to give them good tidings is to convey it to them. So both clauses carry two meanings: a declarative and an imperative. Thus "the believers" here means the believers known from His saying: ﴿Indeed, Allah has purchased from the believers their lives and their wealth﴾ [al-Tawbah: 111].

As for *bishāra* (good tidings), it has been discussed many times before.

[p. 44]

This is a resumption (isti'naf) by which the option (al-takhyir) stated in His words, exalted is He, ﴿Ask forgiveness for them, or do not ask forgiveness for them﴾ [al-Tawbah: 80] was abrogated (naskh, abrogation). That verse placed on equal footing the Prophet ﷺ asking forgiveness for them and his not asking it, since in both cases the most important purpose of seeking forgiveness, which is obtaining forgiveness, is absent. Thus the option retained another purpose: the goodness of speech toward one who the Prophet ﷺ sees as deserving of gentleness, either for his own sake or for the sake of some of his people, as in the story of 'Abd Allah ibn 'Abd Allah ibn Ubayy. God willed to abrogate this after it had already been followed in its application, in accordance with the usual practice of legislation in most cases. Perhaps the purpose for which the option regarding seeking forgiveness for them was kept has weakened: the benefit in it has diminished and the harm in it has been given precedence, through the passing of those who deserved goodness of speech and through the dominance of the rabble of the hypocrites, who suppose that the Prophet's ﷺ asking forgiveness for them will forgive their sins, so that they become joyful, thinking they have gained both bargains and pleased both parties. So God forbade the Prophet ﷺ. Perhaps, when the Muslims heard the Prophet's option regarding asking forgiveness for the polytheists, they began to ask forgiveness for their families and companions among the polytheists, hoping to bring benefit to them in the Hereafter. This became a means (dhari'ah) leading to the belief that the polytheists are equal to the believers in forgiveness, so the distinction that motivates desire for faith would be negated. Therefore God forbade the Prophet ﷺ and the believers together from seeking forgiveness for the polytheists, after having permitted it specifically to the Prophet ﷺ in His words: ﴿Ask forgiveness for them, or do not ask forgiveness for them﴾ [al-Tawbah: 80].

Al-Tirmidhi and al-Nasa'i narrated, "From 'Ali, who said: I heard a man asking forgiveness for his two polytheist parents. He said: So I said to him: Do you ask forgiveness for your parents while they are polytheists? He said: Did not Abraham ask forgiveness for his parents while they were polytheists? So I mentioned that to the Messenger of God ﷺ, and this verse was revealed, up to His words, exalted is He: ﴿Indeed Abraham was tender-hearted and forbearing﴾ [al-Tawbah: 114]." Al-Tirmidhi said: It is a hadith, hasan (good).

Ibn al-'Arabi said in al-'Aridah: It is the weakest of what has been narrated on this subject. As for what has been narrated concerning the occasions of revelation, that this verse was revealed concerning the Prophet's ﷺ asking forgiveness for Abu Talib, or that it was revealed concerning his asking his Lord to forgive his mother Aminah when he visited her grave at al-Abwa', then these are two feeble reports, because this surah was revealed a long time after that.

The prohibitive form came by way of negating the state (nafy al-kawn) together with the emphatic lam of denial (lam al-juhud), as an intensification in declaring oneself free from this seeking of forgiveness, as was discussed earlier at His words, exalted is He: ﴿He said: Glory be to You, it is not for me to say what I have no right to﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 116], at the end of Surat al-'Uqud.

Among the polytheists are included the hypocrites whose hypocrisy the Prophet ﷺ knew, and those whose hypocrisy the Muslims knew through the realization of the attributes that were proclaimed concerning them in this surah and elsewhere.

The addition of ﴿even if they were of near kin﴾ is for the sake of exhausting every circumstance closest to being an excuse, as is the implication of the conjunctive law (law al-wasliyyah, "even if"). That is, the prohibition applies even more so if they are not of near kin. This intensification serves to cut off any excuse for the opponent, and to prepare for teaching the one who was deceived by what the Qur'an related of Abraham asking forgiveness for his father, as in His words, exalted is He: ﴿And forgive my father, for he was of the misguided﴾ [al-Shu'ara': 86]. For this reason He followed it with His words: ﴿And Abraham's asking forgiveness for his father was only because of a promise he had made to him﴾ [al-Tawbah: 114], etc.

The discussion of the conjunctive law (law al-ittisaliyyah, "even if") has already been given at His words, exalted is He: ﴿Even if he were to offer it as ransom﴾ [Al 'Imran: 91] in Surat Al 'Imran.

Ibn 'Ashur's commentary (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on Surah 9, verse 114:

﴿And the request for forgiveness by Abraham for his father was only because of a promise he had made to him. But when it became clear to him that he was an enemy of Allah, he disassociated himself from him. Indeed, Abraham was compassionate and forbearing.﴾

This is coordinated with the clause ﴿It is not for the Prophet﴾ [At-Tawbah: 113], and so forth. It is part of the same verse in view of what it contains of His saying ﴿even if they were relatives﴾ [At-Tawbah: 113], since the rule that what is not fitting for our Prophet Muhammad (ﷺ) is also not fitting for the other messengers (peace be upon them all) is well established, because the majority of their rulings are unified, except for what was specific to our Prophet by way of added excellence. This falls under the question of (the law of those before us is law for us) (a legal principle holding that the revealed law given to earlier communities binds us unless our law abrogates it). Accordingly, what is reported about Abraham's request for forgiveness might seem to create a contradiction between the two verses, and so the Qur'an addressed this objection. The report that this was the occasion of revelation of the verse has already been mentioned just above.

Al-mawida (promise) is a noun for a promise. The promise was certainly made by Abraham's father, as the excuse made on Abraham's behalf indicates. For if Abraham had been the one who promised his father that he would seek forgiveness for him, and his seeking forgiveness for him was in fulfilment of his promise, then the same objection would arise regarding the making of that promise and regarding its fulfilment as arises regarding the occurrence of the request for forgiveness. Therefore, the correct interpretation is that his father promised Abraham that he would believe, so he was in the position of those whose hearts are to be reconciled (al-mu'allafah qulubuhum, those whose hearts are won over by concessions). Abraham sought forgiveness for him because he thought he was wavering in the worship of idols, when he said to him ﴿and leave me for a long time﴾ [Maryam: 46]. So he asked Allah for forgiveness for him, hoping that he would renounce the worship of idols, as is indicated by His saying: ﴿But when it became clear to him that he was an enemy of Allah, he disassociated himself from him﴾.

[p. 46]
The means by which it became clear that he was an enemy of Allah was either revelation, by which Allah forbade him from seeking forgiveness for him, or after he died in polytheism.

Al-tabarri' (disassociation) is a form of (tafa''ul) from (bari'a min kadha), meaning to keep oneself free from something. So al-tabarri' is an intensified form of al-bara'a (freedom from something).

The sentence ﴿Indeed, Abraham was compassionate and forbearing﴾ is a resumptive statement of praise for Abraham. The word (awwah) has been interpreted with meanings that return to tenderheartedness, either toward oneself, in which case it implies humble supplication to Allah and seeking forgiveness, or toward people, in which case it implies compassion for them and praying for them.

The word (awwah) is in the form of an intensive noun: one who frequently says (awwah), in its thirteen dialectal forms which al-Qamus (the dictionary of al-Firuzabadi) enumerates. The most well-known of these is (awwah), with a fatha on the hamza, a fatha on the doubled waw, and a sukun on the ha. Al-Muradi in Sharh al-Tashil (the commentary on al-Tashil by Ibn Malik) said: this is the most well-known of its forms. It is a present-tense verbal noun meaning "I feel pain," used to express the act of feeling pain. However, describing someone as (awwah) is a metaphor for tenderness, softness of heart and humble supplication, when it is applied to one who has no actual pain. The verb from which (awwah) is derived should in principle be triliteral, since intensive forms are derived from triliteral roots. There has been disagreement about the use of a triliteral verb for it: Qutrub affirmed it, while other grammarians rejected this view.

Following (la-awwah) with the description (halim) here, and in many other verses, is an indication of the metaphorical sense and an announcement of what prompts the groaning in him.

Al-halim means the one possessing forbearance (al-hilm). Al-hilm, with a kasra on the ha, is a quality of the soul, namely soundness of intellect, steadiness, gravity, and distance from aggression. It is a quality that entails these matters, and what unites them is the absence of harshness. It does not contradict standing up for the truth, but only without exceeding the measure prescribed by the laws or what people of sound intellect accept.

He said:

"Forbearing when forbearance adorns its people, and together with forbearance he is awe-inspiring in the eyes of his enemy."

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 9, verse 115:

[Page 47]
﴿And Allah would never misguide a people after He had guided them until He makes clear to them what they should avoid. Indeed, Allah is Knowing of all things.﴾

It is a conjunction (ʿatf) upon the clause ﴿And it was not for the Prophet and those who believed to seek forgiveness for the polytheists...﴾ — no, upon the clause ﴿And the request for forgiveness by Ibrahim [for his father] was not except from a promise he had made to him﴾ [al-Tawba: 114], serving as an excuse on behalf of the Prophet and Ibrahim — upon them be blessings and peace — regarding their seeking forgiveness for those among their close kin whom they had asked forgiveness for, such as Abu Talib and Azar, and from the ummah such as ʿAbd Allah ibn Ubayy ibn Salul. The point is that their doing so was nothing but hope from them that guidance would come to him through their seeking forgiveness for him, and assistance for him if Allah willed it for him. Then, when it became clear to them that he had persisted in his disbelief, either by his death upon it or by despair of his faith, they ceased seeking forgiveness for him. All of this was after they had conveyed the message and given sincere counsel to those for whom they sought forgiveness. For this meaning, Allah had already paved the way for their excuse beforehand with His saying: ﴿after it has become clear to them that they are companions of the Hellfire﴾ [al-Tawba: 113], and His saying ﴿And when it became clear to him that he was an enemy of Allah, he disassociated himself from him﴾ [al-Tawba: 114]. In this there is an excuse for the believers who sought forgiveness for polytheists among their close relatives before this prohibition. This is from the category of ﴿Allah pardon you! Why did you give them permission?﴾ [al-Tawba: 43].

It also contains a recording that those polytheists deserve the cessation of forgiveness being sought for them, because the prophets of Allah did not cut it off from them except after they had given them respite, made promises to them, made clear to them, and assisted them through supplication for them; yet that only increased them in transgression.

The meaning of ﴿And Allah would never misguide a people﴾ is that it is not part of His nature and the custom of His majesty to record misguidance upon a people after He has guided them by sending messengers to them and directing them to the truth, until He makes clear to them the things from which He wants them to guard themselves, i.e., avoid them. At that point He conveys to His messengers that those people are among the people of misguidance, so that they abandon seeking forgiveness for them, as He said to Noah — peace be upon him — ﴿So do not ask Me for that of which you have no knowledge﴾ [Hud: 46]. Nor was it part of His nature — exalted is He — to record misguidance upon a people after He has guided them to faith and they have been guided to it, for a deed they performed, until He makes clear to them that He does not approve of that deed.

Furthermore, the wording of the verse is suitable to convey the meaning that Allah does not hold the Prophet ﷺ, nor Ibrahim — peace be upon him — nor the Muslims accountable for their seeking forgiveness for those for whom they sought forgiveness before the prohibition came and the sign of despair of forgiveness became evident;

[Page 48]
because Allah does not hold to account a people whom He has guided to the truth, recording them as astray for sins until He makes clear to them that what they did is disobedience. Therefore, the placement of this verse after all the preceding discourse makes it a comprehensive statement, a concluding summary (tadhyil).

The sentence ﴿Indeed, Allah is Knowing of all things﴾ is a concluding summary (tadhyil) suitable to the preceding sentence, and the occurrence of "inna" at its beginning conveys the sense of a consequence (tafriʿ). The causal explanation is implicit in the preceding sentence, namely that Allah does not misguide a people after having guided them until He makes the truth clear to them.

**Tadhyil** (a concluding statement that generalizes or reinforces what precedes it). This is a second concluding statement, reinforcing His saying: ﴿Indeed, Allah is Knowing of all things﴾ [At-Tawbah: 115]. For this reason it is disjoined without a conjunction, because the fact that dominion over the heavens and the earth belongs to Allah, exalted is He, necessitates that He be knowing of all things. The failure of knowledge to attach to some of what is owned would lead to the neglect of its affairs.

The opening of the sentence with **inna** (indeed), while there is no doubt in the content of the statement, indicates that **inna** here serves merely to emphasize, so it carries the sense of a consequence introduced by "fa" (so) and of causation.

The meaning of **mulk** (dominion) is disposal and management. It has already been discussed under His saying: ﴿Master of the Day of Judgment﴾ [Al-Fatihah: 4].

The addition of the two clauses ﴿He gives life and causes death﴾ serves to depict the meaning of dominion in its most complete perceptible manifestations for people, among whom it is accepted that this is part of Allah's disposal, exalted is He, which no one can prevent or delay.

The conjunction of the clause ﴿And you have not, besides Allah, any protector or any helper﴾ serves to reassure the Muslims that they are victorious in all circumstances, because Allah is their protector, and so He is their helper. It also informs them that they should not fear the disbelievers, because the disbelievers have no protector, since Allah is angry with them, and so He does not help them. This suits the purpose of the discourse, which concerns their seeking forgiveness for the polytheists, indicating that it will not benefit them.

The discussion of **walī** (protector) has already been presented under His saying: ﴿Say: Shall I take other than Allah as a protector?﴾ [Al-An'am: 14], at the beginning of Surat al-An'am.

**Page 49**

**Al-nasir** (the helper) is the one who gives victory. The meaning of **naṣr** (victory) has already been presented under His saying: ﴿Neither will intercession be accepted from it, nor will ransom be taken from it, nor will they be helped﴾ [Al-Baqarah: 48], in Surat al-Baqarah.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 9, verse 117:

﴿Indeed, Allah turned in forgiveness toward the Prophet and the Emigrants and the Helpers who followed him in the hour of hardship, after the hearts of a faction of them had nearly swerved. Then He turned to them in forgiveness. Indeed, He is Kind and Merciful to them.﴾

This is a transition from the exhortation to jihad and the warning against lagging behind, and the rebuke for remaining behind, along with what this exhortation was followed by of the situations of people toward it, the actions of the hypocrites, the weak and the cowardly, to the explanation of the virtue of those who were called to the military campaign and plunged into its hardships. Therefore the sentence is a fresh, initiating resumption (isti'naf ibtida'i).

Its opening with the particle of confirmation (harf al-tahqiq) is an emphasis on its content, which was established in past time, as indicated by the use of all its predicates as past-tense verbs.

Among the embellishments (muhassinat) is the opening of this speech with what signals good news of Allah's pleasure with the believers who campaigned to Tabuk.

The placing of the Prophet ﷺ first in the connection of the verb of repentance with the warriors serves to honor this repentance and its encompassing of all sins, since all Muslims knew that Allah had forgiven the Prophet ﷺ his earlier and later sins.

The meaning of "tāba 'alayhi" is: He forgave him, i.e., He did not hold him accountable for sins, whether he was a sinner or not, as in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿He knew that you would not be able to keep count of it, so He turned to you [in forgiveness]﴾ [al-Muzzammil: 20], i.e., He forgave you and overlooked your shortcomings, and there is no sin nor repentance there. So the meaning of repentance upon the Prophet, the Emigrants and the Helpers who followed him is that Allah does not hold them accountable for what they may think would cause accountability, like the saying of the Prophet ﷺ: "Perhaps Allah looked upon the people of Badr and said: Do whatever you wish, for I have forgiven you."

Page 50
As for Allah's repentance toward the three who were left behind, it is His acceptance of their repentance from their sin.

The Emigrants and the Helpers: they are the totality of the people of Madinah. The army of hardship consisted of them and of others from the tribes around Madinah and Makkah, but they were singled out for praise because they did not hesitate, did not grow sluggish, and were not stingy with their wealth, so they became a model for whoever emulated them from other tribes.

The description of "the Emigrants" and "the Helpers" with ﴿who followed him﴾ serves to indicate that the relative clause is a cause for this forgiveness.

The meaning of "followed him" is that they obeyed him and did not oppose him; so the following is metaphorical.

Al-sā'a (the hour) is a portion of time.

Al-'usra (hardship) is a noun of 'usr, to which the tā' is added for emphasis, and it means severe difficulty. The "hour of hardship" is the time when the Prophet ﷺ called people to the campaign of Tabuk. This is the one to which the reference was previously made in His saying: ﴿O you who believe, what is wrong with you that when you are told, "Go forth in the way of Allah," you cling heavily to the earth?﴾ [al-Tawbah: 38]. Those who were called, prepared, and set out are the ones who followed him. As for what came after the departure to the campaign, that is not the following but rather the jihad itself. What supports this is His saying: ﴿after the hearts of a faction of them had nearly swerved﴾, i.e., of the Emigrants and the Helpers, for it is connected to "followed him", meaning they followed his command after the thought of hesitation, sitting back and disobedience had passed through a faction of them, to the point that they resembled the hypocrites. For that could not be conceived after going forth, and this swerving did not occur, but it came close to occurring.

"Kāda" is one of the verbs of approximation; it operates on two nouns in the manner of "kāna," and its subject here is an implied pronoun of the matter (ḍamīr sha'n), and its predicate is the sentence about the pronoun of the matter. The subject was made a pronoun of the matter here to magnify their state when they came close to swerving.

Al-Jumhur read "tazighu" with the feminine (taʾ) prefix. Hamzah, Hafs from 'Asim, and Khalaf read it with the yā' prefix. These are two valid readings for a verb attributed to a broken plural that is apparent.

Al-zaygh: inclination away from the intended path. It was previously discussed at His saying: ﴿Our Lord, do not let our hearts deviate﴾ [Ali 'Imran: 8] in Surah Ali 'Imran.

The sentence ﴿then He turned to them in forgiveness﴾ is conjoined to the sentence ﴿Allah certainly turned﴾, meaning He turned in forgiveness toward other than this faction absolutely, and He turned toward this faction after their hearts had nearly swerved. Thus "thumma" retains its original sense of delay. This is like His saying in the parallel of this verse: ﴿Then He turned to them so that they might repent﴾ [al-Tawbah: 118]. The meaning: He turned to them, so they became resolved upon it, went forth, and encountered hardship and difficulty. So the pronoun in "'alayhim" refers to "faction". Many exegetes permitted that "thumma" be for sequence in mention only, and the sentence after it be an emphasis of the sentence "Allah turned", so the pronoun refers to all the Emigrants and Helpers.

The sentence ﴿Indeed, He is Kind and Merciful to them﴾ is a reason for what precedes it according to both interpretations.

**Commentary of Ibn ʿAshur (al-Taḥrīr wa al-Tanwīr) on Surah 9, verse 118:**

﴿And [He also turned in forgiveness] toward the three who were left behind, until, when the earth constricted for them despite its vastness, and their souls constricted for them, and they perceived that there is no refuge from Allah except in Him, then He turned to them [in forgiveness] that they might repent. Indeed, Allah is the Accepting of repentance, the Merciful.﴾

﴿And toward the three﴾ is coordinated with "the Prophet" (al-Nabī), with the preposition repeated because the coordinated term is distant from the term it is coordinated with. The meaning is: "and He turned in forgiveness toward the three who were left behind." These are a group with a particular situation among those who stayed behind from the expedition of Tabuk, other than those mentioned in His words: ﴿Those who were left behind rejoiced in their sitting [behind] the Messenger of Allah﴾ [al-Tawbah: 81], and the others mentioned in His words: ﴿And those who made excuses came﴾ [al-Tawbah: 90].

The definite article in "al-thalāthah" (the three) is the definite of prior knowledge (taʿrīf al-ʿahd), for they were known among the people. They were Kaʿb ibn Mālik of Banu Salamah, Murārah ibn al-Rabīʿ al-ʿAmrī of Banu ʿAmr ibn ʿAwf, and Hilāl ibn Umayyah al-Wāqifī of Banu Wāqif. All of them were from the Anṣār, and they stayed behind from the expedition of Tabuk without an excuse. When the Prophet (ﷺ) returned from the expedition of Tabuk, he asked them about their staying behind. They did not lie to him with an excuse, but rather they admitted their sin and grieved. "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) forbade the people from speaking to them, and commanded them to keep away from their wives. Then Allah forgave them after fifty [1]
[Page 52]
nights." The narration of Kaʿb ibn Mālik concerning this story together with the others is in the Ṣaḥīḥ of al-Bukhārī and the Ṣaḥīḥ of Muslim, and it is lengthy and luminous. Al-Baghawī also mentioned it in his tafsīr.

"Khullifū" (were left behind), with the lām doubled, is the intensive form (muḍaʿʿaf) of the unaugmented khalafa, which is an intransitive verb meaning that he was behind others. It is derived from al-khalf, with the lām sukūn, which means "behind." The meaning is that he remained behind others. It is said: "khalafa ʿan aṣḥābihi" when he remained behind his companions in walking, in the present tense "yakhlifu" with the ḍammah on the lām. So the meaning of "khullifū" is that someone left them behind, i.e., he left them behind him, and no one left them behind; rather, they stayed behind by their own action. It is possible that "khullifū" means "they left themselves behind," by the method of tajrīd (abstraction, where the verb is used reflexively in meaning without the reflexive pronoun). It is also possible that the leaving behind is a figurative leaving behind (takhlīf majāzī), used metaphorically for the postponement of the decision about their matter, i.e., those who were left behind from judgment concerning their affair, so the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) neither excused them nor despaired them of repentance as he despaired the hypocrites. Thus "takhlīf" here means "irjāʾ" (postponement). Kaʿb ibn Mālik explained it in this sense in his narration reported in the Ṣaḥīḥ, when he said: "What Allah mentioned of us is not about being left behind from the expedition; rather, it is His leaving us behind (takhlīfuhu iyyānā) and His postponing our matter (irjāʾuhu amrana) concerning those who swore to him and made excuses to him, and he accepted from them." Ended.

That is, the meaning is not that they left themselves behind from the expedition; rather, the meaning is that someone left them behind, i.e., made them the remaining ones (khalaf), and this is a figurative leaving behind, meaning their case was not decided. The agent of the leaving behind may refer to the Prophet (ﷺ) or to Allah, the Exalted.

The passive construction of the verb "khullifū" is taken in its apparent sense, so the intent is not that they left themselves behind.

Attaching the leaving behind to the pronoun of "the three" is an instance of attaching a ruling to the essence (ism al-dhāt). What is intended is attaching it to one of their conditions that is known from the context, like His words: ﴿Forbidden to you is carrion﴾ [al-Māʾidah: 3].

What Kaʿb explained is the one that fits the limit expressed by His words: ﴿until, when the earth constricted for them despite its vastness﴾, because imagining the constriction of the earth upon them and the constriction of their souls is the limit of the postponement of their matter, at which the leaving behind ended. It is not a limit of their staying behind from the expedition, because their staying behind had no end.

[Page 53]
"The constriction of the earth" is a metaphor (istiʿārah), meaning that the earth became as if it were narrow for them, i.e., in their view. That imagery is a metonymy (kināyah) for their distress and for the Muslims' disregard of them. The meaning is that they imagined the earth in their eyes as narrow, as al-Ṭirimmāḥ said:

*I filled the earth around him until it seemed, from the narrowness in his eyes, like the ring of a snare-hunter's net.*

His words "bimā raḥubat" (despite its vastness) form a circumstantial clause (ḥāl) from "the earth," and the bāʾ is for accompaniment (mulābasah), meaning the earth accompanied by its well-known breadth. "Mā" is a verbal-source particle (maṣdariyyah). "Raḥubat" means it became spacious; that is, they imagined the earth narrow while it is the earth described by its well-known breadth.

"The constriction of their souls" is a metaphor for grief and sorrow, because grief is in the soul in the position of narrowness. For this reason it is said of one who is grieved: "his chest became constricted," and of one who is glad: "his chest was expanded."

"Al-ẓann" (thinking, supposing) is used in the sense of certainty and conviction, and this is one of its literal meanings. It was discussed earlier at His words: ﴿those who think that they will meet their Lord and that they will return to Him﴾ [al-Baqarah: 46] in Surah al-Baqarah, and at His words: ﴿And indeed, we think you are among the liars﴾ [al-Aʿrāf: 66] in Surah al-Aʿrāf. The meaning is: and they became certain that the matter of repentance for them is entrusted to Allah alone, by what He reveals to His Messenger; i.e., they took refuge in Allah alone. This is a metonymy for their having repented to Allah and awaited His pardon.

His words ﴿Then He turned to them [in forgiveness]﴾ [al-Tawbah: 117] are coordinated with ﴿the earth constricted for them﴾ and what follows it, meaning: until all of that occurred, then after it He turned to them [in forgiveness].

"Thumma" (then) here indicates succession in time with an interval (al-muhlah wa al-tarākhī al-zamanī), not an interval in rank (al-tarākhī al-rutbī), because what follows it is not higher in rank than what precedes it, by the indication of the context. The context suffices in place of the answer of "idhā" (when), because it conveys its meaning. So, with respect to coordination, it is a conclusion of the limit, and with respect to what is coordinated, it indicates the answer.

The lām in "li-yatūbū" (that they might repent) is for causation (taʿlīl), meaning He turned to them in order that they would refrain from disobedience and keep themselves free from sin, i.e., that they would persist in repentance. So the verb is used in the sense of persistence in being characterized by the verbal noun, not in the sense of bringing the verbal noun into existence.

[Page 54]
The intent is not "that they might sin and then repent," since that does not suit the context of highlighting His turning to them in forgiveness. The clause ﴿Indeed, Allah is the Accepting of repentance, the Merciful﴾ is a concluding clause (tadhyīl) that conveys a sense of favor and grace (imtinān).

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 9, verse 119:

﴿O you who have believed, fear Allah and be with the truthful.﴾

It is apparent that this verse is a conclusion (khatimah) to the verses preceding it, and not the opening (fatihah) of a new theme. In Sahih al-Bukhari, from the hadith of Ka'b ibn Malik when he remained behind from the expedition of Tabuk, he said: "By Allah, I do not know of anyone whom Allah has tested in truthfulness of speech more greatly than He tested me. Since I mentioned that to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), I have not intentionally told a lie up to this day. And Allah revealed to His Messenger: ﴿Allah has certainly turned in forgiveness to the Prophet and the Muhajirin and the Ansar﴾ [al-Tawbah: 117] until His saying ﴿and be with the truthful﴾." End of quotation.

So this verse serves as a concluding summation (tadhyil) of the story. The story includes a people who feared Allah and were truthful in their faith and their striving, so Allah was pleased with them; a people who lied in that matter, fabricated excuses, and swore falsely, so Allah was angry with them; and a people who remained behind from the jihad but were truthful in acknowledging that they had no excuse, so Allah turned to them in forgiveness. Since the cause of the success of the successful in all these circumstances is truthfulness, Allah commanded the believers to have taquwa of Him and to be among the company of the truthful, like those truthful people whom the story encompasses.

The command ﴿be with the truthful﴾ is more emphatic in instilling truthfulness as a character trait than saying "be truthful" (usduqu). Its parallel is ﴿and bow with those who bow﴾ [al-Baqarah: 43]. Likewise, He placed it after "min" (ࣙmin, "from/among") which indicates partiality (tab'idh), and this has already been discussed in His saying: ﴿he refused and was arrogant and was among the disbelievers﴾ [al-Baqarah: 34], and of the same kind is His saying: ﴿He said, "I seek refuge in Allah from being among the ignorant"﴾ [al-Baqarah: 67].

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 9, verse 120:

Page 55
﴿It was not for the people of Medina and those Bedouins around them to stay behind from the Messenger of God, nor to prefer their own selves over his self. That is because they will not suffer thirst, nor fatigue, nor hunger in the way of God, nor tread any ground that enrages the disbelievers, nor gain any gain from an enemy, but that a righteous deed is recorded for them thereby. Indeed God does not waste the reward of the good-doers.﴾

This is an independent (ibtida'i) resumptive statement, making obligatory the military campaign (ghazw) upon the people of Medina and those Bedouins of its desert surroundings who ring Medina when the Prophet ﷺ goes out for the campaign. This is an individual obligation (wujub 'aini) upon these people, whom God honoured by making them the army (jund) of the Prophet ﷺ and the guard of his person.

The Bedouins around Medina are: Muzayna, Ash'ja', Ghifar, Juhayna, and Aslam.

The expression ﴿It was not for the people of Medina﴾ is a declarative form used to express a command, by way of emphasis, since staying behind is made to be something that does not belong to them; they are free of it, so its opposite is established for them, which is going out with the Prophet ﷺ when he campaigns.

In it is praise of the people of Medina and of the Bedouins around them for what they did in the campaign of Tabuk, and it therefore implies exhorting them to that, as indicated by His saying ﴿That is because they will not suffer thirst﴾ etc.

In it is also an implicit reproach (ta'rid) directed at those among the people of Medina and the Bedouins who stayed behind. This indicates the obligation of mobilisation (nafir) upon them when the Prophet ﷺ goes out for the campaign. Qatada and a group said: this ruling is specific to the going out of the Prophet ﷺ, and not to other caliphs or commanders; it is therefore muhkam (not abrogated). Ibn Battal of the Malikis affirmed this. Zayd ibn Aslam and Jabir ibn Zayd said: this was a general ruling at a time when Islam was few and needed a multitude of fighters; then it was abrogated (nusikha) when Islam became strong, by His saying - exalted is He: ﴿And it is not for the believers to go forth all together﴾ [al-Tawba: 122], so that the obligation of jihad became a collective obligation (fard kifaya). Ibn 'Atiyya said: this is the ruling for those whom the Imam summons by designation, because if it were permissible for these to stay behind, the going out would be disrupted. Fakhr al-Din chose this view.

Al-Takhalluf (staying behind): remaining in a place after others with whom one was there have departed. It has been discussed earlier at His saying: ﴿Those who stayed behind rejoiced in their seats, against the Messenger of God﴾ [al-Tawba: 81].

Page 56
Al-raghba is construed with the preposition (fi), which conveys the sense of desiring to attain a thing and being eager for it, and with the preposition ('an), which conveys the sense of aversion from a thing, as has been mentioned earlier in His saying: ﴿And who would turn away from the creed of Abraham﴾ [al-Baqara: 130]. Here it is construed with ('an). What is meant by their turning away from his self is their love for their own selves and their eagerness for their safety, rather than eagerness for the safety of the Messenger's self. It is as if they turned away from his self, since they did not go out with him while attached to their selves, i.e. keeping them safe, because the more of them stay behind, the closer the Messenger's self comes to destruction. So the staying behind of one of them from going out with him is a help in bringing the Messenger's self, peace and blessings be upon him, closer to destruction; therefore the word "turning away" (raghba 'anhu) is borrowed for this staying behind.

The bi in His saying (bi-anfusihim) denotes accompaniment (mulabasa) and is in the position of a circumstantial clause (hal). Holding dear the selves and fearing their destruction came to be expressed by attachment to them in the strongest sense of possession, so the preposition bi denoting accompaniment was used for it. This is a specific accompaniment, although selves are in every case accompanied in this way. This is a wondrously concise construction, extremely eloquent in its inimitability.

Al-Zamakhshari said in the Kashshaf: "They were commanded to expose their selves to hardships such as those his self meets, knowing that his self is the most honoured self before God and the most dear to Him; so when it exposes itself, with its honour and dignity, to plunging into hardship and terror, it is obligatory upon all other selves to hasten to what it has exposed itself to." End of quote.

This is an eloquent prohibition, a rebuke to them, and an incitement to follow him with pride and zeal.

The demonstrative (dhalika) refers to the negation of staying behind from the Messenger being established for them; that is, what they obtain of grace, reward and great recompense requires that it is not for them to stay behind from the Messenger of God.

The bi in (bi-annahum) denotes causation. Zama' is thirst; nasab is fatigue; makhmasa is hunger. It was discussed earlier at His saying: ﴿But whoever is compelled by hunger﴾ [al-Ma'ida: 3] in Surat al-'Uqud.

Al-wat' is treading with the feet. Al-mawti' is a mimi noun (noun of place/manner) from wat'. Treading in the way of God is trampling with the hooves of horses, the soft feet of camels, and the feet of fighters in the enemy's land; this is what enrages the enemy and angers him, since he disdains to have his land trodden by the army. It is also possible that wat' here is used figuratively for humbling the enemy, overpowering and annihilating him, like the saying of al-Harith ibn 'Ulla al-Dhuhli, one of the poets of the Hamasa:

Page 57

"You trampled us with a trampling of rage, the trampling of one fettered, sprouting in old age."

And this is more suitable for attributing the treading to them.

Al-nayl is the verbal noun of (yanaluna). One says: nala minhu, when one strikes him with a calamity. Accordingly, no object is assumed for it. The preposition (min) is used for figurative partitive meaning, realised in the calamity. The calamity inflicted on the enemy may be upon their persons by capture, and may be upon their goods and wealth by plunder and booty.

The exception is detached (mufarragh) from the generality of states. So the clause ﴿a righteous deed is recorded for them thereby﴾ is in the position of a circumstantial clause, and the particle of exception dispenses with its being joined by qad. The pronoun in bihi refers to nasab and what is conjoined to it, either by considering what is mentioned, or because repeating the negative particle made each conjunct as if independently mentioned, so the pronoun was returned to each one in turn, as a singular pronoun is returned to coordinated items joined by (aw), on the basis that that plurality in reality is only one of them. The meaning of "a righteous deed is recorded for them thereby" is that there is recorded for them, for each kind of those deeds, a righteous deed; that is, God makes each of those deeds a righteous deed, even if its doers did not intend by it drawing near to God, for those deeds proceed from their doers while they are heedless, for most of the time or all of it, of their purpose; so they have no intentions of drawing near to God by them. But God, by His grace, makes them acts of nearness for them on account of the nobility of their purpose. That is by making for them a reward upon them, just as He makes a reward for the deeds intended as acts of nearness, as it is related that the sleep of the fasting person is an act of worship.

This meaning is indicated by the concluding clause which gives the reason: ﴿Indeed God does not waste the reward of the good-doers.﴾

This concluding clause indicates that they were good-doers in those deeds, and so they entered under the generality of the principle ﴿Indeed God does not waste the reward of the good-doers﴾ by way of concision.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 9, verse 121:

﴿And they do not spend any expenditure, small or large, nor do they cross a valley, except that it is recorded for them, so that Allah may reward them with the best of what they used to do.﴾

This is a continuation (ʿatf) on the clause ﴿they are not afflicted by thirst﴾ [al-Tawbah: 120], and it is a shift from the enumeration of hardships that befall them without intention in the way of Allah, to some hardships that do not leave those who face them free from the sense that they have endured them in the way of Allah.

Spending in the way of Allah occurs only with intention, by which the one spending remembers that he is striving toward what is a means to supporting the religion. Large expenditure has been brought under the intention, so He draws attention to it and to small expenditure, so that by mentioning the large one the ruling on the small one becomes known, because the reason (ʿillah) in the large one is more apparent. This extended enumeration of their virtues in the expedition serves to depict what they expended in the way of Allah.

Qat' al-wadi (crossing the valley) means passing through it. The literal sense of qat' (cutting) is separating the parts of a body; it is applied to passing through by way of metaphor (isti'arah).

Al-wadi (valley) is the open passage lying between mountains or hills, serving as an outlet for flood waters; for this reason it is derived from wadā, meaning "to flow." Crossing a valley during travel, by its nature, causes travelers to remember that they are journeying toward a certain goal, because it renews a state in the journey that did not exist before. For this reason, pilgrims are recommended to renew the talbiyah when they ascend a height, descend a valley, or meet companions.

The pronoun in (kutiba) refers back to "a righteous deed" (ʿamal ṣāliḥ). The lam of causation (lam al-taʿlil) is connected to (kutiba), meaning: Allah records for them a righteous deed in order to reward them for their best deeds.

Since this is a recompense for their mentioned deed, it is known that this deed of theirs is among their best deeds.

(Ahsana) is in the accusative by the removal of the preposition (naz' al-khafid), meaning: "for the best of what they used to do," or "with the best of what they used to do," like His saying, exalted is He: ﴿That Allah may reward them with the best of what they did and increase them from His bounty﴾ [al-Nur: 38]. As for His saying: ﴿that he may reward you the wage for what you gave to water for us﴾ [al-Qasas: 25], the apparent meaning is that it is of a different kind, and that (ajr) is an absolute object (maf'ul mutlaq).

The mention of "kanu" (they used to) and the use of its predicate in the present tense indicates that such deeds were their habitual practice.

[p. 59]

The bulk of what preceded this surah was an exhortation to jihad and a rebuke of those who fell short in its duty. The preceding discourse concluded by absolving the people of Medina and those around them of staying behind from the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ). Therefore, the force of the speech implied that Muslims must wholly devote themselves to military campaigns. Since one of the aims of Islam is to spread its knowledge and its ethics among the community, and to form groups devoted to the knowledge of religion and to cultivate the minds of Muslims, so that the governance of the community may be sound in the way that religion intends for it, for this reason, the exhortation to jihad was followed by a statement that it is not in the public interest for all Muslims to devote themselves entirely to becoming fighters or soldiers, and that the one who is charged with the duty of teaching does not have a lesser share than the one who fights in the path of Allah, insofar as both perform an act that supports the religion. The former supports it by expanding its authority and multiplying its followers, while the latter supports it by consolidating that authority and preparing it to produce what guarantees the orderly conduct of its affairs and the long duration of its continuance. Indeed, the expansion of conquests and the valor of the community are not sufficient to preserve its rule if it is devoid of a righteous group of scholars, politicians, and people of judgment who are concerned with administering that authority. For this reason, the rule of the Lamtuniyyun (Almoravids) in al-Andalus did not endure except briefly until it contracted, and the state of the Tatars did not become firmly established until after they had merged with the scholars of the cities they had conquered and entrusted the affairs of the state to them.

Since the preceding verse had urged a group of Muslims to rally around the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) in the campaign for the sake of the spread of Islam, it was fitting that it be followed by the mention of a group of believers going forth to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) to gain understanding of the religion, so that they might become guides for their peoples who had entered Islam.

Among the excellences of this exposition is that it matched the form of the exhortation to fighting with a similar form in the exhortation to knowledge. The exhortation to fighting was introduced with the lam al-juhud (the emphatic negative lam, used to deny with force) in His saying: ﴿It was not for the people of Medina and those around them of the Bedouins﴾ [al-Tawbah: 120], and the exhortation to knowledge and understanding was introduced with a similar form when He says: ﴿It was not for the believers to go forth all together﴾.

This sentence is conjoined to the whole of the discourse that precedes it, so it is an independent, resumptive sentence (jumlah ibtida'iyyah mustaʾnafah) for a new purpose arising from His saying: ﴿What is the matter with you, that when you are told, "Go forth in the way of Allah," you cling heavily to the earth?﴾ [al-Tawbah: 38], and then from His saying: ﴿It was not for the people of Medina and those around them of the Bedouins that they should stay behind﴾ [al-Tawbah: 120], and so on. The meaning of "that they should stay behind" [al-Tawbah: 120] is that they should not go forth, so it was fitting that after it there should be mentioned: ﴿It was not for the believers to go forth all together﴾.

[p. 60]

By "going forth" (nafr) in His saying "to go forth" and His saying: ﴿Why did not a group from every faction of them go forth﴾ is meant the going out to military campaign, derived from His saying: ﴿O you who believe, what is the matter with you, that when you are told, "Go forth in the way of Allah," you cling heavily to the earth?﴾ [al-Tawbah: 38]. That is, it was not for the believers to all go forth in that going forth.

The pronoun in His saying "that they may gain understanding of the religion" may refer to "the believers", meaning that the believers should gain understanding. What is meant is that a group from among them should gain understanding, namely the group that did not go forth, as His saying ﴿why did not a group from every faction of them go forth﴾ requires. So it is general in wording but intended in a specific sense.

It is also permissible that the pronoun refers to something understood from the speech, namely from His saying ﴿why did not a group from every faction of them go forth﴾, because its understood meaning is "and there remained a group in order to gain understanding of the religion." So the pronoun is restored to "group" in the plural form, in view of the meaning of "group," as in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And if two groups of the believers fight one another﴾ [al-Hujurat: 9], according to the interpretation that "their group fought".

It is also permissible that the "going forth" in His saying ﴿that they should all go forth, and why did not a group from every faction of them go forth﴾ is a different going forth from the going forth in the way of Allah, namely the going forth to gain understanding of the religion. In that case the repetition of the verbs "they should go forth" (yanfirū) and "went forth" (nafara) is an instance of istikhdam (a rhetorical device in which one word is used with one meaning and its pronoun with another), indicated by the context of His saying "that they may gain understanding of the religion." Then the pronoun in "that they may gain understanding" refers to "group," and His saying "It was not for the believers to all go forth" serves as a preparation for His saying "why did not a group from every faction of them go forth."

Various statements have been transmitted from the leading exegetes and from the reports on the occasions of revelation that accord with both possibilities. The reliance in determining the referents of pronouns is on the contextual indicators of speech, following the habit of the Arabs in brevity and relying on the discernment of the listener, for they are a discerning people.

The use of the form of lam al-juhud is an emphasis of the negation, and it is a statement used in the sense of a prohibition. Its emphasis therefore conveys the emphasis of the prohibition, that is, that it is a firm prohibition requiring its forbiddance. This is because just as going forth to fight is obligatory, since neglecting it wastes the interest of the community, likewise the abstention of a group of Muslims from it is obligatory, since the total devotion of all Muslims to fighting also wastes an interest of the community. Thus the two statements together convey that going forth to fight is an obligation of sufficiency (fard kifayah), that is, upon a group sufficient to achieve the legal purpose of it, and that abstaining from it is required for a group sufficient from among them to achieve the legal purpose of what they were commanded to occupy themselves with, namely knowledge, at the time the other group occupies itself with fighting. This is a restriction of the generality found in the verb "go forth" or a specification of the generality found in the pronoun of "go forth." For this reason this verse is a foundation for the obligation of seeking knowledge upon a great group of Muslims as an obligation of sufficiency, that is, to the degree sufficient to achieve the purpose of that obligation. The negation of the obligation to go forth upon all Muslims, and the affirmation of its obligation upon a group from every faction of them, indicate that those who are obligated to go forth are not more numerous than those who remain for gaining understanding and warning, and that neither of the two states is absolutely preferable to the other. Thus it is known that this is contingent upon the measure of the need that calls for going forth, and that the remainder stays upon the original state. From this it is understood that going forth to jihad is in proportion to what the state of the enemy being fought requires, and that those who remain for gaining understanding remain in the greatest number possible, and that this is equal. It is not proper to rely upon statements that contradict this interpretation regarding the meaning of the verse and its placement among the preceding verses.

"Lawla" (why not / if only) is a particle of urging (harf tahdid).

The firqah (faction) is a group of people who have separated from others in their dwellings; so a tribe is a firqah, and the people of one land are a firqah.

The ṭāʾifah (group) is a company, and it is not restricted to a number. It was discussed earlier at His saying: ﴿So let a group of them stand with you﴾ [al-Nisa': 102] in Surat al-Nisa'.

The indefiniteness of "group" (ṭāʾifah) indicates that going forth to gain understanding of the religion, and what follows from it of warning, is an obligation of sufficiency. The determination of the size of the group and the defining of the limit of understanding is entrusted to the rulers of the affairs of the factions, so the group becomes defined by their appointment, for they are best informed about the measure required by the public interest upon which the obligation of sufficiency rests.

Tafaqquh (gaining understanding) is the effort to attain fiqh (jurisprudential understanding). Fiqh is derived from faqiha (with a kasra on the qaf), meaning he understood what is subtle to understand, so one who does so is faqih. Thus fiqh is more specific than ʿilm (knowledge), and for this reason we find in the Qur'an the use of fiqh for what is hidden in its knowledge, as in His saying: ﴿you do not understand their glorification﴾ [al-Isra': 44]. From it comes faquha (with a damma on the qaf), when fiqh has become one's natural disposition, so one is faqāhah and thus faqih.

Since the becoming of fiqh as a natural disposition is not attained except by practicing what leads to it, the form tafaʿʿul, which indicates effort, is definitively meant here as the effort to attain fiqh, that is, understanding in the religion. In this there is an allusion that understanding the religion is a matter of subtle path that is not attained easily. For this reason the sound hadith says: "Whoever Allah intends good for, He gives him understanding in the religion." For this reason the scholars firmly held that fiqh is the best of the sciences.

The scholars have defined the reality of fiqh as knowledge of the practical legal rulings (al-aḥkām al-shar'iyyah al-ʿamaliyyah) acquired from their detailed evidences through ijtihad (independent reasoning).

Al-inḏār (warning) is informing of what is expected to bring evil. What is meant here is warning against the destructive matters in the Hereafter. From it comes nadhir (warner). It was discussed earlier at His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Indeed, We have sent you with the truth as a bringer of good tidings and a warner﴾ [al-Baqarah: 119] in Surat al-Baqarah. So warning is admonition, and it was restricted to it only because it is more important, since clearing away (takhliyah) precedes adornment (tahliyah), and because there is no guidance to good except that it includes a warning against its opposite. Included in the meaning of warning is teaching people what they use to distinguish between truth and falsehood, and between correctness and error, and that is by the scholar's conveying the sciences of religion to the learners.

The omission of the object of "yaḥdharūn" (they beware) is for generality, that is, they beware what is to be beware of, namely committing the prohibited acts and abandoning the obligatory acts. He restricted it to beware rather than to act for the warning, because the requirement of warning is caution, and you have known that it conveys both matters.

**Commentary of Ibn ʿAshur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on Surah 9, verse 123:**

﴿O you who have believed, fight those adjacent to you of the disbelievers, and let them find in you harshness. And know that Allah is with the righteous.﴾

All of the lands of the Arabs had come under Islam before the Farewell Pilgrimage (ḥajjat al-wadāʿ). The borders of the lands of Islam therefore bordered the lands of al-Shām (Greater Syria), the seat of the Christians of the Arabs, who were under the rule of the Romans. The Battle of Tabuk was the first expedition of Islam to pass beyond the lands of the Arabs to the outskirts of al-Shām. No fighting took place in it, but the jizyah (poll tax) was imposed on Aylah and Busra. That expedition was an intimidation of the Christians. The Surah of Repentance (Barāʾah) was revealed after it,

[Page 63]

and this verse came after it as a charge to continue the campaign against the lands of disbelief that border the lands of Islam. Whenever a land came under Islam and was bordered by lands of disbelief, it became a duty upon the Muslims to campaign against the neighbouring lands. For this reason the caliphs began with the conquest of al-Shām, then Iraq, then Persia, then turned to Egypt, then to Ifriqiya, then to al-Andalus.

Thus the sentence is a new, independent beginning (istiʾnāf ibtidāʾī, a fresh opening sentence), completing the command concerning what is obligatory upon the Muslims in the aftermath of the Battle of Tabuk.

In addressing the believers directly, rather than the Prophet, there is an indication that the Prophet – peace and blessings be upon him – would not campaign after this, and that his noble term of life had drawn near. Perhaps in His saying: ﴿And know that Allah is with the righteous﴾ [al-Tawbah: 36] there is an indication of consolation for the loss of their Prophet – peace and blessings be upon him – and that Allah is with them, like His saying in the other verse: ﴿And Allah will reward the grateful﴾ [Āl ʿImrān: 144].

Al-ghilẓah (with a kasra on the ghayn) means physical severity and roughness. It is used here metaphorically for harmful treatment, as in His saying: ﴿And be harsh against them﴾ [al-Tawbah: 73]. Al-Zamakhshari said in al-Kashshaf: "That combines boldness, steadfastness in fighting, and vehemence in killing and taking captives." End of quotation.

I say: the purpose of this is to cast terror into the hearts of the enemies, so that they fear the consequences of confronting the fighting of the Muslims.

The meaning of commanding the Muslims to bring about what the disbelievers find of the harshness of the believers against them is a command to the believers to be fierce in their fighting. This is an intensification in the command to severity, since they are commanded that the disbelievers should find severity in them. That finding is not realised unless the harshness is of such a kind that it becomes apparent, reaches the enemy, and he perceives it, like His saying – exalted is He – to Moses: ﴿So let not one who does not believe in it turn you away from it﴾ [Ṭā-Hā: 16]. This intensification has occurred because of the strength the enemy possesses, for the intended disbelievers here are the Christians of the Arabs and their helpers, the Romans, who have numbers and equipment. They will not find severity from the believers unless it is a tremendous severity.

[Page 64]

Behind the explicit meaning of this statement there is an allusion to threatening the hypocrites, since their disbelief had become evident while they were closer to the believers in Medina. In this context came His saying – exalted is He: ﴿O Prophet, strive against the disbelievers and the hypocrites, and be harsh against them﴾ [al-Tawbah: 73].

The sentence ﴿And know that Allah is with the righteous﴾ [al-Tawbah: 36] is an affirmation, an encouragement, and a promise of victory if they fear Allah by carrying out the command to jihad.

The sentence was opened with iʿlamū ("know") for emphasis on what knowledge is intended, as was previously mentioned in His saying – exalted is He: ﴿And know that whatever you obtain of spoils…﴾ [al-Anfāl: 41] in Surah al-Anfāl. The companionship (maʿiyyah) here is the companionship of victory and support, like His saying – exalted is He: ﴿When he said to his companion, "Do not grieve; indeed Allah is with us"﴾ [al-Tawbah: 40]. This is a reassurance for them, since they knew the strength of the Romans.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 9, verses 124–125:

﴿When a surah is revealed, some of them say, "Which of you has had its faith increased by this?" As for those who believed, it has increased their faith, and they rejoice.﴾ ﴿As for those in whose hearts is a disease, it has added defilement to their defilement, and they die while still disbelievers.﴾

This is a conjunction (عطف) upon His saying: ﴿And when a surah is revealed, [saying], "Believe in Allah and strive with His Messenger," the men of wealth among them ask your permission﴾ [At-Tawbah: 86]. This is a return to explaining the states of the hypocrites, and what lies between them consists of interjected parentheticals (اعتراضات).

In this verse, ما has been inserted after إذا, and its purpose is emphasis (للتأكيد), that is, to emphasize the meaning of إذا, which is the conditional. This is because this report, given its strangeness, deserved emphasis. Also, the hypocrites deny that it issued from them, unlike the preceding verse, whose content is the narration of their seeking permission, which they do not deny.

This verse does not mention a general summary (إجمال) of what the surahs that were revealed contained, as was mentioned in His saying: ﴿When a surah is revealed, [saying], "Believe in Allah and strive with His Messenger"﴾ [At-Tawbah: 86]. The reason is that all the surahs of the Qur'an are free from neither a call to faith and righteous deeds nor the miraculous nature of their eloquence. Thus the intended meaning is: "When any surah of the Qur'an is revealed." The pronoun in فمنهم refers to the hypocrites, since they are known from the context (للعلم بالمعاد من المقام).

[Page 65]

It comes at the end of the discourse in His saying: ﴿As for those in whose hearts is a disease﴾. Also, because of what was in His saying before this, ﴿Fight those of the disbelievers who are near to you﴾ [At-Tawbah: 123], of allusion (تعريض) to the hypocrites, as was previously mentioned, the hypocrites were floating in the mind of the listener, so bringing a pronoun that refers back to them strengthens that allusion.

Their saying ﴿Which of you has had its faith increased by this?﴾ is a speech of some of them to others, by way of mockery (تهكم) of the believers and of the Qur'an. This is because some verses of the Qur'an explicitly state that the Qur'an increases the faith of the believers. He, the Exalted, said: ﴿The believers are only those who, when Allah is mentioned, their hearts tremble, and when His verses are recited to them, they increase them in faith﴾ [Al-Anfal: 2]. Perhaps the Muslims, when they heard the Qur'an, used to say, "Indeed our faith has increased," like the saying of Mu'adh ibn Jabal to al-Aswad ibn Hilal: "Sit with us, that we may believe for an hour," meaning by discussing the Qur'an and matters of religion (narrated by al-Bukhari in the Book of Faith).

Since the interrogation in their saying "Which of you" was for mockery, it carried the implied meaning of denying that the revelation of the surahs of the Qur'an increases the faith of those who hear them. They supposed that what does not increase their faith does not increase the faith of others, measuring by the states of their own hearts.

The فاء in His saying ﴿As for those who believed﴾ is for sequencing (للتفريع) upon the report of their question, by taking it according to its apparent state and turning it away from their intended purpose. This is the method of the wise style (الأسلوب الحكيم), which is: receiving the addressee with something other than what he expects, by taking his speech to mean other than what he intended, for a subtle point (لنكتة). Here the point is to nullify what they intended, namely the denial that a surah increases anyone's faith, by analogy with the states of their hearts. Their question is therefore answered with this detailed division that follows from it, establishing that a surah does increase the faith of some people, and to a greater degree, namely the arrival of good tidings to them.

In responding to their intended denial, the answer was elevated: the surah is not only one that increases the faith of some people, but the matter is more serious, for it also increases their disbelief. The first category, the believers, the surah increased their faith and brought them glad tidings, so two great benefits accrued to them from it. The second category, those in whose hearts is a disease, it added defilement to their defilement, and they died while still disbelievers. Thus the proper reading is that the clause ﴿and they rejoice﴾ is conjoined to the clause ﴿so it has increased them in faith﴾, and the clause ﴿and they die while still disbelievers﴾ is conjoined to the clause ﴿so it has added defilement to them﴾, because the content of both clauses is what the surah has produced.

[Page 66]

As for the clause ﴿and they are disbelievers﴾ [At-Tawbah: 85], it is a state (حال) from the pronoun in ماتوا.

His saying ﴿and they rejoice﴾ is matched, on the side of the believers, with His saying ﴿and they die while still disbelievers﴾ on the side of the hypocrites, as an embellishment through parallelism (التحسين بالازدواج). Thus the surah had two benefits for the believers and two calamities for the hypocrites. Their dying in disbelief, which is caused by the surah's increase of their disbelief, was placed in the position of a second calamity, distinct from the first, although in reality it is an increase in the first calamity.

This is the reason for the composition of the verse in this fine weave of eloquence and rhetorical beauty. In what I have seen of the tafsir works, this aspect has been overlooked: some of them remained silent about explaining it, and some spread out the meanings of the individual words while leaving aside the aspect of the composition of the speech.

Al-istibshar (الاستبشار) is the effect of good tidings (البشرى) upon the soul. The sin and ta' in it are for emphasis, like استعجم. It was mentioned earlier in His saying: ﴿They rejoice in a blessing from Allah﴾ [Ali 'Imran: 171] in Ali 'Imran, and earlier still in His saying: ﴿So rejoice in your transaction﴾ [At-Tawbah: 111].

The intended meaning of the increase of faith and the increase of defilement is firm establishment and settling within the soul.

Ar-rijs (الرجس) here means disbelief. Its root meaning is a foul thing. This was mentioned earlier at His saying: ﴿an abomination from the work of Satan﴾ [Al-Ma'idah: 90] in Surat al-'Uqud, and at His saying: ﴿Thus Allah places defilement upon those who do not believe﴾ [Al-An'am: 125] in Surat al-An'am.

Disease in the hearts was mentioned earlier at His saying: ﴿In their hearts is a disease﴾ [Al-Baqarah: 10] in Surat al-Baqarah.

The construction of (زادتهم) with (إلى) is because (زاد) has been made to imply the meaning of adding (ضمّ).

The meaning of His saying "As for those who believed" etc. is like the meaning of His saying, the Exalted: ﴿And We send down of the Qur'an that which is a healing and mercy for the believers, and it does not increase the wrongdoers except in loss﴾ [Al-Isra': 82].

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 9, verses 124–125:

﴿When a surah is revealed, some of them say, "Which of you has had its faith increased by this?" As for those who believed, it has increased their faith, and they rejoice.﴾ ﴿As for those in whose hearts is a disease, it has added defilement to their defilement, and they die while still disbelievers.﴾

This is a conjunction (عطف) upon His saying: ﴿And when a surah is revealed, [saying], "Believe in Allah and strive with His Messenger," the men of wealth among them ask your permission﴾ [At-Tawbah: 86]. This is a return to explaining the states of the hypocrites, and what lies between them consists of interjected parentheticals (اعتراضات).

In this verse, ما has been inserted after إذا, and its purpose is emphasis (للتأكيد), that is, to emphasize the meaning of إذا, which is the conditional. This is because this report, given its strangeness, deserved emphasis. Also, the hypocrites deny that it issued from them, unlike the preceding verse, whose content is the narration of their seeking permission, which they do not deny.
