This verse does not mention a general summary (إجمال) of what the surahs that were revealed contained, as was mentioned in His saying: ﴿When a surah is revealed, [saying], "Believe in Allah and strive with His Messenger"﴾ [At-Tawbah: 86]. The reason is that all the surahs of the Qur'an are free from neither a call to faith and righteous deeds nor the miraculous nature of their eloquence. Thus the intended meaning is: "When any surah of the Qur'an is revealed." The pronoun in فمنهم refers to the hypocrites, since they are known from the context (للعلم بالمعاد من المقام).

[Page 65]

It comes at the end of the discourse in His saying: ﴿As for those in whose hearts is a disease﴾. Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 9, verse 126:

[Page 67]
﴿Do they not see that they are tried every year, once or twice? Yet they do not repent, nor do they take heed.﴾
This is a conjunction (ʿatf) upon the clause ﴿So it increased them in uncleanness upon their uncleanness﴾ [al-Tawbah: 125] to its end, so it is part of the elaboration (tafsil).

The interrogative hamza has been placed before the conjunctive particle, following the practice of placing interrogative particles at the beginning (taṣdīr). This placement serves to alert that the sentence is intended as a question.

The interrogation here is a rebuke (inkar) and an expression of wonder (taʿjib) at their failure to see their trial, so that it is not followed by their repentance nor by their remembrance of the command of their Lord. The purpose of this rebuke is to provide evidence for what preceded regarding the increase in the disbelief of the hypocrites and its consolidation, each time a surah of the Qur'an is revealed, by presenting a clear proof that takes the place of the sensible and visible, such that the rebuke is directed at one who does not see it.

Al-fitnah (trial, affliction): the disruption of the usual order of people's condition and the unsettling of their affairs, such as widespread diseases, fighting, and the persistence of fear. Its meaning was previously mentioned at His saying: ﴿And trial is worse than killing﴾ [al-Baqarah: 191] and His saying: ﴿And fight them until there is no more fitnah﴾ [al-Baqarah: 193], in Surah al-Baqarah.

So the meaning of ﴿that they are tried﴾ is that God sends upon them calamities and harms that befall their group, of a kind that the lives of nations do not customarily experience repeatedly, such that the repetition of that indicates that God intends by it to awaken people to the evil of their conduct regarding the right of God, through their failure to be guided to abandon their obstinacy against the Prophet ﷺ. For if they were granted success, they would have awakened from their heedlessness and known that what befalls them every year has only occurred since the time they became entangled in hypocrisy.

There is no doubt that the trial to which the verse alludes was specific to the people of hypocrisy: diseases that strike them, or losses that afflict their wealth, or calamities that strike their crops, or a shortfall in their persons and offspring. Thus, when two such things occur in a year, the trial is twice.

The majority (al-Jumhur) read ﴿Do they not see﴾ with the yāʾ (third-person). Ḥamzah and Yaʿqub read ﴿Do you not see﴾ with the tāʾ (second-person), on the basis that the address is to the Muslims, and it is then a case of treating the one who sees as other than himself, so that the rebuke is directed at him for not seeing what is evident.

[Page 68]
And ﴿thumma﴾ (then) is for graded sequence (al-tartib al-rutbi), because the clause conjoined by it is, in the rank of wonder regarding its state, greater than the clause it is conjoined to. For the occurrence of the trial in itself is astonishing, while their failure to be guided to make amends through repentance and remembrance is even more astonishing. Had ﴿thumma﴾ been for real temporal succession, the object of wonder regarding their condition would have been the delay of their repentance and remembrance.

The clause ﴿nor do they take heed﴾ was introduced with a nominal subject to which a verb is attributed, and he did not say "wa la yadhakkarun," for the purpose of conveying certainty, meaning that the negation of their remembrance is definite.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 9, verse 127:

﴿And when a surah is sent down, some of them look at others, [saying], "Does anyone see you?" Then they turn away. Allah has turned their hearts away, because they are a people who do not understand.﴾

This is a conjunction (ʿatf) upon the clause ﴿And when a surah is sent down, some of them say, "Which of you has this one increased in faith?"﴾ [al-Tawbah: 124]. The apparent intent is that the clause ﴿some of them look at others﴾ is conjoined to the clause ﴿some of them say, "Which of you has this one increased in faith?"﴾ [al-Tawbah: 124]. The conditional clause was repeated either because of the distance between the conjoined clause and the clause of the response, or to indicate the difference in time with respect to the descent in which they say ﴿Which of you has this one increased in faith?﴾ [al-Tawbah: 124], and with respect to the surah during whose descent some of them look at others; or because the two surahs differ, in that what is meant here is a surah containing something specific to them.

The cause for the addition of what follows ﴿idha﴾ (when) in the two verses is one, since its requirement is one.

That some of them look at others at the descent of the surah indicates that they were at that time in the assembly of the Prophet ﷺ, because ﴿some of them looked at others﴾ is connected to the particle of temporality, which is ﴿idha﴾ (when). It is therefore determined that the looking of some of them at others was occurring at the time of the descent of the surah. This is also supported by His saying ﴿then they turned away﴾, i.e., away from that assembly. It also indicates that the surah includes the disclosure of their secrets and the exposure of their scheming, because the looking of some of them at others is a look of astonishment and questioning. He – exalted is He – said in the preceding verse: ﴿The hypocrites fear that a surah will be sent down against them, informing them of what is in their hearts. Say, "Mock, indeed Allah will bring out what you fear."﴾ [al-Tawbah: 64]. It also indicates that they were concealing their astonishment at the manifestation of their conditions, out of fear of acknowledging what was attributed to them; for this reason they were content with exchanging glances rather than speech. So the looking here is a look that signals what is in the heart of the one looking, of astonishment and questioning.

The clause ﴿Does anyone see you?﴾ is an explanation (bayan) of the clause ﴿some of them look at others﴾, because they conveyed by the look what was a secret among them; so, since the look was a look of mutual understanding, it was correct to explain its clause by what indicates the astonished question. Thus in this composition there is a wonderful brevity by omission, indicated by the context. The estimated sense is: "And when a surah is sent down in which their affair is exposed, some of them look at others with furtive glances, questioning and astonished at the Prophet ﷺ's knowledge of their secrets, saying: 'Does anyone see you when you withdraw and plan your affairs?'" For they, in their disbelief, do not believe that Allah informed His Prophet – upon him be prayers and peace – of the hidden matter of their affair.

The addition of the clause ﴿then they turned away﴾ serves to indicate that they gained from the descent of the surah, which exposed the believers to their secrets, neither a lesson nor any nearness to faith; rather, the utmost of their affair was astonishment and doubt as to whether someone had come to know of them and would divulge their secrets. Then they turned away as though there had been no lesson. This is among the trials that befall them: ﴿Then they will not repent, nor will they be reminded.﴾

The clause ﴿Allah has turned their hearts away﴾ is a resumptive clause of explanatory resumption (istinaf bayani), because what the statement ﴿then they turned away﴾ conveys, namely their not benefiting from what is in that surah of informing about unseen matters, which indicates the truthfulness of the Messenger ﷺ, raises the question of one who asks about the cause of their not benefiting from that and not being guided. It is answered that Allah turned their hearts away from understanding by a cosmic (takwini) decree, so they were deprived of benefiting from the most eloquent admonition. This was a punishment for them, because they are ﴿a people who do not understand﴾, i.e., they do not comprehend the proofs, meaning they do not seek guidance through reflection so that they might understand.

Some exegetes made the statement ﴿Allah has turned their hearts away﴾ into an invocation against them, but there is no need for this, because Allah's invoking against His creatures is a cosmic act, as has preceded; and because the causal attribution by His saying ﴿because they are a people who do not understand﴾ rejects it. Moreover, the exegetes have turned away from explaining this verse in a way that shows the meanings are derived from the structure of the speech; instead they have brought statements that the observer feels are forced upon it to fit the intended meaning, and estimations that do not settle the heart.

[Page 70]

﴿There has certainly come to you a Messenger from among yourselves. It grieves him that you suffer hardship. He is anxious over you, and toward the believers he is kind and merciful.﴾ ﴿But if they turn away, say: "Allah is sufficient for me. There is no god but Him. In Him I have placed my trust, and He is Lord of the Mighty Throne."﴾

This surah was a surah of severity and harshness toward the polytheists, the People of the Book, the hypocrites among the people of Madinah, and the Bedouins. It also commanded the believers to engage in jihad and rebuked those who fell short in it. Interspersed within this was praise for the believers who had the opposite qualities: those who emigrated, those who gave help, and those who followed the Messenger in the hour of hardship (al-'usrah).

The surah concludes with these two verses, which remind the people of the favor of Allah in sending Muhammad (ﷺ) and praise his characteristics, which combine all perfections. Among the most distinguishing of these is his eagerness for their guidance, his desire for their faith, and their entry into the community of Islam. He is kind and merciful toward them, so that they may know that the harshness directed at those who turned away from Islam, in word and in deed, was only a means of reforming their condition. This is one of the manifestations of the mercy that Allah, the Exalted, made to accompany the mission of His Messenger (ﷺ), in His saying: ﴿And We did not send you except as a mercy to the worlds﴾ [al-Anbiya' 21:107]. Thus these two verses come with what removes distress from the hearts of the groups about whom the verses of severity were revealed and who were treated harshly, following severity with gentleness and harshness with mercy. This is also the habit of the Qur'an. With these two verses, the door to the enclosure of faith and repentance is opened, so that whoever Allah grants success may enter it.

Thus the sentence is a resumptive sentence beginning a new topic (istinaf ibtida'i). Its occurrence at the end of the surah gives it the meaning of a concluding appendage (tadhyil) and a summary.

The address in His saying "there has come to you" and what follows it of address is directed to the whole community called to Islam. The primary intended audience is those who turned away among the polytheists and hypocrites of the Arabs, as indicated by His saying after the address, ﴿kind and merciful toward the believers﴾. It will come that the intended audience is the Arabs.

[Page 71]

The opening with the two emphasizing particles, the lam and qad, is despite the fact that its content is not something open to denial, in order to draw attention to this sentence because of the importance of the purpose for which it was brought, which we will mention. It is also because what it contains is something the hypocrites deny, namely that he is a Messenger from Allah. It is also because this emphasis makes its addressees treated as if they were deniers of his coming, insofar as they did not benefit themselves by this coming. It is also because this emphasis is a recording against them, intended to hint at the approach of departure. For when the announcement of his coming was repeated, though it had been established for many long years, this was a metonymy (kinaya) for the approach of its ending. It is a record from Him against the believers and a deposit (idda') for the hypocrites and whoever remained of the polytheists. Moreover, other verses addressed to the People of the Book and others were emphasized with less emphasis than this, such as His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿O People of the Book, there has certainly come to you Our Messenger, making clear to you much of what you used to conceal of the Scripture and pardoning much. There has certainly come to you from Allah a light and a clear Book﴾ [al-Ma'idah 5:15], and His saying: ﴿O mankind, there has certainly come to you a proof from your Lord, and We have sent down to you a clear light﴾ [al-Nisa' 4:174]. So the sentence was emphasized in this surah only for a purpose more important than removing denial.

The word "coming" (al-maji') is used figuratively (majaz) for the address of the call to the religion. Its directing toward them is likened to an address they were not expecting, like the arrival of a visitor to people from another place. This is a common usage in the Qur'an.

Al-anfus is the plural of nafs, which means the essence. The word nafs is added to a pronoun, and then it indicates the tribe to which the pronoun refers; that is, he is counted among their lineage, and his belonging to them is not by alliance, clientage, or attachment. One says: "He is a Qurayshi from among them," and one says: "The Qurayshi is their mawla or their ally." So the meaning of "from among yourselves" is "from the pure core of your lineage." It is thus determined that the address is to the Arabs, because at the time of the revelation, the Arabs did not count as their own those who allied with them or became their clients, such as Salman al-Farisi and Bilal al-Habashi. In this there is a favor to the Arabs and an alert to their excellence. In it there is also an indirect exhortation to follow him and not to oppose him, and that the most fitting for them is to take pride in him and to rally around him, as He said, may He be exalted, about the Qur'an: ﴿And indeed it is a reminder for you and for your people﴾ [al-Zukhruf 43:44], meaning that a good remembrance of you will remain through it.

[Page 72]

Al-'aziz means the dominant one. Al-'izzah means dominance. One says 'azzahu when he overcame him. From this is His saying: ﴿and he overpowered me in speech﴾ [Sad 38:23]. When it is followed by 'ala, it indicates the meaning of heaviness and severity upon the self. Bishr ibn 'Awanah said, mentioning his killing of the lion and his wrestling with it:

"I said to him: It grieves me that I killed my kinsman by force and by subjugation."

The ma here is a verbal-masdar particle (masdariyyah).

'Anittum means you suffered hardship. Al-'anat is hardship, that is: your distress and your suffering were heavy upon him. This is like His saying: ﴿Perhaps you would kill yourself with grief that they do not become believers﴾ [al-Shu'ara' 26:3]. This was mentioned in the description of the Messenger, peace be upon him, and it indicates that this is a disposition of his. Its effect is gentleness toward the community and caution against what would throw them into punishment in this world and the next. Among the effects of this is his intercession for all people on the Day of Standing (al-mawqif), to hasten the reckoning. Furthermore, this implies that his law came in harmony with his character, so hardship and difficulty were removed from it. He said: ﴿Allah intends for you ease and does not intend for you hardship﴾ [al-Baqarah 2:185], and He said: ﴿And He has not placed upon you in the religion any difficulty﴾ [al-Hajj 22:78].

The departure from using the explicit verbal noun 'anat to using the verb with ma, which in combination forms a verbal noun, is a subtle point (nukta). It conveys that the hardship that befell them in the past, which had already occurred, was grievous to him. That was by what they suffered from the killing of their people, from captivity in the raids, and from the dire threats and warnings of the Qur'an. If the verbal noun had been used, it would not have referred to a specific hardship or to a hardship that had occurred, because the verbal noun has no tense. It would have been open to meaning that it grieved him by keeping it away from them. But the coming of the verbal noun formed from a past verb makes it a verbal noun restricted to occurrence in the past. Do you not see that you may paraphrase it thus: "It grieves him, the hardship you suffered in the past," so that this verse serves as an alert that what they suffered of severity was only for the reform of their condition, that perhaps after it they would lower their arrogance, turn back from their error, and perceive the goodness of their affairs.

Al-hirs is an intense desire for a thing and eagerness toward it. Since it transitively reaches the pronoun of the addressees, which refers to their persons, and the persons are not the object of the eagerness here, it is necessary to supply an elided noun understood from the context of the discourse, so it is taken as: "over your faith" or "over your guidance."

[Page 73]

Al-ra'uf means the one of intense tenderness. Al-rahim means the one of intense mercy, because these two are intensive forms (sigha mubalaghah). They both govern the prepositional phrase connected to them, which is "toward the believers" (bil-mu'minin).

Al-ra'fah is a tenderness that arises when harm befalls the one who is treated with it. One says: ra'uf rahim. Al-rahmah is a tenderness that calls for kindness to the one who is shown mercy. Between them there is a general and specific relation in an absolute sense, and for this reason they are combined here, though their implications differ. The ra'fah was mentioned earlier at His saying: ﴿And Allah would never have caused your faith to be lost. Indeed, Allah is toward the people ra'uf and rahim﴾ [al-Baqarah 2:143] in Surat al-Baqarah. And the rahmah in Surat al-Fatihah.

The fronting of the complement before its two governing words, which contend for it, in His saying: ﴿toward the believers ra'uf rahim﴾ is for the purpose of drawing attention to the believers, in the direction of the two attributes of His tenderness and mercy toward them. As for His general mercy, established by His saying: ﴿And We did not send you except as a mercy to the worlds﴾ [al-Anbiya' 21:107], it is a mercy mixed with severity toward non-believers. So toward non-believers he is ra'uf and rahim, but one does not say "ra'uf rahim toward them."

The fa' in His saying: ﴿But if they turn away﴾ is for the purpose of deriving a consequence from the sending of the Prophet (ﷺ), the bearer of these attributes, to them. For his mentioned attributes require of every sound-minded person among the Arabs faith in him and following him, because he is one of their own and loves their good, and is ra'uf and rahim toward whoever follows him among them. So it is consequently required of them to believe in him. If they believe, that is well. If they do not believe, then Allah is his Reckoner and Sufficient. The conditional has indicated its opposite, because "but if they turn away" implies the supposition of its contrary, which is that they submit in faith.

After the derivation, the speech shifts from addressing the Arabs to addressing the Prophet (ﷺ), with what the apparent form would have required them to be addressed with, relying on the indication of the particle of consequence. So he was told: ﴿But if they turn away, say: "Allah is sufficient for me."﴾ The implied meaning is: "If you turn away from him, then Allah is sufficient for him; and say: 'Allah is sufficient for me.'"

Thus this wondrously concise arrangement was brought, with what it contains of excellent allusion to their not being worthy of the address of Allah in the case of their turning away.

Al-tawalli means turning away and retreating. It is used here figuratively for stubbornness and obstinacy.

[Page 74]

Al-hasb means the sufficient one. That is: He is sufficient for you against the evil of their turning away, for if they turn away after this, they turn away out of envy and rage. That is a state that suggests they would strive in plotting and harm.

The meaning of the command to say "Allah is sufficient for me" is that he should say it as a statement arising from the firm resolve of the heart upon it. That is: know that Allah is sufficient for you, and say, "Allah is sufficient for me," because speech confirms what is known and fixes it in the soul of the one who knows it, and because in this statement there is a message to those who turn away from him that Allah is sufficient for him against them.

Al-tawakkul means entrusting. It is an intensive form of wakala.

This verse conveys the honoring of this blessed phrase, because he was commanded to say this very phrase, and he was not commanded merely to rely upon Allah, as he was commanded in His saying: ﴿So rely upon Allah; indeed, you are upon the clear truth﴾ [al-Naml 27:79].

Nor was the statement that Allah is his sufficiency merely a report, as in His saying: ﴿Indeed, Allah is sufficient for you﴾ [al-Anfal 8:62].

The sentence "There is no god but Him" is a resumptive sentence for praise, or it is in the position of a circumstantial clause (hal), and it is a praise of His oneness.

It is conjoined to it by the sentence "and He is the Lord of the Mighty Throne," for praise of His great power, because whoever is Lord of the Mighty Throne is established as Powerful, since it is well known that the Throne is the greatest of creatures, and for this reason it is described as "mighty." So "mighty" in this verse is an attribute of the Throne, and therefore it is in the genitive case.

In these two verses there is an indication of the deposit (idda') and the excuse given to people, and an alert to the urgency of seizing the opportunity of the Messenger's (ﷺ) presence among them, so that they may be honored by faith in him while they see him and draw light from the radiance of his guidance. For being guided by seeing him and receiving directly from him is more hopeful for attaining the completeness of faith and benefiting in a short time, to obtain abundant good that cannot be obtained in its like over many times longer.

Also in them is a hint of the approach of the appointed term of the Prophet (ﷺ), because the reminder with His saying "there has certainly come to you" indicates that this coming, which has passed through a long time, is about to end, for every arrival has a departure, and every rising has a setting. It has been reported from Ubayy ibn Ka'b and Qatadah that these two verses are the most recent of the Qur'an in terms of their time with Allah, meaning the last of what was revealed of the Qur'an.

[Page 75]

It was also said: the last of the Qur'an to be revealed is the verse of al-kalalah, which ends Surat al-Nisa'. And it was said: the last of it to be revealed is His saying: ﴿And fear a Day when you will be returned therein to Allah; then every soul will be paid in full what it earned, and they will not be wronged﴾ [al-Baqarah 2:281], from Surat al-Baqarah.

[p. 77]

Grievous to him is your suffering; he is ardently concerned for you﴾" to the end of them. And by way of Ibrahim ibn Sa'd, from al-Zuhri, [it is narrated] with Abu Khuzayma al-Ansari. The meaning of this is that he (Zayd) searched for these two verses in what had been written down of the Qur'an, and did not find them, while he knew that at the end of Surat al-Tawba there are two concluding verses, or that he himself had them memorized. (For Zayd was careful, in collecting the Qur'an, to rely on memorization, on tracing what had been written down at the dictation of the Prophet ﷺ, and on the recitation of the Qur'an's memorizers other than himself.) Then he found that Khuzayma, or Abu Khuzayma, had them memorized. When Khuzayma, or Abu Khuzayma, dictated them to him, Zayd recalled their wording, and those among the Companions who had heard them recited also recalled them. How so, when Ubayy ibn Ka'b had said: "They are the last of what was revealed." So their wording is established by consensus (ijma'), and their mass transmission (tawatur) is attained, since no one doubted them. Their establishment is not limited to the report of Khuzayma or Abu Khuzayma.

In the name of Allah, the Most Merciful, the Especially Merciful

Surat Yunus

It is named in the codices (mushafat) and in the books of tafsir (exegesis, the explanation of the Qur'an) and sunnah (the Prophet's teachings and practice) "Surat Yunus," because it alone mentions a particular matter concerning the people of Yunus (Jonah): that they believed after their Messenger had threatened them with the descent of punishment, so Allah pardoned them when they believed. This is in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Why was there not a city that believed and whose faith benefited it, except the people of Jonah? When they believed, We removed from them the punishment of disgrace in the worldly life, and We let them enjoy for a time﴾ [Yunus: 98]. That distinction is an honour for Yunus, peace be upon him, and there is no mention of Yunus in it other than that. Yunus is mentioned in Surat al-Saffat in more detail than in this surah, but the reason for the naming does not necessitate it.

What appears to me most likely is that it was attributed to Yunus to distinguish it from its four sister surahs that open with ﴿Alif, Lam, Ra﴾ [Yunus: 1]. For this reason each of them was attributed to a prophet or to a prophet's people, instead of being called "the first ﴿Alif, Lam, Ra﴾ [Yunus: 1]" and "the second ﴿Alif, Lam, Ra﴾ [Yunus: 1]." Thus, the surahs' becoming known by their names first spread among the Muslims through the first words in them, especially when their openings were disjoined letters. They would call those surahs by "Ha-Mim" and "Alif-Lam-Ra" and the like.

It is Meccan according to the majority. This is what is narrated from Ibn 'Abbas, according to the more sound report from him. In al-Itqan (of al-Suyuti), on the authority of 'Ata', from him, it is said to be Medinan. In al-Qurtubi, on the authority of Ibn 'Abbas, three of its verses are Medinan, and they are His saying, exalted is He: ﴿So if you are in doubt about what We have sent down to you﴾ [Yunus: 94] up to His saying ﴿until they see the painful punishment﴾ [Yunus: 88]. al-Qummi al-Nisaburi affirmed this. In Ibn 'Atiyya, on the authority of Muqatil, two verses are Medinan, namely ("So if you are in doubt") up to His saying ("among the losers"). In the same source, on the authority of al-Kalbi, one verse was revealed in Medina, and it is His saying, exalted is He: (﴿And among them are those who believe in it﴾ [Yunus: 40]) up to ("Allah is most knowing of the corrupters"). It was revealed concerning the Jews.

[p. 80]

Ibn 'Atiyya said: A group said: about forty verses from its beginning were revealed in Mecca, and the rest of it was revealed in Medina. He did not attribute this to a specific source. I suppose that these opinions arise from the assumption that whatever disputation with the People of the Book is in the Qur'an was revealed only in Medina. If that is so, the assumption of these people is mistaken. This will be pointed out later.

Its number of verses is one hundred and nine in the count of most of the regional centres, and one hundred and ten in the count of the people of al-Sham.

It is the fifty-first surah in the order of revelation of the surahs. It was revealed after Surat Bani Isra'il and before Surat Hud. I suppose it was revealed in the eleventh year after the Call (al-ba'tha), on account of what will come at His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And when We let people taste mercy after adversity has touched them, at once they conspire against Our signs﴾ [Yunus: 21].

* * *

Among the aims of this surah:

It begins with the purpose of establishing the prophethood of Muhammad ﷺ by the evidence of the inability of the polytheists to produce the like of the Qur'an, an evidence indicated through a subtle allusive style built on the implication of the disjoined letters at the opening of the surah, as already explained at the beginning of Surat al-Baqara. For this reason those letters are followed by His saying, exalted is He: ﴿These are the verses of the wise Book﴾ [Yunus: 1], indicating that its inimitability for them is the proof that it is from Allah. What was implied here has been stated explicitly in His saying: ﴿Say: Then bring a surah like it﴾ [Yunus: 38].

This is followed by the establishment of the prophethood of Muhammad ﷺ and the refutation of the polytheists' claim that it is impossible for Allah to send a human as a Messenger.

From that it moves to establishing that Allah, exalted is He, alone is God, by the evidence that He is the Creator of the world and its Governor. This leads to refuting the idea that Allah has partners in His divinity, and to refuting the excuses of the polytheists that their idols are intercessors with Allah.

[p. 81]

This is followed by establishing the gathering (of the dead) and recompense. That is the refutation of the roots of polytheism.

Interwoven with this are indications from created things, an explanation of the wisdom of recompense, the nature of recompense, the wisdom and benefits for people in the signs found in created things, a warning to those who deny resurrection and turn away from the signs of Allah, and, in contrast to them, the promise given to those who believe. Most of this surah therefore revolves around the axis of affirming these foundations.

Among these is the reminder that Allah's granting respite to the disbelievers rather than hastening punishment is a wisdom from Him.

Among these too is the reminder of what befell the peoples of earlier generations when they associated partners with Allah and denied the Messengers.

Also: taking lessons from the abilities Allah created for people to travel on land and sea, and from the subtle favours found in the conditions of sea travel.

And the striking of a parable for the worldly life, its splendour and its passing, and that the Hereafter is the abode of peace.

And the differing states of believers and disbelievers in the Hereafter, and the disavowal by false deities of their worshippers.

And the refutation of the divinity of any other than Allah, exalted is He, by the proof that they cannot benefit people at all, in this world or the Hereafter.

And the establishment that the Qur'an is sent down from Allah, and that the proofs that it is fabricated are manifest.

And the challenge to the polytheists to produce a surah like it, but misguidance blinded the eyes of the obstinate.

And the warning to the polytheists of the consequences of what befell the nations that denied the Messengers, and that if the punishment comes upon them, their faith will not benefit them. And that this did not overtake the people of Yunus, because their coming to faith happened before the punishment arrived.

And the rebuke of the polytheists for forbidding what Allah had made lawful of provision.

And the establishment of Allah's comprehensive knowledge, exalted is He.

[p. 82]

And the good news for the friends of Allah in this world and in the Hereafter.

And the consolation of the Messenger for what the disbelievers say.

And that had He willed, all who are on earth would have believed, all of them.

Then it arrives at taking lessons from the earlier Messengers: Nuh, and Messengers after him, then Musa and Harun.

Then the truthfulness of the prophethood of Muhammad ﷺ is affirmed by the testimony of the People of the Book.

The surah concludes with instructing the Messenger, peace be upon him, in what he may use as an excuse toward those who doubt the religion of Islam: that whoever is guided is guided for his own sake, and whoever goes astray goes astray to its detriment, and that Allah will judge between him and his opponents.

[Page 70]

﴿There has certainly come to you a Messenger from among yourselves. It grieves him that you suffer hardship. He is anxious over you, and toward the believers he is kind and merciful.﴾ ﴿But if they turn away, say: "Allah is sufficient for me. There is no god but Him. In Him I have placed my trust, and He is Lord of the Mighty Throne."﴾

This surah was a surah of severity and harshness toward the polytheists, the People of the Book, the hypocrites among the people of Madinah, and the Bedouins. It also commanded the believers to engage in jihad and rebuked those who fell short in it. Interspersed within this was praise for the believers who had the opposite qualities: those who emigrated, those who gave help, and those who followed the Messenger in the hour of hardship (al-'usrah).

The surah concludes with these two verses, which remind the people of the favor of Allah in sending Muhammad (ﷺ) and praise his characteristics, which combine all perfections. Among the most distinguishing of these is his eagerness for their guidance, his desire for their faith, and their entry into the community of Islam. He is kind and merciful toward them, so that they may know that the harshness directed at those who turned away from Islam, in word and in deed, was only a means of reforming their condition. This is one of the manifestations of the mercy that Allah, the Exalted, made to accompany the mission of His Messenger (ﷺ), in His saying: ﴿And We did not send you except as a mercy to the worlds﴾ [al-Anbiya' 21:107]. Thus these two verses come with what removes distress from the hearts of the groups about whom the verses of severity were revealed and who were treated harshly, following severity with gentleness and harshness with mercy. This is also the habit of the Qur'an. With these two verses, the door to the enclosure of faith and repentance is opened, so that whoever Allah grants success may enter it.

Thus the sentence is a resumptive sentence beginning a new topic (istinaf ibtida'i). Its occurrence at the end of the surah gives it the meaning of a concluding appendage (tadhyil) and a summary.

The address in His saying "there has come to you" and what follows it of address is directed to the whole community called to Islam. The primary intended audience is those who turned away among the polytheists and hypocrites of the Arabs, as indicated by His saying after the address, ﴿kind and merciful toward the believers﴾. It will come that the intended audience is the Arabs.

[Page 71]

The opening with the two emphasizing particles, the lam and qad, is despite the fact that its content is not something open to denial, in order to draw attention to this sentence because of the importance of the purpose for which it was brought, which we will mention. It is also because what it contains is something the hypocrites deny, namely that he is a Messenger from Allah. It is also because this emphasis makes its addressees treated as if they were deniers of his coming, insofar as they did not benefit themselves by this coming. It is also because this emphasis is a recording against them, intended to hint at the approach of departure. For when the announcement of his coming was repeated, though it had been established for many long years, this was a metonymy (kinaya) for the approach of its ending. It is a record from Him against the believers and a deposit (idda') for the hypocrites and whoever remained of the polytheists. Moreover, other verses addressed to the People of the Book and others were emphasized with less emphasis than this, such as His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿O People of the Book, there has certainly come to you Our Messenger, making clear to you much of what you used to conceal of the Scripture and pardoning much. There has certainly come to you from Allah a light and a clear Book﴾ [al-Ma'idah 5:15], and His saying: ﴿O mankind, there has certainly come to you a proof from your Lord, and We have sent down to you a clear light﴾ [al-Nisa' 4:174]. So the sentence was emphasized in this surah only for a purpose more important than removing denial.

The word "coming" (al-maji') is used figuratively (majaz) for the address of the call to the religion. Its directing toward them is likened to an address they were not expecting, like the arrival of a visitor to people from another place. This is a common usage in the Qur'an.

Al-anfus is the plural of nafs, which means the essence. The word nafs is added to a pronoun, and then it indicates the tribe to which the pronoun refers; that is, he is counted among their lineage, and his belonging to them is not by alliance, clientage, or attachment. One says: "He is a Qurayshi from among them," and one says: "The Qurayshi is their mawla or their ally." So the meaning of "from among yourselves" is "from the pure core of your lineage." It is thus determined that the address is to the Arabs, because at the time of the revelation, the Arabs did not count as their own those who allied with them or became their clients, such as Salman al-Farisi and Bilal al-Habashi. In this there is a favor to the Arabs and an alert to their excellence. In it there is also an indirect exhortation to follow him and not to oppose him, and that the most fitting for them is to take pride in him and to rally around him, as He said, may He be exalted, about the Qur'an: ﴿And indeed it is a reminder for you and for your people﴾ [al-Zukhruf 43:44], meaning that a good remembrance of you will remain through it.

[Page 72]

Al-'aziz means the dominant one. Al-'izzah means dominance. One says 'azzahu when he overcame him. From this is His saying: ﴿and he overpowered me in speech﴾ [Sad 38:23]. When it is followed by 'ala, it indicates the meaning of heaviness and severity upon the self. Bishr ibn 'Awanah said, mentioning his killing of the lion and his wrestling with it:

"I said to him: It grieves me that I killed my kinsman by force and by subjugation."

The ma here is a verbal-masdar particle (masdariyyah).

'Anittum means you suffered hardship. Al-'anat is hardship, that is: your distress and your suffering were heavy upon him. This is like His saying: ﴿Perhaps you would kill yourself with grief that they do not become believers﴾ [al-Shu'ara' 26:3]. This was mentioned in the description of the Messenger, peace be upon him, and it indicates that this is a disposition of his. Its effect is gentleness toward the community and caution against what would throw them into punishment in this world and the next. Among the effects of this is his intercession for all people on the Day of Standing (al-mawqif), to hasten the reckoning. Furthermore, this implies that his law came in harmony with his character, so hardship and difficulty were removed from it. He said: ﴿Allah intends for you ease and does not intend for you hardship﴾ [al-Baqarah 2:185], and He said: ﴿And He has not placed upon you in the religion any difficulty﴾ [al-Hajj 22:78].

The departure from using the explicit verbal noun 'anat to using the verb with ma, which in combination forms a verbal noun, is a subtle point (nukta). It conveys that the hardship that befell them in the past, which had already occurred, was grievous to him. That was by what they suffered from the killing of their people, from captivity in the raids, and from the dire threats and warnings of the Qur'an. If the verbal noun had been used, it would not have referred to a specific hardship or to a hardship that had occurred, because the verbal noun has no tense. It would have been open to meaning that it grieved him by keeping it away from them. But the coming of the verbal noun formed from a past verb makes it a verbal noun restricted to occurrence in the past. Do you not see that you may paraphrase it thus: "It grieves him, the hardship you suffered in the past," so that this verse serves as an alert that what they suffered of severity was only for the reform of their condition, that perhaps after it they would lower their arrogance, turn back from their error, and perceive the goodness of their affairs.

Al-hirs is an intense desire for a thing and eagerness toward it. Since it transitively reaches the pronoun of the addressees, which refers to their persons, and the persons are not the object of the eagerness here, it is necessary to supply an elided noun understood from the context of the discourse, so it is taken as: "over your faith" or "over your guidance."

Al-ra'fah is a tenderness that arises when harm befalls the one who is treated with it. One says: ra'uf rahim. Al-rahmah is a tenderness that calls for kindness to the one who is shown mercy. In the name of Allah, the Most Merciful, the Especially Merciful

Surat Yunus

It is named in the codices (mushafat) and in the books of tafsir (exegesis, the explanation of the Qur'an) and sunnah (the Prophet's teachings and practice) "Surat Yunus," because it alone mentions a particular matter concerning the people of Yunus (Jonah): that they believed after their Messenger had threatened them with the descent of punishment, so Allah pardoned them when they believed. This is in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Why was there not a city that believed and whose faith benefited it, except the people of Jonah? When they believed, We removed from them the punishment of disgrace in the worldly life, and We let them enjoy for a time﴾ [Yunus: 98]. That distinction is an honour for Yunus, peace be upon him, and there is no mention of Yunus in it other than that. Yunus is mentioned in Surat al-Saffat in more detail than in this surah, but the reason for the naming does not necessitate it.

What appears to me most likely is that it was attributed to Yunus to distinguish it from its four sister surahs that open with ﴿Alif, Lam, Ra﴾ [Yunus: 1]. For this reason each of them was attributed to a prophet or to a prophet's people, instead of being called "the first ﴿Alif, Lam, Ra﴾ [Yunus: 1]" and "the second ﴿Alif, Lam, Ra﴾ [Yunus: 1]." Thus, the surahs' becoming known by their names first spread among the Muslims through the first words in them, especially when their openings were disjoined letters. They would call those surahs by "Ha-Mim" and "Alif-Lam-Ra" and the like.

It is Meccan according to the majority. This is what is narrated from Ibn 'Abbas, according to the more sound report from him. In al-Itqan (of al-Suyuti), on the authority of 'Ata', from him, it is said to be Medinan. In al-Qurtubi, on the authority of Ibn 'Abbas, three of its verses are Medinan, and they are His saying, exalted is He: ﴿So if you are in doubt about what We have sent down to you﴾ [Yunus: 94] up to His saying ﴿until they see the painful punishment﴾ [Yunus: 88]. al-Qummi al-Nisaburi affirmed this. In Ibn 'Atiyya, on the authority of Muqatil, two verses are Medinan, namely ("So if you are in doubt") up to His saying ("among the losers"). In the same source, on the authority of al-Kalbi, one verse was revealed in Medina, and it is His saying, exalted is He: (﴿And among them are those who believe in it﴾ [Yunus: 40]) up to ("Allah is most knowing of the corrupters"). It was revealed concerning the Jews.

[p. 80]

Ibn 'Atiyya said: A group said: about forty verses from its beginning were revealed in Mecca, and the rest of it was revealed in Medina. He did not attribute this to a specific source. I suppose that these opinions arise from the assumption that whatever disputation with the People of the Book is in the Qur'an was revealed only in Medina. If that is so, the assumption of these people is mistaken. This will be pointed out later.

Its number of verses is one hundred and nine in the count of most of the regional centres, and one hundred and ten in the count of the people of al-Sham.

It is the fifty-first surah in the order of revelation of the surahs. It was revealed after Surat Bani Isra'il and before Surat Hud. I suppose it was revealed in the eleventh year after the Call (al-ba'tha), on account of what will come at His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And when We let people taste mercy after adversity has touched them, at once they conspire against Our signs﴾ [Yunus: 21].

* * *

Among the aims of this surah:

It begins with the purpose of establishing the prophethood of Muhammad ﷺ by the evidence of the inability of the polytheists to produce the like of the Qur'an, an evidence indicated through a subtle allusive style built on the implication of the disjoined letters at the opening of the surah, as already explained at the beginning of Surat al-Baqara. For this reason those letters are followed by His saying, exalted is He: ﴿These are the verses of the wise Book﴾ [Yunus: 1], indicating that its inimitability for them is the proof that it is from Allah. What was implied here has been stated explicitly in His saying: ﴿Say: Then bring a surah like it﴾ [Yunus: 38].

This is followed by the establishment of the prophethood of Muhammad ﷺ and the refutation of the polytheists' claim that it is impossible for Allah to send a human as a Messenger.

From that it moves to establishing that Allah, exalted is He, alone is God, by the evidence that He is the Creator of the world and its Governor. This leads to refuting the idea that Allah has partners in His divinity, and to refuting the excuses of the polytheists that their idols are intercessors with Allah.

[p. 81]

This is followed by establishing the gathering (of the dead) and recompense. That is the refutation of the roots of polytheism.

Interwoven with this are indications from created things, an explanation of the wisdom of recompense, the nature of recompense, the wisdom and benefits for people in the signs found in created things, a warning to those who deny resurrection and turn away from the signs of Allah, and, in contrast to them, the promise given to those who believe. Most of this surah therefore revolves around the axis of affirming these foundations.

Among these is the reminder that Allah's granting respite to the disbelievers rather than hastening punishment is a wisdom from Him.

Among these too is the reminder of what befell the peoples of earlier generations when they associated partners with Allah and denied the Messengers.

Also: taking lessons from the abilities Allah created for people to travel on land and sea, and from the subtle favours found in the conditions of sea travel.

And the striking of a parable for the worldly life, its splendour and its passing, and that the Hereafter is the abode of peace.

And the differing states of believers and disbelievers in the Hereafter, and the disavowal by false deities of their worshippers.

And the refutation of the divinity of any other than Allah, exalted is He, by the proof that they cannot benefit people at all, in this world or the Hereafter.

And the establishment that the Qur'an is sent down from Allah, and that the proofs that it is fabricated are manifest.

And the challenge to the polytheists to produce a surah like it, but misguidance blinded the eyes of the obstinate.

And the warning to the polytheists of the consequences of what befell the nations that denied the Messengers, and that if the punishment comes upon them, their faith will not benefit them. And that this did not overtake the people of Yunus, because their coming to faith happened before the punishment arrived.

And the rebuke of the polytheists for forbidding what Allah had made lawful of provision.

And the establishment of Allah's comprehensive knowledge, exalted is He.

[p. 82]

And the good news for the friends of Allah in this world and in the Hereafter.

And the consolation of the Messenger for what the disbelievers say.

And that had He willed, all who are on earth would have believed, all of them.

Then it arrives at taking lessons from the earlier Messengers: Nuh, and Messengers after him, then Musa and Harun.

Then the truthfulness of the prophethood of Muhammad ﷺ is affirmed by the testimony of the People of the Book.

The surah concludes with instructing the Messenger, peace be upon him, in what he may use as an excuse toward those who doubt the religion of Islam: that whoever is guided is guided for his own sake, and whoever goes astray goes astray to its detriment, and that Allah will judge between him and his opponents.
